This game reminded me of The Pagemaster. An animated film from 1994 about classic fantasy protagonists embarking on a common quest. I could say the same of Torn Tales’ plot line but if you know me or my reviews, the only thing I hate more than spoilers, are the dimwits which spread them. At least the dev team isn’t formed out of Steam rookies. They have released two other games which portray certain aspects of strategy. So far, so good.
I enjoyed Torn Tales and not just for giving another spin to established fairy tales. It’s essentially a squad-based RPG at its heart, yet still manages to hint at more than just another hack ‘n’ slash. The term “ARPG” is used more often nowadays, with “A” standing for “Action”.  Ironically, while I’m usually an outspoken critic of multiplayer-centric titles, I find the complete abscence of an MP mode from Torn Tales, to be a missed opportunity. At least local co-op if nothing else, since the AI isn’t making things any easier, that’s for certain. Not much of a challenge though, as I was able to breeze through hordes even as my two AI-controlled companions were more likely to cheer me up from the sides, than take active part in the actual combat. The fact that you can switch between them at all times, represents the saving grace of an otherwise atrocious artificial intelligence.
So who are the three legendary heroes that form an unlikely alliance? None other than Robin Hood (everyone’s favorite highwayman with a heart of gold), Snow White (somehow, a mage in this game) and Dr. Jekyll (also known as Mr. Hyde, if any of his friends would have survived the encounter). Archer, Wizard and Melee Warrior. Is this Trine on steroids? At least no obnoxious or fruity puzzles in sight! Instead these three companions are in the business of killing. As you can imagine for any self-respectable ARG, business is booming.
Some quests and boss fights try their best to break the monotony but Torn Tales still suffers from too much repetitiveness, in both assets and the action itself. Victor Vran and the Van Helsing trilogy never gave their players a chance to get bored since the enemy types and scenery were constantly shifting. So it’s not a question of much more variety, simply in game design choices and how well can the assets on hand be used, in full effect. One might argue that the production costs and price tag of Torn Tales, cannot rival the aforementioned similar titles. And that would be correct.
Overall, Torn Tales is a decent representative of its genre and one that isn’t overpriced either. Plenty of Achievements and Trading Cards sweeten the deal and you won’t feel sorry for your bucks if you buy the game outside of a Steam Sale or bundled deal. Just have a lot of patience until you pass the first few levels and you will surely enjoy the experience of hacking away minion after minion. Game progression is given sufficient attention, in the form of upgradable skill trees for all three protagonists as well as an inventory/load-out system, for maximum fighing effiency. You can't ask more of this game and I don't want to hear another word on DLC. Erase that thought immediately!
+ Pleasant graphics and sounds.
+ Clear gameplay distinction between characters.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
- Occasionally gets repetitive.
- Lacks in NPC interaction.
- AI and pathfinding issues.

Torn Tales is a party based action-RPG set in a dark fantasy world.  Take control of three well-known characters (Snow White, Robin Hood & Dr.Jekyll/Mr. Hyde.)  Mix and match a dynamic mix of specific abilities to define your party's combat style.  Control them through twenty levels of linear driven combat against various fairly-tale themed enemies.  Find and collect magical rings and amulets to augment character abilities.  Defeat the end of level bosses to progress and eventually defeat the evil Story-Teller.
+ Good range of character skills make for some varied tactical party combos.
+ Fairly balanced character levelling.  Earned skillpoints can be allocated regularly.
+ Nice cutscenes between each level with excellent voice-over narration.
+ Pretty graphics. Stable engine. (PC/Win 10)
+ Auto and manual savepoints.  In a good spread of locations.
- Linear clicker-type gameplay.  Some alternative sidepaths to item chests.
- Very limited inventory/loot.  Virtually no item farming/grinding.  Only three equippable items, 2x rings and amulet.
- No NPC or enivornment interaction.
- No co-op/multiplayer unfortunately.
* Twenty self-contained areas across five different distinct environments.
* Nice easy going music which changes depending on the game situation.
* Decent range of enemy types.  Varied boss fights.
* Rudimentary AI behaviour settings for non-controlled party members.  Mostly works well.
* Decent skill/spell animations though only some of the character abilities truly stand out.
As an invited beta-tester I received a free copy of this game.  TBH this isnt the sort of game I would necessarily choose to play.  Yet it was remarkable to see how this game progressed from its early stages to release.  There is no doubt that Twistplay/Chilled Mouse put alot of hard work and love into this title.  Though I did not start out appreciating the concept or gameplay at the end after my initial playthrough, I was actually won over.
If you are expecting an action-RPG such as Van Helsing or Grim Dawn you should consider if Torn Tales is a game for you.  At times it seems more RTS than RPG.  Infact its strongest feature is the combat - specifically the configurable aspect of skill composition.   You can decide what sort of archetype you wish each character to be from: damage-dealer, tank, healer, close combat or ranged specialist, stat agumenter or a mix depending on which skills or items you equip.  Artwork, graphics and audio are pleasing and present a wonderful fairy-taleseque ambience.  With the narration and voice-overs being particularly favourable.
Perhaps the biggest disppointments are a lack of loot farming and click-fest nature of gameplay.  Loot is limted to a range of magical fairy-tale derived rings and amulets can be collected and stored in a small party inventory to be swapped in and out of character slot but like skill selections, once you set on a style of play these rarely change.
As others have pointed out the gameplay can feel almost like you're playing a clicker.  Once the party's skills and AI behaviour are set, you only click to move the party forward, select the enem(y)ies to attack and click on the skill or amulet you wish to use at a certain time during battles.  Then wait for the skill cooldown to pass.  Occasionally you will move to a treasure chest to collect a new ring or amulet, clean-up your inventory or allocate skill points across five minor and two major skills, when a character levels up.  Rinse and repeat.  Thats pretty much it!
The core campaign is fairly short.  Ten levels split across five chapters. With an additional two optional levels in each, making for twenty levels in total.  My playthrough lasted around under thirteen hours.  Hardcore mode add replayability and seems to be more challenging.  Fans of casual gameplay will be pleased that standard mode very forgiving.  If a character dies you can either go back to the last savepoint or try to progress with those still alive.  A bolt-on arena mode prolongs whatever longevity there is.  Where you can test your skills against waves of enemies across standard, hardcore and infinite difficulties, but for me it seemed a disappointing afterthought.  Not what I would play the game for.  Others will disagree.
In keeping with the fairy tale theme, enemies come in a fair range of guises each with their own abilities, strength and weaknesses.  Essentially they are very similar even if there are two types: standard and elite.  Elites drop item chests.  Some end of level bosses though provide a nice experience to overcome.  The AI is rudimentary but works well.  Party controls are also fine yet there still seem to be issues with AI controlled party members despite the developers putting alot of effort into perfecting them.
Torn Tales is a solid if lite APRG-esque game.  Its pretty to look at and though gameplay is linear and at times can feel like a click fest, it can be a fun for casual ARPGers or those that are after something with a tactical focus.  Overall the different components of the game work very well but if you are after more of a loot-farming, level-grinding experience then I suggest you look elsewhere.  Those looking for a modestly priced party-focused ARPG that is a little different than games like Grim Dawn or Van Helsing then this could be for you.

Squad based RPGs are not games I typically play, but Torn Tales had me coming back time and time again for a really enjoyable experience.
It reminds me a lot of League of Legends - a game that I think has an interesting playstyle, but I am not a fan of the full multiplayer experience. Torn Tales is a great alternative, having a similar playstyle but instead of humans, you are fighting through groups of AI enemies.
The feeling of having Jekyll tear through a mob of enemies with his cane cyclone is immensely satisfying, all the while Snow White hurls spells of poison and healing to make you feel awesome. I love the rune system, when you level up your skills it has a random chance to pick a sort of modifier for your skill, such as making you do more damage every time you hit. These really vary your playstyle and different runes can be swapped out depending on the situation you have at hand.
The game has a nice balance of easy enemies to beat your way through and tough ones that require a little more strategy. Every time I died I felt like it was my fault for being too bold or not using my characters strengths correctly and it just motivated me to go back and have another go.
I'm also a big fan of the earlier levels having side quests with very high leveled enemies so there is reason to go back to the beginning and play the levels again.
The game runs fine on my laptop, I don't have any issues with it.
I would definitely recommend this game, especially for £10.

I like this game, the idea is original and the gameplay is almost there. The story is based around an evil story writer who mashes together 3 stories in an attempt for revenge, Robin Hood (The hybrid) Snow White (The Mage) and Dr.Jekyll & Mr. Hyde (The tank/bruiser) are together in a team to try and fight their way through to the truth. The game works well, employing hack n' slash mmo and rpg games into one, the wide range of weapons and levels give way to hours of gameplay and endless amounts of exploration.

The game starts off with a decent narrator explaining bits of story and you set out with Snow White and Robin Hood.
You basically walk to where you click and can even use the mouse button held however holding the button spams the animation of the pointer which was a little annoying.
Having the controls down you get put on a linear path to your goal with some dead ends that would have been worth exploring had there actually been something there.
After killing a few rats and being directed forward the whole time you find Dr Jekyll fighting some wolves.
Turns out that combat is just like a clicker game and all you have to do is move your “too stupid to do it myself” AI buddies out of the way of major boss attacks and use Snow White’s heal every now and then.
Moving your team out of telegraphs can be a pain as they tend to either run back in to them or the attack is too fast to move all of them out of it.
Abysmal combat aside, there are lots of unused spaces on the map and it feels lifeless and empty apart from the few groups of mobs scattered around it.
Nearing the end of the map you get to fight The Huntsman and suddenly your group of overpowered characters dies to 1-2 hits of this boss’ heavy attacks, difficulty curve oh where have you gone?
After beating him you finally get a piece of loot in the form of a ring or amulet.
Suddenly the many dead ends that lead to nowhere now lead to treasure that will most likely never see the light of day as the game taught us that we only need to go forward and that exploring is a waste of time.
By now I’ve leveled up a few times and what you get to do is pick a skill and upgrade it. You also unlock traits that alter the skill in some way like adding a cleanse on Snow White’s heal. This was a little neat but since combat is so underwhelming it’s potential goes to waste.
After having played for more than a good hour I just felt like the games was cobbled together with little to no regard as to their design choices.

Lost Planet: Extreme Condition is a third-person action game made and published by Capcom. It throws you into the role of Wayne Holden, a Snow Pirate trying to rid the planet E.D.N. III of monstrous beasts known as the Akrid. These creatures when killed, give you "thermal energy" which is used to power your armor or mechs known as V.S. Suits, and provide a shield much like that found in Halo.
Graphics: For a game released in 2007, the graphics are still great for today's standards. Every inch of snow, V.S. Suit, Akrid and weapon are rendered with sharp detail and the textures good.
Sound: The ring of bullets piercing through the air or the screech of a two-story high Akrid are captured beautifully and really immerse the player in the game.
Gameplay: The game is a fast-paced and arcadey shooter, with fluid controls and this allows for great mobility of both Wayne and his V.S. Suits. The gameplay is easy to get into and the gamepad configuration is laid out well enough for anyone to master.
All in all, Lost Planet is one of my favourite games and I would give it a 7.5/10.

LEVEL DESIGN: 6/10

Relaxed 2D Moba

I bought this game back when I was in high school. In fact, this was one of the first games I bought on Steam along with Rogue Legacy. Awesomenauts is a 2D side scrolling MOBA, basically the forbidden love child of League of Legends and Super Smash Bros. The game features a quirky Saturday morning cartoon art style, with each character looking and feeling incredibly distinct. The game also has a superb soundtrack, with every single character having 2 versions of their theme song. Before going free to play on May 24th, the game used to have expansions you could buy in a similar fashion to Blizzard titles or MMOs, but now features a variant of the tried and true League of Legends model with a weekly rotation and being able to purchase Nauts with real money or in game currency. The game has gone through many changes over the years, with the removal of pre-set loadouts for upgrades, the addition of a team experience system similar to Heroes of the Storm, several art redesigns for the older characters, and of course, pulling a TF2 and going F2P. The game is fast paced and hectic, with several maps but slightly less emphasis on map objectives than HotS. Overall, a solid game back when I bought it and a solid game now.

There was actual heart and effort put into the game, which makes my following words all the more painful to say...
The game itself is horrible. Overly simple game mechanics and the use of Q, W, and E keys for special abilities? As I said in my review that is posted above, think an Alpha version of Dragon Age: Origins blended with an MMO and a mobile game. And then lobotomized. And then kicked squarely in the nuts. Terrible AI, ineffectual control capability, and needless and painfully tedius backtracking every time your AI companions manage to get themselves killed.
A game that, for right now, is utterly horrendous. However, there is a kernel of a good game and a solid premise underneath everything that is wrong. This is a title that, if the Developer were to revisit some specific components and re-work them, then we would be looking at an exceptionally solid title. Imperium Galactica 1, the first amazing 3 in 1 game (Master of Orion, Sim City and C&C/Dune style gameplays) that started it all. Well okay, not quite for me as admittedly I didn’t play it until after playing its sequel IG2! However that didn’t make me love it any less, in fact there are parts of IG1 that I love even more than IG2.
For instance in IG1 you are located on the bridge of your command ship and the games various screens (galaxy view, planet view, research, production & diplomacy) are all accessed via different panels on your bridge. Even cooler is that you can get up out of your command chair and walk around your ship visiting your quarters or the local bar to talk to your crew (usually to further the games story) and as you’re promoted through the ranks you are given bigger and better battleships to command and explore. The only game to recreate this experience since that I can think of was the brilliant Starcraft 2 Wings of Liberty campaign where I used to spend just as much time exploring the ship & talking to people in the bar as I did playing the actual missions lol, I just love that level of immersion.
Other highlights in IG1 are the cool unique alien buildings each race gets (they’re all human looking in IG2 sadly) and a nice day/night cycle for all your planets that make all your buildings & roads turn on lights in the dark. There are also many cool Star Wars & Babylon 5 inspired custscenes of huge fleet battles and impressive landing sequences (Scorpion 4 base is my favourite vid) during the games campaign story that up the immersion even further.
IG1 is set in a distant future where after years of civil war and alien aggression the human empire is falling apart and is vulnerable to a new suer powerful alien invader. You must expand the empire again, research new technologies and form alliances with other empires to defeat the Dargslan threat.
IG1 was quite popular when it came out however it was punished for some of its shortcomings such as its large cumbersome interface, no Master of Orion style sandbox/skirmish multiplayer mode outside of the main campaign spoiling replayability and finally like many RTS games of the time the spaceship and tank pathfinding was terrible with units tripping over each other endlessly!
Fortunately the game was still utterly brilliant and all of these issues have since been fixed in the brilliant fan made remake OpenIG. I strongly recommend you check it out!

I'm writing this review because of the lack of any objective or relevant review on the steam store(At the time of writing). This was my first time playing, so i have no nostalgia toward the game. I was pleasantly suprised by this two decades old gem of a game.
Its your classic 4x with a strong yet very campy narrative. It has space and ground combat (rts-mechanics), both are quite quirky and i would not recommend you buy it for that. Its strenght is the planetary management and immersion(compared to other 4x). By immersion i mean how you start of as a small time sector commander, en end up becomming the grand admiral of the human empire, all this with dialoges and lot of cinematics. I felt a lot more engaged with my planets/empire then I do in other 4x.
One big negative could be the punishing nature of the game, certain event happen at certain times and if you are not prepared you will lose, and the game will not hint at these events. So if you want to be prepared i would advice you to google for a walkthrough, those could also help with explaining some of the more "complex" mechanics.
A technical side note: This game is run with dosbox, and the default settings as they where for me are not recommended. My advice would be to set the cpu cycle at 35k, and not leave it on its default settings. That way you have a good speed during combat, but not to slow fade transitions between screens. (Alt + Enter > Cpu > Set Cycles) If these instruction confuse now, they will make sense when you play the game.

First things first: I have only played one ending to this game, I am led to believe there are many.
Despite the above I feel I am qualified to give a review of a large portion of the content, since the core backstory is static.
This game is wonderful. It happens to be my favorite game in the world, but that is a subjective assessment and I intend for this to be an objective review so I will explain WHY my opinon has formed the way it has.
First: the world is unique.  The spectacularly different setting in which the protagonist finds himself is interesting and deeply realized. I found that as I played this game I wanted to learn more and more about the backstory, the reason things were the way they were. It is likely that not everyone will have this response but I found that the somehow quite human cyberpunk characters drew me in. The robotic population of this game have dreams, hopes, and problems which make them relatable, but also special. They are obviously not human, but the similarities between them and humanity are evident in many portions of the game. That, however, is not to say there are no differences. Indeed some of the differences are what drove me to be more industrious in my exploration of the world.
Second: the voice acting is stellar. While the voice acting is not particularly flashy, it has an underplayed value in making the protagonist and his little helper come to life. Throughout it gives simple but essential relatability with the main character, putting the player in his shoes so to speak. The voices are diverse and unique and this additionally draws the player into the world, which now not only has depth, but also seems broad.
Third: the art is dead center with the rest of the game's feel. Though robotic, many tubes and unique shapes cascade through the art design, giving the machines an organic feel (this is not the only game I've seen do this but this game does it well). Most of the tones are dead-feeling beiges and browns but there are many glowing lights throughout the game that give the overall impression of a world with a soul beneath all the lifeless metal. Again this fits perfectly with the world's history and vibe.
Fourth: the audio is wonderfully immersive. The sound is electronic with a common use of ethnic sounding pad synths. Deep, slow rhythms give the game a dark and somber feel which meshes perfectly with the mechanized art and characters. There is at least one old record you can listen to, which deepens the games portrayal of the world's past.
Fifth: the gameplay is solid. The puzzles are not hard, but they have an obvious digital slant that only increases immersion and interest. Each one is unique, although each of thier formats is fairly standard for point and click games. If this game had to have a weakness it would be the puzzles, if you don't play this game for the story and immersion, I think you're not playing to the game's amazing strengths. If you don't like stories/worlds that you can lose yourself in and just want hard puzzles, don't play this. However, if you've ever been interested in a cyberpunk world, or a fantasy story, or even basic philosophy/worldviews, let this game tell you a story. It does it well.
Sixth: no spoilers in this review but I will say the ending I found was amazing.

I thought Primordia was a very good game, and I would recommend it both in terms of mechanics and story. I am a big fan of the Blackwell games, and this game has many of the same strengths.
Pros:
+ Excellent story. There's legitimately a lot to think about in this game, including political, religious, and social commentary. The game is set in a world where humans are extinct and only robots are left. We see how the society they create is a very clever mirror of our own, with plenty of parody of our own flaws along the way.
+ The point and click puzzles are solid. They are somewhat difficult, but solvable without having to consult a walkthrough because the solutions make sense once you get them. To me, this is one of the most important things about gameplay in a point and click. You have to use your brain to solve the puzzles.
+ If you do start struggling, you can get hints by talking to people (especially your sidekick Crispin), which again means you don't need to consult the internet to get a nudge in the right direction. Normally, he will give you a clue about which area you should be searching, or which object you should be fiddling with.
+ The art and aesthetics in the game are good. The characters are interesting-looking, and the world is very neat.
+ The game is paced well. It does a nice job of moving you from place to place, advancing the story and revealing the mysteries by steps.
Cons:
- Hard to think of any. I suppose the UI can be a bit clunky until you get used to it, especially how you access your inventory.

This game is very indicative of the landscape of terrible gaming today. No matter whether you look at indie studios or big AAA companies, there is no such thing as a complete game anymore. They are just tiny gimmicks attempting to make a brief artistic statement on some unimportant aspect of life. You spend an hour playing through a glorified tutorial before finding out that the entire game is a tutorial. All of the things that you want to do as a player are blocked off, either because you haven't earned the right to play that part of the game yet, or they decided for you that freedom is stupid and you should feel bad for expecting to have fun. Exploration should not be punished, dissapointing, or a massive chore. But that's basically this entire game in a nut shell. You're always chasing the start of the game, and never get anything short of a sick joke making fun of actual game play.
And to be honest, I'd have kept this entire opinion to myself if this game didn't offer itself up as such a wonderful treat for your steam controller. Guess what. It's broken. You have to use weird work arounds to get the steam controller to work, and even when it works once, there is no gaurantee that it won't break again between turning it off and on again.
If you're up for wasting time, this one is the one for you. But don't expect to have fun or get your controller to work.

Pros
- Very charming art style. The loading screens, the characters, the world, its all very pretty. One of the main reasons I keep coming back to it. Very good soundtrack too. The stories behind the factions and the faction quests give this game an additional depth which makes it enjoyable even when playing alone.
- the tech tree is very easy to navigate for beginners. But this may also make it repetitive as you play more. Unlike civ 5, some buildings require strategic resources to build which will affect your research order. This keeps the game fresh in a way.
- The combat is very unique. It gives an extra layer of strategy flavour to the game because of mechanics like positioning and action-queing. However, the issue I had with this was when all your guys have lower initiative, none of your orders will get through and you get really disadvantaged because you can no longer focus down enemy units or retreat your weakened units.
- I am writting this lengthy review in the middle of the night even though I have school in the morning and this will probably be buried under numerous other review.
Cons
- My main problem with this game is the leveling system of military units. The level of the armies matter so much to the point that it almost makes technological advantage obsolete. You have to try to keep a sizable army from the start of the game otherwise, you will just get out-scaled hard. This makes some factions much weaker than others because of their play style. which brings me to my next point
- This game is not very balanced for multiplayer. Certain factions are definitely stronger than others. But this can be overcomed by everyone playing the same faction or customised factions which is still very enjoyable.
- Strength of your armies are also determined by the strategic resources you possess since you can edit their equiptment individually. So if you get screwed by your starting location, you will also get screwed in the military race. Interesting mechanic but makes the game a little imbalanced.
If you're looking for a 4x game you can enjoy playing alone, you should definitely get it. However, if multiplayer player is the main reason you want to get into this game, you may want to reconsider.

Excellent! A classically styled adventure point-and-click, Primordia has incredible visual identity, background story, and voiceovers. The puzzles aren't too hard, the tips for them are close by, and there are various choices, hidden information and multiple, well-written endings.

A mysterious past is slowly unveiled in a post-apocalyptic art-noveau cyberpunk world.
If you like robots, themes of AI, and/or adventure games - especially classic ones - this game is for you.
The game follows the pretty standard adventure mechanic - click on things to make things happen - sometimes click on things with things from your inventory, or mix things in your inventory together until they become clickable on other things.  Take notes.  (Most of which actually happens for you with the in-game "data-pad".)  Solve puzzles with said notes.
The game runs at 640x400 resolution - which can be off-putting to some, but really lends to the retro-adventure feel of the game, and I've come to love it.  (On my 1080p tv, it won't actually fill up the whole screen, but it doesn't really bother me.)  That said - I highly recommend going into the options menu and chosing the "DX" display mode as opposed to D3D if it works for you - the sprites mesh with the backgrounds much better this way in my opinion.  DOS nostalgia!
What really shines in Primordia is the story - and the art.  They come together to create a fascinating atmosphere that makes me want to revisit the game again and again - and the developer commentary is great on a second or third playthrough.  The excellent voice acting and seven or so potential endings don't hurt, either.  (The narrator from Bastion plays the main character - and the sidekick that follows you through the game is entertaining at every turn.)  The music and sound mesh well with the art to create an engrossing atmosphere - despite the retro low-res graphics.
There aren't many puzzles in the "puzzle game" sense - but there is plenty of puzzling to be done in the game in terms of figuring out how things fit together, what things mean, and what the significance of certain items or pieces of information may be.  The story is mostly linear, but there are a few opportunities to take different approaches to solve situations - especially near the end.  Observation and careful contemplation are rewarded.
The setting is in the distant future in a post-human world - no organic life is to be found anywhere - even the bugs and little things swimming in the sewers are machines - but make no mistake, they have lives and thoughts of their own, and are no less interesting than any human character.  And for the robot fan, there are references to other robots from both popular and obscure culture everywhere - along with a videogame reference or two.  MST3K, Short Circuit, Metropolis, and Fallout - just to name a few.
I would highly recommend this game to any fan of classic graphic adventures, narrative-driven games, or robots.

Primordia is not what it first appears.
It's description is: "What happened to the Humans", but that isn't what the game is about.
I thought this would be an Adeptus Mechanicus themed Adventure game with a Sam and Max buddyish element, but was actually wrong.
Instead, this is a game about logic, law, and a divide between liberty and community.
The main characters are both charming and the other characters all have little quirks that ensures there is no "that guy" of the game. The puzzles are good without ever being too challenging and the story is tightly knit, with only about 10-11 locations and about 15 characters in the entire game. It's concise without any red herrings. Actually, because the game is so tightly knit, some important secrets are left out in plain sight, which makes it interesting to replay.
What I also like about the puzzles in this game are that there's dialouge if the game understands what you were trying to do with a puzzle, but you were using the wrong piece and there's multiple ways to solve several of the puzzles. In fact, the biggest and longest puzzle of the game can literally be bypassed from the moment you enter the second act.
My only complaint with the game would be the antagonist. The antagonist has a trait that they can "never lie" but then you manage to catch them in lies several times and when confronted with this, the antagonist says "no player, you must be mistaken because I am not". In a game where the entire second act is about logic, it just seems silly. Additionally, my other problem with the antagonist is that at one point the antagonist just says "I know you have a lot of questions about the world and history of this game world, so let me answer all of them for you".
However, that small gripe aside, this game had me engaged and immersed the whole time, trying to figure out its secrets and lore (until the minute that it got bored and laid out its cards on the table).

Great concept with a solid artistic and technical delivery, but featuring ludicrously shallow gameplay.
Evoland delivers on all it's ideas. Its an adventure through gaming. From 8bit 2D adveture, to 2.5D "HD" hack and slash, to pre-rendered backgrounds, to turn based RPG, to even ARPG, etc. It accomplishes them all and presents them in a cohesive way with dashes of lighthearted homages and references to the games it is emulating. It definitely "brings you back" to the eras. But all of it comes with extremely shallow and downright silly easy gameplay. Turn based is unlimited heal and attack, your numbers always win. 2D adventure is single hit bland enemies with easy pathways. Most of the 2.5D adventure is actually clunky on top of being simplistic. And anything else is just button mashing. Its a shame too, because the foundation could support a skyscraper, but all we got was a hut.
That being said, I still had enough fun. I spent my time searching for all the 100% achievement stuff to find the fun though. Some of the hidden chests and puzzles off the beaten path were the best bits of fun to be had. There's a couple levels where you actually actively switch between eras of game style to solve puzzles. Almost feel like with how atrocious the gameplay was otherwise perhaps this game would've been better served as more of a puzzle oriented game.
Its painful to to start thinking about all the missed opportunists here, which seems to be an all too common theme amongst this genre on PC. I have reserved, but optimistic, hopes for the sequel though. And plan to play it soon. Because there is indeed that foundation there... Fingers crossed for marked improvements! The game is interesting enough in what it does accomplish conceptually that I definitely recommend it if it looks appealing to you. But pull back and reel in those expectations as far as you absolutely can when it comes to gameplay. I'll also say that I've seen it on sale for 90% off and in bundles plenty of other times (I got it in a bundle somewhere along the lines), and those are probably the only prices I'd recommend but its your money.

Evoland's gimmick is a progression through different graphical and gameplay styles using the usual fantasy adventure and RPG tropes. As you progress through the game, you discover different graphical upgrades (from black and white to color, from 2D to 3D, etc.) and gameplay systems (now you have save points!). Different areas of the game feature different combat mechanics, from sword-swinging action to turn-based RPG battles to point-and-click ARPG encounters.
Evoland is both a parody and homage at the same time, primarily riffing on the Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, and Diablo (but there are nods to others). It's appreciation for the source material is obvious, but it's not afraid to poke fun at the tropes, either. Some of the humor didn't hit squarely for me, and produced more eye rolls than laughs, but it didn't detract from my overall enjoyment of the game.
The gameplay is neither long nor deep, but if you have an affinity for the source material it draws from, Evoland is an enjoyable way to spend a weekend.

Pochwa (łac. vagogo) – odcinek żeńskich dróg rodnych. Jest przewodem mięśniowo-błoniastym, silnie rozciągliwym i elastycznym, długości 5 cm do 14 cm (zazwyczaj 6 cm do 8 cm), stanowiącym połączenie między macicą a przedsionkiem pochwy, będącym częścią sromu (pudendum feminum). Najwęższa w swojej dolnej części stopniowo się rozszerza. W części środkowej ma około 2 cm do 3 cm szerokości. Pochwa stanowi miejsce wprowadzenia nasienia, obejmując prącie w czasie kopulacji oraz drogę, którą wydostaje się płód podczas porodu, a także drogę odpływu krwi menstruacyjnej. W czasie rozwoju płodowego powstaje z połączenia części dystalnych przewodów przyśródnerczowych (przewodów Müllera). Położona jest w płaszczyźnie pośrodkowej ciała, nieomal w całości w miednicy mniejszej. Końcowy, krótki odcinek przebija przeponę moczowo-płciową. Pozwala to na wyróżnienie części śródmiedniczej (pars intrapelvina) i części przeponowej (pars diaphragmatica).
Ku przodowi znajduje się pęcherz moczowy, a między pęcherzem i pochwą biegną oba moczowody. Poniżej biegnie cewka moczowa połączona z przednią ścianą pochwy przegrodą cewkowo-pochwową (septum urethro♥♥♥♥♥♥le), która wypełnia przestrzeń cewkowo-pochwową (spatium urethro♥♥♥♥♥♥le).
Ku tyłowi – górną część pochwy (1 cm do 2 cm) pokrywa otrzewna, która następnie przechodzi na bańkę odbytnicy, tworząc dno zagłębienia odbytniczo-macicznego, stanowiącego zazwyczaj szczelinowatą przestrzeń. Czasem wnikają w nią pętle jelita cienkiego lub inne, położone nieprawidłowo narządy (np. jajnik). Poniżej znajduje się przestrzeń odbytniczo-pochwowa (spatium recto♥♥♥♥♥♥le), którą wypełnia tkanka łączna (u góry wiotka, ku dołowi coraz bardziej zbita), tworząca przegrodę odbytniczo-pochwową (septum recto♥♥♥♥♥♥le).

A two button hack and slash quick time event-fest. Tedious and really really-really easy.
At the beginning of the game you have two tiers of upgrades: recruit and soldier. With centurion and legendary skills locked off.  Before the game introduced the focus mechanic i'd already gotten enough points to get soldier tier skills in everything but focus. Then, Hilariously enough. After i finished upgrading i killed some barbarians and got a popup saying "centurion skills unlocked" There's 4 tiers of upgrades in total and i'd already unlocked 3. On the highest difficulty avalible for my first playthrough. I was an unkillable god before the game even introduced all of the mechanics...
Now, You know how i mention you have two buttons? yeah, Sword and Bash. And all the combat is: Slash with your sword twice. Press shield bash. Repeat. No enemy can touch you if you do this. Now, You're thinking there has to be more right? Well yeah. You can deflect attacks, But it's really easy and feels so bad. There's no talent or skill. Just press A and all attacks get deflected. There's no thinking or strategy involved.
When a enemy is low health you can execute them. Which is pretty boring. They glow blue? press X. they glow yellow? press Y, And you get ridiculous buffs. Heal yourself, More damage, More XP, And focus which is basically i'm bored and want to finish this level faster. Let me wipe out the entire enemy sqaud with minimal effort.
The worst thing about this game though. Is the uninteractive boring first person / third person shooter segments. I wish i was kidding. But all you have to do is hold LT and RT and it auto aims for you. The only time you have to aim is when the game is like "shoot these red barrels to make EXPLOSIONS!" Which is really hard. Because whenever you try to aim at the red barrels the game auto aims / aim bots a random enemy soldier instead.
+Graphics are nice
+Runs well. Not having FPS drops like others are reporting
-Game is way too easy. I picked the hardest difficulty i could and it was laughingly easy. Even if you're more of a casual player i'd recommend playing on centurion as i can't imagine how pathetic this game would be on the easier difficulties.
-Player interactivity is low. It's a very 'cinematic' game meaning sometimes your player input isn't worth a damn.
-Protagonist isn't interesting at all. But annoying enough to where you can't self insert yourself.
-Melee combat is pretty repetitive you press X twice and Y once to defeat every enemy in the game
-Quick time events get old. I was starting to recognize the same animations during the tutorial
-Quick time events take away from the games pace by slowing down time and making you wait
-Turret sections in a game about ROME
tl;dr I feel bad for anyone who bought this game at full price. I got it in the humble monthly. If you're like me, And was interested in the game because they thought it looked cool and wanted to try it. Either buy it on sale, Or set a timer for under two hours and then request a refund.
I personally would request a refund if i bought the game through steam.

Lost Planet: Extreme Conditions is the first game on Lost Planet franchise. Developed and Published by Capcom, it was originally designed to be an Xbox 360 (2006) exclusive but was later released for the PC (2007) and subsequently, the Playstation 3 (2008).
The player takes the role of Wayne Holden, a Snow Pirate surviving in a failed colonization project of an alien world known as E.D.N. III. Said planet was a prospective new home planet for humanity until it was discovered that: 1. Its covered in perpetual winter. 2. Its home to a hostile alien species known as the Akrid. Wayne, along with his father was supposed to be hunting a particularly powerful Akrid but it proved too powerful and soon things went from bad to worst as Wayne finds himself left for dead in the frozen surface of the planet. He was later recovered and revived (with amnesia) by another group of Snow Pirates who came across his frozen body. Join Wayne in his quest to recover his memories and piece together a conspiracy by a mysterious corporation known as NEVEC.
+ Graphically and Visually stunning despite being 8 years old at the time of writing this review (2014).
+ Vital Suits (V.S.) are fun to pilot and to play
+ Healthy amount of Variety on the above mentioned VS, each having their own strengths and weaknesses
+ Good Music and Sound Effects (although the voice acting could have used a bit more work)
+ Good enemy variety
+ Epic boss battles
+ Large enough levels for exploration however...(See CON #7)
+ Great environment, level design and refreshing new setting (abandoned frozen planet)
+ Performance Test functionality (which is proper since the game HAD a heavy system requirement back in 2007 for the PC version)
- Voice acting could have been better (or they could have used the original Japanese with english subtitles)
- Story line is a bit hard to follow if you're not paying attention
- Not very memorable characters
- The jumps between cutscenes and missions are sometimes disconnected.
- Poor A.I. (You'll see more intelligence in a Coma patient than the Human Enemy AI in this game.)
- Repetitive combat
- Unrewarding and pointless collectibles that serve no purpose in gameplay or story. (You don't get rewarded for exploration.)
Its a NICE game that could have been done better. I can still give it my RECOMMENDATION because I particularly liked my experience with it. It can get a boring at times, but Lost Planet: Extreme Conditions does make for a good pass time since the levels are interesting and satisfying to play through.
The visuals are great which are complemented with good music and sound effects however, the voice acting is tolerable at best. The combat gets too repetitive at times and the human enemy AI is woefully underwhelming but the fun and excitement found when using the Vital Suits does make up for it.
All in all, its an AVERAGE game. RECOMMENDED to be bought on a SALE rather than full price.

If you take this file out of play (by removing or renaming it) the pad.exe will work, and if run will tell you what it sees as the controller. Point-and-click adventure games were one of the first things I ever played: When I got my first computer around 1994-’95 I played Discworld with my dad. We had a walkthrough since neither of us could understand English. Since then I have gone mostly to other genres but the adventuring spark were left in me somewhere. That’s why I have bought a great many point-and-click games but every time I play one the same thing happens: I click around for a while and get bored. They just don’t get a grip on me. That was until Primordia.
The player takes role of Horatio and his sidekick Crispin, who live in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. What seems like a peaceful existence is interrupted when a robot crashes through their wall and steals a power core that is keeping the two alive. The game is a quest to find and get back the power core. The mood is melancholic and sad but is lighten up by Crispin’s surprisingly funny dialog. Every other character was also fascinating and had some personality to them.
This was the first ever adventure game that I completed without looking at a walkthrough. Most of the puzzles are logical in a sense that if you have an item that might fit it most likely does. Every solution made sense. The puzzles are quite varied: There are use-item-on-item puzzles but also drawing, memorization, code breaking and so on. I was surprised at how many different kind of obstacles the creators had thought out. It took 7 hours to complete the game, though length varies greatly depending on how fast you solve the puzzles. There appears to be different endings and outcomes since I only got half of the achievements on single playthrough.
The graphics in this are amazing. Everything is a post-apocalyptic bleak wasteland but the world that was destroyed has this art deco kind of style (think Bioshock) that is really nice. The game actually runs at the tiniest of resolutions but is stretched to full screen. Not a lot of pixels to work with but what has been achieved is wonderful. I’d love to see full resolution images of the art since it’s so great. This is also why the game probably runs on pretty much any potato as long as there is electricity. For some strange reason in one room, after certain thing happens, my fps dropped to single digits but it was solved after I got out of the room. You cannot die and there is no rush so it doesn’t matter. Even better than the visuals is the sound and music. I think the voice acting is great but, together with the art, it’s the music that shines the most.
If you have any interest in point-and-click Primordia is a must play, no doubt about that. For someone new to the genre it’s also a good place to start since it’s not as far-out weird with its puzzles as some games in the genre. I can only give a big recommend for this wonderful game!

Primordia... This game is easily the best point and click adventure game there is. The pixalated look takes a moment to get used to but it quickly makes things look like works of art. The dialogue is both very funny, witty, and sad in this dystopian society where machines rule. It gives life to and great character work to what apear to be hunks of metal. I got very attached and played it through in two sitting with it's difficult puzzles and advanced but easy to follow plots. A must to any readers and adventurers :)

The puzzles can get a bit too adventure-gamey and the tone of your robot sidekick doesn't really match the rest of the game, but it's worth playing for the excellent art and unique post apocalyptic scenario alone. It's like a combination of salvador dali and hr giger.

Among the many things that make Primordia great are:
+ fantastic, gripping storyline, taking you on an adventure through a dieing world
+ unique art style and music that will highjack your imagination
+ great voice acting - hey, Logan Cunningham is here!
+ humor, and lots of it
+ characters you really care about
+ puzzles that will make you think
+ you don't have to worry that you will be stuck at some point (Crispin will give you a hint if needed)
+ commentary and blooper tracks added as an option
+ many possible endings - it's all up to you
+ developers that really care about the users and will help you out with the game if there is any issue.

Best horse game on steam. If you like horses and horse riding you will love this game. You are the owner of a stables and must look after the horses by cleaning, feeding and teaching them. Later in the game you can have guests stay and ride horses too.

As an avid equestrian since childhood, I have played several horse games, and this is by far the best one I've ever played. One of the most impressive points for me was the riding. It's not perfect, but the horses look better than in any other horse game I've played. Their gaits look realistic and when you turn them while trotting or cantering their heads actually look pretty. Their legs don't look all wonky and weird. The riding controls are very simple- click the left mouse button to speed up and the right to slow down. You don't have to make the horse jump yourself, but you do have to set them up right for it by taking them straight at it (most of the time, sometimes they jump at crazy angles) or the will refuse the jump. There are so may aspects of horse care (grooming, bathing, picking hooves, massaging), growing your farm (building a training facility, therapy center, guest house, and breeding center), and riding and competing ( There are 3 races in each area. The areas are the field, forest, and mountains). It is a very involved game with more goals than simply competing and brushing your horse. You earn money by training foals, massaging client's horses, breeding foals for clients, and booking guests. You can also breed your own foals and sell them. You can buy 3 different types of feed, supplements, a general vaccine, and a myriad of other medications to cure your horse of ailments (you'd only need them if you didn't keep your horses' health up, and it's very easy to keep them healthy). You can also buy show coats, boots, saddles, casual clothing, and books (which increase the amount of money you earn for each activity). Your focus it to achieve the next star rating by meeting all of the requirments for each level. It is very addictive and very fun!

It's not bad. I've played many horse games over the years, and this is one of the best. That said, even the best wasn't that great. It might just be that I'm picky, though. It IS the best horse game currently on Steam, in my opinion.
Note that this review is from the POV of an equestrian, and is probably best targeted at someone similar. This is mostly me being picky.
Things I like:
- I like that you can lead your horse. It takes goddamn forever, but I recently realized I could speed up the game (hotkey 1 to speed up/slow down) while leading my horse or doing other similarly slow tasks to speed them up.
- I like the upgrades to the facilities even though it's slightly linear as to what you can do, and when
- I like the animations, which are very good compared to many other games with horses in (though not necessarily horse games)
- I like the riding activity. I've only got the first field unlocked, but it's nice, and I like that there are bonus points scattered around for you to find.
Things I don't like:
- You can tell whoever they hired is not totally on the up-and-up on all things horses. This list is primarily going to revolve around that.
- Lunging foals that look like they haven't even been weaned? And on tiny circles? If you did that in real life you'd have a broke♥♥♥♥♥(and not in the good way) horse within a year. Their joints would just disintegrate (not a technical term) with the stress.
- There are only three breeds. Hanoverian, Friesian and Andalusian. Not bad breeds, but who the hell's idea was it to put Friesians in the game? Friesians only come in solid black, in reality. It's kind of their thing. In this game, they can come in any damn colour. NO. NOT RIGHT. WRONG. D: Hanoverians and Andalusians do not come in cream, either. Totally inaccurate. Not even close. They could have improved the realism tenfold just by adding a few more breeds, making them actually look like those breeds, and STICKING TO REALITY. Having a gray (white), palomino or spotty Friesian is the equivalent of having a purple polkadotted pony. It's not possible.
- Only being able to gallop over jumps, when in reality you want to NOT speed over jumps, usually. That's how you break legs.
- Lack of show jumping or dressage. The best horse game I ever played incorporated all three branches of eventing. Sadly, it lacked in other areas. I have yet to find one that hits every note.

This is a silly little game that takes itself far too seriously.
For a game that pretends to be plot-driven it has a total lack of urgency about itself which is actually kind of nice.  It gives you a series of instructions to complete ‘when you feel like it’ and turns you loose.  It lets you get your feet without pressuring you overmuch… but it’s also not challenging.  You learn to feel for how much time your tasks take and plan around them, you learn where everything is so you don’t waste time going back and forth and back again because you forgot to do something in one area earlier.  (Eventually. The map’s not very easy to read.)
The HUD’s pretty awkward to manage too. There’s a function where if you click a certain button it’ll bring up your current attributes, and if you walk near a horse it’ll show the horse’s stats.  The only problem with this is that it takes up half the screen and doesn’t show anything relevant about the yard – the horse section’s pretty good, but having the human one show how much feed you had, the overall dirtiness of the stable/horses in the stable/tasks completed for the day would actually have been useful. I can think of like six ways off the top of my head that could have been implemented better.
The minigames are dull and unrealistic in terms of actual horse activities. I won’t bicker too much about them as I realise there’s a limit to coding, but there’s a hell of a lot more involved in foal training than making it walk in a circle, and I’m BORED.  It’s kind of like level grinding in terms of boring and pointless.  And the less said about the breeding mechanics, the better, though I suppose for a beginner it would be more than enough.  It’s certainly interesting… Let’s just say the system isn’t based on genetics as I know it and leave it at that.
The controls are clunky and unintuitive, but they’re not *broken* or anything.  You’ll spend about half an hour cursing out your monitor every time they introduce something new and then you’ll get the hang of it, still mumbling occasionally about how idiotic the control scheme is. I have never before wished with such fervour that a game had been made aware of the WASD system.
It doesn’t help that the game isn’t very good at explaining what it wants you to do, though, and isn’t always that good at responding even when you are using the right combination of keystrokes, though maybe that’s just my keyboard.  Protip: when the game tells you how to do something, take it with a grain of salt, and experiment, because chances are it forgot to tell you how to do B and C while vaguely instructing you on how to do A.
The soundtrack is uninspired and highly repetitive but at least not catchy enough to drive me crazy. I turned the music off and played my own for background.  In another case of being somewhere in the middle of the scale the graphics aren’t cutting-edge but they aren’t hideous either.  I have some issues with the horse movement models they use, but again, it’s functional. There’s *some* customisation available for your avatar and horse, but not much. Coat colours and patterns are limited and use terminology that makes my head hurt with its inaccuracy, but it’s a kid’s game, so I can cope.
And frankly when I bought this that was what I wanted.  A silly game that didn’t ask too much of me while still managing to be interesting enough that I could kill a few hours when I got bored with studying.  This fits the bill.  It’s not amazing, but it’s playable.  If you’re thinking of buying it, go watch someone playing it on youtube for half an hour or so – that will pretty much tell you if it’s what you’re after or not. Metal Gear Solid's hallmarks have never been represented better than in Ground Zeroes, the prologue chapter to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. It combines tense stealth and best-in-class cutscene direction, and these aspects stand above any other game in the series, but naturally, the narrative ultimately concludes sooner than you'd like. It may only take you an hour or two to finish the main objective, but the game doesn't totally end there. In addition to filling in some of the gaps between Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and the Phantom Pain, Ground Zeroes introduces a new stealth system and an open-world format that's perfect for experimentation. Even though you're prepared for the next chapter, what's the rush? After the credits roll on the main mission and a handful of side activities unlock, the best part of Ground Zeroes is just getting started. With a wealth of secrets to find, and new challenges to master, chasing the endgame will keep you entertained for hours on end.
Aged graphics and AI bugs galore, but it's all worth it for the story.

This game in my perspective is still one of Bioware's best works.
Even though I had the story spoiled for me before playing this game I still enjoyed the plot overall. Sure the twists lack impact but at least they made sense and weren't just twists for the sake of it. Had I not been spoiled I'm sure I would have a greater appreciation. Although I'm sure most people already know about the plot at this point. You also dictate your own morality to the force, and this will affect the plot.
The characters for the most part are interesting, each with their own backstory. They have reasons for accompanying you and it will be your curiosity that dictates whether you wish to explore it (hint: you should it adds plot plus Exp). Some may get on your nerves, but others have some immense one-liners.
Now the 1st part of the game that truly shines is the gameplay. A fantastic combat system that is simple to understand, but still offers some difficulty at points. Some enemies will be a pebble for you to step over, others will beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you if you lack a plan. With a strategy in mind you can push on through these battles, and achieve a great amount of satisfaction from your victories. This is more in the early game however, as if you know how to build your characters you can make some incredibly overpowered parties that steamroll most enemies.
At some point during the game you will travel to a planet and acquire your Jedi (or sith) powers. This adds even more to the character as you now have even more skills and powers to use in combat. There are a decent amount of powers too. Each will be suited to paticular classes and some are just too good not to use. Your morality will also have an effect on your force powers too with force point costs altering depending on your allegiance. I found this to be rewarding when my characters level up and increase their repertoire of powers, allowing them absolute domination in battles. Still the non-force users in this game are still equally effective in their own right, perhaps acquiring some of the most potent equipment in this game.
There are various planets you explore in this game, most of them being mandatory (Yavin is DLC included in the game that sells you various equipment that you MUST ACQUIRE if you fancy a shot at godhood). Some planets were highly enjoyable, but others felt reather sluggish in their pacing, and ultimately were relatively boring. This depends on what order you visit the planets though as you can push your least favourites out of the way going to them first, then visit the more amusing planets later. I did appreciate this as it gives you the choice, giving you a sense of freedom a captain of a spaceship would have.
I have to make note of some glitches I expereince however. Sometimes the characters would lock up and refuse to move, usually after combat. This is easily rectified however by entering the options menu and turning on the VSYNC int he advanced graphics setting. Also in a few cutscenes the lines of the characters were automatically skipped. This made some elements of the story hard to understand and there seemes to be no solution I can find for it. This only happens once or twice but it is a nuisance. One of my saves also became corrupted at one point losing me five hours of game time (not the games fault I should have saved more frequently). I am unsure if the game is responsible for this, or if my PC was momentarily force persuaded to corrupt my save, but it only happened once.
To summarise if you enjoy any of Bioware's other RPGs or a Star Wars enthusiast do yourself a favour and buy this game. It has everything a good RPG needs to have, while adding replayability for those that can't get enough. It's cheap too (only £6.49 or something?). Even if you know the plot of the game and haven't played it you will still get something out of the gameplay I assure you.

Champions Online: Free for All
By far, the worst MMORPG I have ever played.
Refered by many reviewers as "The best 'free to play' Superhero MMORPG", Champions Online is by no means "Free for All". Whilst you can download and play through the first missions for free, the archetypes (power sets) the game provides free (silver) players with are by no means 'ballanced'. You get to pick one of the three. Healing, Damage, and defense. This was the idea the developers had to convince the players to subscribe and go freeform, allowing Gold (subscription) players to choose any power from any powerset as they wish. This already had made the game extremely unballanced, giving Silver players no chance at PVP. And how can you achieve this Gold membership you ask? By only 15€/month, OR, a crushing 299€ for a lifetime subscription.
However it does not end there.
Allong the years, freeform players have studied (copied) builds from other players, builds called 'Flavour of the Month'. Well, the last Flavour of the Month build has been going on for six months straight. This shows us the Developers not only refuse to 'nerf' these skills the community refers to as "overpowered", they actually could not care less about the game's ballance.
As for PVE? For Silver players? Nearly impossible. For gold members? Unchallenging. Dull. Hold a button down and you've killed ten enemies within three seconds. Again, this is a mechanic the developers came up with to convince players to subscribe.
As for the "variety of costume options"? Also a lie. Allthough you can create your own character freely, to obtain the actual good-looking armour sets, you'd be required to (who'd have thought?) spend even more money at least 5€/per costume set. Not to mention -no- vehicle in the game is free either. You'd have to take your chance with lockboxes (5 euros for each 5 pack-which, contrary to popular belief, rarely reward you with any vehicles whatsoever) OR purchace ZEN to buy them directly from the store. How much would a vehicle cost, you ask? From 15 to 20€, each.
Final veredict? Do NOT recomend, unless you've got more money than you can spend, but then again, you'd be investing on a broken game that is slowly falling to pieces.

Positives
+ Interesting lore and quests for each faction
+ Factions have very distinct play styles which are layed out for you on the faction selection screen.
+ MANY ways to win a game, can win without entering combat at all if you like.
+ Non linear progression system. Can research technology how you like which provides flexibility
in game.
+ Great visuals
+ Can create custom factions to cater to your specific play style (personally i feel the default factions are perfectly fine)
+ RTS Style combat that uses the world map
+ Can upgrade Units and Heroes with equipment and items earned from quests or built within
your empire.
+ One of the easier 4x games to "break you in" to the genre
+ Great customisation options for games such as world generation options, victory conditions enabled/disabled and turn  limit.
Negatives
- Tad too easy on normal difficulty. Start your first game on normal but jump up in difficulty when you understand how the game works.
- Although i said the game is one of the easier games in the 4x genre to pick up there are a few elements that aren't explained brilliantly. Combat for example can be a bit tricky if you don't know that if you want to stand a chance in  combat, upgrading units is essential. Also keep in mind positioning, get to the high ground whenever you can. The diplomacy victory option is also tough to keep track of if you don't know where to find the diplomacy point value you generate per turn. Don't worry if this all sounds confusing, google is your friend! Although i count it as a negative against any game if i have to resort to google for any reason.
- Like other reviews have said; the victory screen could use some work. A single image with the victory type achieved below it seems a bit "meh" for all the effort. An ending cinematic would have been nice for each faction!

Overall
One of my favourite 4x games ever. The diversity in the factions makes this a great game to replay as each playthrough feels different.

Homestar Runner is one of those long standing institutions of internet culture that has refused to die, but not like other series at the time like Madness Combat. No Homestar has managed to remain the same and yet still be just as funny as it was a decade ago. And I've grown up watching pretty much every episode, short, email and more. The main element that sells this game is the fact it's a Homestar Runner episode running on for a lot longer than usual. That's a double edged sword in my opinion, as it makes the game entertaining but sticks a timer on it. The good is that the humor you expect from this game is definitely there, all the little jokes that Strong Bad can make are included with gusto. Everyone is voiced by who they're supposed to, so no bootleg Bubs's can be found. The problem comes in that after a while, you begin to hit the same old voice lines over and over and over again.
That's the only problem I have with this game, it's Telltale making it. It feels as clunky and convaluted as any other Telltale game that didn't try to force you down a path. It has that old timey point-and-click problem of "If you don't know what the devs were thinking, then you're gonna have to break out da walkthrough" and then the issue is once you read/watch a walkthrough, you know the whole game.
I feel like this needs to be way cheaper than it is, maybe 10-15 dolalrs instead of 20. It's a very good game and the Brothers Chapman definitely made what feels like 5 extended Homestar Runner cartoons, but the Telltale side of the game just feels annoying. If I can reccomend how you get this game, do it like this. Wait for a sale like Steam Summer/Autumn/Winter/Gaben's bank account is low Sale and then buy this at a reduced price. It makes the stingy Telltale gameplay slightly less painful.

One of the best point & click games I've had the pleasure of playing. Despite the 'outdated' graphical appearance, the art was top-notch, as was the overall feel and atmosphere. But what really seperates fantastic point & click games from the mediocre ones, is the writing and the quality of the dialogue and plot in Primordia is absolutely stunning. Characters were also very likeable, in part due to the great voice acting.

Planescape: Torment is a major inspiration here; the initial hook of the story, Crispin/Morte, emphasis on the past, it's all here. Much like Torment, Primordia is filled with sad moments, funny moments, philosophical themes and one hell of a cathartic ending (at least the one I got).
Puzzles were decent and quite logical, although at times the game had too many red herrings going on, which made some puzzles a bit difficult for me. Still, only in one puzzle I had to go to a walkthrough and check it out.
All in all, a very solid old school adventure game with insanely good story, one that I am unlikely to ever forget.

Beautiful (if grim) setting and atmosphere. Excellent dialogs.
The puzzles are quite intuitive (after thinking for a bit! =), at least some of them have multiple solutions (I finished the game without solving every puzzle), and the game has a very robust hint system which is nicely integrated into the narrative.
I enjoyed the retro/pixelated visual style, but since mileage varies greatly do check screenshots and videos and see for yourself.
Maybe a tad short, as adventure games tend to be (about 5-8 hours in this case) but you can save the game at any point (and you have as many save slots as you want), which encourages exploring alternative solutions & dialog choices.
***
Personally, I play adventure games mostly for the story, setting, and characters, with a bit of puzzle-solving to spice the mix. As noted above, in this genre I don't care much for AAA high-end graphics as long as what's on the screen is clear.
"Primordia" delivers on all counts:
> The setting is amazing: robots in a post-apocalyptic, nearly Mad-Maxian world (minus the cars), with an orwellian Big Brother on top. Although, to make it better, the mood is nostalgic and bittersweet rather than oppressive.
> The plot is itself quite good.
> I found most characters to be very well crafted. The protagonist's companion deserves a mention of his own: not only he fulfills his Sassy Sidekick role and provides the humor this otherwise grim tale needs, he's also part of a very comprehensive hint system (and seamlessly integrated into the narrative)
> The puzzles themselves are quite intuitive, and the few that may be too obscure are enlightened by the hint system. Several puzzles have multiple solutions, too (I finished the game without solving every puzzle), and at least a few of them affect the endings of the story.
"Primordia" (as other adventure games) may feel a bit too short when comparing the playtime/cost ratio with other genres, but IMHO it's the price of well crafted plot & characters... and, perhaps more important, of setting and themes you keep thinking about even after finishing the game.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

There are serious problems with this game. Serious enough that this game's development cannot be said to be complete. There are game-breaking performance issues, game-breaking UI bugs, and the AI wasn't finished being programmed.
1. Laggy. I don't have a power gaming rig, but neither should I need one for a game like this. My computer has a decent processor and subpar graphics card, but the amount of lag is unreasonable. The big problem with this is that the way the physics engine has been programmed, the game physics slow down when the GPU can't keep up. Consequently, I often find myself unable to determine whether I'm flying at slow speed or experiencing physics lag. This often makes me crash into things and makes flight uncontrollable in general because I can't determine my actual in-game speed.
This is an unneccessary issue, as it's possible to program a physics engine with a fixed timestep that only draws frames as the graphics card can keep up. So there's no excuse for physics lag, really, even if the user has a subpar graphics card. It's just poorly programmed.
I'm quite sure the issue is with the video card not keeping up, since I have a pretty good CPU.
2. Bug: You can change the mouse-bindings on your ship to control what is activated by the left, middle and right clicks. However, if I go into the menu to change this binding then exit, it NEVER sticks. It doesn't save the change. I've been able to work around this a couple of times, I think by alterring something in the physical construction of my ship which 'tricks' the game into recognizing that some change needs to be saved.
3. Bug: There's no point having a child ship spawn order option if the game doesn't pay attention to it. You can set four ships to spawn from your own, and the order in which it will happen. The first one to spawn for me was number 4, then number 1. So there's no discernible order here.
4. Controls: I can't gel with twinstick shooters, so I opted for the keyboard and mouse. The game seems to be designed around this anyhow. You control your ship using the WASD keys, but the W key doesn't make you go up. Nope. It makes you fly forward with respect to the current direction your reticle (mouse) is from your ship. I find this counterintuitive, but perhaps there's a good game design reason for this.
Also, it's impossible to shoot in a direction other than the one where you're ship is facing (or currently turning to face). Why? The turrets are capable of pivoting, and if for example set to "Point Defense", will automatically shoot at enemies no matter which direction you're facing.
5. AI:
I find there to be way too many ships around stations owned by the player faction. It wouldn't matter, except that they crash into you. A lot. They don't seem to have any desire to avoid crashing at all.
For some reason, laser/beam/idunno weapons set to "Point Defense" will not shoot down enemy rockets, even if they have nothing else to do. Why? I can shoot them down manually with these weapons, so the capability is there. It's just unfinished AI.
6. Limited Ship Building parts:
From what I can tell, there's no 'structural integrity' component to designing ships. Parts don't experience torque or rip off or anything like that; I think the way it works is that each part is rigidly attached to every other part, until it takes sufficient damage to disappear and disconnect anything that was connected to it. That's fine.
The problem is that sometimes you want to connect an important part (say the ship's shield) to multiple other parts of the ship so that there isn't just one link in the chain that needs to be broken for it to fall off of your ship. You can sometimes do this, but often there are times when parts are *almost* snapping together but there's a teeny bit of space between them. This comes about from the developer not paying enough attention to the geometry of the parts provided to ensure that this will happen less frequently. An easy way to solve this would be to put in a sort of 'strut' part that can have variable length and just serves to connect two bits of the ship. But nope, that's not in the game either.
I appreciate the detailed options available in this game. You can change the number of physics timesteps per second, V-sync, and various gamepad options. I can't think of anything else good to say about this game, as my experience was so seriously hampered by physics lag.

If you are looking for a well rounded horse game, then this is a *very* well rounded horse game. It covers many aspects of horse life that other games do not usually include. These aspects include, but not limited to, horse riding, horse caring (beyond just cleaning and feeding), training, working with multiple horses, breeding and selling said horses, and running a profitable stable yard (where guests can rent your horses).
It takes a realistic approach to horses where it can while keeping in perspective that it is still a game. Some of these realities are the fact that your horse does get tired if run for too long, can get stressed, and even sick if not properly taken care of.
The in-game books (used for increasing skill levels) are not limited to in-game information, but rather information on the game's aspects in general, such as actual horse care, behavior to be taken when caring for a foal, etc.
As far as the technical aspects of the game goes, there are many positives. The graphics are not as realistic as most modern games, however, what it does have is beautiful. The controls are extremely simple, even if the concepts of the game are more for children 8+. The game restricts the player to an "8 hour day" where it will auto-save at the end of said day, so no night rides.
I would recommend this game for children 8+ and can go as high as teens to twenties. Definitely a fun, well rounded game for children and adults of all ages.

Background: Kinda enjoyed Lost Planet 3 and had always been interested in playing the first two since before. Not interesting in multiplayer so didn't even try.
The Good:
* Big bugs are fun and rewarding to fight
* Simple controls and movement with an often useless map
* Looks OK for it's age with some has great alien design
* Decent story and characters keep things moving
* Good weapons and great damage feedback gives impact to battles
* Grapple works really well but could have been necessary more often
The Bad:
* Graphics look bland and dated in places (not badly so)
* Keyboard bindings sometimes ignored by in-game feedback
* ConsolePortitus in the menus, movement and gunplay too
* Small Bugs feel like cannonfodder and aren't ever a challenge
* Walking speed feels sluggish and you rely on jump and slide
* Thermal tick down could have been more interestingly used
Impressions: Overall I liked the game and it's design work and mechanics even if it was rather simple to beat and outside of boss battles it's mostly unmemorable.
It might be unfair to expect more from a game of this age but I was left feeling that there was a cracking experience here that was dragged down by console port limitations. To be fair they give you a lot of rendering options for compatibility but sadly it didn't extending into updating the in-game feedback for what keyboard button to press in some situations.
Recommended for:
Conclusion: 6/10. A fun retro console like diversion that feel unambitious.
