A really nice game if you want an action-packed adventure with some environmental exploration and great freedom of approach.
The thermal energy mechanic might take a little while to get used to, but as soon as you wrap your head around it you'll be feeling like a real scavenger, looking around for every container and such, to get that glowing liquid that lets you survive, and you might also want to optimize your ammo usage for that extra survival flavour.
The setting is very fascinating,although its background is too vaguely described.
Enemies are varied and have cool designs, and they are quite aggressive and will swarm you if you're not careful.
Bosses are usually huge and ensue epic battles.
There are some cool weapons, but the best feature is the robots, there are different models that handle differently and have special moves and abilities, very nice. The stronger the robot, the more thermal energy it consumes, so it's all balanced and you gotta be a good player to survive.
The grappling hook is very cool, you can do some nifty tricks with it, too bad that the game doesn't mention them in any way.
There are some collectibles, not sure what they are for since I didn't look for them.
Sniping makes the game easier but I recommend it on some very hard parts of the game, e.g. you on foot vs. 6 robots and 12 soldiers.
It's playable with m&k, very very enjoyable, only the last "corridor" suffers from this layout.
The multiplayer in this version seems to be unusable, what a pity.
Had problems running it in dx10 with my 7870, played it in dx9 without problems, all to the max at 1920x1080.
All in all an excellent shooty-shoot fest with a good japanese flavour that gives it a feel of a lovingly crafted capcom game.
Took me 12 hours to play the campaign on normal, I'm an explorative player though, no point in rushing the experience. So if you're an ocd zergling it will probably last less.

Discovered Realm™: Manageable Weather is a pest-killer simulation in which you play as Wayne Brady trapped in a blizzard with a severe ant problem. Eventually the pest-control group called NEVEC which stands for "Never encounter venemous Eriophyidae caryana" That seeks to destroy nut-tree-eating gall/and or rust mites, thus leading to a heated conflict amidst the blizzard as both battle for dominance of the pest-control market.
In your battles, the harmonica system given to Wayne by Gale Harold will prove to be invaluable; healing his injuries by using the points that you collect from exterminated insects, essentially making you invincible until you run out of points.
There are a few clunky sections in which your exterminator tools will not work properly and the crosshair seems a little sluggish without any option to change it in-game, but for a PC port of a very early Xbox 360 game, it still looks very good and performs well enough; the bugs look very detailed and insectious.
Overall, if I had to rate it, I'd give it a 5/10 from an outside point-of-view. You like it or you don't; but personally, if I gave a rating on my own feelings, it would be a 7.5/10 for the impressiveness at the time of release and inventive mechanics. The story and cutscenes make no sense, though.

Don't buy this game... not recommended at least.
Where do I start with this piece of junk...?
It's a third person shooter alright. it has some interesting options for aim customization (you can adjust the way the crosshair moves relative to your character and such) but that's about all that's positive about the game. Even with highest graphics settings, the game looks basically just cheap compared to what was first shown as ingame footage. Aside from all that the Gameplay sucks. I started the game on medium difficulty (there's three in total) because I wanted to get a quick impression... ended up continuing it because I just didn't want to play all that again. The thing is. the game is just ridiculously easy, very few of the enemies barely even manage to attack you at all most of the smaller monster just seem to... be there to be shot and not much more. They move like half a kilometer per hour and do some (very well animated though) moves... but they don't attack... at least they didn't attack me. Human enemies just stand still at their predefined spot most of the time and act as if they were shooting in your general direction, though I have yet to be significantly hit... they just can't shoot straight. Except for Rocket Launchers... those things, even if they hit somewhere remotely close to you, will send you flying (they don't actually do much damage though) which get's me to the next point: Ridiculously large health pool, constantly refilling too from a pool of "thermal energy" which can be found in simply everything (frozen old cars, barrels, EVERY SINGLE ENEMY ... you get the idea) so dying is basically not an option, aside from Capcom's typical animated special killmoves that some bosses do.
Leveldesign and story are in equal parts boring and rightout stupid. In fact, starting a mission will give you a screen telling you "Objectives: Go there and clear the place out." ... no kidding... that's actually exactly what every mission comes down to. Then you'll start the mission, instantly standing somewhere between a few dozen small enemies and a lot of stuff lying around that needs to be broken to fuel up on some energy and ammunition. Then you try to find where the heck you're supposed to go since it's sometimes completely unobvious (there's lightposts pointing in the direction where you need to go) and end up fighting a slightly harder foe (usually a mech with rocket launchers that moves around completely stupidly or a giant monster with some nice special animations.... and not much else), then the screen goes "Mission Complete" ... mission over... cutscene with some horribly bad written plot and next mission. The Game does not feature any kind of advanced combat mechanics like cover, zoomed aiming or such, so basically.. it's generally uninteresting and unrewarding.
I've never got so bored from playing a shooter... seriously...
The game DOES feature a rather well-modeled kind of sympathetic main character though... if it's any help....

One of the more interesting action roguelikes to come out.   This one kind of flew under the radar even though it came out at a time when theses kinds of games felt new and were receiving a lot of attention.
Solid twin stick gameplay with permadeath,  random levels,  and persistent class unlocks and perk upgrades.  The persistent upgrades and unlocks help make death less frustrating but you don't feel like you're grinding for these upgrades or that the game can't be won without them.   Easy to learn controls plus enough special abilities to keep things interesting.  One unique touch not often seen in this kind of game is the map screen similar to super mario 3 where you choose the level you want to go to and avoid certain types of levels if you want.
Excellent audio visual presentation with a unique voodoo theme.   A lot of indie games go for a retro pixel look or if they try for 3d end up looking cheap and stiff.   Everything looks very fluid in this and has a lot of personality.
Like many roguelikes of any kind this is very difficult and so is something you can play for a long time.  It rarely gets overly frustrating though.  Because of the well done presentation and fun gameplay you won't mind replaying levels.   It even has multiplayer though I haven't tried it.
Highly recommended and well worth the price.

This used to be a great game and everyone used to compliment its huge character creation possibilities... until they decided to make you pay for all that, leaving you with barely anything to make your characters look unique! This used to be one of my favorite games of all time until the developers decided to ruin it. R.I.P. Champions Online

I'm an old veteran of City of Heroes and City of Villains, and have played a large array of various MMORPGs. Champions Online: Free For All has been the perfect scratch to an itch I've had regarding both MMOs and superhero games. While a lot of options are locked behind the Freemium wall, there is enough available for free to satisfy what I'm looking for in a PC game right now. Available archetypes are varied enough, and two character slots, while limited, forces me to explore those characters rather than spend hours making new ones who will only be deleted in short order.
Content is streamlined and fun. I'm still getting used to all of the different currencies in the game (Zen, Resources, Millenium City Recognition Points, UNTIL Recognition Points, among others), as well as the layout of the game world, but if Millenium City isn't enough, you can complete multiple-mission story arcs in other locales, such as Canada (in 'Whiteout', a comic-book equivalent of John Carpenter's The Thing), Africa, and other areas. If that isn't your thing, run 'dungeons' for your hero by participating in Alerts, where a group of five heroes team up to stop bank robberies, museum heists, time displacements, and others.
While there is a large amount of content that can only be accessed by paying, Champions does allow me play an online superhero game that offers just enough customizable options without requiring tons of hours of gameplay or a monthly subscription.

General Notes: My never-ending quest for the Perfect Turn Based Strategy Game found its way to the Endless Legend Pre-Release. Having come off of 2 years of Endless Space I was all for that traditional old timey feel of having my boots on the ground again. Having just gotten the last achievement I feel like I need to say something about the Legendary Deed quests. Holy Crap.
The Story: The Story is surprisingly deep for a Turn Based Strategy. Sure every game has some measure of Lore, but Endless Legend tells a story about each Race with Unique overarching story quests and deeds that really get you to care about each race. They also help define the playstyle and unique characteristics of each race and embodies them like fine wine.  It reminds me of Warcraft, but on a grand scale.
Game Mechanic Highlights:
Dynamic 2-Phase Weather System: The Game exists in Winter and Not-Winter. Winter requires cities to tap into their stored food instead of the Production of Non-Winter.
Non-Linear Research: There is no Direct Path in how your Research develops, only a set marker of X many research projects completed to reach the next tier which promotes varying playstyles without sacrificing Research Level.
Unit Customization: Any fan of the Warhammer games will be ardently familiar with how Endless Legend presents itself, but so will Veterans of Endless Space. Units are customizable down to their Armor, Weapons, and Trinkets. Leader Units also have customizable Traits that help them in their Role.
World Map Based Combat: Combat takes place on the Actual Map that you navigate on, so planning your Position at the start of a battle can be the difference between success and failure.
No Pay to Win Store: No Pay to Wind Store. I must state this because there is that Pay to Win Turn Based Strategy game out there presently on the Steam Store with animals and stuff. Anyways…
This is not Civilization: Let’s get this out in the open, this is by no means a Civ game, though it shares many similarities I think by now we can expect the core concepts to be similar to Civ like every MMO is to World of Warcraft. Everyone’s a critic.
Final Thoughts: The Game by itself is a great game with a nice sound track. It does share a lot of similarities with other Amplitude Games like Endless Space so Veterans of their work may feel like its too close to the same formula but that does not detract from the Story.
As Always, Watch Gameplay Footage Before Buying!

Reassembly is a sure way to have a ton of fun. Its simple, and doesn't have much in it - but its just so beautifully executed that I have a hard time criticizing it. The first thing you'll notice is just how damn good it looks. The simple style mixed with the flashy bright particle effects make every ship look fantastic, even if your not a skilled builder. Basically, you start as a faction with a little plot of territory in the galaxy, and must build ships with increasing size and power, collect resources, conquer and annihlate opposing factions, and eventually control the whole galaxy.
You manage your faction in a simple screen that essentially says "what ships should we build?." Not every ship you construct will be your own, you'll find yourself making everything from Carriers to Gatherers to Melee brawlers, all supporting your faction on a galactic scale, not just following you around.
Pros
-Visuals: Just look at them. They're mesmorizing...
-Simplicity: This may not be for everyone, dont expect complexity and depth. Though this DOES NOT MEAN ITS NOT SKILL BASED, more on that later. The simple building system allows you to make pretty ships that are functional in minutes, and make enormous detailed bohemoths in about 20 minutes. Its just so easy to do,  you dont even have to be creative, really. (That is not saying there isn't lots of room for creativty.)
-Skill: Outside of building, you've got to know how to pilot your ship. ou can die fairly easy and lose control of your entire fleet, so you've got to be careful. You can play just bumrushing everything, but you'll die a lot. I recommend lots of mobility, even in ships that wouldn't ordinarily need it. I cant count the amount of times I failed to remember to make good thruster systems and ended up with a floaty brick.
-Faction Growing: By far the games greatest strong point. Over time, as you see A.I. ships you created flying about and taking territory for you, it gives you a nice feeling of progression. You can even costomize what the stations you capture will look like. I found myself building unarmed civilian vessels and giant mining ships just so that our territory would seem lived in. I build a cheap but huge metropolis that I spammed all over my land so that it looked like there were cities.
This stuff is not entirely nonefunctional. I found that building mini mining ships that gathered all the R (resource) they could, letting all my stations spam them out, then just recruit them all so they'd give me more R then it costed C (credits) to hire them. I would then sell the R for C and make a fortune.
-The organic galaxy: Unlike most games, the galaxy is all in one map. Its not particularly big, you can fly across it in five to ten minutes with a fast ship. (Though you likely wont make it, the amount of enemies flying around and waring with eachother will kind of get in the way.) However, I think the map is better off small. You see, if it were big like actual space, it'd be empty. This map is anything empty. In fact, its a bit of a cluster****, and thats a good thing. The map is one giant asteroid field, inhabited by countless factions all fighting for territory. Whilst exploring, you will frequently find crashed and destroyed ships, stations, etc. And there will always be plenty of ships to fight. Once you get bigger, most of them wont be two much of a threat. But every now and then, a giant mothership will pop out of nowehere and blow you to pieces.
Ships dont just spawn when you get close, they all came from somewhere. And you can, if you blow enough of them up, completely genocide them. The factions will all be trying to do this to eachother (though they likely wont ever succeed due to the sheer amount of eachother) and you will constantly stumble across epic space battles and land grabs. Indeed, the whole galaxy is a warzone, and a chaotic one at that. There will sometimes be so much going on screen all you can see are particle effects( despite this and my fairly low end PC, the games runs like butter) Being able to zoom in and out greatly adds to the games scale as well. Oh yeah.. And also, SPACE PLANTS! SPAAACE PLAAANTS!
-Soundtrack: The fantastic ambient space music fits the game perfectly, with its Psychill electronic style making for a very relaxing genocide war.
-Tournements: I had a fun time with two friends, just playing the game locally during a get together, in which we all build ships of the same P limit and made them fight in the tounrement. Making your ships fight eachother is addictive enough without it being a competition between friends, so I recommend checking it out.
-Gameplay: It plays a lot like the old arcade space shooters, just far smoother and a bit more physicsy (eiiy? Eee?) This works really well with the open world aspect, making it a joy to play. Works really well as both a timewaster and a longer effort. There are a number of ways to play Reassembly, you can spend all your time making perfectly crafted fleets and sending them through wormholes to fight other players, or you can just make one ship and be a lone wolf, building your ship to perfection over time. Me? I prefer to play it on a large scale, assembling fleets and building military strength.
-Agent System: One of the better semi-online systems I've seen. Basically, you can upload your best fleets into wormholes, and they will appear in other players worlds to wreak havoc. Its kind of like Dark Souls's world invasion thing, but you dont control the fleets you send out. They are A.I. cotrolled. Agents appear as little red triangles, and vary in strength. (depending on the P (ship size) of the fleet the player sends out). If you destroy their flagship, the fleet breaks up and stops building new ships. They will spread out, raiding your stations, but will eventually all die.
This is a fantastic way for players to show off their creations. Although you will inevitably see a few giant blocks full of guns, most of the designs I've seen have been quite good looking.
Cons
-Lack of weapon variety: Weapons are a crucial part of the game. Sadly, most weapons are just generic projectile weapons, with some doing more damage then others. To be fair, there are lasers, drones, missiles, AoEs, but every faction seems to have most of those. The faction variation is more in their visual style and armour then their actual difference in combat. There are some more interesting weapons, such as the Proton Sword, the Borg Drones (Yes, Borg), and it seems as though every faction has at least one special gun, I would like to see more weapon types in the future. Stuff like wave guns, tracking lasers, force guns to blow enemies away from you, etc.
-Can get repetitive: Make sure to play this game in successive bursts. Playing for hours and days at a time will get boring fast, its better picked up and played for a few hours every now and then.
Procons?
-Balance issues: I dont really know about this one, its undeniable some factions are better then others (Red sucks, Crystalline are gud) but I wouldn't really call it a bad thing. Its more of a progression system, as the tougher factions are usually closer to the centre of the map. Make of this what you may.
Overall - worth a buy. One of the best games I've seen come off Steam, and an excellent example of what Indie Devs can do!

Do you like the Legend of Zelda? Final Fantasy? Dragon Quest? Diablo? Many more? Well I guess you could give this a go. A nice throwback to the classics, visiting upon game mechanics with the use of evolving gameplay, unlocking elements as you play such as antialiasing and 3D movement. It's a fun way to show the evolution of gaming throughout the years. The story is short, having completed it in 2 hours while taking my time. There's no shortage of game references that you'll most likely recognize if you liked any of the previously mentioned titles, some subtle and others blatantly obvious. For example, your protagonist is Clink, a blonde, spiky haired boy wearing a green tunic. Gasp, spoiler alert, you get a buster sword too. But that just adds to the humor.
There are a couple of issues, such as unresponsive menus in battle and the inability to use potions unless you're in battle, but they're hardly game-breaking. If anything, you can chalk it up as another reference to the olden days when glitches and errors were a dime a dozen in any number of classic titles. Overall, not a bad experience, though you may find it lacking if you're jumping in without any prior knowledge of older games.

This is a really good MOBA and everyone should try and play it. The characters are simple enough to learn and get the hang of and has a great verity within the cast. Maybe it's a bit of a bold statement but I think Primordia is a memorable game, so much so that I'm writing this review to recommend it.
I'm a story guy and this game delivers it in spades both at a macro level (the main story arch) and micro level (the single scenes). It does suffer a bit from the puzzle adventure syndrome, that is, it's not always clear how to solve a problem with the stuff you have, even when you have everything that's needed. I know this is to be expected in a way but it still bothers me.
The old nerd in me suspected some of the details revealed in the final scenes right from the start but the game was compelling enough to just draw me in the atmospheric setting and make me concentrate on what was happening at a certain point. Hard to say the same about most games I've tried.
The music may be a bit repetitive in the long run but it really adds to the mood, it fits perfectly. So much so that I actually noticed, appreciated and left it on: in other games I usually have it on low volume or off entirely.
The graphics are retro, but in a good way. A shiny AAA engine would only marginally enhance the game. Some may even think that this old school style is actually better/more suited to this kind of game, can't say they are completely wrong.
Again, highly recommended, best game I've played in a long while.

The evolving, AI equivalent of sea monkeys! Or if you like, an evolving AI ant farm. Featuring actual neural network based brains. (Sort of.)
An artificial life, natural selection simulation. One of the few truly easy to use, easy (with some time) to comprehend, sims of its kind. Complex enough for real neural nets to exist and self-replicate (though there is not, to my knowledge, any deep or reinforcement learning happening here - just pure natural selection,) and for interesting behaviors to evolve over time.
Definitely not a game so much as a simulation though, and the user interface is a bit opaque, so expect a learning curve. Fortunately, the simulation handles most of the work for you, so you can simply let it run and observe until you're ready to make changes yourself and experiment.
Map editing tools allow creation of specific experimental designs intended to test how the simulation's natural selection process "responds" to specific challenges, and tweaking things like the energy consumption required for certain neurons to exist, the level of friction or damage in certain terrains, etc. allow for even more control.
I had been on something of a deep reinforcement learning kick when I stumbled upon this sim, and while it does not (that I can tell) feature any true "learning," it may be the finest, easiest to use natural selection AI simulator I've found so far.
I am by no means an intellectual - I have little education, and am a complete layperson when it comes to artificial intelligence. But here is a program complicated enough for more intelligent people to run full experimental studies with - assuming proper experimental design of course - yet simple enough for a dolt like myself to use, tweak, and observe effectively enough to still learn something. It truly is endlessly fascinating.
The premise couldn't be simpler. A grid - size of your choice - which continually populates with food (the green squares,) and random creatures. Its border is (at least by default) surrounded by deadly lava. Each creature consists of a membrane (a colored square,) and neurons (inputs for sensing the environment, a middle layer, and outputs for affecting the world and the creature's actions within it: grabbing, turning, feeding, moving, signaling, etc.)
DNA, which mutates randomly, determines the neural network and the properties of the neurons. (E.g. what the neurons do is already established on a neuron by neuron basis beforehand, but the DNA tells each neuron what its specific threshold for signaling is, where in the network they are positioned, which neurons exist or get deleted each generation, etc. etc.)
Each membrane can hold a configuration of input, middle, and output neurons (a neural network) at a maximum of 9x9x9.  So these are extremely rudimentary creatures, indeed.
However, the random generation of these creatures' neural configurations, combined with genetic mutation and drift over  successive generations, means that natural selection over time takes place, and those creatures more specialized to find food, reproduce quickly, and avoid death, naturally tend to dominate.
Given enough time complex and interesting behaviors naturally emerge.
One of the most intriguing things to observe in Gridworld, is how "eras" or "epochs" of specific traits seem to naturally emerge.
For example: early in the simulation, there tends to be a life explosion. This is quickly counterbalanced by food scarcity. Those creatures which survive the ensuing starvation then pass their genes on to subsequent generations.
Another example may come when creatures evolve to be more rapid, more efficient food seekers. A particular mutation - such as the ability to turn toward food for instance - may allow a creature with those specific traits to rapidly outproduce others, leading to their competitors' extinction and their own domination of the world. However, this too can be self-limiting, as eventually they can become so good at finding food, they begin to starve. Or, in the pursuit of food, they grow so fast that the speed with which they dive into the deadly lava at the world's border may outstrip the pace at which they can reproduce. In either case, and in others, they may eventually die out, or get out-evolved by another, more conservative species.
For this reason, faster/better/more neural activity is not always the recipe for success. A simpler creature with a better balance between food seeking, energy efficiency, and reproductive rate - perhaps with a random tendency to change direction more often, lessening the likelihood that they will run straight into the lava - may be more successful than bigger brained competitors.
All of this means the game goes through phases of rapid evolution and dominance by a single creature type, followed by some sort of impact on the world by said creature's ubiquity and behavior, until such time as a new equilibrium can be reached... either by the creature itself evolving to adapt, or a new creature outperforming it. This cyclical process of "epochs" is truly random, emergent, and unpredictable. Which makes it extremely compelling/entertaining to observe!
One of the most interesting and popular behaviors evolved by some, is the ability to detect and avoid lava. This is held up by many as an example of successful evolution, and many have expressed frustration and dismay at the rarity of this trait.
It's important to remember however, that we are not talking about true intelligence or learning, here. We are simply dealing with rudimentary natural selection. In practice what this means, is that an advanced ability such as the detection of danger and the capacity to steer away from it, is not necessarily always the greatest sign of fitness to survive in Gridworld. Simpler organisms that reproduce faster may overtake these more advanced creatures, by sheer numerical superiority and food consumption. Which of the two then survives that mass starvation will depend not on who is better equipped to avoid lava, but on who is best able to find food and reproduce.
This introduces an intrinsic and common limiting factor in Gridworld that some find disappointing. But make no mistake... it's entirely possible, however rare, for the perfect combination of food seeking, turning, danger avoidance, speed, and reproductivity to evolve. When and if that happens, you'll see very fast, very "smart" (not literally) agents avoiding danger and popping out babies like there's no tomorrow, while also not inducing a mass extinction because of their energy efficiency which requires less food.
and as such, species can go "backwards," or reach evolutionary dead ends. Especially if you start changing the environment. Creatures well adapted to the previous status quo may die out, unable to cope with the changes, prompting newer adaptations to usurp their position in the food chain.
True neural approximations of brains
Natural selection driven emergent behavior & adaptation
Can be run passively, taking an extremely hands-off approach
Fascinating to observe
Easy for anyone to understand with some time and effort
Creature capturing, importing, & exporting between different experimental grids
User editing of world grids, energy cost, types of neurons that can be generated, amount & rate of mutation, & much more.
Very RAM intensive at high creature and neuron counts.
Somewhat difficult to understand user interface.
No reinforcement learning.
If you find sea monkeys or ants boring, you probably won't like this more than that.
Very accessible, powerful sim, demonstrating true natural selection.

This simulation is really cool. Notice how I say simulation. This is not a game. You can influence the simulation with MANY different factors, or save creatures from their inevitable death. This is a simulation about evolution. In the simpliest simulation, you have a world of food surrounded by lava. Randomly generated creatures will begin to spawn. Creatures that are 100% random. You will quickly learn that the chance for a species that can sustain itself is extremely low. It can take hours before you find a creature that starts reproducing. It may seem awful that all you find are creatures that only know how to spin in place or don't even have a mouth to eat. When you do find it, it feels awesome. AND THE BEST PART: It is totally random. You may find your typical creature who just runs, eats, and reproduces, but you can also find cool creatures. In one simulation, I decided to put a big lake in the middle to see if it could change anything. Suprisingly, a creature which I call the "Shore dweller" arose. It lay dormant on the shore, conserving energy, until it reproduced another along the shore. There was just a pack of them wading beside the lake, living for an extremely long time. Recently, I started a game. Many creatures were spawning that were able to move and eat, but when it reproduced, it created imperfect, lifeless creatures which would die. Then the "Rollers" came along. A species that produced, yet seemed to also product those same imperfect babies. So how did they reproduce? Appearently, these acted as eggs. Something unique about these rollers is that they would roll things in a circle around their body if they touched something. They would roll the eggs, feeding them, and they would then "hatch," being like all the others. Seeing these cool things like this make you feel good. Sadly, this creature relied on a huge amount of food and didn't like turning. I made a river that split this world in half, so they only had 2 real ways to go (Unless they had abilities to cross the river, which though they made some progress, not enough.) They went into my lava border and their species was wiped out, along with all food in the area. If you decide to play this game, there is a pretty good chance you will have a unique creature to rule your simulation. Or 2, if you try and segregate areas to attempt to get multiple creatures.
ALSO, you should totally check out Rickashay's steam guide on the Boom Bust Cycle. It shows you another awesome example of a creature and they tell you about a cool cycle to fluctuate creature size.
I'm not really a fan of these types of game, but I can't say it's bad. I would recommend this if you enjoy life simulation games of this kind.

The premise of this game is kinda dumb and I wasn't so sure about it. However, it became side-splitting fun very quickly. Basically what you're doing is setting up one of your two customizable characters in a sandbox track type environment for various ways to do serious bodily harm to them.  Its basically like when you were a little kid and would set up a toy soldier on a little obstacle course with cars, explosions, and all of that sort of thing except it is virtual and freeking hilarious.  I've also heard this called a crash test dummy sim and I suppose that is fair too.  All I know is I think other people with a childish sense of humor like mine who like games will probably enjoy Turbo Dismount.  The gamer chooses a course, sets up some obstacles, picks a mode of transportation (cars, bikes, skateboard, etc) a customizable Mr or Ms Dismount character, and the position on the vehicle for the character, then sends them on the way to certain death.  Once the dismount is achieved the whole scenario can be rewound and played back at various speeds to your liking either for your own entertainment or to help decide how to tweak the course.  Everything in the game seems well done.  I haven't encountered anything to complain about.  The graphics are simple but highly adequate and the camera system is great.  If I had to complain about any one thing is that I'd like to see more obstacles and perhaps a user picked starting point.  Its not a big deal and perhaps is something left for the next version.  I'm not much of a multi-player type of person for the most part but I can see where this would be fun to play with someone else.

I was quickly able to beat back weaker factions, and help my faction grow to a decent size.
An economic boom occured, as stations sprung in high density around a resource rich field of asteroids, just down of my starting area. My ships were still hardly better than my neighbors, who stood very close and inbetween my land. I had to push them further.
Eventually, I would overcome them. Continuing to push the remaining factions further away, I noticed something. A red blip, was headed straight for my territory. They were tough for a single weak ship, but I brought more and waited for them. They came, and I wiped the floor! But, another comes, and was easily defeated as the ships were inferior. I continued to push out rivals, and explore new lands.
However, nothing could prepare me for what would arrive next. A fleet, with a captain who I shall refer to as bent. Bent had brought very special ships. It was far more advanced than what I had come up with. His ships were a horrid blue and white. The majority of the fleet spawned drones, however one ship design would utterly bring me to my knees. Master, that's the name of it. With a factory lodged in it's center, and several drone spawners, it would prove to be my ultimate quest to destroy.
Bent's fleet had cut across my territories, in a sparsely populated region. They quickly defeated all ships, and stations in the area, but they could not cut through the denser areas. I went in, time and time again, capturing derelict stations in a grind that would eventually help me fund a better ship. Even after I built it, it was still no match for the swarms of drones. I then attempted to develop my own spawner. Capable of launching thirty drones at once, it helped me slowly push back Bent's remaining forces.
I had now established myself, as a force to be reckoned with. The old neighbors I had forgotten about, became weak. Then, while designing a ship tto hunt down the remaining Masters, I had an inspiration, to create a style. I quickly switched my colors to Gold, and white. I redesigned my entire fleet with wing-like designs, and I gave my fleet the moniker, Imperial Navy.
Since then, I've spent my time eliminating more invaders, and destroying the last of the Masters, An almost futile effort, considering the trail they left. But I have the greatest fleet to ever sail the deep space.

Just One Line is a fantastic concept that I really hope succeeds.
The basis of Just One Line is rather simple, you create an adventurer and fulfill quests that end up on a tavern job board in order to gain money, fame, glory, et cetera. It's a simple concept that the developer has turned into an extremely engaging experience with a good deal of replay value.
So you create your character and choose what you want them to specialise in. You choose either power, wit, or cunning. Basically you are good at smashing things, figuring things out or persuading people. There are different races and classes to choose from that each have their own traits, though only a few are currently implemented in the game.
Once you create your character you are suddenly in a tavern menu with a job board. After you spend some money getting basic gear, you choose from the available quests to complete during your adventure.
Each quest is a short text adventure. There is little traditional gameplay and most of it is spent reading and making choices during the quest. These choices can affect whether you pass or fail the quest, what rewards you receive and generally how people see you.
It might not sound like much, but the quests involved are all well written and offer a great amount of choices in how you complete them. There are no fail states other than dying during the quest. If you run away or refuse to do something, the quest just ends and you continue your adventure. The game is all about defining your character stories and who they are. There were times when I failed a quest but was still rewarded because I did something they didn't want me to such as literally robbing a farmer's house when he got lost. Having those choices really makes it engaging.
The quests are written very well with a few spelling errors that I noticed but nothing major. Just minor things like mispelling "the" as "teh" once or twice.
The goal of the game is to unlock more adventurers as you play by getting to certain milestones, doing certain things and the like. You can retire adventurers and make a new one to lead on a completely seperate path. The game is designed to be experienced a few times.
The game is helped tremendously by the art style. This game does a wonderful job with making a text adventure feel alive and fun to play. There are background environments and a fantastic fantasy cartoon setting that gives the game a ton of personality. More choose your own adventure games need to incorporate this because it makes the experience much more enjoyable.
There are only a handful of quests currently available for about an hour of content if you want try out a couple different characters. The developer stated they will be adding more in and also announced what I believe will be the feature that makes the game have lasting power and become popular.
The developer wants to put in the ability for players to make their own quests. This could potentially spawn an endless amount of new content for players to experience and form a great community around the game. I would advise that there be a system to help reduce griefing, as I'm sure there will be many meme related quests and the like. A list of different quest catagories would be great that players could turn on or off. That way meme or joke quests could be seperated and not forced onto players that might want something a bit more serious.
Overall, Just One Line is an absolutely fantastic idea and I genuinly cannot wait to see where this one goes. You've done good JOL Studios.

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Twin Stick Rogue-lite
The Good
+ 8 characters to choose from each with their own passive and active abilities. Each one plays very differently from one another, encouraging you to try every one.
+ Multiple passive abilities that you can upgrade and add to your character, .ie. more health, damage, more critical etc.
+ 4 main scenarios that have their own quests. Each scenario has randomized levels
+ 5 difficulty levels that change things dramatically
+ Lots of items to collect. Each run is completely randomized in terms of which items you receive
+Items include a description so you know how it helps/hurt you
+ Survival mode - play against hordes of enemies
The Average
Takes a long time to unlock and upgrade everything. The game seems to be designed around grinding. Nothing serious but you may have to grind out a few levels to unlock everything.
The Bad
-Despite  the randomness of the levels, the game feel very repetitive especially if you are playing single player. After completing the game a few times, there is really no incentive to go back to it.
- Multiplayer is dead, this is a game that would seem more fun if you had a co-op partner to play with
Conclusion
Despite its shortcomings, I had fun with my time with the game but I see little reason to go back to it. I would recommend the game only if you're a fan of the rogue genre.

So good! I was skeptical about the gameplay when I used to watch videos of this game but it works really well.
You have 20 levels to rank up jedi powers, combat skills and feats (your starting class determines which of these 3 categories gets the most points per level up). A jedi power available is force lightning, a combat skill is something like flurry which increases your number of attacks but they deal less damage and might not hit and a feat is which type of armour you can wear or other passive benefits.
Combat is played on a turn-based dice roll system which might sound off-putting but works out well. Throughout the game you will meet characters who join you on your spaceship and you may choose 2 of them to accompany you outside of the ship. Companions will have their own stats, gear and skills so you can play around this (if you come across a companion with high lockpicking you might choose not to level your own and swap to this companion to unlock things for you). You can choose to level up your companions skills manually or automatically.
You can choose preset combat manoeuvres for yourself and companions such as ranged attacking or jedi support (buffs and heals) or you can choose to manually decide you and your parties actions by pausing the combat and assign attacks and items to a queue. You also don't have to use companions at all, you can elect to play in a solo mode where all the exp gained from enemies will go straight to your character. You also don't have to worry about this mode because companions will automatically be boosted to your level if you haven't used them.
How you play the game is up to you. I went for a dual-lightsaber character with light armour and attack bonus jedi powers but you can play as a sniper, explosives expert, jedi caster or even unarmed fighting.
The story is really what made the experience for me however. You will travel to multiple planets, gain your own starship, meet interesting characters and get to interact with almost every NPC you come across with multiple lines of dialogue and character development.
One downside to this game is that you can't play in a widescreen resolution without using mods (although guides can be found for this on the forums here on steam, along with HD mods and many others).

As I have now actually completed all five episodes of
, I can give the game a proper review instead of just saying that it's a cool game for attractive people, even though, you know, it kind of is.
First of all, we'll get this out of the way: Unless you are a fan of the Homestar Runner universe, there is a probability that you won't enjoy this game. It makes endless references and jokes related to the series that you wouldn't understand unless you've seen some of the episodes in question. That isn't to say that you shouldn't buy it just because you might not understand some of the jokes though, either way this game is extremely funny and the humour is very dry, as you would expect from a game where you're controling Strong Bad.
This is what you would expect from a typical Telltale Game, it's a (mostly) point and click adventure with clever and satisfying puzzle solving which ultimately turned out to be a lot of fun. The puzzles make sense, the controls are simple (though sometimes a little clunky) and the dialog is hilarious.
The gameplay is relatively simple and easy to get into, some mini-games and particular inventory items help to break things up nicely so that it doesn't feel too repetitive. There are a total of five episodes for Season 1, all of which are relatively short but sweet, I'd estimate that they take around an average of 3 hours each to complete.
I really enjoyed my time playing this, and while it may not be to the taste of a number of people, I defintiely recommend it to those of you with a good sense of humour, whether you are a fan of the Homestar Runner series or not, episodes 4 and 5 were particularly excellent and stood out the most to me among the bunch, especially in the humourous department.
Lastly, the standard sale price is a little bit steep for the amount of gameplay that the game offers to you overall so I would recommend buying it while it's on sale. Either way, you'll get your share of laughs playing this game.

From the Telltale Games that brought you Sam & Max 1-5, and Videlectrix that made Trogdor: Let's Burninate Phonics, Trogdor & Rabbit Algebra comes Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive People or SBCG4AP for short. It's got the Complete Cast from
(Plus the Lame Ones too!). You'll go to all the cool places they go in the Homestar Runner cartoons in 5 totally awesome monthly episodes after you Purchase them & download them for the PC, Nintendo Wii's WiiWare & the PlaySstation 3's PSN Store through your Internet Connection.
In Episode 1:
Strong Bad receives an email suggesting he "beat the snot out of" his long-time rival Homestar Runner. When he gets there, however, he discovers Homestar has entered the Free Country USA Tri-annual Race to the End of the Race & decides it would be even more fun to beat Homestar at his own game than to simply beat him up. He disguises himself as Homestar, keeps him distracted away from the race & loses the race. The resulting chaos turns Homestar into a loser, earns him a criminal record, and makes his girlfriend Marzipan break up with him. Though Strong Bad is initially proud of himself for ruining Homestar's life, these efforts backfire when Homestar moves into Strong Bad's house, believing him to be "the only friend I've got". In an attempt to get Homestar out of his house, Strong Bad must undo the harm he did to Homestar's life.
In Episode 2:
The King of Town institutes an email tax. Strong Bad is the most heavily affected. However, being unaware of the existence of the tax, he is put under house arrest (with an explosive collar around his neck), a predicament that leads him to unite the citizens to rise up against the authorities. Strong Bad then declares his own plot of land (an empty lot featuring a fence, a spare tire, and a graffiti'd stop sign, which Strong Bad has named "Strong Badia") an independent nation. The inspirational speech he gives to the citizens inspires them to create their own independent countries. In order to overthrow the King of Town, Strong Bad must work his way through the countries and unite Free Country USA once again under the Strong Badian flag.
In Episode 3:
Strong Bad's FunMachine (an Atari 2600-like video game system) suddenly breaks. Strong Bad does not have the money to get it fixed, however. In an attempt to get money, he organizes a Battle Royale of the Bands, complete with local bands and celebrity guest stars; the 80's hair band Limozeen. When this still does not cover the fee, Strong Bad is forced to compete with his own rock band and claim the cash prize.
In Episode 4:
Strong Bad has finally finished his long awaited film and invites his friends over to his basement for the film's premiere of Dangeresque 3. The player then assumes the role of Dangeresque, embracing the cliches and tropes of the action film genre, with the movie looking like a very low-budget film.
In Episode 5:
Strong Bad jumps off of the couch and hits the Trogdor arcade machine. The Trogdor arcade machine grows an arm, legs and wings and comes to life. Strong Sad claims that Strong Bad damaged the 8-Bit containment field and needs to order a replacement. Sadly, through an odd series of events, the containment field is broken, resulting in the world of videogames and the world of Free Country USA combining. Video Game Elements & Characters begin invading the real world, and vice versa. In the ensuing chaos, Trogdor escapes his game and "Burninates" Strong Badia. Strong Bad must defeat his fiery creation once and for all, by getting party members from other games to advance to the dungeon of the beast and restore balance between the two worlds. But there's just one problem, does anybody know how to kill a dragon?

Reassembly is the "Love-it, else Hate-it" tittle. What you see on the store page is what you get. It is well-worth my purchase. Here is my opinion;
You start with a predefined ship. Explore, gather resource, destroy enemies, build/upgrade your ship, then repeat the whole process until you conquer the space, perfect your ship as far as your idea can go.
IMHO, this is where it determines Love/Hate opinions. If you like the concept, you will love the game as it has been executed very well, but for those that turns off by this kind of gameplay, it is a skip for Reassembly.
One of the two main core element. It has very common control for the genre, which can be floaty, weird, need some get used to.
The combat is rather simple from the looks, but actually there are some depth behind that plain looking combat. Weapon positions, projectile ranges, projectile speeds, special attributes, timing, and elae play the major role in the combat.
These come down to the second core element ...
Simple, easy to use, but powerful ship editor. It's snap'n build style, so it is easy to understand, and to get into. You can turn you ship into anything limited to your imagination, and ... system limitation, not the all you can build.
Each part you put into your design has its purpose, and different in stat. They will affect how your ship fly, either for exploration or combat. I haven't gone much deeper into this, but it is trials and errors until perfection, imo.
You can have AI-squadmates too, which is positively nice, but a little annoyance at times.
Here comes the twist, you can fly into other players creation during your gameplay. They are AIs with custom ships, which can be ranged from wackiest ship that annoy you to hell, or the flying box of death.
It is a good game for this genre at this price. Recommended !

This is a really fun game that bears a resemblence, visually, to the old vector-graphics games such as Battlezone or Asteroids, but bought forward into a much more modern environment.
Like many space games of this type, you start out with almost nothing, a tiny ship with very little firepower that is going to die against most other ships it encounters, but that's ok, because you aren't alone. Scattered around near you are bases and ships of your own faction that you can, with a bit of strategic thinking, use to your advantage to defeat even large enemies. Just be careful not to drag anything TOO powerful over to one of your bases.
You can earn money by gathering resources and selling them. These can be obtained from harvesting space 'plants' that can produce resources in various ways, or from destroyed vessels. This money can then be spent on parts that can be added to your ship, and that's where the real fun begins.
The ship editor is, simply put, brilliant. You can drag and drop parts onto your ship to create a vast array of different craft, and once a craft is designed, your own faction stations will ALSO build those ships (alongside the standard designs), so you will see your own vessels and stations being used as part of the overall design of the map.
Physics apply, it might seem like a good idea to build a small ship with an enormous cannon on it (or a large ship with several), until you find yourself being thrown backwards every time you shoot, the positioning of things like thrusters will affect the manouverability of your ship etc, which means you actually have to think about the design of your vessel, and yet somehow the whole thing feels simple to use and doesn't over-complicate itself. Each faction is unique and requires a different approach to vessel design and gameplay, so you can either choose a faction that suits your style, or attempt the challenge of one that requires you to leave your gaming comfort-zone.
The music works incredibly well with the game, and takes me instantly back to the late '90's with groups such as 'Future Sound of London', and that works incredibly well with the visual themes.
Even the issues I CAN think of are largely based around things like Mods that use vast quantities of things like drones or missiles, causing the game to AI-lag or possibly even crash, or the fact that, in factions that have resource-generation modules such as Solar Panels, you can build an enormous ship filled with these modules and your factions A.I will become obsessed with them, pumping them out seemingly in preference to fighting-vessels.
In summary, this is a 4x game stripped down to its core, and it works brilliantly. Very much worth the investment.

Full disclosure, I love Endless Legend.
I love how it takes the Civilzation formula and puts its own unique spin on it. I love how the asymmetric factions drastically increase replayability and interest in the backstory. But most of all I love the feel. Plenty of others have talked about the gameplay aspects, so lets dig into what makes Endless Legend
so good.
Endless Legend has a pervasive sense of melancholy that permeates all aspects of the experience. The opening cinematic is narrated by the game's setting Auriga and tells of her impending demise. During these last rites she talks of her concern for what will become of her children, the races of Auriga. After this the main menu loads and we get our first taste of the glorious soundtrack by FlybyNo. This soundtrack plays a key role in defining the feel of the game, since the hours spent playing are accompanied by a mournful and sorrowful accompaniment, all of which reinforces the mood set in the cinematic.
Once the game actually starts, the music becomes more upbeat and optimistic, and the player goes about doing standard 4X things and all is well. But after a few turns, winter descends. City's production takes a hit and movement on all of your units is reduced; you can almost
them wading through snow drifts. The first time this happens is quite a surprise, but it soon passes and things returns to normal with bright sunshine and sanguine music. But then it happens again, and then again, and each time is longer than the last and we start to realise that Auriga was right. She is dying.
Even progress through the tech tree reinforces this vision of the oncoming demise. Unlocking sufficient technologies advances the world eras in standard 4X fashion, but in Endless Legend they are accompanied with increasingly apocalyptic images, culminating in Era VI, the End of Ages.
In terms of referencing games with a comparable
, the only ones I can think of are Journey, ICO and Shadow of the Colussus. These are quite rightly considered classics, and I think that Endless Legend can stand alongside these revered titles.
In summary, come for the excellent gameplay and replayability, stay for the character, unity of design and
.

The fantasy aspect of the game is tantalizing, but that being said the game could use more empires with a larger variety. Gameplay is engaging and makes you think about your actions in the long term instead of playing move by move, and the technology and combat factors are much more interesting and rewarding than those in Civ. The DLC for this game also adds a lot of fun features, and the developers have allowed people that do not own the DLC to experience it in multiplayer games where others have it which is an awesome feature. Great game, highly recommended for strategy lovers.

This game was a pleasant surprise, to be certain. I could tell just from looking at the trailer and screenshots of this game that it looked interesting, and that "Overwhelmingly Positive" next to the user reviews made it seem like a no-brainer. So, finally I picked up this game and boy, I am not disappointed.
Let's get the bad out of the way first.
This game runs in a very small resolution, at least for most modern monitors. The highest resolution possible is 1280x800, which looks best in a window. It was also a bit annoying that the only way I could find to change these settings was by a launcher in the actual folder containing the game files. I only found that much by perusing the game forum when I was disappointed with the resolution.
There isn't much replayability. I can definitely see myself trying this game again to do a few things different, but overall it is a story-driven and therefore linear experience. It has several endings, but most of those endings are decided at your own whim by how you play out the final scenes.
Now, the good.
The obvious first thing you'll notice about this game is that artwork. I found it to be very cool to look at and definitely gives you that feeling of despair - a world wasting away around you as you desperately try to rebuild what you can. You also have atmospheric music that adds to these scenes but mostly stays in the background. It adds a lot, but doesn't overtake it. Instead, it's all just working together to give you an experience.
The voice acting is likewise excellent. The main character and his sidekick both do most of the talking, so it's great to see them so well performed. It's easy to pick up on their personalities and they're both likeable.
I'm always a bit bad at puzzles in games, but I thought the ones here were challenging but always possible. Nothing ever felt frustrating or beyond my abilities to figure out. I did get "stuck" in a few places where I had no idea what to do, but it usually came down to me not thinking about the situation well enough or remembering details that I simply overlooked. It's worth saying, almost everything matters in this game. There are few things that are superfluous.
Overall it took me about six hours to complete this game. I would have liked for it to be longer, but I could say that for any good game.
If you're interested in this game at all, check it out.

On the surface this is a 3rd person fighting/ combat game. You lock onto different targets, block attackers and use a combination of different attack styles to defeat different enemies.
The Campaign is 6 hours long and while the storyline is pretty straight forward to what you'd expect of a game based in this time there are many twists and turns along the way with the biggest of all at the end that changes everything.
There is also an Arena Mode which is where the game shines most in my opinion. Getting back to that feeling of being a Gladiator and fighting in the arena. However it’s not as simple as just kill everyone, there are different arena layouts and objectives to complete as though you are taking part in a part of the Roman History rather than a tournament where only the strongest survive.
The Graphics are incredible, Could not fault a single thing there, Very Immersive but not surprising as it was developed by CryTek who are known for benchmark standard games like Crysis.
ONLY Negatives would be 100% Achievements are a no go here as the Multiplayer community is non-existent and quite a few are Multiplayer required. Possible with a friend but otherwise nope.
QuickTime Combat also becomes a bore after a while and I ended up only using it if I needed Health Regen.

Ryse was a mixed bag for me.  While I love ancient history, the gameplay was off from what I expected.  First off, let me say that the story and graphics were quite enjoyable. Really neat little game, it's a Choose Your Own Adventure book that'll have essentially endless possibilities further into development. Playing back through the same quests after losing your character to permadeath doesn't always result in the same end point either, so there isn't a playing it safe kind of option. Definitely worth multiple trips through to see all possible quest ends.
Couple dings against it, there's not a whole lot of content here yet for the price point but what is, is well done with solid humour. English writing of said content could use some proofreading though, as it's got a spelling mistake or two in several quests.
Side note: The suggestion of installing this on an SSD to improve load times is strange, as it loaded perfectly fine on my standard HD.

It's cute, it's cartoony, it's simple, and it doesn't (at least for now) take itself seriously. It's basically a "choose your own adventure" game in bite-sized chunks, in which you get quests from a quest board at the tavern, perform them through a series of text choices, succeed (or fail) and get rewarded, as well as unlock other races and classes. The production values are good, with a consistent art style. No crashes in 30 minutes of play.
- The overall feel for the game and fact it can be played in short sessions makes me believe it would do well on mobile platforms. The engine could allow for other genres as well.
- To the devs: you will need a native English speaker to write your text. It is never possible to do this well if English is not your first language. The current English is passable, but contains odd phrases and some incorrect words and grammar. For example, many quests refer to the "Reign", when the word you wanted was "Realm". But fixing small mistakes such as this won't get you AAA text -- that needs to be done by a good, native English speaker.
The game world feels fairly random, though I can tell some thought went into the lore. The problem here is that you're presented with everything at once -- all the races, factions, etc, and it's simply too much to consider at the start of the game. The game really needs a good, epic story mode that allow unlocking of new content (perhaps new quest hubs with new quests as factions slowly unlock?) as one progresses through the story; right now the quests feel fairly random and artificial. Allowing players to create DLC as mentioned in the description, could increase longevity / replayability by allowing for essentially endless content. I am not convinced the current design of leaderboards is the way to go, as they feel artificial and are not satisfying on an emotional / storytelling level.
Some other thoughts:
- It is not clear to how difficult a quest will be vs. my abilities before I take it. The same goes for engaging in combat. The "3 skulls" interface is a good start, but it's still fairly vague and doesn't give me a good idea of what my chances are.
- In addition to a better ability to sense my chances of success (understanding that the way things are designed, this would probably have to be displayed on every choice), it would be nice to see the dice rolls. It would make things feel more like I was participating. Right now whether I succeed or fail feels like the game has made an arbitrary decision.
- The once per fight special ability: right now I cannot think of a reason not to use thisat the start of every fight, which begs the question -- why have it at all?.I like the idea, but not the current implementation. Perhaps this should only be available at certain parts of the fight, and only if the choices match (for example,
- I would like more ways to obtain quests than the quest board in the inn. NPCs who sometimes appear in the tavern with random quests would be fun, as would quests that open up "in the field" while you're on another quest. A quest board is fairly sterile and lends to the artificial feeling of the lore.
The game engine is great. It just needs careful content curation to reach its full potential.

Telltale Games joined forces with Videlectrix to use computers to make video games, and their collaboration brought us the coolest guy on the internet since 2000: the one and only STRONG BAD!
(Kids, ask your parents who Strong Bad is!)
But I digress: Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive People captures everything from the Homestar Runner universe that we all know and love. Strong Bad checks his emails. He pesters everyone. He kicks The Cheat. He plays his Fun Machine. Coach Z has that weird accent. All that good stuff.
The first episode has Strong Bad ruining Homestar's reputation, then having to undo all the damage. It's a good start to the game, with plenty of funny dialogue, decent puzzles, and of course, plenty of in-jokes everywhere. Not everyone may understand the jokes or references, but there are plenty of Homestar Runner cartoons on YouTube you can watch to get with it all. Telltale went all out to assure that the game would perfectly capture the look and feel of a H*R cartoon, and they didn't disappoint.

The gameplay wouldn't have been affected, and where necessary it could've occasionally switched to a 3D sequence. Other than that, it's just not really as funny as the web cartoons. The dialogue for those is usually short and snappy, and here you get kind of mired in the necessary conversations for adventure game dialogue. A lot of the references to stuff from the web cartoons feel kind of tired. I've been playing it for a while now and after 10-15 minutes I just have to save my game and go do something else for a while.
I will say the adventure game aspect of the game is pretty solid, it can get tricky without becoming frustrating. It's not a bad game series, but a little disappointing.

When I started into the universe of Reassembly, I wasn't really certain what to expect. What I got for a 15 dollar game was something amazing. You start with only one faction which you then are to use to take out at least one capital ship of another faction to unlock it. You start out tiny. As you explore and grow, learning lessons and tricks, dropping starbases and capital ships across the universe- and other universes for that matter, you will find yourself just looking to find something new. The thing is, every new discovery just sets the stage for the next new find. Different factions play radically differently, some with powerful custom built cannons, to another with few weapons, but a severe penchant for ramming- and the equipment to make it hurt when they do.
Perhaps the most striking thing of this game, to me, is the amount of thought that has gone into it. Want to build a starbase? Build a design including a factory but no thrusters. A monster capital ship which can build more of itself? No problem, include plenty of storage. Almost everything can be resized. Changing sizes increases mass, storage(if applicable) and armor, which means you’ll need more thrust to maneuver. You can not only build other ships, but build ships which can build other ships. Then tell them what you want them to build.
All and all great fun.
Edit: Just a small addition to this to round out this review. I have found after a while the game can grow repetative. I would dare say this does not happen untill you have at least tested each faction.
This game is RAD.

I was COMPLETELY WRONG.
Reassembly is much deeper than you'd suspect, offering many hours of gameplay due to its well-executed procedural generation, plenty of weapons and a dozen factions. Although the game lets you roam free immediately after the short but very good tutorial (it teaches you all the basics while still letting you free to do as you please, and you'll have to learn the rest by playing), there is more than enough to do. You can build a sizeable fleet, design perfect ships, take over all space stations, wipe a faction off the map, destroy asteroid fortresses, take down strong fleets created by other players, or warp to an entire new map with your fleet.
Combine the simple, yet deep and very addictive gameplay with the amazing, trance electro music and the colourful, pleasing graphics, and you've got a great game for a great price.
I absolutely recommend it as long as you like top down / twin stick shooters and constantly tweaking your ship designs.

Bought this for $7.50 during the Summer Sale, along with literally $100 worth of other games (including MGS: V). I even got a Bottle of Bourbon for the night, to make it a little special (coz you know, $100). 11 Hours in and I've yet to play any other games.
It's like SPAZ, but you can COMLEPETELY customize your ship. You'll spend an hour finding a great design only for it to become obsolete 45 minutes later, but it doesn't feel infuriating, it feels like I've moved closer to becoming the king of this little castle. You'll get cooler guns, bigger Shields, bigger engines, and find different ways to make bigger, cooler ships.
Some CONS:
The Ship Builder often doesn't line up how you'd like and there aren’t enough sizes of different things. Seems like a minor thing, but in a game that’s built around designing ships, when you have to literally entirely redesign your ship just so you don't have big holes in it that can’t be patched, it starts to matter.
Not as many Upgrades as one would like. A good few hours and you'll have pretty much unlocked it all. It's still fun exploring all the things you can make but with the tech limit such as it is, you can very much see an expiration date.
All that being said, 11 hours in and MGS: V is still waiting.
7/10 would get much higher marks for greater longevity, but a GREAT little game nonetheless.

Overall, I've greatly enjoyed this game. I wasn't expecting much going in because this isn't the type of game I typically play, but I've been very impressed. The open-world style keeps the gameplay interesting, and the ship-building aspect makes for a nearly infinitely customizable experience. The process of acquiring credits to buy new ship components and weapons is a bit of a grind, but the addictive aspects of this game make that issue disappear relatlively quickly. And once you've built up to capital ships with relatively few challenges from default factions, the agent fleets mostly present consistent challenges. Additionally, with Steam Workshop support, there are many customization options.
All together, it's a highly addictive game that I've probably spent too much time playing.

A hidden gem on the Steam store, Primordia is a game that is about robots in a world where their creators have long since been gone. You are a robot named Horatio Nullbuilt with his best friend Crispin Harotiobuilt, and you two are living in a wasteland. This game is great at charather development and world building.
Man is a god among robots and some say Man never existed. Some robots are barely surviving in the dying world they find themselves in. Others live together in Metro city, a strange place that seems like the last civil place on earth. This is a great 4x game, but a few aspects force me to give it a negative review.  Anyone who plays 4x games knows what makes a great one, so I will simply list the bad parts and let you make up your own mind if you try it.
1. The optimisation and performance is pretty terrible.  Even with a good system your turns will start to take longer and longer and longer as you explore more of the map.  This problem is much more prevalent the larger your map size is as well.  After exploring the full map, you will generally have to wait for the game to "refresh the map" every.. Single.. TIME.. you move it.  Additionally, the AI turns can take 3 seconds, or they can take 30 seconds depending on how much map is explored and how many opponents you have.
2. Winter is coming.  This game has randomized seasons; The standard game, ie summer, and the progressivly worse penalty season known as winter.  You will learn to hate it with a passion, as winters (and summers) have a huge randomness of duration so you could have 6-7 turn summers followed by 15 turns of winter.  Additionally, there is no option to remove winter, and by late game it gets longer than your very short summers, making movement of units, resource gain, production, etc all cut by 50-75%.

The trap of lazy and obtuse puzzle design is one that many developers fall into. Indulge me, if you will, and I will tell you a story.
Long ago, in a land far, far away, I read Hamlet by Shakespeare. When I finished it late at night, I had the strange idea to look it up on steam. Lo and behold, a game existed that was based off of the infamous play for a very reasonable five bucks. It appeared to be a point-and-click adventure game, but that didn't matter to me. It was too odd, too coincidental, for me to pass up. It downloaded quickly, and I began an hour journey of puzzles with no clear answers, walkthroughs, and a very loose interpetation of Hamlet. This is what I have come to expect from point-and-click adventure games. Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive People changes the formula to be less... awful. The puzzles in this
I know, that's crazy.
Alright, not all of them make sense, but most of them do. I can imagine it being hard to make puzzles that are difficult and coherent, but when it is the norm rather than the exception to have stupidly specific puzzle solutions in games, we've done something wrong. Point-and-click adventure games are notorious for having these sorts of puzzles, and that's because they miss something fundamental in making a puzzle: simplicity. Not simplicity in the answer or in the visual design (although that can help), but simplicity in the tools you are given. Think back to your favorite puzzle game. For a lot of you, it's probably Portal. Portal's central mechanic is deceptively simple; you shoot two portals, and walking into one brings you out of the other. But with that simple central mechanic comes the possibilty of twisting it into new shapes using physics and other, smaller tools and obstacles. Spacechem and Infinifactory are also great puzzle games, and their premise is simple as well. "Make specific things with these tools," the game says to the player, but the creators stretch and mould what it is the player needs to make. This most important of concepts is never used in point-and-click adventure games, but it is in Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive people.
There are some strangely specific puzzles, but most of them are pretty well done. Part of it is that there is no item combination. In most adventure games, the player is forced to combine everything in their inventory to find the solution to a problem, but Strong Bad eliminates that by removing that facet of gameplay. You just have stuff, and you can use it all with your environment. Many things only work in specific places, but those place also make sense. In Episode 2, for example, ypu get a lighter. Throughout the rest of the episode you can use that lighter on burnable objects. Makes sense, right? I'm glad to finally see a really good adventure game, but it
a Telltale game, and this is what they do best.
Strong Bad's Cool Game for Attractive People is fun and challengining, and I very much recommend it.

I'm not a Strong Bad fan especially (though I enjoy the flash games on the site), but having just finished Episode 1, I have to recommend this game. It's a pre-TWD Telltale episodic adventure, set in the wacky town of Homestar Runner. It's funny, the puzzles make sense, and it's overall a blast to play.

There are certain companies in the gaming world that dominate a specific genre of games. In TellTale's case, it would be point-and-click adventure games. These people know how to make a fantastic adventure game with wonderfully designed puzzes and great story execution.
SBCG4AP is based off Homestar Runner, a long running and very entertaining flash cartoon website with a fantastic cast of diverse and easily recognizabe characters. As such, being a fan of Homestar Runner is definitely reccommended for full enjoyment of this game, otherwise you'll probably have no idea what's going on, and in the case of a few of the puzzles where a bit of knowledge about the characters really helps, you might find yourself having a lot of issues.
As for the puzzles themselves, they seem vary in difficulty from episode to episode. I feel like episode 4 is the easiest, but I don't really know which episode I should consider the hardest. Puzzles in just one episode can also have varied difficulty, meaning they don't just increase in difficulty as the episode goes on. And since this is a Point-and-Click Adventure, that of course means that getting stuck will probably lead to the age old method of trying everything with everything. However, you can turn hints on if you have too much trouble, or if you want to hear additional funny dialogue, whichever works.
The control is as simple as you would expect in a game like this, point to where you want to go, and click to move there. Hold the mouse to move faster, and while I know you can run, I'm not entirely sure how to get it to work, I think you double-click, but it doesn't always work. Moving to where you want to go can be a bit finicky though when you're on the grassy roundabout for a majority of the game's locations (Bubs' Concession Stand, The Stick, Strong Badia, The Cool Car, The Whale and the like). Your inventory is easy to find and navigate and talking to the other inhabitants of Free Country, USA is as simple as clicking on them and choosing an image from a little chat bubble for your response. Saving your game is easy and in general the game is very streamlined to make playing it simpler and removing a lot of needless menu navigation.
In terms of the graphics, voice acting and sound, they're all pretty darn good. The character models look like the characters' 2D flash puppets were just taken and rendered into 3D. All of the locations that Homestar Runner fans recognize are here and accounted for, and there are even other references like the Geddup Noise, that painting of a demon holding a torch (why is he holding that torch?), and there's even a minigame in one episode where you can make a Teen Girl Squad comic. The voices are done by The Brothers Chaps and Missy themselves, and they deliver the characters just as they would in the cartoons. And the music is perfectly like the cartoons, and some are just taken directly from them (One for example is specifically taken from "Strong Bad is in Jail Cartoon"). Essentially, they feel like you're playing an hour or so long Homestar Runner cartoon, and it's a joy from beginning to end.
Overall, a fantastic buy for Point-and-Click enthusiasts, especially those who are fans of Homestar Runner, but you might be able to enjoy it just fine even if you aren't a fan.
