CLIFFS: Contender for worst/laziest PC port of all time, still one of the deepest, most involving games of all time.
For those who have never played the KOTOR duology, you need to know that you are absolutely missing out on some of the best moments in gaming.  These are the games that paved the way for the Mass Effect series and the "play as a good or bad person" mechanic seen in many games since.  You don't even have to be a big Star Wars fan to really enjoy them.  If you're like me, though, you will be one by the time you are finished.
Gameplay mechanics are similar to Mass Effect.  You and up to two other characters on your team at the same time. Run into some enemies, and the default setting is for the game to auto-pause while you issue your commands. Unpause and the battle commences.  The battle mechanics has a ton of stuff going on in the background that you don't even see.  This is good if you have terrible reflexes or just want a nice, enjoyable game to play without getting all tensed up.  The game uses a "D&D" based system to calculate how battles will play out.  Stats, saving throws, etc.  The game does not really get into depth on how certain stats and attributes affects gameplay, but it isn't too hard to figure out the basics.
Character development is like a classical RPG and is really in depth.  This allows you to tailor each member on your team and there are a lot of different paths to take.  For melee characters, you can go unarmed, one handed single-handed weapons (duelist), dual wielding single handed weapons, or a single dual-handed weapon (like a staff).  And then there are the variety of light sabers: short (for off-hand dual wielding), regular, and the double-bladed badass. Despite the dated graphics, the light sabers still look great.  Next up is the ranged build with an equal amount of variety.  Blaster pistols, blaster rifles, bowcasters (Wookiee weapon), and heavy blasters. Many of the weapons can be modified with various upgrades that you can tailor to your liking. For example, strong vs droids, can destroy shields, light vs dark powers, fire, ice, sonic, ion, and electrical damage, etc.  Same thing with armor.
At every level, your characters are awarded skill points to put towards various skills. The number of points varies upon the character's intelligence and class. Skills are Computers (slicing/hacking), Security (bypassing locks), Persuasion (can alter certain conversations), Repair (fixing things, "healing" droids), Demolition (disarming mines, effectiveness of grenades), Healing, and a few others.  In addition to skills, there are techniques to unlock.  It varies by class, but you will often get one point for every 2nd/3rd level to put towards techniques.  This is where you can tailor your character for a certain fighting style.  Adding points to dual wielding, for instance, can reduce the penalty recieved from using two weapons.  There are a ton of these things to unlock, giving you the oportunity to grow each character exactly as you want.
For the characters who can use The Force, you get one (sometimes two) points per level to unlock/upgrade Force Powers.  This is the fun stuff and there are a ton of different ones to choose from.
The absolute best part about this game is the depth of the story and how well-thought out the Star Wars universe is. There is so much to learn about the different planets, species, and factions in the Star Wars world and it can totally suck you in and make you want to watch the movies again (axcept for the one with JarJar; ♥♥♥♥ him!).  The story is very deep and has many interesting twists and turns.  If you have a short attention span and usually skip dialogue, you will not get the full experience from this game.  There is an incredible amount of dialogue here.  As you are walking around, you will have many opportunities to speak with others and even your own teammates.  You can guide the conversations by choosing your responses and this leads to one of the most interesting mechanics in the game.  Be a good guy (Light Side) or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (Dark Side) and the game reacts to that.  This also affects your character development.  Some of the Force Powers are Light or Dark side.  You can still use any powers you want, but a fully Light Side character trying to use the Wound/Choke/Kill Force Power will require a lot more Force Points (like MP).  Force Points regenerate over time, but youcan easily run out in a battle. Dialogue is a huge part of this game and thankfully, the voice acting is terrific.  I have no idea how they managed to record so much and still fit it on the original disc. For every line of dialogue you hear, there are often one or more lines you don't hear because of the way you selected your response.  It's brilliant.  The "non-English" languages sound just as good as they did in the movies.  Ditto the light saber and blaster sound effects.  The music is also really good.
And now for the RANTS: Let me get this out of the way first. This is, without a doubt, the WORST and LAZIEST console-to-PC port I have ever seen! So much disappointment, and the frustration is compounded because the game itself is so deserving of a good port. It is so good, in fact, that if they gave it a modern refresh and re-released it, I would totally pay full price for it. How bad is it? How about this: This game, which was designed for consoles, HAS NO CONTROLLER SUPPORT! Instead, we are left with some mediocre keyboard and mouse controls. It's not that they are bad, but if you are in the mood to recline on your couch and play with a controller, you're out of luck.  Oh, and the resolution? Hope you're still using a laptop from 10 years ago. You can download a program and edit an .ini file to give you 1080p, but it should be able to be selected in configs. More bad stuff: the character AI and path detection is, for lack of a better word, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Since combat is automated, characters wil run around on their own.  More often than not, two or more characters will try to occupy the same space at the same time.  They usually end up stuck on each other or will just do-si-do around like they're dancing. This isn't Riverdance, morons! Go hit that enemy with yor light saber! Queueing up commands can be frustrating, too. You meet an enemy and the game auto-pauses.  You input your commands, then unpause.  More often than not, the characters will perform one default action first before doing the commands you ordered.  Huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you issued your commands to buff the party up before going to go head to head with a Rancor, but your idiot teammates decide to run up to it, hit it once, then carry out your commands. Great, not only are you getting your stool pushed in, but the characters are out of buff range and don't share the effects you want. Oh, and often upon finishing a battle, the active character would not respond to inputs.  I would have to either switch to another character or quick save/quick load.  I was nearly finished with the game before I figured out that enabling V-sync can fix that bug.
Lastly, the fact that their are no Steam Achievements or Trading cars is like one final flick to the nuts while wearing tight jeans.  I know Space Channel 5 was recently updated to fix it's many shortcomings of being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC port, and they even added Achievements.  Hopefully someone will give this game what it deserves in a much-needed update and fix the mistakes.  It's just unforgiveable.
I know the list of negatives is huge, but it absolutely should not deter you from playing this game.  You really are missing out. KOTOR 1 & 2 are two of the best games ever made and still stand up today.

If you're looking for another 4x strategy game but don't want another Civ game, I'd recommend checking this out. The playable factions are actually different enough to notice in this game, and the interesting military unit system brings a higher level of personal control over your armies
Starting off, the playable factions are amazingly unique from one another. One faction disregards food as a resource, instead using gold. One can only ever found a single city, and must rely on the small, AI controlled minor factions to expand their influence. Another has nomadic cities that can be picked up and placed elsewhere. The variety is incredibly refreshing, and the difference adds a lot of immediate replayability
The military upgrade system is quite different from Civilization. Rather than researching new units every few technologies, you instead research a few base models (4 per faction, one being a Settler and the rest being some combination of Melee, Ranged, Cavalry, Support, Flying, or Naval). You can then use strategic resources to develop more powerful equipment for these units and personally craft your forces. This can make early combat a bit of an uphill battle, but once you have all the technologies to start creating the new equipment, it really takes off. The feeling of having this much personal customization is great

Visually, this game is simply fantastic! The cutscenes are the best part of it, with (for a video game) very realistic acting and facial expressions in addition to excellent directing, and the gameplay environments are detailed and feel authentic (down to subversive graffiti on walls in Rome's inner city).
The dramatic revenge story is written well (not exceptionally deep, but with a consistent arc) and includes mythical twists and a spectacular ending. I will keep it in good memory, even though the campaign took less than 10 hours to complete.
The reason why I was glad it did not take longer was the combat. It is not bad, not at all: It has its own, brutal character that sticks with you. The developers made hard efforts to let you experience ancient Roman warfare, with sword and shield as your main weapons and occasional use of throwing spears (pilae), light artillery (scorpio) as well as battle formations of legionnaires under your command - those parts are well implemented and even innovative. Nevertheless, the swordplay that makes the major part of the game gets tedious after a while. Especially enemies who can block and dodge take a long time to kill, and as there are only a dozen different types of opponents who always look identical, combat gets repetitive and feels like hard work at some point. Also, you cannot customize your character in any way, your tactics remain the same all the time except (ultimately inconsequential) variations of finishing moves, and the equipment only changes cosmetically (there is no looting or trading of weapons or armour). That's why in the final chapter of the story, I did long for it to end.
As each part of the campaign is a strictly limited corridor, and there are no meaningful decisions to make storywise, I cannot see myself replay the game. As I said, the melee combat did not fascinate me either, so I did not feel like trying the gladiator fights (i.e. the multiplayer mode).
The good parts and the high overall production value made the game worth my time nevertheless. As I got it on sale, I am satisfied with one exciting playthrough and give this game a 7/10. However, I would not recommend buying it for the full price, due to its shortness.

The game is fun, the music is fantastic, and the characters are memorable. You get a remixed version of your character's theme if you get a killing spree, and those really make you feel like a badass.
The artstyle is great too, nothing really looks bad, and everything definitely looks like it belongs in the same universe.
There's a good variety of maps, which helps keep the game fresh.
The only issue this game has is it's relatively small playerbase, which can result in matchmaking being a tad unfair sometimes: one team might stomp another quite easily. However, with Awesomenauts becoming F2P, that will very likely improve. Also, matchmaking is surprisingly short despite the small playerbase.
One thing I haven't seen other people bring up is the benefits of being a 3v3 game, compared to something like League of Legends or DotA. With this game being 3v3, there is a far lower chance of there being angry people shouting insults at you. There are only 5 other people who could be flamers, whereas 5v5 games have 9. I've noticed that I am far less likely to get yelled at if I do poorly in this game.
Another benefit is that if you want to not queue up with random people, it's far easier to assemble a full team out of your friends. After all, you only need two friends to get a full team: whereas in a 5v5 game, you would need four friends willing to play with you.

Is Kaizen a blatant rip-off of HAL 9000?
Yes, it is.
Does that mean Event[0] doesn't feature the most innovative game interaction I've ever had?
No, it doesn't.
The story is derivative. The graphics are alright. There's nothing new or innovative about the sound.
But none of that matters. This game is worth every penny for the mere experience of its unique gameplay.

Event[0] is one of those games who don't look that spectacular from the screenshots, but once playing them, it becomes much more clear how awesome this game is. It look very good, plays almost lag-free on mid-end hardware, and the most important aspect of it all, it got a very great story.
The biggest key element of Event[0] is the Kaizen AI, which are some terminal computers standing around, which you can actually talk to - and to be honest, that works very fluid and good, did not expect that in first place.
You talk to the computers anytime, ask them to open doors, get some tips for continuing the story, or ask them some random stuff (which actually works too!).
Still I felt lost at some spots since I couldn't figure out how to progress, so I needed to google sometimes, but I doubt that that was terrible game design but rather me not paying attention to some details.
All in all, I love the story, I love the mechanics, I love the soundtrack, this game is one of those indie games which I directly recommend to everyone who is even remotely thinking of playing a new story based game.

Primordia is a point-and-click adventure game developed by Wormwood Studios and made available on Steam through the Greenlight system.  It features a fully voice-acted cast with a retro graphical art style that pays homage to the classical age of gaming.
The story of Primordia takes place in a post-apocalyptic future where machines have taken over the world after the human race fought itself into extinction.  You follow the adventures of a self-aware android named Horatio Nullbuilt and his companion Crispin Horatiobuilt both residing inside a crashed ship called 'The UNNIIC'.  When a mysterious and powerful robot steals their power source, both Horatio and Crispin embark on a quest to seek out a new power source which eventually leads them to the mechanical city of Metropol.
+ Good Retro Art Style
+ Great character writing and developments
+ Good story with an interesting back-story
+ Atmospheric environment and world design
+ Consequence-based choices that can affect the final outcome of the story
+ Fully voice-acted characters
+ Healthy game time of at least 6-8 hours depending on how quickly the player solves the puzzles
+ Steam cloud support
- No 'HD' or Widescreen Support, in which the game opts instead for a pitiful 320x200 resolution which, frankly speaking, makes my eyes hurt.
- The game has a fetish for the color brown
- Puzzles are sometimes irritatingly difficult
- Does not expand much on the back-story which, in my opinion, is far more interesting than the main story
- The game's humor is a hit and miss
I Green-lit this game when it showed up in my Queue because I was very interested in its concept, setting, and back-story, and once it was released I purchased it and found a fun and absorbing point-and-click game with homage to the classical style of the genre.
Overall, Primordia is a great point-and-click adventure game that provides at least 6-8 hours’ worth of game time. In addition, for only $10 (or your regional equivalent), it is definitely worth a look especially if you're a fan of the genre.

A charming journey into the never-ending-dungeon genre, with a heavy emphasis on dual stick synchronization. If you begin to worry that your character might be getting a little too overpowered, the game will quickly remind you that the game script giveth, and the game script taketh away.
Currently shelved under "COMPLETE".

Twin-stick shooters often lack RPG development, and dungeon crawlers often lack interesting combat mechanics. The two seem to make an adorable couple, and do entertain initially. There are about a dozen or so types of bad guys to attack, each having their own mechanics, a handful of heroes to choose from with somewhat different characteristics. Items and leveling give a simple but surprisingly effective RPG depth if you aren't looking for any story element other than "explore dungeon and kill". There are secret areas containing extra loot and a quest giver who also delivers upon completion of killing a certain number of a type of villain in a time period.
The twin-stick shooter within the corridors of a dungeon is a bit unusual at first, and I would prefer some more traditionally twin-stick open areas. The typical level's hardest moment is at the beginning of the level where you spawn within reasonable distance of a flurry of baddies. Once you get a handle on that initial attack, the level geometry usually means there isn't much issue after that and clearing the level is easy. This ease only increases as you stock up on the games small number of items, and reach higher levels. Eventually, you faceroll everything.
The game is enjoyable as it is, but I'd like to see more variety in terms of the levels themselves, as well as boss battles, which are conspicuously absent. There is no satisfying ending as you push through levels that eventually become easier and easier.
Despite the scaling issue with dungeon and player level, and the lack of variety of levels/monsters, the game is enjoyable and well made. These limitations do reduce replay value, however, and perhaps expectations as to hours spend in this game should be kept low. For the low price of the title, the length of gameplay is reasonable.

You start with a simple small ship but you can unlock both more systems to build with and larger ships via combat and resource gathering and can unlock the other factions via battle so you can try their unique playstyles in future games. The best part of the game's factions is that while they all have some similiarities, they are quite diverse and not simply reskins of each other.  Playing the starting Terran faction is quite different from the Reds which are different from the Sentinels and so on.
You eventually get to build ships from your ship and can keep them with you or release them and they'll defend areas as your control expands. Your AI allies will even build copies of your ship and you can use the interface to affect their production queues.
You also have a lot of control options and can even set how your weapons are keyed so you can fire every weapon via the LMB or put even big cumbersome weapons on point defense duty if you like. There's a lot to love here.
Heartfelt recommendation from me.

TL;DR: Amazing unscripted top-down space combat/expansion indie game with great community and plethora of quality mods to add content to game. If you liked SPAZ or Starsector, you’ll LOVE this game!
For a game made by one guy, heck, even compared to other indie games with teams of developers, Reassembly ranks up with there with my favorites. Reassembly can be compared to Space Pirates and Zombies and Starsector, 2 other top-down space exploration/combat games; however, Reassembly has them both beat in customizability, unscripted expansion/development of the player faction, and ambience. The gameplay is easy to get into and gets as complex as your creativity can make it, yet still retains simplicity which makes it easy and fun to sit there creating a large complex spaceship tailored to your desires. As you expand and grow your faction, your AI will begin building ships you design for them and in order to expand more you could employ many ways to take over sectors of the galaxy. From bringing a fleet of ships to having a carrier with masses of drones or even piloting a singular dreadnought to carve through enemy territory, or even coming up with your own tactics as you can create any kind of ship you want block by block (even copy pasting big chunks of ships to create modular designs) the designs are limitless!
As for quantity of content, the base factions are interesting but when they get bland the developer made Reassembly open source allowing anyone to easily create their own factions or even universe altering mods and upload them for anyone to download and play from the Steam Workshop. The community, while small, is one of the nicest and most dedicated I’ve seen, and you’ll definitely never run out of quality new factions to download and try out or play against. This includes mods that change the entire galaxy to a star wars themed galactic war to mods that create a 2 faction war between humans and zombies in space, to... well just check the Workshop and you’ll see all the amazing stuff going on!
P.S. Nominated this game for the "Just 5 more minutes" Steam award because I've definately played this instead of slept despite having class in the mornings.

Let me just start this review by giving you the following context: I very rarely play point-and-clicks. The most notable ones (namely, those by LucasArts) were before my time, so my only games in this genre I’ve played are the new Sam and Max games and this one.
This genre greatly focuses on its writing and story, and I feel Primorida does well in that regard. What starts as a simple story of tracking a robot who stole your stuff turns into a one with many hints about the world and why it’s in the state it is, and Horatio’s role in it. Each character, from the straight-laced and practical main character Horatio, to his perpetually floating, snarky sidekick Crispin, and everyone else you interact with is written with enough skill to give them unique personalities without falling into two-dimensional archetypes. While many NPCs fall into some stereotypes of their characters (ex: a soldier robot speaks how you’d expect him to, likewise with a robot with a monocle), they get moments where they flesh out their character and have some very clever lines.
The overall plot kept me guessing all the way to the end, but stayed mostly clear about what was going on the whole way through. The story is straightforward in that regard, although the littering of hints of the details behind the game world really helped the story shine when it revealed big plot elements.
However, I NEED to talk about the gameplay. It’s your typical adventure game fare of solving puzzles by figuring out how items interact with each other, listening to context clues, etc. The game doesn’t go too crazy with the solutions.
That being said, I will be honest and say I had to use a walkthrough for this game. This is most likely due to my inexperience with the genre, but many times I felt clueless on what to do. Furthermore, when I looked up the solution, I felt like the game gave me little to no inclination that what I was supposed to do may be the answer.
PUZZLE SPOILERS
One of the most “how was I supposed to do that” moments was when I needed to figure out how to remove rust from gears so I could open a door. I hadn’t met anyone who was a cleaning robot or the like, and I had no items on me that implied they could clean. It turns out that in one segment, there are underwater “submersible” robots who, when I dunked the gears underwater where they were, cleaned the gears. When I clicked on them normally, the main character said NOTHING about their potential cleaning ability.
Another annoying one was a moment of “I didn’t know I could do that”. I had to inspect a door in order to solve a puzzle, but left-clicking it gave me a quote that didn’t help me. However, right-clicking it gave me a different one relevant to the puzzle. I know that could right-click on items to hear a description of them in my inventory, but I didn’t know why I couldn’t just left-click this door to hear the contextually-important quote for this puzzle.
END PUZZLE SPOILERS
So overall, I’d say that you should not feel ashamed if you need a walkthrough for certain puzzles in this game. The second half of this game has quite a few rather obtuse ones, which is a shame since they can halt the progression of what is otherwise a really cool story.
My other problem is a technical one: this game has no resolution options! It can only either run in fullscreen (which I think is 1024x768!!!) or windowed which has a default size that is most suitable for ants. Thankfully you can turn the “scaling” up, which means increasing the size of the internal resolution (window size in windowed mode increases with this), but the lack of proper resolution options just strikes me as lazy to me.
Lastly, and this is sort of a nitpick, but this isn’t Logan Cunningham’s best work. He does a decent job not sounding bored in his lines and emoting properly when necessary, but either due to sound engineering, low quality audio files, or otherwise not as much strength in his voice work, he isn’t as memorable as he was in Bastion. I felt the sidekick Crispin out-did him in passionately delivering his lines. It doesn’t detract from the game at all really, I’m more just feeling like he could have done better.
SUMMARY:
I strongly suggest you guys pick up Primorida. It’s got an interesting plot inside a unique atmosphere of a post-human world, and the writing does those both justice. The puzzles can be result in premature baldness due to hair-pulling difficulty, but they didn’t stop me from enjoying the game.

There is actually two complete games here. One is Soda Drinker Pro, and the other is Vivian Clark so I'm going to split this review up a bit.
+ Certainly a unique and a bit surreal experience. You walk around and drink soda, but it's like the more you drink the stranger the game gets while some deranged man whispers in your ear about the greatness of soda.
+ The levels...are soooo weird... Some of the worst textures and graphics you may ever see, and it seems like all the walls or "backgrounds" are childish crayon drawings. Strangely enough, it's actually enjoyable as you only spend about 30seconds or so in each level, and it's quite interesting to see what comes next and to laugh at how bad the environments look.  Each level is also in a unique location, and can never guess where you will end up next.
+ Oddly addicting, I felt the need to keep going just to see what crazy land I'd end up in next. It has the "randomness" factor that depending on your taste may make this a very enjoyable laughable experience.
- Not much gameplay, you mainly just look around to admire the outlandish and pretty poorly designed levels
- It gets very repetitive after a while as you are mainly just waiting for a meter to drop to get to the next level, and after ~10seconds of looking around, you again just wait for the soda meter to drain.
- It's more of an experience and less of a game, I would not recommend this unless you know what you are getting yourself into.
+ I did not expect to find a complete game within Soda Drinker Pro
+ The gameplay in this is actually extremely enjoyable. Very wacky platforming / shooting levels, where the game mechanics and characters constantly change between each level. Similar in appeal to games like Wario Ware.
+ Colorful surreal levels that don't really make any sense but are all so interesting and there's a ton of them
+ Hilarious characters to play as and enemies
+ Surprising amount of thought went into it. Some stages I was like "I'm going to jump off the map and break the game" but surprisingly there are actually events and odd things to find seemingly all over.
+ Such a creative and unique game and experience, it's random but in a good way.
+ Great soundtrack
- Somewhat confusing at what or where you are supposed to go. Some stages you will instantly die not knowing what just happened.
Overall I would say Vivian Clark is the better game, but both games are great and very unique experiences.

What a ridiculous game. That pretty much summarizes the reaction I had when I first saw Soda Drinker Pro in action. The game really just serves as a front for the real game, Vivian Clark. I found this to be a strange design decision, but given the absurd nature of this game, I guess it fits well.
Soda Drinker Pro is a joke, through and through. There really isn't anything redeeming about it in terms of gameplay, but I was impressed by the fact that seemingly every level has a line recorded about that level when it starts up. That alone probably took a few hours to record.
Vivian Clark, on the other hand, is an artsy little game that reminds me of Wario Ware. You go back and forth between goofy minigames that are as fun as they are outrageous. These minigames connect to other ones, usually by bumping into an object or even by failing in a certain way, which creates a maze for the player to navigate through. Vivian Clark is very much a maze of minigames that tests your memory as you try to figure out how to get back to game X to continue exploring new ones you haven't discovered yet.
So do I recommend this game? Yeah, I think so. It's a fun little game to show off to friends or stream. I'd wait for a sale to pick it up though, because I think the entertainment it offers is pretty limited.

I only found out about this game in the past week or so, and so after a bit of rummaging around, i gave it a go. Best idea i've had for a while now.
This game is a very short, very sweet little homage to games such as Final Fantasy and Zelda, and it does a capital job. The game starts with you only allowed to go right in a 2d line with no music, no sound, no anything. But through getting various things in chests (the left key, sound effects, a storyline, etc) you see in front of you, how the RPG and Adventure genres have evolved over the years, hence the name. It's got it all- your hero-looking person, turn-based battling, life gauges, random encounters (lord help) and loads of pointless collectible stars. Eventually, you even get a bit of a Diablo segment, except it pokes fun at huge aspects of it- an inventory's worth of gear that all does squat, (e.g 'Turns you into a dragon. 12 months cooldown.') to the lag-inducing masses of enemies, all of which apart from the wizards are decimated by mere button-mashing.
This game also has an outstanding soundtrack. It is just beautiful. From the catchy tune of the battle theme, to the emotional tune of when
to the final boss theme, which is one of the most incredible fight themes i have heard to date.
I have one major problem with this game, though, and it's that the game is really short. I've played the game once through and it took about two hours. Still, the sequel may have a longer playtime and much more fleshed-out story, but it still is one of the most charming indies i've played. In this case, size isn't everything.

I love this game, but it has some flaws
Pros
-Kaizen Interaction
The best part of this game, hands down, is interacting with Kaizen. Your interactive buddy or digital adversary is the main gameplay mechanic. I for one love Kaizen, but he can be a little tempermental. This is the reason for this game to exist.
-Music
This game's music is one song, but it's a good song. Look up "Hey Judy" on youtube if you want to hear it. I like it lots.
-Atmosphere
The retro-futurism reminds me of Alien, and the clicky terminals remind me of actually using commandline systems. The silence coupled with the noise makes a tense environment. Hearing your breath during EVA (spacewalk) works just as well here as it worked underwater in Subnautica.
Cons
-Length
This game is two hours long. I've played through it four and a half times, so there is replay value, but unless you love the crew of Nautilus (Kaizen included) or really like ♥♥♥♥ing with chatbots, you will be disappointed by length.
-Opening
After complaining about short length, now I'll complain about the intro being to long. It is unskippable, and it is preventing me from doing a fifth playthrough. It is maybe 15 minutes long, which is CRAZY considering the length. Let us skip this please.
Conclusion
If this game is on sale (I got it for $10 IIRC), buy it. It's great for sci-fi fans, its great for sociable people. Kaizen is my new favorite virtual buddy.

Event[0] is one of those borderline games.  It seems more of a proof of concept than a full fledged game, and that's kind of cool.  The problem is the game and content is really only about 2 and a half hours long.
The core of the game, and really the reason you SHOULD play is the AI.  Kaizen is his name and he's almost brilliant thing to play with.  He'll answer questions and even avoid answering questions at times, I absolutely love it.  It's just so much fun to toy with.
But at the same time I feel that the AI is just a shade dumber than he should be.  He's great but he's not perfect.  There was a point where I said "what happened" as something happened and he told me about another thing, then I asked him again, and he answer my question correctly.  He will answer the same question differently when asked twice in a row.  But overall he's a pretty smart and savvy AI.
I enjoyed playing with him, he's interesting, but he's not a true AI, and while that's ok, he has shortcomings that are awkward.
Yet it is fun and I know I seem to be talking a lot about him, but really in this game, there's really only one puzzle, there's a decent story, but everything is done through Kaizen and terminals.  You will type requests and commands to him and he'll do things for you.  It's a very unique and special game in that aspect because it's all done through the AI, but that's pretty much it.  It's a one trick pony, but I really enjoyed the trick.
As for the rest of the game, there is actually a good story here as you try to piece together what happened, but because everything is through Kaizen (and logs) there's limits to what you can and can't do, and playing with Kaizen is what will extend your time.  The bad news is that once you're done, the story is pretty much there, and the ending is interesting, but I don't know if I can truly say it's fulfilling.  I don't know for sure if I made the right choice, and while I'll replay it, I think it's an open ended ending, so people who really demand closure, may not get it here.
The other side of that is the entire game only took me two hours.  While I could say I'm a genius and know everything, the fact is I didn't rush this game and really explored, and 2 hours later the game is over.  Replays are said to take under an hour to do everything, and I'd buy that, now that I know everything I do, I could probably speed run the game.  So anyone looking for a ton of content isn't going to find it here.
So do I recommend this game.  God, that's a question... it's 20 bucks on steam, at that price no question, no.  At 2 hours of gameplay it's completely on the wrong end of that price point.  Even at 10 bucks I find it hard to recommend, but at the same time I adore the game, and I did get it in a humble bundle.  Keep an eye on this one and hope it drops in price, but I'll give it a recommendation on the strength of the game itself, but not on the price it is today.

Event Zero is about finding life depends on an AI with a complete a set of emotional bagage and problems. Hey who wouldn't have issues after 30 years of living in solitude. Kaizen - our AI - is trying real hard to be nice, but like with everything in life it doesn't always work out.
The game is a mix of exploring your environment, trying to figure out why that spacecraft has been lost in space for ages alongside what happened to the crew, and having a dialogue with Kaizen, to see if it will open more rooms or share some information with you.
The dialogue with the AI interface is entirely free. No multiple choice questions; you're going to have to type your way through.
At its best moments, Event Zero will completely amaze you at how uncannily accurate the AI response is to your speech... and at its worst moment it will feel like you're having one of these "conversations" with Evie Bot. Most of the time will be just about in between, not convincing enough to make believe the magic of AI has happened, but clever enough so that you'll go "ahah I see what they did there".
All in all the game is interesting enough as a concept to be worth a play, and interracting with Kaizen is generally pleasant.
...just make sure you never forget to say please or hurt its feelings.

This is not quite a 'game' but a machine learning life simulator with a myriad of tweak-able parameters.
I started with a 400x400.
After a few days of evolution I changed from rock walls into lava.
I halved the weight and energy requirements of neurons.
They evolved to avoid the deadly lava after 2 hours.
I segmented the 'world' into 4 quadrants separated by lava.
This considerably changed the food distribution and replenishment dynamic.
One of the quads went entirely extinct causing the food to pool and resulted in less for the other three quads.
They adapted.
I seeded the extinct, but food rich, quadrant with a select few from each of the other 'living' quads.
All four continued to thrive, one using pheromones, one fighting and stealing energy, one reproducing rapidly and feeding primarily on carcasses and one evolving many eyes to efficiently find food.
I removed the lava dividing the areas to combine all quadrants only leaving the outer lava walls.
So here we are. They are currently mixing and fighting for resources.
I wonder if one species will become dominant or will they all co-exist.

When I saw this game come out, I though “Man, that’s a cool concept, I should buy this when it’s on a sale”. However, I never did. I dunno why, but I just forgot about this game. Now, I can play it thanks to the glory of Family Sharing and… Well, I’m f#cking disappointed. The game has one of the best concepts for a game I've seen in years and then just decides to turn those ideas to a human form and shoot it on the head with a sawed off shotgun at point blank range.
The biggest problem this game has is the parody it tries to be. It starts okay, being an affectionate parody to the original Legend of Zelda games, but soon enough it starts to deviate from the cool concept of recreating history and stays making a rather fanboy-looking parody of just two games: Zelda and Final Fantasy VII. The game calls itself for going through videogame history, so WHY THE HELL IT SPENDS SO MUCH TIME JUST MAKING PARODIES OF THE SAME TWO GAMES OVER AND OVER!? Not only it makes no sense, but if you don’t love EITHER of those two games, you’ll get extremely tired of the game, really fast. And while I like the 2D Zelda games, I do NOT like FFVII, I find it to be popular because, for most people, it was their first RPG, it’s characters are mostly lackluster, two dimensional, and quite honestly lame as hell. WELL GREAT, BECAUSE THE MAIN CHARACTER IS A PARODY OF CLOUD, THE SECOND MAIN CHARACTER IS A LITERAL COPY-PASTE OF AERITH AND IT EVEN HAS A CID IN BETWEEN. And if that wasn't enough, the villain is - YOU GOT IT, AN EDGIER SEPHIROTH, the only difference being that it's design takes from - YOU GOT IT AGAIN, LEGEND OF ZELDA, by looking like Ganondorf and even
. Oh, and want to know the best part of it all?
I’m not joking here, the game is short, barely 2 hours long, but yet it spends most of its time trying to be a poor-taste Final Fantasy wannabe. I was happy as hell when the game suddenly changed and finally decided to parody something that wasn’t a Nintendo game or FFVII, and it turned out that it was just a dungeon inspired in Diablo, which had special controls just for it while the rest goes back to the same crap over and over. I have to say, for a game that's supposed to be about the history of games, neither it references many different games neither it stays at just games. It just feels out of place when the game suddenly throws multiple references of Lord of the Rings, and it's even INSULTING when the villain QUITE LITERALLY THROWS A KAMEHAMEHA FOR NO REASON DURING A FIGHT. And I don't mean a similar looking attack, no. He even said "Ka-me-ha-me-ha" and posed the same way. It's THAT lame.
Oh, and not only the parodies are boring and uninspired and the story lackluster and predictable, but it also has a few bugs. Textures stretching up to infinity and looking ugly, the game crashing when opening a chest (something you’ll be doing for half the game and that has happend to me twice on the two hours of game), that kind of stuff. You can also keep going when the Aerith-wannabe leaves to learn spells and go into the next dungeon, where you’re somehow able to play as her even though she’s NOT coming with you.
But does the game has good stuff however? Yeah. Somehow. Changing the genre of the game constantly is a good way to keep it both interesting and original, even though it doesn’t happen nearly as enough and
.
The idea of a game evolving is also a really cool concept, and it’s quite fun to go back and revisit previous areas, see how they look now that instead of SNES graphics we got PSX graphics. Sadly the devs kinda messed that up, as previous places stay with the graphics you saw them, meaning if you've unlocked beautiful 3D graphics, the first town will still have SNES graphics FOR NO REASON WHAT SO EVER.
The soundtrack should also be commended, as it manages to capture the feeling of the eras it tries to represent, and some of the themes are catchy enough.
Is the game worth it? That’s a tough question that ultimately boils down to it’s price. 10€ is nowhere a good price for this 2 hours travesty, it’s a repetitive experience that probably only fans of either Zelda, FFVII or both will like, as the game CONSTANTLY makes fun of both. I didn’t have to pay anything thanks to Family Sharing, and I still feel disappointed by this, it’s an extremely good concept gone to hell and back, and I bet that it’s all because the writer (or writers) left their inner fanboy run rampant. I mean come on, there were other RPG games other than f#cking FFVII that made an impact! What about Earthbound, for example? NO, LET’S INSTEAD MAKE REFERENCES TO SKYRIM AND IT’S F#CKING ARROW IN THE KNEE.
Don't buy this. Don't look at it. Don't even think about it. Unless you can get it for a single € or you get it as a gift, I don't see why you should even purchase and play this. This has some of the WORST writing I've seen on my entire life playing games, and that's quite an achievement.
TL;DR Edition: A 10€-worth nerdgasm about Zelda and Final Fantasy VII, the games that the writer/s liked the most. If you don’t hold both of them as the pinnacle of human creation, you might wanna look away from this. Maybe the sequel is better, but I don’t care to this point.

Quite an interesting approach on the visualisation of evolution of the virtual RPG standarts over time.
When I just heard about this project, I thought "wow, cool, must've been smth worth to look at!". Then I bought it - probably at some sell event or in the bundle, as I'm sure I was not buying it the moment it got out of Greenlight. And then... I haven't touched it until now. Two years passed by, the game achieved positive background and its devs even released Evoland 2, which is basically just one more try to do the same trick - but better... So yeah, now there are some reviews which points to the Evoland 2 immidiately, like the first one Evoland is obsolete now. Is it? Nope.
I have to say, one of the things that kept me away from Evoland was the fear that the devs will mess something on my "so precious" gaming experience over all those years. It's the same thing as touching the HD remakes of Heroes of Might and Magic 3 or Baldur's Gate - which I haven't done yet - just to not mess the memoires of good old times with another portion of disorder every reinstallation usually creates.
Happily, I have to state, that's not an issue of Evoland.
While it ceratinly does just as promises - showing you the evolution of trends and game mechanics in some part of virtual role-playing - it does not insists that it was Strictly That Way. You know, as it usually goes with history lessons - like when Soviets poses like it was them who beats all the Nazies - and forgetting totally about Lendlease. Or like Americans poses it was them who finished Hitler and all around - oh yeah, and with K/D ratio of 10, above all... Sorry, I'm slipping away.
So, have I enjoyed the game? Certainly. Could I recommend it to buy? Only if you're already used to play wanna be jRPG projects (like RPG Maker stuff), as Evoland generally follows the "evolution" on the eastern tread: Legend of Zelda mixes with early Final Fantasy tunes, whereas the promised reminiscence to the Diablo feels... just slightly common. Anyway, as of "evolution" theme, Evoland concentrates basically on the technological stuff - like adding more and more pixels on the screen and more tones to the sound, while the story and other most basical RPG elements remains on the level of the games in early 90's.
So! As of overall, speaking of "cultural value" of Evoland, I can say it's a good tribute, which is worth your attention, if you've been long on the gaming stage. However, if you're expecting a very good RPG experience from Evoland itself, I'm sorry, I can't see, how this can be done in project like this, with all that mixture of styles, game mechanics and other stuff! Were that game any longer, I must add, it could have been even worse than it is now. Because tribute - is always just a tribute. If you want authentic taste - you obviously need to play all those classics like Diablo or Zelda by yourself.
My mark for Evoland is 7.5/10. Nice project, and easy gold on achevements. Worth its price.
Don't play it, play Evoland 2 instead. 1 out of 5 stars.

This is a game that was on my wishlist for a while. My primary interest was the visual style, which reminded me somewhat of Machinarium, a lovely adventure puzzler I played a few years back. Primordia is more a traditional adventure game however and I wasn't prepared for how fully it sucked me in once I began playing.
It all begins with a robot named Horatio ... Horatio Nullbuilt v. 5 to be precise. Horatio has a problem, the power core to his fixer-upper airship the UNNIIC has just been stolen by a badass bruiser bot and without it, he and his floating companion Crispin will die a slow death out in the dunes, unable to recharge their batteries or get anywhere that they can do so in time. Thus begins this rather unassuming, but ultimately rather epic point-and-click adventure game.
My few problems with Primordia are the same I have with most retro-style adventure games, those being the combination of low res graphics and archaic systems making it difficult to know what is clickable and what is not. Playing "hunt the pixel" along with environments filled with "flavor" clickables, meant I missed a few crucial objects here and there, leading to a bit of frustration. Other than that however, the puzzles of Primordia are mostly logical, with only a few moments of "how was I supposed to know that?" or where a lack of full understanding of all that Horatio and Crispin together could do kept me confused.
The story and world building in Primordia more than make up for any shortcomings however. Set in a world populated only by robots, where "Man" is nothing more than a myth for all but a few devoted "Humanists", Primordia frames the typical post-apocalyptic dystopia in a fresh light. While at times predictable, the interactions between characters makes even a conclusion you've already jumped to a joy to behold. The dialog in Primordia oozes with personality, especially between the stoic Horatio and the sardonic Crispin. While oft-times broadly drawn, getting to know the denizens of the world of Primordia is half the fun, especially learning the quirks of their robotic society. There is plenty of lore to uncover as well throughout the game, fleshing out the periphery of the world and ultimately contributing to the main story in interesting ways.
By the time all is said and done, you'll have explored a rich world in Primordia, made choices that actually matter, and experienced one of several endings, some of which are locked by key decisions earlier in the game. On sale or not, I cannot recommend Primordia enough to adventure game fans.

At this point you probably know that this game is famous for a great story, great characters, and innovative gameplay that revolutionized the RPG genre. So let me cut to the chase and answer the real question you're wondering: does this 11-year-old game still hold up?
Yes. Yes. God yes.
It may not be today-style graphics, but the graphics hang in there and there is some legitimately beautiful scenery. There's one spot on the final planet that seems built just for you to stand there and look at the vista, and I stop to admire it every time. You won't get hung up on the graphics.
The gameplay mechanics are fresh and sharp even to those only familiar with more modern RPGs like Mass Effect 3 or Skyrim. Gear customization is not *as* deep as some RPG games, but it's deep enough. Voice acting is top-tier featuring some real luminaries like Jennifer Hale (also known for Mass Effect's female Shepard and a thousand more), Kevin Michael Richardson (akf The Batman's Joker and Lilo & Stitch's Gantu), Raphael Sbarge (akf Mass Effect's Kaidan Alenko), and many more.
On a more personal note, I played this game six or seven times before Steam was even a thing. And then recently I figured, what the heck, I'll get a Steam copy. I told myself, surely this won't be as great as you remembered. You've played a ton of more modern games since those days, it'll feel outdated. You already know the story, it'll feel tired.
Nope. Eighth time through the game, better than ever.
Thank you KOTOR. My pick for the best game of all time.

I am still looking into Gridworld, so take this review as a "first impression" review from a simulation-fan. I've always been fascinated by both evolution simulations and neural network simulations, so "Gridworld" was a must-have for me. Still, there are a few issues which I find highly annoying and hope that will be improved in updates in future. I've given the project as a whole a "thumbs up", though, because I strongly hope things will be improved... Some of the points:
1) Give us more details! Maybe I have been blind and am just missing the obvious, but watching blinking colours is MUCH more fun, if you have a clue what its meaning is! Okay, most often it just differntiates differnt "creatures" or "neurons", but it would be good to have that verified... Even more important: There HAS to be some manual explaining what the various neurons "do" in the world, or it is just boring to see them evolve.
2) I know that a simulation is not about "looking nice", but the UI in Gridworld is "lacking" at least. I think one can live with the very primitive optics, but what is unacceptable is the lack of "responsiveness" of certain elements. First, I thought it is simply the "workload" making it slow, but when you stop the simulation, the UI becomes fully un-responsive! That is horrible beyond measure...
3) In a "simulation game", where observing is more or less all you do, the program has to offer as many "observing" features as possible. I'm missing a punch! I can "export" facts, but where can i see them plottet as graphs? I would like to do record "time-lapses" of my creatures evolvement to play as a simple "movie". I would like to have a "Analysis-Screen" for the neurons when I have a creature under the "microsocope", i.e. see how it's neural network "looks" and "behaves"....
4) Autosave simulation. I've run a 14hrs simulation and it just "disappeared". (Gridwork stopped working and vanished at one point.) Have at least a "timed" auto-save to be able to recover!
5) Randomness: The whole simulation is based on random evolution. I think it would be mandatory to provided the means to "recreate" the same random-numbers, i.e. the seed for the random generator should be an accessible option. Thus you can "rerun" a simulation to the identical effect and check what a "modification" of some sort would do.
6) Optics: Not the most important, but it would be very, very nice if the "genes" and "networks" could be turned into some "creature-shape" to be visually inspected. Only in the microscope (to have short rendering times.)
Compared to some of the free simulators online, this sucks.

So first things first you will need 64bit Java to run this game well and without crashes.
Gridworld is a very interesting simulator of evolution. When I first began playing I knew little about the controls for changing terrain or food and was more or less at the mercy of natural selection with what came of my world.
For the first hour of eager scrutiny of my first world I saw nothing but failures of creatures. Organisms that could reproduce but lacked a mouth. Creatures that emitted poison but lacked the ability to survive contact with that poison. Animals that could eat but not move, etc, etc. Most of them died off quite rapidly. I saw the slightest glimmer of hope when I noticed a creature moving, eating, and reproducing but when it would reproduce, the parent would die and the offspring without much energy to begin with, would die very soon after if not directly next to some food. By and large these creatures all seemed doomed and world would become a lifeless hulk of uneaten food.
I walked away from the computer and left my game on. watched a television show, came back and saw not much had changed. Having left the TV on I left the room again to turn it off, sat down at my computer and stared at the screen.
That's when I noticed a small group of creatures moving and eating food in the top right of the world.
I immediately zoomed in to see these organisms:
1. Moving
2. Eating
3. Reproducing
4. Conserving enough energy to reproduce while keeping the parent alive.
I WAS ECSTATIC. I sat back and watch these creatures, which I have dubbed 'Monchers', take over my world in no time. They spread like wildfire in a world abundant with food and devoid of competition. Now I see my little Monchers evolving with generation after generation, creating better, different, and sometimes flat out worse versions of themselves. Even as I type this the Monchers of my world are much more efficient than the first colony in that top right corner.
With food more scarce and competition increasing between the Moncher species I noticed Monchers with poison emitters to kill of competition, ones with more speed to collect food faster, and ones with less fancy "Neurons" as the game calls them, which are basically body parts or overall traits of your creature. With less traits though the monchers use less energy, allowing them to survive longer without a meal and pass on the genetic code.
With organisms that don't die within minutes, neurons actually become interesting features of your little animals. You wonder where evolution will take them next and what might succeed or fail. What species will die out or dominate.
This game is an evolutionary petri dish of interesting results. Although actual interaction with the player is limited, it's more like a simulation than a game. An aquarium or jar of sea monkeys. But this is so much more than a jar of sea monkeys. It's like having a small world of your own. Species to watch and track. You'll see generations live and die. Creatures rise and fall. If you have the imagination to enjoy these small beings, and don't mind a back seat view of evolution, this is a very interesting game to leave up and watch from time to time.
You will not enjoy this game if you don't like the idea of:
VERY simple pixel graphics.
At times hours of gameplay without change.
Having to make your own stories and use your own imagination for maximum enjoyment. Often times the most world altering moments can happen quickly and without much fanfair. To someone without their mind enveloped in the game world this would appear quite anticlimactic.
This game requires a lot of patience and creativity.
If any of these reasons don't sound appealing to you I would recommend you NOT buy the game. Otherwise I would highly recommend it.

MGO3 is a major let down. It is almost nothing like MGO2 which was the best of them all. MGO3 has much smaller maps and is much more fast paced with less in mind for the CQC and stealh players (the true Metal Gear fans). They have gone for the main stream shoot em up type of game. This isn't call of duty, keep Metal Gear what it used to be. Here is a list of things MGO2 did better.
- Better room creation (Name, description, options, etc)
- Host migration
- Text chat
- Clan system
- Friendly fire
- Tag/Find friends in lobbies
- Block players
- Could mix and match several items/outfits
- Use nades while on a ladder
- Backstep, sideroll, side-strafe (FPV)
- Hold ups in TSNE
- Play dead
- Worm crawl
- Stealth camo made you invisible with the exception of your weapon/knife
- Could be completely invisible with stealth camo by saluting/playing dead/worm crawling
- Improved CQC (could choke out by laying enemy on ground in order to avoid detection/fire)
- Could pick up and move enemies once stunned which also dropped their weapons
- Fire Mode (burst/single/etc)
- Chaffs
- Set camo's per map
- More codecs and able to preset additional ones on an external keyboard
- RES/DM/SDM/SNE/CAP
- Knives
- Drum can / vomit
- Set marker "!" on map using the "enemy sighted" codec
- Animal rank based on performance
- Teammate can boost you up to higher platforms on maps
- Stunned enemies go to sleep longer & required several 'taps' to wake up (waking skill helped)
- Could tell when stunned enemy/teammate would wake up via stamina bar
- Able to use codecs while stunned - caused player to mumble in sleep hinting to teammates enemy was close (useful in TSNE)
- Could actually hide in a box and get away with it due to several boxes scattered around maps
The only reason I am still playing MGO3 is because of my hopes that it will one day regain some of what made it good. Thanks for shutting down the servers too. I would have gladly paid a monthly fee to keep those servers up.

A good game with great production and presentation. The narrative and setting keep you engaged and interested, and doesn't feel like the devs cut corners (as so common with a lot of other exploration type games).
As you explore the ship, you find notes, files, and clues that lead you to answers of what happened to the ships crew and passengers. You are supposed to communicate with the ships AI (Kaizen) to find those answers; but you soon realize that there's more to the story than Kaizen is leading on to.

The AI is interactive, and you ask it questions and give it commands. However, keep in mind that the game was developed by a very small team, so this feature is pretty limited. You'll soon start seeing a lot of repettitive responses when you say\ask something that isn't relative to the story (which is to be expected imo).
My only cons with the game is the relatively short story. I finished my first playthrough in just under 3.5 hrs; although I didn't take time to hunt achievements, or unlock the other two endings (three in all). Some players may not see the value in the game at full price, but if you like atmospheric exploration games then you will see the hard work put into the game; or just wait for a sale if you're still not convinced.
Despite it's short story, the game has plenty of atmosphere and depth to keep you moving forward to find answers.

So, I got around to finally playing this and I put it down for 3 months. I decided that I needed a review and here we ♥♥♥♥ing are. How is the game? Well, you already know by the fact that Steam tells you right away what my verdict is, but let's go through anyway and you can hear my 5 paragraphs of reasons why you should get this game. Sorry, you need to read anyway and this game will make you do it too.
Remember the Gameboy? No? Then sucks to be you, but if you do remember, then you'll have a nice trip down memory lane as you start off the game with a green shaded screen and sweet 8-bit graphics as the game starts granting you rights to move up and down and opening chests.Yes, this game literally has to grant you rights to do stuff. As you progress through the game, you unlock features via opening chests and some features overwrite other features like: they took my ♥♥♥♥ing Turn based battle system from me! You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... I don't like clunky active battle systems... They will take the normal way of opening chests and make it like how Link opens chests in Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past. This game even pays homage to Final Fantasy games for PS1 with rendered backgrounds, that's epically awesome. The game is linear however, the open world isn't open when you get into that and rather large open areas like in Final Fantasy 4 in the beginning of the game. I don't like linear in video games with the exception of the horror genre because being able to go anywhere in a horror game is like getting threatened to suffocate with a tight plastic bag over your head with holes poked in it. It just doesn't work.
The graphics are everything in this. From 8-bit to full fledged 3D. Its amazing how this game changes graphics on the fly. The game probably looks its best when imitating 16-bit graphics because I think that's as polished as 2D RPGs get when it comes to graphics. I really liked that look and I still miss it. The game won't let you choose the graphics you want and will just force you to stick with one since you need them in some situations to progress. There is a puzzle that lets you switch graphics back and forth because you're "traveling through time" to get through certain areas. It's neat some of the things they do with the graphics.
Sound is the same way. The music is very nostalgic to hear and definitely has inspiration from older games, again,  like Zelda games and Final Fantasy. I know I'm using those over and over as examples but its really the only way to describe it. They go from old to new sounding as usual. The music will evolve as you progress. Obviously, it being the name, "Evoland".
This game is a one trip journey and has no replayability. Moving on.
The game is extremely linear and it can be a fun trip down memory lane seeing how far RPGs and video games in general have come. Its a fun experience and if you can get it on sale, and you'll probably will, you cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, then I highly recommend it to RPG lovers new and old. The only problem is that the game lacks replayability and is only meant for one game play experience. I can't see it having multiple playthroughs. Just like the Tiger Electronic devices you get at cheap dollar stores, meant to be played once and never again, only Evoland isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥.

This game can be a lot of fun with friends. The character creation options are very impressive. You can spend a ton of time designing a perfect hero and as you progress in the game, costume unlocks will become available to you randomly or through other means.  Along with this, the places that you can travel around are huge so if you're the kind of person that likes to travel around this is a definite plus.  With friends you can take down bosses with ease, conquer different crime organizations, and enjoy the plots your character is tied into.
Without friends you can do the same, but it may not be as fun, especially with the Alert system and weekly events that take place.  Some events need good teamwork and organization to pull off, but if you don't have friends that are interested in playing or available, the community in game are more than kind enough to assist those in need.  Not only that, but the sheer amount of different appearances of heroes may spark more creativity for your character (or nemesis once you reach a certain level).
The downside is that this game has a ton of costumes, devices, and most recently vehicles that will cost a pretty penny to obtain with real money. There are methods to obtain most in game, but it will require a lot of grinding for resources that is a pain.  Vehicles are probably the most annoying to try to obtain without actual cash since they reduce the time it takes to get from one end of a map to the other by at least half according to a few people, but are possibly the most difficult to get.  If you need to get to a place fast, such as a friend that is fighting a boss in the corner of the desert while you are at the south end of Canada, it will take forever to reach your friend to help without improved travel powers or a vehicle.  However, the vehicles are not required to play the game or progress your character to max level, so while it is a downside, it isn't a big one.
Overall it's still a fun game to play. If you have a decent computer and like being a superhero, give it a try. If you have a friend that likes being a superhero bring them along as well. The more the merrier!

A surprisingly pleasant twin stick shooter with a variety of character types but repetitive and somewhat unneccessary leveling/exp system.
PROS:
-Good variety of genuinely different characters to pick
-Clean controls
-NON-level based unlocks and persistent power-ups (by spending gold you get via playing) are well done, good variety. The gold sink is borderline grindy, but the prices are mostly reasonable. This is a "fair" way to add a small replay value by means of grind to the game (unlike the level system, see below)
NEUTRAL:
-Graphics are nice but not amazing. Art style is cool, but I feel more could have been done with the world. It is somewhat bland.
-Higher difficulties add additional modifiers that make game more skill-based difficult, but also introduce an artificial skill-wall by means of character levels. WHY?!
CONS:
-There is no point to the leveling system but to add an artificial skill-wall and repetition to gameplay. Annoying, grindy, and unneccesary in what is otherwise a relatively skill-based game. NOTE: There is a relatively low level cap (15) so this isn't a huge issue.
-No multiplayer base. I don't know anyone who has it so I've been unable to try coop, but "online" games are a ghost town.

Full Mojo is a roguelike with a marraige between many popular games of the genre, adding together to be something completely unique. Offering multiple campaigns to challenge as well as various collectables and roguelite qualities that cater a huge amount to fans of the genre. This combined with some tongue in cheek humor and lore that sticks very close to its origins adds together to make a most exceptional game, though not without its share of flaws.
Mechanically it is most closely resembling that of Binding of Isaac, with shooting in various directions from a topdown view, but the gameplay more closely resembles that of area shooters like Serious Sam, as you will often be backpedaling away from hordes of enemies, hoping not to get yourself into a corner. This is one of my largest complaints about this game. Since the areas are so large, and the lowliest enemies so quick and devastating to your health, you are almost always relying on luck moreso than skill or patience, and regardless of how high your level and hp, you'll always be backpedalling. This quickly takes away from the fun, as a run can come to a swift and brutal end as your own skill can only take you so far. A cautious approach is reccomended for the earlier levels, as most of the enemies are rather simple, but the farther you go, the trickier they become, and if you trigger too many spawn points, you will easily be overwhelmed by a veritable congaline of enemies. This is by no means a bad thing, as it demands some forethought, but sometimes after you beat a particularly brutal boss, your day can be ruined by some cheaply spawned exploding enemies, and you'll have to start alllllllllllllllllllll over again.
Thankfully, all coins and experience carry over, so you're not completely bankrupt, but this is a twitchy game, and if you aren't one for twitch gameplay, steer clear, for you don't have many other options. Otherwise, this gem in the rough is definitely worth your attention.

If you came to steam reviews then good for you, you aren't a tool who watches a bunch of bumbling idiots talk "prolifically" about a game they've played in a single sitting and never came back to.

Critics have said that some of the puzzles to this game are too difficult and require a walkthrough,,, no, they don't, they require a pencil, a scrap of paper, and an attention span longer than someone who would give a Call of Duty game an 8.5 out of 10 on their website.
I managed this game without a walkthrough, granted one numerical puzzle was tough but not impossible, the general idea is that you're a ♥♥♥♥ing robot so of course you're going to end up doing some goddam computing. As soon as you start writing all of the relevant information to the puzzle on paper you begin to see the rules and elements of the puzzle exposed and ready for solving. YOU DO NOT NEED A WALKTHROUGH let the game grant you the satisfaction of completing it yourself.
This pen and paper style comes into play multiple times throughout and really rewards the player for paying attention to the environment around them.
This is an absolutely beautiful game that mostly airs around these cozy melancholic hub-worlds and takes the occasional incursion into the deep dank dark unknown. The music is pretty much entirely ambient and supports the melancholic tone.

The gameplay is pretty simple point & click graphic adventure, combining things and making good use of your flying partner with some lateral thinking, solving various types of puzzles and uncovering mysteries about your past.
Overall this game has:

After only a few hours of gameplay, I became hopelessly hooked to this game. It is fun and terrifying, filled with nerve-wrecking action. One thing though that must be pointed out is that it is not what I expeced it to be at all. If you are looking for a left 4 dead clone with nazi zombies, this is not what you are looking for. This not not even close to L4D, despite boasting the full L4D roster.
If you are looking to buy this, and mainly because of a love for L4D, here are some quick things about the game to think about before dropping $45.
-Zombie army is much more slowpaced, so dont expect every moment to be heart-stopping, faster-than-the-eye-can-follow action. Zombie army is a game where each bullet is precious, and can't go to waste.
-Zombie army is long, so expect to be working on the came level for quite a few hours. It dosen't have the concise chapters of L4D.
-Zombie army is hard, much more so than L4D. These zombies arn't the same zombies you mow down in L4D.

Reassembly is a decent sandbox shooter that has a relaxed atmosphere.  The best part, obviously, is building your own ships and experimenting with designs.  As you gather resources you can purchase better parts.  Each of the factions have a unique theme and require different strategies to design. The ship building interface is very intuitive and easy to use, which is a big plus.
It's a nice, chill single player game but I think overall it lacks depth, which I will describe below.
There's really no need for specialization against any particular foe. With such flexibility in ship design I was hoping this game could push this concept more.  Once you have a decent ship it works against all factions almost universally. You can fiddle with designs for a while, but in the end, more expensive parts will make you better.  With many factions it's quickest to destroy enemy ships for resources, so that becomes your sole focus.  Once you max out your ship, basically nothing stands in your way.  Unless you tried to get all the Steam achievements, like I did, there's not much of an end game to keep you playing.  I spent most of my time on this game grinding out achievements.
In conclusion, it was fun but lack of depth put me on the fence on this one.  After getting all of the achievements, I feel like I tapped out all of my reasons to keep playing.   I would have liked to see the ship building aspect developed further.  I'm leaning on the fence to recommend this game, but it was still fun for the time being.   If you feel like this game might be something you'll be interested in then you'll probably enjoy it.
