Cons:
1) The game is very different in many ways, and while I am not saying being different is a bad thing it is something that takes a while to learn. Big learning curve and tutorial is all text that you must read, making it more of a daunting task to get into.
2) Cities can be infiltrated very early in the game with lots of damaging affects...techs, skilsl and equipment to counter this are not available until late game. This means you have no choice but to deal with this annoyance until later tech ages.
3) The ability to construct buildings that do damage to enemy units in your territory passivly cannot be built until your game has experienced at least 2 or 3 winters.
4) One of the game's factions cannot be played unless you own the game "Dungeons of the Endless"
5) Each round of combat has you issuing orders and then not being able to issue new ones until next round. So you give all your units the order but if things don't go as planed you cannot do anything to change the orders until everyone on battlefield has moved.
All in all it is a great strategy game and one that I love dearly but it is very different in a lot of ways. Seriously spend some time watching lets plays or gameplay in general before buying, especially vidoes showing the combat system. This is honestly not a game that "everyone should play." The game set out to be different and I love that difference but for others it may not be what they are looking for. I would best describe it as a turn-based strategy RPG, and a good one at that, but like I said with my review of Lords of magic it is differnt and different is not a bad thing just know what you are getting into.

Evoland is basically every bad old RPG rolled up into one. Boring enemies, boring combat, excuse plot, character who dies who you just don’t care about at all (or indeed, care about any of the characters at all), ect.
The game is meant to poke fun at old RPGs, including Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, Zelda, Diablo, and others, but frankly, it falls flat. All of the “humor” in the game is basically the game pointing and saying “isn’t this dumb?” It is basically explaining the joke, except there is no joke, just a reference to an older game which isn’t very funny.
The game seems to suggest that you’re going to gradually move through various eras of games, but by about a third of the way into the game, you’re already up to 3D graphics, and it doesn’t really go beyond that. The game feels almost as if it has to rush through to unlock all the earlier stuff and then get to 3D for some reason, even though, quite frankly, the 3D gameplay isn’t very good (but then, neither is the 2D gameplay).
Ultimately, the game is meant to be funny, but isn’t, and is meant to be fun, and also isn’t. The gameplay is as tedious as any old, poorly designed game with very little content; the JRPG overworld encounters happen every five steps or so and are pointless and tedious, while the dungeon Zelda-type movement is very basic, containing very little variety of monsters, none of which are particularly interesting to fight. The game contains three bosses, two of which are pretty boring; one of them is basically “stand there and hit it until it dies”, and another is a standard “dodge the charge and hit them” boss. Only the final boss shows any signs of real gameplay, and even there, it was kind of tepid.
There’s just nothing here for anyone. If you’re looking for humor, the game isn’t funny; if you’re looking for a game which is fun to play, this isn’t. It doesn’t even feel original, as literally everything in it is referential, meaning any “originality” it might have from the whole idea of evolving into the modern day of gameplay is basically dead on arrival, buried under a pile of old video game references.

Evoland is a journey through the first few generations of video games. Starting with simple black and white 8-bit graphics that resemble the earliest GameBoys, it slowly evolves into Nintendo 64 era features. Each time the player opens one of many treasure chests scattered across the worlds, new graphical, musical, or sound effects are "unlocked." In this way, the game slowly progresses through the history of action/adventure video games.
Obviously inspired by classics like The Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, and Diablo, this game appeals to fans of those games, like myself. Highlights of the game include the unique evolution style, decent music (though sometimes overly repetitive), and a great homage to classic games. On the negative side, the game was a bit too long for me, but only because I searched for every secret room and hidden items. So, without the side-questing, I am sure the game would have been less of a drag. There was included as well in the game a side mini-game, called Double Twin. This was a basic card game twist of tic-tac-toe. Again, an interesting idea, but only good for a few plays, not for prolonged play-time.
This also marks the first time that I have gained all the achievements for a game on Steam... No reward for that except a little self-pride...

Why don't I like this game? When I go to play a classic RPG, I think it looks beautiful, but now I want to play it on an emulator because without the option to speed up the game I just feel like I'm wasting my time.
Games used to have more of a public stigma and were often called a "waste of time." For some reason Evoland doesn't want to move past that, but, intentionally or not, it seems to imply that /this/ is the pinnacle of gaming. These loathsome turn-based battles wherein I'm not scared I'm going to die from facing four enemies, no, I am scared of the animation of four different characters, which means each. One. Hits. Then. You. Attack. And. Oh. You. Didn't. Kill. It. So. Let's. Do. Another. Four. Attacks. For some reason Evoland stops in this weird middle-ground of floaty combat, dull puzzles, and poorly written dialogue.

Perhaps worse, is that this was a perfect chance to play with genre tropes and yet Evoland decides to mimic tired mechanics.
I don't know. If you like Big Bang Theory's or Family Guy's referential "humor" and you like Zelda and FF7 then I guess this the game is for you. This "humor" is encapsulated by the annoying "beeping" sound when you get to critical health. The game even points it out. "Remember how annoying that was in Zelda? DO YOU REMEMBER?!"
Play the Ludum Dare entry and save your money and, most importantly, time.

What exactly was wrong with the game?
It wasn't just one thing. It was a bunch of small things that slowly angered me until I was utterly infuriated. The gameplay I experienced can only be described like this: It's like trying to stick your fork into the last pea on your plate. Whenever you think you got it the thing rolls away and you're left wondering why you've been punished.
Similarly, it also leaves you feeling unsatisfied. Sure, you have the whole game. But that one last bite is still missing. That something was the soul of a theme park. I never actually felt as if I was playing a theme park simulator. It was simply too boring.

But just as I tried to open the ride...bam...the freaking path trolled me again by breaking. Then I fixed the path...only for it to break in another location. I googled this and realized other people also have this issue. I tried to follow their recommendations...I really tried. I never managed to get past two rides because that path be failing every time.
Everything in the game takes too much time. Going through the menu takes time, building things takes forever. (And don't think you'll be building awesome rides at first because that takes too long). Seriously, I get that there's a bit of a learning curve but after a while that just fails to excite. After all, I play games so I can instill the fake belief that I'm actually good at things, not to remind myself that I can't get my act together in a game either.
I could still deal with all the time consuming parts in the game, the swarm of bugs and long tutorials, if it wasn't for the paths. I know I mentioned it before but I cannot stress enough how much the paths ruined my life. It was a when a path screamed its final hoorah and broke one time too many that I flew into a rage and uninstalled the game.
Whenever I think about this game and the money I spent on it I become so horribly enraged. I'm normally a calm person but I doubt anything I can say will ever be able to capture the pure passion with which I hate this game. I truly wish I had a physical copy of this game. Why? Primordia is a point and click adventure game that more than rivals titles like "I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, Machinarium, Botanicula, etc." It takes place in a post human world, where advanced AI have claimed what is left of the wasteland that is the planet.
The voice acting in this game is top notch, incorporating even the talents of Logan Cunningham. The characterization of the entire cast though, hinges on the environment they are thrust in. And how each sentience has chosen to deal with their circumstances.
The game itself is quite serious in tone and changes in severity depending on which ending you achieve. Though there are many breaks from this dark nature when Horatio and Crispin interact with one another, often ending in clever word play or sarcastic optimism. It's something I hope they continue with a sequel or a run off featuring different characters. This is the type of game that would make a wonderful animation on the silver screen.

What is there to say, more importantly what do I have to say?
Well, Despite not having hundreds of hours on my account, (at the time of this review) that does not mean I haven't played it WAY too much, seeing as I'd probably have 1000+ hours if you threw in my time on XBox.
Now, to the review!
The Story:
The story is set roughly 4000 years before the events of the movies, as to avoid going against the established timeline and lore from the movies. Since this is a long time before the movies somethings will of course be different. For one, people still use swords to kill each other despite never really seeing that in the movies, but don't worry! They are special swords that can block lightsaber blades because of the metal they are produced from. Anyway, You take control of a soldier for the Republic who can be seen as the "peacekeepers" of the galaxy and are essentially the good guys. However, the ship you are on, The Endar Spire is attacked and destroyed as you flee in an escape pod with fellow soldier Carth Onasi, and you also have to save a jedi named Bastilla who has a special power. Now I could go further but I don't want to ruin much of the story and the game will explain things better than I probably will ever. Oh and don't worry, you can become a jedi as you could probably tell from the screenshots :)
Combat Gameplay:
This is where the game shows some of it's age with a little bit dated combat system where you can miss at melee range with a sword... yep it's one of those games. That's not to say the combat is bad, as long as you don't invest half of your points into something worthless like Charisma because you WILL have to fight and no talking will ever get you out of it, then yeah you should be fine; just make sure to keep some medpacs handy for those tougher battles. This is where I mention that there are a few ways to engage combat: Stabby Stabby (Melee) Shooty Shooty (Ranged) or Force Power Force Power (Mage-like) of the three I think Force Power Force Power is the hardest to do right, and I will be honest, I don't like ranged, it always feels like I miss way more than I should but then again, I probably just suck anyway, as for melee, well... melee is dominate in my opinion.
Non-Combat Gameplay:
When you aren't running from your life from some giant monster that wants to eat you and you decided that melee was a good idea, you are usually talking to people trying to find out what you need to do to complete your objective, there are side quests of course like I remember having to help one of my companions find his son who just so happened to be at a local sith academy probably plotting my friend's demise. There are other things to distract you too like the card game Pazaak that I really suck at, swoop racing which I also suck at, or my favorite, selling my 20 extra lightsabers from all the dark jedi I killed in self defense, it was not murder! Life is good...
You the character:
As being the one person who seems to be leading everyone because you happen to be the center of the plot (or at least part of the center) you will have control over where you go, what you do, and what side of the force you will follow. Obviously being on the light side without choice can be pretty stupid so there's the complete opposite: be mean to everyone because you wanted to be dark side! There is a morality system and while your morality itself will not matter much in the grand scheme of things, (you can be full evil and decide to be good at any time) that isn't to say it doesn't have it's uses. Being on one side of the force means you have to expend less force to cast that side's powers and that means quite alot since only one of the jedi classes can use the force beyond healing and buffs plus the occasional force attack; but this is where things become painful, you see you'd imagine the dark side has all the battle powers that are useful and you'd be right where as the light side gets things to destroy droids (which aren't rare but they aren't common either) or remove all force buffs on an enemy, which WOULD be cool if you actually fought force users often! Seriously, the only reason you'd choose the light side would be for role-playing reasons or all the seemingly useless buffs they get that wear off before you can cast them all... except force speed, force speed is awesome. It comes down to you choosing the dark side for all the pros and then switching light side at the last moment for the light side ending. (There is a light side and dark side ending, no neutral)
Oh and you have amnesia, go figure.
Overall:
By now you either are just skipping to see my final verdict or you seriously read all of that and that is dedication and you should get a star for that.

This game is a simple concept expanded upon and made extremely entertaining (read: addicting). All you do is build a ship out of 2D shapes, shoot other ships, and try not to get blown up, all while making your blocky ship bigger and better. And yet, the game manages to do for me what even big-production space titles like Elite: Dangerous couldn't: absorb me in an expansive, living universe that I got hours of fun out of. It's easy to jump into, there's unlimited creative potential in making your ships, the destruction effects are satisfying, and you never run out of things to shoot, because the only thing there really is to do is expand your territory by destroying enemy ships, of which there are in (sometimes frustrating) abundance.
The "passive mulitplayer" mechanic is enjoyable, because while you can't very well taunt over the wreckage of destroyed player ships hoping to give your enemy some quality killcam footage, you can still feel smug knowing you just trashed the MVP of someone else's universe without expecting them to come back for revenge.
The game world in its geometric minimalism is surprisingly atmospheric, almost organic, and this feeling is certainly helped by the Brian Eno-esque music. There's no real plot that ties the 6 factions together as far as I know, but I feel like any kind of story would weigh down the smooth simplicity of the gameplay.
All in all, Reassembly is probably the most fun you can have in space without doing cargo runs.
(For bonus funtimes: Be the Sentinel. Get the Armor Spikes. Make buzzsaws. Be unstoppable.)

I feel there are two main problems with this game:
- Far too short
- Not clear what to do
There are also some smaller problems, like the game occasionally freezing and having to be restarted (happened to me twice on Mac) and Kaizen not understanding follow up questions/responses, but these are the two main ones.
Just as I had gotten to what seemed like the inciting incident of the story, the credits began. The game seems like a very long prologue, with much left unexplored. It gives the impression that there is lots to be uncovered about the ship and what happened on it, but unfortunately we don't get a chance to uncover it.
It's often not clear what to do. I found myself stumbling around for ages trying to get something to work, then realising I just had to ask the terminal in for a third time. Some of the things you have to do just don't make much sense, like playing on a piano through a computer terminal to unlock the 'manual' mode for some probes so that I can smash them into a window. Was I meant to work that out for myself?
What I did like:
- Interesting AI personality, I was never sure if I could trust it or not
- Space station looks very nice, I just wish I could have played it without all my graphics turned down (I guess that's a Mac thing)
- The climax was very enjoyable
- Cool name :)
Had some quick freezes and hiccups but it was a cool experience.

this game is what you want to play if you ever wanted to play as your own created superhero. having more customization with appearence and travel powers is what sets this game apart from another superhero mmo that has more publicity. this game has lots of heart and is surprisingly fun for a game that appears to be losing steam. with that being said there are minor flaws i found in the game that are both small nitpicky (albeit rational) and the kind that will have you shouting. power customization is little to none unless you decide to pay for membership, in which case the powers are fun with the different classes and you can even make a class from scratch. you are also limited to 2 characters associated with your account, unless... you pay. there are vehicles your hero or heroine can own to fly around in style... if you pay for them. and last but certainly not least in any sense, boss fights are stupidly frustrating later on even with friends, during a mission me and a friend were fighting a boss whose health would hardly decrease, we had an NCP that was supposed to do a majority of the damage needed to progress but the NCP would not stop getting beaten down so that he needed rest. during the same boss fight my friend and i also both managed to man up and get the boss's heath down to next to nothing but since i had died and for some reason got locked out of the combat zone he ended up dying and once i was finally able to go through the invisible wall keeping me back we both went back to the boss and he had full health... the NCP was resting, and just like that 2 hours were wasted. i know what youre thinking "maybe you just got unlucky or its just part of the game that you can't lose." i tried again twice once alone and with the same friend. with my friend he ended up dying like i did before and i was strong enough to beat him with some grinding, wouldnt you know it when i was two hits away from victory, BOOM! boss is full health and fighting the good fight. when alone the same thing happened and no matter what i did the NCP did nothing and the boss refused to accept defeat from me. all in all this game is good fun and is best played with a controller, i like this game a whole lot and aside from the immortal boss fight with the useless NCP the game was fun and is worth a look if you want something new out of an mmorpg. if i were to give it a rating i would give a 7/10. its fun and i liked the customization very much, the emphasis of having to pay for things that would make the game a good f2p is annoying at times and some features require many players to work and since this game is so under the radar it is not able to be what it should. finally i enjoyed the look of the game and how it was made to look like a stylized comic book. i recommend this game to mmorpg fans and superhero fans alike

Similarly, it also leaves you feeling unsatisfied. Sure, you have the whole game. But that one last bite is still missing. That something was the soul of a theme park. I never actually felt as if I was playing a theme park simulator. It was simply too boring.
I've always been a fan of tycoon games but I've never felt so enraged by a game in my life. I played through all the tutorials, read everything and made sure I understood everything. Yet the paths...the paths were acting like freaking hoodlums. Breaking whenever I thought I finally managed to build the path correctly and will be able to open the ride. But just as I tried to open the ride...bam...the freaking path trolled me again by breaking. Then I fixed the path...only for it to break in another location. I googled this and realized other people also have this issue. I tried to follow their recommendations...I really tried. I never managed to get past two rides because that path be failing every time.
Everything in the game takes too much time. Going through the menu takes time, building things takes forever. (And don't think you'll be building awesome rides at first because that takes too long). Seriously, I get that there's a bit of a learning curve but after a while that just fails to excite. After all, I play games so I can instill the fake belief that I'm actually good at things, not to remind myself that I can't get my act together in a game either.
I could still deal with all the time consuming parts in the game, the swarm of bugs and long tutorials, if it wasn't for the paths. I know I mentioned it before but I cannot stress enough how much the paths ruined my life. It was a when a path screamed its final hoorah and broke one time too many that I flew into a rage and uninstalled the game.
Whenever I think about this game and the money I spent on it I become so horribly enraged. I'm normally a calm person but I doubt anything I can say will ever be able to capture the pure passion with which I hate this game. I truly wish I had a physical copy of this game. Why? So I can either A. rip it to shreds while I cry from frustration or B. eat it and have my body dissolve it into the poop that it was to me.
I can make all the things that shouldn't happen at an ammusement park; happen. What more could you want?

A fantastic point-and-click adventure brimming with atmosphere and clever puzzle design, with barely any flaws to speak of.
So let's get those out of the way first. The biggest flaw is that the game occasionally has pixel-hunting puzzles, which are never good. Bad developers. Only time in the game I looked at guides was when I was missing something from pixel hunting (random LCD screen, bah, random floating junk, what even?)
The palette's also a bit dull overall; I get the point of having so much brown but it gets a little tiring to look at after a while, though the game's gorgeous looking otherwise.
That aside, only the postitives left. The two protagonist characters each have quite a bit of personality to them and play off each other well for plenty of amusing moments, though the game still keeps a fairly serious and dark tone throughout. The other various characters are all quite unique and memorable and serve the overall plot in interesting ways, usually having their own mini-arcs. The backstory and worldbuilding is also very rich, not outright saying a lot but leaving the pieces scattered for the player to put together.
The puzzles are also generally good. Plenty of the standard item-trading things but there's no moon logic present there. And there's straight up logic puzzles on occasion, too, which are probably the most fun. There's no need to memorize strings of numbers or information, either; the game auto-saves all relevant data in the main character's datapouch, as well as providing a map for quick travel. It's got a lot of old-school adventure game design with a more modern feel to it, making it both well-crafted and elegant in execution.
There's a lot to like here and little to dislike, I heavily recommend it to, well, pretty much anyone really, but especially point-and-click enthusiasts, because this is certainly top-tier in that regard.

TLDR:  If you want the game then get it for the story and the art and not the puzzles.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is an RPG created by BioWare, the company that made classics such as Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights, and would later go on to make the critically acclaimed Mass Effect series. However, I think that this game and its sequel are some of their best work in the genre.
KotOR runs a simplified version of Neverwinter Nights 2's character and combat engine. It is easy to pick up and understand. Character creation isn't a hassle, and combat feels natural. You can take complete control of the fight, choosing attacks and Force powers for each ally, or just focus on your own character and let the capable AI choose your teammates' attacks.
As far as the story goes, it is well-written and keeps you interested the whole way through. As you work to uncover the secret of an ancient war machine, you will learn about your allies, and grow fond of them... Or learn to despise them. Each ally you can obtain has different values, and views on right and wrong. Unfortunately, how your allies view you doesn't impact much in this game; this will be expanded upon in the sequel.
The morality system of Light and Dark Side works well. If you adhere to the Jedi Code, your character will positively gleam with the Light Side of the Force; but drift toward the Dark Side, and your character will start to visibly change to represent that - scars and blemishes will appear on your model, to show how twisted you have become. In the end, though, this doesn't affect much more than Force costs in combat, as you can choose the Light or Dark Side endings no matter your alignment. Again, this is handled better in the sequel.
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 8/10. This is one of my favorite PC games of all time, and for good reason. The game works well, but it does have some flaws that are handled far better in the second game. If you like Star Wars, I'd definitely recommend picking this game up. And if you enjoy this, You should definitely check out its superior sequel.

After some ridiculous number of hours assembling fleets of warships from fighter to super-death-machine 2X, I decided that this is probably the best top-down shooter I've ever played. Whether your death-machine is incredibly manueverable and flies circles while spraying white-hot death, or a slow-moving tank that absorbs hundreds of shots on its mile-thick armor plating before its quintuple banks of burst lasers burn through the enemy to the core, you'll have fun dismantling it, making it better, over and over again, unlocking new parts, more points to use on them, as your drone-launching, resource-harvesting, station/fleet-building monstrosity burns its way through the universe.
After I maxed out the first race, of course I did the same with every one, having fun the whole time, testing my ships against the normal ones as well as the user-designed ones until I had achieved the proper mix of lethality and style.

Reassembly is the game I never knew I wanted, but man, did I want it badly.
A 2D top-down shooter not unlike space invaders or asteroids in the sense that you fly around and shoot stuff. Reassembly takes it to a whole new level, allowing you complete customization of your ship. You can connect various parts, which snap together at points like legos, to create whatever your mind can come up with. At the beginning of a playthrough, your ships will be small and fairly weak, but as you advance you will be able to fly massive frigates followed by your very own custom fleet.
One of my favorite parts of ship creation is the physics of thruster placement. Where you put your thrusters actually matters a lot; your ship won't be able to turn very well if you only place them on the back. This also lets you build some funny creations such as ships that travel by spinning. It also means that if you are having trouble progressing, you can completely change the feel of your vehicle by moving or adding a thruster.
Creation aside, the game revolves around the aquisition of currency (called "C") and resource (called "R"). You get both of these basically by blowing up your enemies, the other ship factions. You use your C to buy upgrades and new parts for your fleet, allowing you to take on bigger enemies. If you manage to conquer your whole galaxy, no big deal, the game allows you to jump into a wormhole to enter a new galaxy with your fleet. You can also unlock new factions to play as; all of them utilize different base shapes for their ships, meaning you can create entirely new ideas playing one faction that you couldn't with another.
If you feel like you've peaked, you can upload your fleet, sending it to other players' games as a powerful opponent called an Agent. This is a really great part of the game, it keeps things challenging and fresh.
Overall, I put this game in the same circle as Spore. You create cool things and share it with others. The game is fun to look at, very colorful, and it has an awesome soundtrack. If you like building things, if you like space, or you like shooting the hell out of ships, just go buy Reassembly.

I suppose this one already has zillions of positive reviews. I don't care - I'll add another one. I played for... maybe an hour? and I can already see this is a pretty good game. I thought I would have to play Shogun 2 for the rest of my life but Endless Legend might save me.
In short, this is probably your game if:
-you liked Eador/Broken World but wanted it to be a bit more complex
-you liked Civilization and wished it would go fantasy
-you liked Civ and wanted a bit better battle system
-you like games where skill and luck both play a part
-you like customisable games
-you are not a big hack&slash fan but rather like to plan and learn
-you like large games with specific goals
-you like the idea of combined adventure and empire building
One of the best features so far: the game got stuck when a battle was just starting (waiting for opponent). Most games would have crashed at this point, but EL let me save the game, reload it, and start the battle - this time successfully. This is some good coding the way I see it.
(The rest of the review is mostly just rambling. tl;dr works here.)
After playing for a day or so:
I'm hooked. I don't know if this game is much deeper than the ordinary 4X game, but it feels that way. It seems as if the designers have taken the best bits of several different games of different genres and slapped together a frankensteinian.... you get the point. Let me elaborate a bit:
-you get tasks, major and minor. Some are very easy and can be completed on the spot if you have the right resources about you, some take at least 50 turns to complete. This alone keeps the game going for me.
-you battle against different beings with VERY customisable armies (and the customization actually makes a difference).
-you have heroes that progress and can use different weapons, armor and trinkets. This is one of my favourite aspects of any game.
-you develop your empire. This works pretty much the same as in Civ: grow too fast (or too large) and the people will rebel. Science seems to be the key, along with a few other factors. More interesting mechanics than in any comparable game I've played.
-tactics and strategy work together in (at least) a couple of different ways. Not sure yet if it gets more complicated/many-sided as the game progresses. I hope it does.
-winter. A great idea.
-empire boosters. A great idea.
The battle screen could be better... I would be overawed if this game had similar battles as Total War games have - but this is no big deal. The strategic side is more important.
The game, all in all, is like a souped-up version of Heroes of Might and Magic or similar, if you want it in a nutshell. Like a rocket is a souped-up version of a slingshot missile.
After two days of play:
It's hard to quit and go to bed. Very immersive. The graphics look great - at first they looked a bit clumsy but the idea is that different elevations of landscape are easier to see.
Fun to play. Challenging enough. Looks good. What else could you ask of a video game? Non-stop action perhaps, but that one's not my thing. I have an attention span.
I will edit this review after getting through some campaigns.

Words cannot describe how much fun this game can be. It's easy to start, but It's also complex and diverse enough to have a learning curvew for gameplay for the first few weeks of playing it. Then, after you have learned all about the intricities of the factions, fighting them, and generaly playing the game, you get to ship design. Another main part of the game, but one that will keep you entertained like Legos.
The game is bassed in around the designing and flying of peice-built spaceships. Enimies are diverse, and tactics complicated. There is faction warfare, between all the races, not just your own. There are no aliances, but some are peaceful unless provoked. There are 7 playable races, each have strengths, weaknesses, and their own aray of wepon systems. The world is proceduraly generated, and you can chose to leave it to go to a new one through a wormhole. This spawns in another galaxy for you to fight against. Scaterd through each world are "Agents", fleets designed by other players.  At a wormhole you can chose to either travel through it, or to upload your fleet. These uploaded fleets randomly have a chance to apear as agents in another player's game.
My only twwo dislikes for the game:
Factionl Controll:
While the factonal controll system is fine, and killing things is easy, truly dominating the entire galaxy is nearly imposible. I wish there were a better, more defined way of determining who controlls a secotor than by who has the most ships in it.
Self-replicating system cluster♥♥♥♥s:
Ya know how there are scifi horor movies and books that had robots that became sentient and learned how to build more of themselves? THERES A REASON FOR IT. Two of the games factions, Flies and Spikey Plant, can spread like wildfire if not contained. And truly eradicating them is imposible. A serious problem, though, lies not in the game's factions, but in agents. Plenty of players equip their ships with Factory moduels to make more ships. But with an agent fleet, which is already hard to defeat, the ability to have that fleet self-replicate and replenish itself? It becomes an epic killing macine. I've seen agent fleets take more than a quarter of the map (a titanic feat) by reproducing off of the resources from killing me. Literaly nothing stands a chance against these monstrosities, Even after killing their lead ships, they stay behind as a permanant force. Luckly, the method of loading tthe game from a save file results in these fleets being dimished in power after a restart from a difernt area.  But at any rate, a self-replicating object is dangerous. No matter the details.
With these all of this taken into accound, I rate the game 10/10. For the sheer amount of content that can be had, similar to games like The Binding of Iasac, Rebirth. And for it's building system that alows you to be creative. The two dislikes I have for it can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥at rare times, but don't hurt the gameplay as a whole.
And to the guy with top comment reguarding glitches, not sure how old that is. I've played for a week and only seen an ocasional glitch where the screen doesn't folow the ship for a seccond, then snaps back into place. I have yet to see a single crash.
And also direguard the 6.1 hours in game. I bought the game elsewhere before I got it from steam. I have been playing for two weeks, from arround 2:00 PM to 4:00 AM off and on. I have at LEAST 50 hours.

*WARNING TO ANYONE BUYING:  AWESOMENAUTS WILL BE GOING FREE-TO-PLAY MAY 24 - BUYING THE GAME AS OF RIGHT NOW WILL GIVE YOU 20/29 IN-GAME CHARACTERS AND WILL SAVE YOU TIME*
Awesomenauts is an entertaining, casual MOBA that will be going free-to-play on May 24.  Instead of being 5v5 as most traditional MOBAs are, it takes a different approach as a platforming 3v3 MOBA.  It is far more casual and easy to learn/pick-up than any of the big name MOBAs out there (League of Legends, DOTA 2, Smite, Heroes of the Storm, etc.) and beginner friendly.  There are three different abilities each character has - either a ranged/melee basic attack and two other character-specific abilities.  Each character in this game has a different approach to them, truly making playing every character feel unique when playing.  The same principles of gameplay from MOBAs appear in Awesomenauts, but at a less intense level.  This minimizes snowballing and makes matches seem a lot more fair and winnable, which is definitely appreciated (especially if you're new to the game).  Mechanics don't take long to pick up and understand and don't get too complicated.  There are multiple maps that the game will assign you to play, each of which having unique layouts, hazards, and features.  Characters are balanced pretty decently as well (currently L4 and haven't seen too many characters that severly overpower others or ruin matches), which helps keep the game enjoyable.
As for buying the game before it goes free-to-play, I would only do so if you are into these type of games or if it looks appealing in any sense, as you will have to grind through a lot of matches to unlock the in-game characters before you'll either have to shell out cash or grind for in-game currency for them.  If not, definitely check this game out when it turns free-to-play.

Champions Online was one of my favorite MMOs, period. I spent hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of hours in this game, mostly playing with other players like one should in an mmo. I don't actually play there anymore, but felt the game deserved at least an honest review from someone who spent and enjoyed so much time in it. Keep in mind my opinion may be a bit bias because of this, but know I'll be trying to be as fair as possible as a reviewer.
The game has a MASSIVE focus on character customization that puts others in its genre to shame (and I've played plenty of them, trust me). You will spend a good half hour or more messing around with the look of your first character before you actually get into the game. And the best part is you can change it at any time. The appearance of your character is completely cosmetic and unrelated to your character's actual equipment, so you don't have to spend hours and hours and hours trying to find gear that you like the look of. It's already there for you at any time. There are so many options revolving around the appearance of your character and whatever they're wearing, that it's worth trying out alone just to see and believe. The game oozes content, has fun and engaging pvp, cool superpowers, and a lot of lore to help get you immersed in the universe. Combat in general feels like it has impact or effect. The world is very detailed and varied with multiple, large areas (such as the city, the canadian wilderness, undersea, etc.) with plentiful dungeons, bosses, and monster variation to boot. My favorite battles were the ones with epic bosses (yes, the game has those) that didn't require a 30-man group to slay so much as a competent, small party. And I know some people may not understand where I'm coming from, but I'm not a fan of games that force you to grind to level 80-100 to get the end-game. The level cap on this game is (last time I checked) level 40, which is fairly easy to get to within a reasonable amount of time when compared to other mmos. So if you're worried about this being a grindy game, don't worry, the trip is shorter than others.
The game did have problems though. For one thing, the quests are fairly generic. Which is forgiveable, given the date this game was released, but it's not going to astound you with its structure. Pretty standard stuff; kill ten of these guys or go get three of these items, etc. This made the pve element of the game fairly boring unfortunately. The A.I in the game occassionally had something new to throw, but again, do not expect mind-blowing A.I to regroup or use successive abilities in perfect synchronization on you or anything like that (boss fights vary). There's also a -really- painful lack of character development for your hero. It's not like Star Wars the Old Republic where you're making decisions that have an impact on your alignment or anything; everything is set in stone. You can not play a villain, only a hero, which may dissapoint or even turn away some fans of hero mmos. I completely understand as I often wish there was a villain faction to fight the hero faction in the open world. You do get a nemesis at some point, which is essentially an npc villain you make, but that's about it. I personally found it a dissapointing feature, as you're only ever going to see that npc when you get randomly attacked by minions of it and get a quest-item drop to go into a dungeon or see your nemesis during alerts (which are essentially quick-action dungeons or game modes with random party members). The music was great sometimes, but unfortunately had a looping issue which made the game very quiet. The fighting animations, while cool to look at when executed properly, did seem unpolished at times (if you ever played Warhammer Online, you'll have a general idea of what I'm talking about). The voice acting is also inconsistent and either hit or miss.
Finally, the free-to-play model that I have mixed feelings about. After I went gold, I simply couldn't go back to silver out of my need for freeform building (which essentially allows you to  structure your abilities as well as color them however you like), and need for more customization options, which does come with it. When it came to pvp, subscribers dominated as freeform allows for some insanely powerful builds that just aren't available to free players. Even though there's a que for pvp for non-freeforms, it still cuts off free players from a massive portion of the community and makes que times much longer. There were times when the free-to-play model worked though. You could buy exclusive outfits, consumeables, travel powers (yes, there's more than just flying and running), hideouts, boosts, and more in the cash shop. None of these were required to really succede at the game, but instead offered either conveinance or added to it. There was some really cool cosmetic stuff in it that was reasonably priced (most of it anyway), and felt like a good exchange to keep the game going.
If I had any suggestions to improve the game in its current state, the main one would be to stop dividing the player population between subscribers and non-subscribers by removing the gold status requirement for freeform (can still keep some power types locked off for non-subscribers). It makes the game feel pay-to-win and just made me irritated getting locked off from my freeform character until I dished out another monthly payment. Also implement a supergroup v.s supergroup (guilds) element so that players can battle it out in the streets whenever their supergroups desire.
I know I complained a lot in this little review, but trust me when I say the game is worth taking a look at. It's far from perfect, but has solid combat, plenty of content, MASSIVE customization, and a pretty decent community (from my experience at least). Game gets a 7/10 from me, despite the fact it may be a bit out of date. Go ahead and try this game out if you're even remotely interested in playing a superhero mmo that actually makes you FEEL super. You got nothing to lose.

It's just too short to recommend.

A short but good game, which offers a rather unique experience since all interactions other than exploration are made by conversing with an artificial intelligence.
The AI is essentially a chatbox that relies mostly on keywords to interprete what you are trying to say, so nothing groundbreaking for the world of AI, but it still makes for entertaining gameplay, and the AI understands enough to get you through the game and trigger some entertaining interactions. Just don't expect to hold an actual conversation with it.
The story is interesting, and when you piece together all of the pieces of information available here and there, you get the full picture.
The ship's interiors are rather beautiful, but it is also sadly very small, and the game is, consequently, quite short. Still, as short as it is, it is a good experience. If you have the budget for it, that's what matters most.
I definitly hope to see future games based on this concept. With a bigger budget, this could lead to something really exceptional. A bigger ship, of course, more complicated and numerous puzzles, speech-to-text and voice commands, VR... and of course a smartest AI which would be allowed to take into account the structures of your sentences and deduce meaning from the context. Some researchers do very impressive work on this.
If you do not mind a short game and are not looking for a challenge, but rather to experience something different with a good story, this game is for you.

Okay, let's jump right into this one! Visually it is pretty unimpressive, but that is to be expected from a game of its age. The audio is solid, though I did find that the sound of lurking zombies is not always a good guide as to how close they may be, or what direction they may be coming from. Just seems a lot more manageable that way, and the player revives make a huge difference taking away a lot of the frustration that was experienced when playing alone. Finding a group doesn't take too long but this game is flying under most people's radar so the community really isn't there.
I did find the X-Ray kill system to be quite fun, as it made me want to get more headshots, and the ability to punt kick a zombie's head off was just awesome.

Evoland 1 is a fun action RPG, basically a mix of Final Fantasy and Zelda through the years. The gameplay is pretty solid as you evolve along with the story, but there is very little to distinguish this game as something that stands apart from its inspirations. The story is about as derivative as it could possibly be, and I don't think there's an original idea here except the actual 'evolving' as you play. It's fun to watch the graphics and gameplay style improve as you go, but some aspects never catch up. Could I get a run button or even a back button? Where is a list of the cards or stars I've collected? I was missing one of each by the end of the game, and there's no way I want to retread the entire map with an online guide to figure out which 2 chests in the whole game I missed. Also, this would be so much better with actual controller support. It feels even more disconnected from old school games when I'm using arrow keys and the space bar. Overall, it's still fun to play, but I wish it could stand on its own a bit better.

Bloody, gorey, and intense combat-oriented game. The graphics are outstanding, and the game mechanics are thoughtful and intuitive. The story is simply amazing, and held my attention through the entire game.
That being said, the game does tend to be repetitive after a few hours. Completing the game on the easiest level, casually, took about six hours. I'm not the fastest gamer, and I prefer story elements over powering through something. However, even going for a more difficult setting, I found the combat system weighs heavier - as is to be expected - but sadly I can't recommend the game soley for it's combat.
You earn points to redeem on special execution animations, health stats, focus, and so on. While it's an interesting concept, the execution of the system leaves me disinterested at best. It's a way to "level up" your character for future playthroughs, of course, but doesn't provide much in the way of changing gameplay.
The Vistas and Scrolls collection is for those completion-hunters out there. Some are very obvious, some require wandering off the path a ways. I haven't completed any of the side achievements for that, so I can't say what sort of bonuses it provides.
Overall, though, this game is well worth the price. I'd like to see a sequel in the works, or another game set in the same setting.

I bought this expecting a rogue-like. In that sense, I was disappointed. Although it has stiff penalties for death and levels are randomly generated, you keep your stats between replays and can continue your next game on the same quest. The random level generation adds some variety but does not make each replay significantly different (think Diablo, not Brogue). So don't buy this expecing a wildly random experience like Binding of Isaac or FTL.
So it fails as a rogue-like... but it succeeds as an action RPG. The actual combat plays like a twin-stick shooter and the outcome is determined as much by aim and dodging as by stats. The graphics are great, filled with comedic voodoo iconography. Most of the abilities have excessively long cooldowns so you'll find yourself using the basic attack most of the time. This isn't so bad since the basic attack is satisfying enough.
The two-player co-op is fun and the networking code works very well.
I do have a few quibbles, though:
- Some of the dialog boxes have timers which arbitrarily prevent you from closing them immediately to proceed with the game.  Fortunately, they're not very common.
- When playing multiplayer, your group is disbanded after each quest and you must re-form the group to continue.
- The lack of variety will likely hurt the game's long-term replayability.
On the whole, this is a fun, polished, and bug-free experience, but don't expect it to hold your interest for more than 10 hours.

If you didn't think there was enough "Gauntlet" in "Gauntlet", you should probably invest in this. I will mention Gauntlet rather a lot in this "review", btw.
The first point, and it's a reasonably large one, that this game scores over Gauntlet is that it has genuinely random (thus replayable ad inifinitum*) levels and a fairly expansive character customization section make this a far more worthwhile purchase. Gauntlet promised randomised, limitless levels and failed to deliver, preferring instead to rotate a level through 180degrees or make you do them "the opposite way round" (from start to finish in a 'death' level, for example). It's obvious, woeful and does nothing to hide the fact that you're always playing from a small group of levels that can easily be remembered, no matter what way round they are.
There are also more "world types" than in Gauntlet.
The player upgrade system is somewhat similar but, again, full mojo rampage has a better one. There's more to spend your ingame currency on and the prices of everything gets quite high so you need to take time to find cash. This isn't annoying, however. Also, found items can be sold in the shops ingame, which produces a lot of extra cash. Item drops are random and there are a LOT of different items that you can find. You can also mix together 2 items to get a single item with all the effects of the 2 individual ones. This is a fun way to make interesting "charms" to equip and also an interesting way to cause a sort of "inventory game" to arise, wherein the player must decide what stuff to keep/dump in favour of potentially more useful items. You can also expand your inventory, too, so it's possible to carry more. I liked this aspect of the game as, again, it adds another random dimension to things that makes each playthrough different.
I've put a fair amount of time into the game and I still find it fun to go back and play more. Also, I have yet to complete all of the levels on "hardcore" difficulty, which requires a more levelled up character. I think, beyond that, there's "nightmare" or "insane", something like that, so there's plenty of reason to return and play more*. I will be trying to finish all the levels at all skills and will probably wind up doing so at some point. I see this definitely as a game I can return to in future as I've enjoyed it and it does a lot of things that I, personally, like in games.
Some people have said this is tough but I think it's reasonably easy, it's far easier to solo than Gauntlet, for example, which is easy enough but you have to adhere to a plan/play style to get through. You have much more option to just "muck around" in full mojo rampage, as a result of the levels being more open and monsters spawning/wandering randomly instead of coming from "summoning stones" in closed rooms (another bad point about the new version of gauntlet).
Finally, it's not really a roguelike, tbh. There's a lot of games called Roguelikes these days but I would say this has much more in common with something like Gauntlet or Alien Syndrome. Neither of which are roguelikes. Unless you count Gauntlet 4. People seldom do, despite it being by far the best version (genesis cart, have a look if you like Gauntlet). HOWEVER, I did play one game where I was transported to a random dungeon that was made of ascii and I had to fight various "G" and "M" symbols. This was excellent and I would probably play the whole game in this manner if the option existed. There are some nice little diversions like this in the game. As I've mentioned, you're never quite sure what's going to pop up and, for this reason and the others above, I rate this as a really good and fun game.
The online works well, too.
*If you enjoy the premise and play style of the game, of course.

I really loved Primordia it took me back to the days when Sierra, Revolution and Lucas Arts created some truly unique games and Primordia stands perfectly in their company. The voice acting is very good and there is a lot of humorous references to pop, computing and gaming culture. Primordia gives the player many choices for a game in this genre with various ways to solve puzzles and multiple endings that have very different outcomes. A few puzzles might be considered difficult, but most will keep you entertained without causing frustration. It took me about 8 hours to finish before going back to try different solutions to see the all the endings. I think Primordia is well worth the asking price and I found it more enjoyable than some newer click adventures 2-3 times more expensive. If you enjoyed games like Beneath A Steel Sky, The Dig or Ring World you won't be disappointed in Primordia.

This game has an excellent story and a unique and interesting setting filled with charmingly colorful characters.  It is thoughtful and meaningful, and addresses some serious theological and philosophical points, while remaining mysterious and exciting (most of the time).  However, I found the gameplay to be very lacking, in a number of ways.  I'm now going to complain about all the things I need to complain about, but do please recall that I actually enjoyed this game :)
The puzzles in this game were difficult, and not in a good way.  While many of them had "cool" solutions - which would be awesome in a movie, for example - they were often not cleanly solvable, in the sense that they were the only plausible solution and made everything "make sense" when you figured it out.  For me, a lot of the reason I want to play a puzzle game is for that awesome feeling of everything coming together when I figure it out.  This is not the sort of game that does that for me.  Here's a few of the problems that I saw:
1. Trying to create a clever solution rather than a good puzzle.  The solutions to puzzles are often the sort of zany solutions that are fun to watch heroes think of in movies, but not reasonable to force the player to think of.  In other words, they don't feel like THE solution, just A solution (and yet in the confines of the game, they are THE solution).
2. Tooooo many items.  Unlike a lot of games, in Primordia you almost never get an item taken out of your inventory when you are done using it.  By the end of the game, I have so much stuff in my inventory that the task of getting through a locked door has dozens of reasonable-sounding solutions - crowbar, plasma torch, signal transmitter to pick the lock, etc, etc - but only one of them is right (and it's probably none of the standard things I've learned how to do throughout the game, because that would be to easy).
3. Generic, reusable items.  This is one of my pet peeves in puzzle games.  When you have a generic item like a hammer, there's a trillion and five ways that the player can think of to use this item.  Even if the game designer could think of all of those, allowing those solutions would make many of their puzzles too easy.  Anyway, this game is full of generic items that you use again and again throughout the game (but are never allowed to use when you think of it).
4. Confusing items.  I had a whole bunch of electronic gadgets and doodads that it took me a long time to figure out how they worked - a signal transmitter, a decryption device, a memory reader, etc.  All of these could be used only in very specific circumstances (i.e. as far as I can tell, the memory reader can only be used to access memories from a severed robot head - which you encounter in this game a lot more than you would think!), but this information is never explicitly told to you (I never really figured out what the rules for the decryption device were).
5. Just too much going on at once.  The game is basically divided into two parts.  During each part, you slowly unlock more areas, and then can travel freely between all areas that you have unlocked during that part, which by the end of each part results in a huge environment in which to look for a small number of remains tasks.
The end result of all of this was that I played the game with a walkthrough constantly ready.  And I do not regret it :)  Most of the things I had to get help on ("most" because I started getting lazy near the end), I think I would have felt frustrated rather than satisfied if I took the time to solve myself.
The interface is unfathomably archaic and unintuitive.  For example, the process of using an item - one of the most base necessities of a point and click game - requires (1) hovering near the top of the screen to open the tool bar, (2) selecting the inventory button to open your inventory, (3) selecting the item from the inventory, (4) clicking outside the inventory to close it, then finally (5) clicking on the thing in the world that you want to use the item on.  On all the interfaces mentioned, there are also many confusing and sometimes unnecessary/duplicate buttons.  The datachron (which automatically takes notes on things you have learned) has a horrific interface that looks something like an old school gameboy, with giant text on a tiny screen, and buttons (that you have to click with your mouse) for scolling up and down.  Similarly, the signal transmitter - on which you frequently need to set a 4-digit number to transmit - is pretty obnoxious, requiring you to click on the left and right sides of two dials (not even buttons that you can see, so it's hard to find the sweet spot to actually click on) - one to cycle through numbers, and one to cycle through DIGITS.  DIGITS.
All that being said, however, I think this game is definitely worth playing for the story alone, which like I said is fantastic.
Play it. Really, you have no excuse not to.

Champions Online. To put it simply this game is limited to the users imagination. If you can think of an idea, let it flow and give it shape. Download this game. Don't even second guess yourself. If you want customization, crazy worlds. Things you thought impossible. Well. I'm telling you its all perfectly possible. Now then. Onto an actual review of this game.
Once it went Free to Play, naturally i jumped at the oppertunity to play such a game, but i was disappointed and surpised on a number of areas. The first being the silver and gold platforms for playing. (Silver being the base model of F2P and Gold being a subscriber status of the game) If you want some neat features, extra perks. I highly recommend you buy Gold membership (Never been gold but i am ashamed to say i have pumped far too much money into this game.) For the small pricetag you pay your getting alot, this is including the "Freeform" character feature. (I'll touch on this later!)
Not too mention the new aura system and dare I say it.. Vehicles. Ugh. (Not as good as they sound.. Keep reading for my opinion on these.)
So before i continue i want to sidetrack with you with abit of history of the point of view from a Veteran Silver. Content has really, REALLY been lacking these past few months. With most of the attention shifting to "STO" (Star Trek Online) One of Cryptics other ventures before being brought out. So yeah. Theres been little to no quality control and content added to the game recently. Even old features such as missions from Adventure packs - (Buyable DLC expansion packs which were made free by Perfect World Entertainment) remain just undoable because of heavy bugs from the game. (Which probably won't ever get fixed..)
Freeform your characters.
Its exactly as it sounds. Want a fire character who can shoot electricity? You can do it. Want a sorcerer with a cheeky sidearm? Why not! How about a robot who has floating drones.. Or even Ice wolves as pets!? Do it already! Freeform is your golden ticket into the chocolate factory. Imagine, Create and have Fun! If you are subscribed to the membership system ingame you will automatically have access to this feature. Silvers can also buy access to this feature.. For the small sum of £50 or $50, in the respected countries. Soo yeah. Thankyou PWE for this but.. I think its best we wait for Half-price sales.
Vehicles.
Oh my gosh.. Just a waste of money. They might look cool but you will barely ever use them. Weapons do limited damage. If anything they are useable trophies. (Did i mention you can only use them outside?) Just save yourself some money. Say NO to vehicles!
To put this bluntly. Most of these new features is to keep the playerbase for hanging on. The game is dying. I'm sorry but it is. I can recommend this, but it probably won't be around for the remainder of 2014.

Loved the first Boo Bunny, (Do recommend you get it)
However this one....not so much.
I did like it, just not as much as i hoped.
Although the game is short, it's is...lacking.
This might be from the fact it's very arcadish in design, however the game doesn't move fast enough to warrant this and becomes a slug as you go on. A multiplayer mode could have fixed this however there isn't one.
Where to start?
The Story:
Basic Plot: After 2 kids berate them, Boo Bunny and Co. enter a competition against other bands for a magic wish.
The story doesn't really have anything to it, it just rides along till it ends. Not developing or doing much un-like the last game. Except for the end where i was pleasently surprised before it did another 180 and just went somewhere else.
The boss's for the other bands sadly arn't much. If the story had each of the boss's as part of one band and you versed each member seperatly it could have been better.
The Meat:
A good part of the game is spent going through 2 levels between boss's killing or running past cannon fodder that has no real purpose. Levelling up, from finding items only, grants health and special usage but it's somewhat redundant when the specials do almost the same thing as basic hitting. So in a way, progress doesn't really exist in the game besides getting to the end of the level, by either running past everything or slowly clearing the floor.
And in a weird twist, the boss's go down easier than the cannon fodder. Theres also a good amount of nothing happening in the levels. If there where puzzles or quests or something just to fill the excuse for the long levels besides get from A to B with hordes of cannon fodder. But repitition is what you'll face.
A Multiplayer mode would have done the job as well breaking up the repitition or speeding it up.
There's also no real reset for failing in the game unless you pick the "rouge" option which limits you to one go. If you do fail on the normal difficulty, prepare to re-walk the level to where you failed. Filled with no cannon fodder now since you removed them.
Same goes for boss's, if you fail oddly enough the fight doesn't reset.
The Controls:
If you do get this, FOR BOO BUNNY'S SAKE, use a controller. If you use a mouse and keyboard you'll end up with your character attacking everything nearby. (Yes i know theres a button to stop that from happening but it never worked)
Other things i came across where the characters unresponsivness at times to move or attack. Also found the hud to be in the way when not using a controller and trying to walk around.
Other Characters:
This is a great addition and pretty cool. Sadly the lack of a multiplayer mode could of made this better.
Music:
It's good, but somewhat lacking from the first game.
Humor:
Felt more refrential this time around towards other things, Not saying it wasn't bad, but about more than half of it is refrencing to other things.
Other:
Camera Angle was not the best, stuff behind the walls closest to the camera couldn't be seen.
To sum it up, It's a mini condensed top down hack and slash, which if you have the patience for (lots of) repitition and want something to blast away the afternoon, will be a great blast for 3-5 hours.

So to start and to get the ugly out of the way, This is a spinoff/sequel to the last game, "Boo Bunny Plague." Which was a buggy, so-so, third person hack n slash game. If you looked at gameplay alone, it probably wouldn't gain too much of your interest.
BUT, the game was genuinely funny and really charming, with a lot of self-aware humor. On top of that, a really amusing soundtrack to boot. Like I said, it wasn't going to win awards but it was certainly entertaining. And this new installment much like that too.
Save for this time, they've taken a more traditional top-down dungeon crawler approach. If you go in expecting Diablo level quality, you'll be disappointed. But for a small indie developer? It's a really nice evolution from the last game and you know they want to improve. And their unique sense of humor is still present and amusingly goofy.
And if you did play the last game, you'll be happy to see other characters be playable and see more from them.
It does have its problems. In my short time with it so far, it has been a little buggy and sometimes things don't trigger like they should ( ihad a cutscene audio start up but I was still stuck in ganeplay.) So I won't say it doesn't have flaws.
But there's far worse out there that's made by people who care way less. There's a lot of heart put into these two games and I highly reccomend giving them a little support.

My recommendation hinges entirely on whether someone wants to play this multiplayer.
This is generally a thumbs up. It's mostly solid. It has gorgeous graphics (and performed well even on my old mediocre PC), a nice soundtrack, and has a lot of interesting additions. There is a large amount of diversity in the factions, some of which drastically change the way the game is played. The game is rich with varied mechanics, to the point that you might find you've played multiple games without even realizing certain systems in the game exist!
It has its quirks. The AI pathing can be extremely irritating in combat, as your guys will sometimes start travelling a path they can't possibly reach by the end of combat when a path is just temporarily blocked. I've read that one of the end talents has been broken from the beginning.
In many ways, it makes for a more interesting game than Civ 5. However, I would stop short of recommending it over Civ 6. I feel the districts system in Endless Legend is a little more stale and boring compared to Civ 6. While I like the idea that districts change which tiles can be exploited, you are pressured to make your city into certain shapes, which are often not what you want.
Overall, this game is a solid addition to the genre, as a single player game.
To put it simply, this game is a mess multiplayer. It's often unplayable. It's the worst network handling of a game that I can recall since CivNet in 1991.
In more than half the games I've played, the game would report that the client and host were out of sync. Re-syncing forces rejoining the game, sometimes causing the client to lose actions. I've never had re-sync work. It always would go out of sync in a turn or 2. You don't know how serious it is, or whether you can just keep playing. Last game, we tried to keep playing, and eventually things just stopped working for us.
But worse than that, every game I've played has encountered a bug that could cause the game to grind to a halt. The client will issue perform an action (move a unit, change research queue, change build queue, etc) and the game won't recognize that it happened. Then no actions will register for minutes. Sometimes the actions will resolve after you hit End Turn, but sometimes they don't. When this happens, both players will be in a state that shows them waiting for the other player, and the game just seems to be stuck for minutes at a time. In late games, these bugs could sometimes add 5 minutes to trying to perform each turn. It is painfully frustrating.
This game is a mostly great game, but the terrible multiplayer experience causes me to become soured toward the game overall.
Endless Legend completely changed my view of the 4x strategy genre. It's one of those games that somehow pushes all the right buttons at just the right time.

Metal Gear Solid's hallmarks have never been represented better than in Ground Zeroes, the prologue chapter to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. It combines tense stealth and best-in-class cutscene direction, and these aspects stand above any other game in the series, but naturally, the narrative ultimately concludes sooner than you'd like. In addition to filling in some of the gaps between Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and the Phantom Pain, Ground Zeroes introduces a new stealth system and an open-world format that's perfect for experimentation.With Ground Zeroes’ minimal HUD, a narrow third-person camera angle, and a sprawling base filled with potential threats , sneaking behind enemy lines has rarely felt so tense and immersive. Metal Gear famously stars characters with exceptional sneaking skills, but they also come equipped with fantastical gadgets that make their jobs easier by revealing enemy locations and alert states.Though it's unusual for everything to take place in a single location, there's so much to do and see, and whether you take a stealthy or head-on approach, infiltrating Camp Omega is a thrilling experience that shouldn't be missed.

Primordia is a point and click adventure game set in a post-apocalyptic world strewn with pieces of machinery.  You play as Horatio Nullbuild, who has a rather peaceful existence ruined when a powerful robot steals the power source of his ship.  Horatio and his companion Crispin leave their home and head for the city of glass and light - Metropol.  Here, you will uncover secrets of your past and gain a better understanding of humans who previously walked there.
Primordia does not reinvent the genre, it is a sci fi adventure game that offers a dark and meaningful story - something lost in some modern point and click games.  The game provides excellent atmosphere, a rich script, solid puzzles and an art style that is really captivating.  It is the sort of game that tries to restore the classic point and click genre and I believe it has truly nailed it.  It feels like the 90's, but shows that with careful animations, voice acting and intricate details, that 'modern' resolutions and graphics are not always necessary.
I wanted to find out more and had to see the different endings, take different paths and look for more information online.  The only fault would be that it is perhaps too short, especially if you are used to classic adventure games.  Some puzzles were pretty difficult and there were a few moments of "That doesn't make much sense", though that's something I always expect from these games.
It is not really going to interest people who don't play point and click games.  It is for people who miss games like The Dig, Beneath a Steel Sky and maybe even the classic Fallout games (in terms of atmosphere).  It has replay value, great soundtrack, top storytelling and is certainly difficult enough to stump you in a few places.  Highly recommended.

Primordia, a point and click adventure game that has quite good story with challenging puzzles. More or less like The Cat Lady... the good and the bad. To sum it up:
Pros:
- Great/Mature story
- Multiple endings
- Challenging puzzles... to the point I required help from walkthrough *ahem*
- Funny dialogues
- Great voice actors
- Decent price point
Bad:
- Weak graphic engine, seriously. I even had a Developer helped me to get the game up and running.
- Art isn't up to my standard.
- A bit short game (approx 5 hours), but for 2.5 USD when discounted/on sale (or bundled), well... I guess  can't be helped.
The gameplay is just another point and click adventure. You pick up one object, deliver it to one character, get another item to unlock another area... rinse and repeat. You also are required to pay attention to hints collected. Not so much new invention in this aspect.
Story, well, I can't say much without spoiling anything, but the story is interesting enough. In fact, I wouldn't have completed the game had the story been bad. It's like, again, The Cat Lady - light story in the beginning and developing slowly until the finale.
Soundtrack is so-so, not that good but not that bad. Voice actors, however, are top notch. They really portray the characters well. Oh yes, don't forget about hilarious exchanges between Horatio and Chrispin throughout the game. More often than not I laughed on many occasions thanks to that funny Chrispin.
Overall, Wormwood Studios, I think, have a success creating a good game for us all. Moreover, they are willing to interact and listen to their playerbase as well: see
. I wish them luck with their future projects, too bad it won't be Primordia 2 (as has been said by the Developer himself).

This game is good, the stories a bit so-so (i am not a sci-fi fan, so this may not be the case for you), but there is a depth to the world that makes exploration satisfying. For an adventure game (and a sci-fi), it's not bad. Adventure games are usually sold based on their stroy, or their atmosphere and world; this one falls squarely with the interesting world brand of adventure games. It takes a serious stance to its story, so if you wanted another monkey island-ish adventure game, keep looking. The visuals are solid, and what humor there is (mainly in the form of referenceses, such as the crowbar) isn't very satisfying, but it's harmless.
Where the game lost me is its choice on puzzle design. There comes a time when you have to do some tasks, like convince 2 robots to stop arguing. The problem i have with it is they don't give you the information for long, so you either have to write it down or memorize it. Only after writing it down can you try to solve the riddle. It's a bit backwards, where you have to work around outdated, missing, or omited mechanics to get to the puzzle before you've even had a chance to ponder it. There is a device that records important pieces of information, but what it deems as important can be hit or miss sometimes (such as the robot diologue riddles, where the riddles aren't written down).
The game also does a very poor job of giving hints if your stuck. This problem, and a few others, are indicitive of the genre. One such problem is having puzzles where you have to guess at what the developer wanted you to use to progress. An example would be ruining soup in some adventure game, where you have mud, shoe polish, and a rat. Only one will ruin the soup, despite all of them being viable in a realist sense.
In the end, this is an adventure game, so replayability is already low. I'd rather not waste my time reruning the same diologue trees over and over, which is what i found i had to do for the robot riddle puzzles. If I couldn't write fast enough (cus memorizing the jargen and name drops was not easy), i would have to guess and restart. There are i believe 5 riddles or so, so having to restart from the 4th on can be annoying to say the least. At this point, the game felt more like work then fun, so i gave up on it. I didn't want to put in that much effort for what i felt was not enough in return.
You are expected to bring a lot to the table to get through the game. Good memory, write stuff down, and replay the same section over if you experiment. You will find that trying to force your way through diologue puzzles is very time consuming. If you get stuck and fall back on this, you might feel inticed to cheat (as i was). When i feel like i have to resort to a walkthrough to make progress, the game begins to feels like a chore. It's not fun when you have to use a walkthrough for an adventure game, because relying on it really takes you out of the world. Personally, i call it quits at that point, as i did here
To reiterate, this is not a bad game. It's a game with a vision that i fell outside of. If you played a lot of old-school adventure games, or you're a sci-fi fan, you might find a lot to like. If you find you didn't like older adventure games (or Daedelic's brand of adventure games, like The Dark Eye or Memoria), or you gravitate towards newer games like the Telltale brand of adventure games, this game may not be to you're liking.
If an old-school sci-fi adventure game with some of the problems of older games, as well a bit unforgiving approach to game design (in that you will solve problems for yourself, without more help then the developer deems nessassary) sound good to you, then this might be a game you will enjoy.
