I am not trying to be harsh.  This game has a few good points but also there are some major flaws that I have experienced in my first half hour of playing.  I will first elucidate the good, and then the bad.
Good:
- Its a pretty game.  Fairly unique style of graphics.
-Seems fun enough. Its nice to collect things and it seems like there is a decent bit to unlock.
-Has online multiplayer.
Bad:
-Erases game progress.  In my first play session I got to level 2.  My second play sessions I beat level 2 and unlocked a new item.  There is no way to equip items without first going to the main menu, so i quit (the game is supposed to auto save) equipped the item, and loaded my game back.  It put me back to level 1.  Keep in mind that moments before when I had loaded the game it had me on level 2, so this is not a case of the game simply not saving.  It ERASED the progress that I had made days previously.  This is a huge error that needs to be fixed before I will spend 1 more minute on this game.
-Too similiar to other games.  The voodoo theme is kinda fresh but other than that the game just plays like a tired twin stick shooter.  The controls feel clunky and the special attacks have terrible accuracy so you are forced to rely on your pathetic normal firing mode.  Kinds feels like a diablo III with worse graphics, worse controls, and way less content.
-like I mentioned above, the user interface is poor, forcing you to retreat to the main menu in order to equip a new item.  This is a bad system, or a terrible oversight in the game design.
-Zero online community.  I waited 20 minutes to find one game, hit refresh several times and no games at all.  Thought it might be better with some co-op action.
Overall:
If the game erasing bug were fixed, if there was an online community, and if the controls were a tad tighter I might recommend this game.  Right now however, I feel that there are plenty of roguelikes to choose from that are better than this one.  Nothing is particularly wrong with this game (besides haivng progress erased) but there is also nothing that sets this one apart.  These are the reasons that I would not recommend this game.

After a seven year break, I recently rediscovered RCT3 thanks to Steam - I used to have the whole collection on disc.
As this was the first game in the series to jump to real time 3D graphics, it somewhat polarised people during it's initial release - long term fans of the series were excited and intrepid in equal measure. Even today, the game isn't as highly regarded as it's two prequels; a view point I absolutely disagree with.
Roller Coaster Tycoon 3 is the pinnacle of the series, especially here in it's 'Platinum' form. The complexity of earlier games is still there, although managing the paths your peeps take and where they spend their money is somewhat easier and more intuitive. The 3D graphics allow you to explore the park as if you were a guest, and you can ride every creation in first person, whether the gentle spin of the teacups or the stomach churning corkscrews of your own personal magnum opus. The game has extensive tutorials which cover everything the game has to offer, and the same level of in depth tutition is available for both of the included expansion packs.
Creating coasters can still be done on the fly while you're in the middle of the games campaign mode, or it can be accomplished in a dedicated in-game tool, allowing you to build and test the coaster of your dreams without limitations. You can then save these designs to your very own catalogue, where they will be given a cash value based on the number and type of parts used. If you then wish to use this design during your main game, in any mode, you purchase it from the catalogue just as you would with other built-in designs.
Adding to the depth of creativity is the building designer. Now this is seriously impressive: You use geometric shapes and parts to literally create buildings from the ground up. It's like having a 3D jigsaw but with a limitless number of pieces, allowing you to create any shape you like, and then apply any texture you like to them. Again, this tool is available in-game straight from the main menu, and whether you use it to recreate the Tower of London or your favourite sweet shop from Blackpool Pleasure Beach, it's powerful stuff. Of course, dozens of building designs are included in game, and just like the coaster tools, you're not forced to create them from scratch if you don't want to.
The final tool to complete this insanely customisable trilogy of creation is the Peep Designer! That's right, you can create your own individuals - families, even - and customise them with your own names and such. Graphically you don't get much for the peeps, unlike the rest of the game which looks fantastic, because they're low poly models as you will have literally hundreds of them exploring your theme park at once. But it's still cool to be able to put your family in the game, and track them throughout sandboxes and scenarios.
As well as all of the above, you have the game itself. Anyone who claims that the complexity and intricacy of the earlier games has been lost, well you're playing a different game to me! Shops, finances, entrance fees, peep personalities, disasters, employees and all the minutae they involve have to be managed by you, and it's as engrossing as ever.
When you add in the superb expansions, allowing you to build swimming pools of any shape you desire, and water flumes with the same levels of complexity as the coasters, it becomes a no-brainer for fans of strategy games and Theme Park. With the addition of the included Wild expansion, you can even set up zoos and safaris, either independently or as part of your main park. Pens, viewing platforms, making sure people don't get mauled by a tiger that's chewed through a cheap fence you traded off to built a better log flume... It's all there.
The game runs really nice and smoothly and still looks great, right down to the little details like peeps throwing their arms in the air when the reach the peak of a coaster before a big drop... It is, without a doubt, the best theme park management game ever made, and an easy recommendation.

When you start off the game, everything is 8-bit. The graphics, the sounds, the music, etc. In fact, when you start the game you don't even have that much. This game starts as a parody... a journey through some rpg story. Or maybe I must say Final Fantasy, Zelda and Diablo story. You keep finding chests to unveil some new graphic mode or mechanism. It is fun through the first hour.
The minute you reach "the town", the whole game begins to fall apart. That town, OMG that town. NPCs make yo go through screens over and over again. Then the Diablo-like dungeon... it was somewhat fun, but not that much. Then that forest where you need to torch some bushes over and over and over again touching crystals going from present to past... over and over and over again!
I really tried to like this game. But it is an exercise on patience against boredom. Some people say it is a short game. I think it should've been even shorter.

I would have to say I both recommend and don't recommend this game. But the end of this review, I'll have decided which I would rather say overall, but I'll explain my reasonings:
The concept of this game is great; a journey through the history of video games where you unlock the different things through finding them in chests. This is a very charming game and probably worth playing at least a little while just for the concept. If you are huge into RPGs and even other games, such as Minecraft, you will be able to enjoy the references and easter eggs throughout. (Yes, they make a reference to Minecraft once).
However, these qualities can be overshadowed by the fact that the game feels like it's just stealing a bunch of games and mashing them together and the difficulty becomes increasingly frustrating. There is also one portion where you are able to choose between the male and female characters, and I had to restart my playthrough because playing as the girl made it much more difficult than when I went to play with the guy character. And in that same region, there are some minor graphical errors. The final boss battle is also pretty frustrating. It's simple, but it gives you absolutely no extra time to put in hits. The difficulty is frustrating at times, but as are a lot of games, so that attribute can be considered both a quality and an impedement.
I did enjoy the minigame "Double Twin", I'm not sure how original it is, but it is fun.
Overall, this is a pretty fun game. Enjoyable, although it does have its downsides. If you are bored and don't have anything else to play, it's an alright option.

Among its strengths are:
1.Pretty nice looking. Even if not the most visually intense game it's filled with a original flair and style that make it stand apart and not look ''standart''.
2.Unlike other games in this or similar genres differences in factions here mean a lot. You have a faction that cannot declare war on others. Another that cannot have more than 1 city. And one that cannot use food as a resource.
3.Using all of the DLC ( for when this review was posted ) you can have a surprisingly complex and deep game mechanically speaking.
And now to it's weaknesses:
1.Even as someone who is familiar with this genre it takes a while to get used to all its quirks and mechanics. This might make the first few tries frustrating.
2.One of the reasons why it's difficult to get into is probably because the game doesn't tell you very much about the characteristics and requierments for many things. Mind you they are almost never hidden from you but you need to know where to look.
3.And while the enormous differences among the factions might make them far more unique compared to other games they also mean that some factions are way harder for newbies to play as than others.

What can I say about this game, well I'm no hardcore legacy MGS fan and I couldn't give a donkey toss who Hideo Kojima is. I have fond memories of the 1998 PS1 MGS and that is about it.
I got this in a flash sale for about £3.50
The errr, game (I can't call it that; I'll just say 'mission') - can be rushed in about 15-20 minutes if you are running and gunning which is huge fun, but I was severly affronted when it ended... I actually said very loud and very clear; Really?
However, the depth to the mission while stealthing is huge and is really where this shines. Lots of nice options when dealing with enemies like neutralising, disarming, KO'ing, killing, interrigating, stabbing, chatting to then putting to sleep etc. Lots of routes, lots of options to the objectives. A small mix of vehicles, a surprising selection of weapons and some pretty decent voice acting - Even got Kiefer Sutherland as Snake... although he must say about 8 words throughout the mission in total. Its a got a lot of good things going for it.
The mission WILL catch you out plenty if you want to ghost it... this isn't a 'KO/Kill everyone on the map' type of game - As the mission progresses things change and that option / route you thought you left open for later, probably won't be, you'll be forced out of your comfort zone and forced to think and improvise - which coming my worlds of Thief / Splinter Cell / Dishonored - Is refreshing.
There are some 'grown up' themes thrown in to the plot, at least one actually hard-to-watch cutscene and a completely non-sensical story....
The mission is not worth more than a fiver though.... with the main game, mission, being so astonishingly, unjustifiably unbelieveably short. This is a bit like the Hitman: Sniper Challenge - A precursor to a bigger and proper, fully fledged game (The Phantom Pain obvs) which I'm looking forward to eventually playing thanks to this.
Saying all this there is plenty of re-play value, extra missions (rehashing the same 'map' / base used in different ways) and an absolute bucket load of easter eggs, secrets and fun to be had - So I'd recommend it to anyone into similar titles to Splinter Cell - but pick it up cheap... dead cheap.

Tough, but (almost always) fair, puzzles? Done. A compelling narrative? Oh yeah. This game has all of two downsides - first, that clues are sprinkled into the dialogue, but there isn't a way to reexamine or replay it, so sometimes you're left guessing. Second, the game is short - but this is more of a nitpick than anything, because its actual length belies the completeness which the game concludes with. Ultimately, this is a great work by a talented team, and the only real reason you wouldn't like it is because you don't like point and click adventures.

I'm not giving a thumbs down because I out and out dislike the game - I'm not not entirely sure if it's worth the trailer hype and full price purchase given the shortcomings. Feels like a spiritual successor of sorts to Beneath A Steel Sky, something I'm surprised more people didn't pick up on. Visually it all works and the music pleasantly chugs along - Along with some humour from Horatio and Crispin.
Here's the problem though; Just as the game allows you to get more comfortable and eager to explore the story more, it stops becoming fun. The middle section of the game has some painful 'swap this for that' puzzle sequences that become a chore, and you are only driven to continue because of the story, and trust me, you will be looking at a walkthrough at some point, some of the puzzles are too obtuse.
It also ends far too soon - overall only having 2 main environments in the whole game is not that satisfying at all, and what could have been quite atmospheric starts to feel a little brownwashed. The character development was never built up long enough for me to feel any emotional connections with the characters, and there were some uninspired and cliched plot turns. Beneath A Steel Sky never varied too much in environment either but at least it stayed enjoyable right to the end. There are multiple paths in the game to take which will lead to different endings - but it really depends on whether you enjoyed the first run to want to do this, and I'm not entirely sure if I want to play this game again for a while. Shame there's no windowed mode either, can appreciate the Lucasarts style resolution/graphics decision but couldn't easily leave the window or tweak anything.
I'm not saying it's a bad game, trust me, it isn't - I would just suggest you wait for it to go on sale, as there's a chance you could be disappointed like I was.

Overall satisfying adventure game with only a few caveats.  Most of all I recommend this game.
Pros:
• Thought-provoking story full of moral ambiguities and juxtaposed viewpoints making you question your own judgments of the characters and their actions.
• Good interface with a minimum of unnecessary clicking and waiting.
• Varied endings dependant on choices made by the player.
• Interesting scenery, good voice acting, and excellent atmosphereic soundtrack.
Cons:
• Completely unnecessary gender references at various points.  It's a world full of robots... Why does there need to be a "female" robot with boob-curves, or gender binary relationship references between androgynous mechanoids?
• Serious tone somewhat undermined by numerous 4th-wall jokes by  a main character.
• Lots of back-tracking and occasionally preposterous leaps in logic were needed to solve puzzles.  Several times I found myself resorting to "randomly combine junk until something happens" or having to look up walkthroughs, and being utterly baffled how someone would arrive at that solution.
As stated above, I do highly recommend this game, and I enjoyed the story.  You should check it out!

All the while, Horatio simply wants his power core.
A brilliant, rich and enticing game. It asks more questions that it answers, while playing with your imagination and leaves you wanting more from this universe. All in all, if you're looking for a game that challenges your logic and problem-solving skills, while experiencing a well-developed world and excellent cast of characters, look no further.

I, for one, continue to welcome our Neo-Roguelike caretakers (ALL WILL BOW BEFORE THE MIGHT OF THE HEGONOMY OF DARK SOULS CLONES).
First things first. Yes, Full Mojo Rampage *is* like that Binding Of Isaac game. In that same way that BoI is like Berserk; Improved upon in virtually every way. It's like if Blizzard decided to put their unique, super-effective pass of polish and gloss on a BoI game.
- The Mojo/Relic/Inventory system is a nice 'tactical balance' constant decision spot for the player to get caught up in, as are shops at which you can buy AND sell, and the Mojo Mixer, which lets you meld 2 individual powerups into a dual (cannot be melded further).
- All Character Classes can be unlocked just by expending 10 Medallions (used to purchase Masks/Classes/Playthrough Bonuses), which are reasonably easy to find (can easily find 10 in a decent run - not even a good run). The Classes themselves have a good amount of playstyles represented, with the exception of a melee (although there is a close range / melee-esque class).
- There are Persistent Systems for Player Level (each level you can upgrade one Stat slightly) and Gold, which can be spent in shops, or spent on upgrading persistent "Pins", which provide bonuses to your character such as extra inventory slots, more health or damage or critical chance, faster spell cooldowns, a chance to poison or slow enemies, etc. (you can carry 1-5 pins with you (Player level dependent) of the 25 or so available). Pins drop randomly during gameplay (I have yet to find a duplicate, but I still have 4 or so to find).
- The level layout is randomized, as is the order or appearance of levels in the 'overworld map', for an extra layer of difference in each playthrough. Different Acts (Quests) have a very different base layout (in particular, Exploration Time Before Boss Fight decreases as you advance through the Quests).
- Uses the same Elite Monster paradigm as Isaac/Risk Of Rain (and you know, Diablo/ Titan Quest), but I'm into the 3rd Act, and there definitely are not as many unique Bosses/Sub-Bosses as in Isaac.
- Already has native gamepad support and genuinely good graphics (although I actually prefer the mouse aiming to twinstick shooting).
- Has 2 Player Local and 4 Player Online Co-Op play (I have not yet sampled these modes)
The long and short of this is that Full Mojo Rampage gives me that 'Just one more game' feeling, as well as that pleasant surprise of getting that one item that saves your run, as well as that shock when your stupendously overpowered character dies miserably. Which brings me back around to just one more game.

This game is like a memento for classic RPG games, and it's a good one. The story is nothing special, and random encounters at one point can be rather boring/annoying, but the overall atmosphere and difficulty are compensating that.

This was certainly better and longer than expected.
In its core it is mostly Zelda and final fantasy gameplaywise, with short references into other games, thus this being part of what (admittedly small) length it has.  It uses those 2 rather well though, allthough the random encounters felt far too frequent. You unlock new graphics etc. by opening chests zeldastyle.
To get 100% you will probably need a couple more hours without google, since the game is pretty good at hiding goodies or even entire areas and at locking them behind puzzles. Without any sidedestractions id say you will beat this in 3 hours at most though.
There isnt a reason to go 100% other than the sense of achievement either, since the game isnt exactly keen on giving away cool stuff, which is also part of what bothered me: I beat your little mini cardgame with 10 cards, in every difficulty I dont WANT the other 13, I dont WANT another hidden star, i want some cool kind of equipment.
The music is pretty decent sometimes but mostly just gets the job done. Perhaps I entirely missed so many hidden audial messages in the music, aside from the expected 8-bit to 16-bit etc switch, but in case I didnt I think it would have been decent to think of something there, since this tries to represent the evolution of games and boy did music evolve with it.
Graphicwise it is pretty cool that they added quite a few layers between first and final graphics (with jabs at "HD" versions of stuff from the past that still looked like crap), but I still feel like they could have done more steps in between, and the final graphics look kind of ugly in my opinion as well. Going fruther than that would have also enabled more steps in between.
The story is absolutely not worth mentioning, it wont be why you played this, same goes for character development etc.
All together I love it though, it is full of hidden references, it copy pastes gameplay from the other games in ways that work well and I love the idea in general, very decent for a part 1 gonna play part 2 now and hope a lot of things improved. Is it worth 10 dollars though? Hmmm that depends on if "well that was kinda fun" as a result after 3 hours is worth 10 dollars to you. I guess most would say no and should wait on a sale

Really well made nostalgia trip for any jRPG fan, but not necessarily a good game on its own. Evoland takes you through the "evolution" of the genre with ideas and mechanics taken from titles such as Zelda, Final Fantasy, and even Diablo. It's really clever, original and quite accurate, as it shows not only how the games changed from the gameplay standpoint, but also on the audiovisual level.
That said, on its own Evoland is not a great game. It's simple, linear, often tedious. About halfway through you unlock the "final" graphics style, but there's still a lot to do. At this point the game starts to drag on, as none of the combat systems is fleshed out, enemy variety is very small, levels are hard to navigate without a map, and the story is basic and straightforward.
I'd still recommend it as a cute and funny experience. Any person familiar with some of the old-school RPGs will find a lot of references here. Plus, the game isn't long, so it may be worth getting during a sale.

2 hours in and I knew it was a great game, 15 hours in I had to tell others about it!  So here I am.
A 2D top down space shooter whilst accurate, is a poor description for this game as there is much more to it than that.  The graphics although basic are perfect for the game.  The sound is also well chosen.
You start in a pre-designed ship but as time goes on you can add to the design or just create a new one from scratch.  There are a decent variety of weapons and other modules to choose from, like rockets, missiles, torpedoes, mines, lasers, projectile based weapons and crazier ones.  Your ships can also house a factory to build other ships on the fly, which in turn can have a factory and can build.  With a bit of time you can have a fleet of AI controlled ships following you around until you dismiss them to do their own thing, and they do.  AI ships not under your control will continue to gather resources and contribute to your factions efforts.  Time to colonise and control the galaxy!
The map is large, and the factions varied, although I am now starting to get slightly bored of the existing factions, but there are many more in the Steam Workshop.
My only criticisms of the game are as follows; Agents, which are player made ships that spawn into the game and severely ruin your day, are often too good and numerous when they first appear.  You could ignore them until stronger, however once you give them a foothold in the galaxy they are really hard to remove.  In addition, you reach the endgame of progression in terms of unlocking blocks and maximum ship size too soon, normally after a couple of hours.
All being told, an excellent buy.
EDIT: Nominated it for the Steam Award “I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award” Award.

You know, I've been waiting for a game like this to appear. I love space, spaceships, and I love games where there's something that lets my creativity run wild. Glad I found this gem!
This is a game where you control a single ship of faction you choose at the beginning of the game. You can customize it however you want it with the pieces the faction provides. Each faction is unique in a way and none are the same. You fly around, you shoot enemies, gather resources, unlock new modules, grow in power, build up your ship to become an unstoppable destroyer, unlock other factions to play as, and so on.
Of course you don't need to fly alone, you can build up your fleet, or hire pilots from your faction to join you and fly with it. You'll soon be able to conquer the entire galaxy. Also, the galaxy has a fair amount of 'agents', which are fleets that were made by other players. Most of the ones I've seen so far were pretty formidable so if you see a red arrow, you should run until you really feel confident you'll break their ships with ease. Oh, and if you're done playing in that one galaxy you started in? Use a wormhole to fly to another one! This will also upload your current fleet, and chances are, someone, somewhere, on planet Earth, will be soon encountering your very own fleet on their computer. And he'll probably have trouble destroying you.
What's truly beatiful about this game is how simple it looks, and how complex it actually is. You could actually consider this game some sort of art. You start in a tiny sector, and you can see pretty early on how dynamic the world is. The AI harvests the minerals, grows in size, expands, it gets better with you, and so on. For example, I once built a single ship that could build stations. I manufactured it from my flagship, kicked it from the fleet so it could be independent, and guess what. Soon enough, when I came back, there were like, 15 stations there, and a whole lot of tiny little fighter ships scuttling around. It was an awesome sight. To be honest, the game kinda looks more organic than scientific. It's like actual organisms battling against each other. Sort of.
Well, either way, if you like space, spaceships, and space battles, if you like being creative, if you like shooting stuff up, if you like seeing your ship grow from a super fast tickling drone to a slow, massive hulking beast of absolute annihilation, if you like sending your enemies to oblivion, then chances are you're going to appreciate this game. It's got a fair amount of replayability, and even though it looks simple, it's really lots of fun.

+Gameplay and mechanics are quite good, however I wish Snake could do a little bit more climbing. He is kind of limited and can only climb when a prompt appears on the screen in front of ledges and what now. There were a few instances where I felt limited, but it wasn't game breaking.
+The locked missions are great and full of easter eggs and throwbacks. The locked mission De Javu lets you recreate scenes from the original MGS game the challenge is to find the locations on the map based on the photos given to you at the start of the mission.
+You get to play as Raiden from Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance in the locked Jamais Tu mission.
+Decent replayability for each mission due to achievements and challenges if you are into that sort of thing.
+There is a background section to bring you up to speed on who Snake is and the motherbase if you aren't familiar with the Metal Gear universe.
+The missions all offer individual unique challenges to include rescue. extraction, assassination, destroying emplacements, and collecting intelligence.
Cons:
- The only way to play the locked missions is to find these XOF patches that are scattered all over the map in the main mission. The problem is that you have no idea at all where to find them and they are almost impossible to see. There are 9 in total.  The odds of you coming across all of them without knowing where to look are next to impossible. You can sneak up behind guards and interrogate them and they tell you random information about where to find ammo, locations etc and you never know from game to game what they will tell you. Sometimes its a patch location sometimes a cassette, it is very tedious I found 2 patches on my own and didn't want to spend another 10 hours or so playing the mission over and over again hoping the guards would tell me, so I looked up a guide.
- Ending credits at the end of each mission that can be sped up but annoying nonetheless.
- Short story can be seen as a money grab by some, for 20 USD though it isn't too bad and if you take advantage of all the game has to offer.
If you are on the fence about buying MGSV The Phantom Pain pay less and play this one first, if you like it like I did, chances are you will feel comfortable purchasing it.
TLDR: Good game if short with good easter eggs (which are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to unlock )and high replaybility. The perfect  prologue for the potential MGSV buyer.

Primordia is quite good overall. Among its best assets are its strong sense of style and its audio.  Both the music and the voice acting are excellent. I liked it a lot. It's dark and grim. It's about "Horatio Nullbuilt", a somewhat stoic and secretive humanoid robot living alone in some long-stranded organic-looking airship in the middle of some barren brown desert. Humans are long gone, only machines remain, some worship them - or their legacy - in a secluded and lonesome manner as Horatio does. He has a self-built low-grade flying companion robot, "Crispin Horatiobuilt", who is an obvious sidekick, who keeps refering to himself as that and who is supposed to be a constant contrast to his builder for he is not as nearly withdrawn as him but more humorous, even on a meta-like level for example when he comments your futile efforts to do the same thing over and over and expecting different results.
There are more interesting characters to see. All kinds of machines who inhabit the few remaining places in the world. Be it a bomb from some long-past war that never detonated and which is worshipped for it is a creation of man, the remains of colossal titan robots buried deep within the desert or old human cities maintained by robots just enough not to collapse totally.
Primorida is a middle-scaled adventure for what I can tell. It has an interesting story, great characters, powerful voice acting (every character is voiced - and those robots who cannot talk bleep around in their own manner) and a significant amount of puzzling too. If I remember right I had to look up a walkthrough a few times, though I guess I was just blind on one eye for the solutions seemed reasonable afterwards. There are several endings, they all seem fitting and interesting in their way, and while the decision which you will see is made very lately in the game it is still somewhat relevant what you do mid-game.
There is a significant amount of lore background. You will meet characters who share their stories and views on the world. You will learn more about them, their motivations and failures. There is a robot society that kinda imitates human society. It has it's own leadership and entities. However barely anything about is perfect. It is in demise, and Horatio is trying to find his way through. He is connected to the world around him more than he admits, and getting to know him better was done very well I think, from robots remembering him to data logs hidden within the places he visits. The art is nice, there are some great dark or soothing music tunes, everything seemed crafted together well and I thought I was satisfied with all aspects of the game even though it has been a long while since I've played it. Definitely the best adventure from Wadjet Eye Games I've played thus far.

Ryse: Son of Rome is pretty cool, I guess.
You play as Titus Marius, a man with a very cool name.
Titus is a new recruit in the Roman Legions, assigned to the 2nd and soon to be off to Alexandria. But when his family is murdered, he's enlisted into the XIV Legion by Commander Vitallion. From there, Titus goes on a field trip to Britannia where he embarks on a mission of war, revenge, patriotism, and betrayal.
Also, he gets a really, really cool looking sword.
Ryse: Daughter of Greece is a third person action game in vain of other games like God of War and Batman. Titus is armed with a Gladius (That looks really cool), a shield, and a handful of javelins known as pilums. I would recommend playing this game with a controller, but do what you want, I'm not your dad.
Your face buttons cover the basics, you have an attack, a shield bash, a block that doubles as a counter if you time it right, and a dodge button. So it plays like Batman, yeah, but it also has the added bonus (or negative depending on who you ask) that Titus comes equipped with a good number of fatalities you can pull off on any mook that is marked with a skull over their head after you do enough damage. Although flashy and nice to look at, they, much like my criminal record, tend to repeat.
The game tries to even this out by adding a little color coated quick time event during these scenes, you don't HAVE to press anything while they play out, but if you don't you  miss out on extra experience. Experience is used on what you expect, increasing things like your health, your focus meter, and even spending experience so you can gain more experience overall.
One of Ryse's strongest points is its cinematography and choreography. As simple as the story is, it's actually rather entertaining to watch when you aren't slicing people up and taking their property. Characters are surprisingly life-like in the way they move and speak. John Hopkins and Tim Treloar take it home with their performances of Marius and Vitallion, bringing a sense of life and personality to the characters that would have sounded like gruff generic guys if anyone else were to do it.
The Roman Empire as shown in Ryse is also pretty asthetic. Armors are ornamental and weapons are very flashy. Titus' Gladius has a outward curve to it that makes it look like something someone would use in a Dungeons and Dragons game, and any important character seems to have their own personalized weapon, like they were custom made just for them. It also helps that I want to have a romantic relationship with Roman architecture and themes in general, and maybe a little bit of a relationship with Titus.
Because he's hunky.
But, if you're looking for historical accuracy, you should go look somewhere else. Ryse's depiction of the Roman empire is very fantastical and different. Damocles isn't really a "Spirit of Vengence", considering it's a Greek tale about how riches and power also grants peril and anxiety.
Commodus was actually the son of Marcus Aurelius instead of Nero. Boudica's army never made it out of Briton, let alone reach Rome, and I have no idea what Boudica's real father's name was, nobody apparently does.
There's also other glaring things, the Roman Scutum is way too small in this game for what it actually was used for. And for being one of the most organized and professional army the world has ever seen, the Romans in this game sure are unorganized, only taking formation and not fighting like unruly brawlers when Titus or Vitallion tell them to fight like how they're supposed to.
See, you learned something today.
But should you play Ryse: Son of Rome?
I got it for 5 dollars, which is a good price for what it is. It took me around 5 hours to complete with one extra hour screwing around on the multiplayer mode, which itself is just a two player horde mode type ordeal. But the story is entertaining and the voice acting is pretty great. And for what it is, the combat is also pretty good for the 5 or so hours you can to play with it.
The game however, is also pretty easy. The only reason why I didn't beat it on Legendary is because I had to actually beat the game first to play on legendary, and the difficulty right under it wasn't all that tough. Still, if you can get it on sale, I don't see why you shouldn't give Ryse a go.

So this is going to be a lengthy one, the game is at the quality all Indie Early Access games should be at release! It is not perfect in any way but it is solid and playable! I will go through the different aspects of the game to cover them!
Graphics: The graphics are good and i think this might be the first game where it looks better in-game than on the screenshots. The style is obviously toony but it fits well! The menu is also really cool!

Champions Online... where to begin with this one? Probably with a bit of history, for your personal culture. On the 28th September 2006, Microsoft Game Studios and Cryptic Studios announced a brand new multiplayer game for the Xbox 360 known as Marvel Universe Online. The only thing we can all Google about this project is a short teaser with an epic music that shows actually nothing revelant about the game itself but it was here... until the 11th February 2008 when Marvel decided to cancel everything without explaination.
Ending with an almost completed game in their hands, Cryptic Studios didn't really want to lose this investment although they lost the Marvel licence for publication. So they played it smart : just looking for another super-heroic universe, they found a table-top roleplaying game called Champions created by George MacDonald, Steve Peterson, Bruce Harlick and Ray Greer in 1981. It was more or less the same thing as Marvel and DC so they exploited this newly acquired licence to quickly rebuild their game, renaming it Champions Online at the same time.
Fact is, when you look at Champions' lore it seems quite dark, mature like DC because when we think Marvel many people instantly remember Spider Man, Deadpool and other cheerful characters. The best example for this argument could be the fact that one vigilante from Champions (named Nighthawk) looks shockingly like Batman from DC, and we can even find some kind of Joker in characters like Black Harlequin or Jack Fool... but that's probably me being nitpicky over the cell-shading technology employed in this game, while the feeling of the characters and places seem darker than that?
Anyway, back to the game itself! I would recommand Champions Online for one thing mainly : near limitless character creation and customisation. If you've played City of Heroes before, you see what I mean instantly, it should be the spark that will ignite your wild imagination. For the new players who never got the chance to play this game (now lost because NCSoft have decided to shut it down, mostly to capitalise on the Guild Wars franchise) just give it a try, considering that it's free to play and nothing there will force you to open your wallet just to enjoy the game entirely... unlike what Electronic Arts have done with the "free" to play model of Star Wars The Old Republic.
Indeed, the gameplay is repetitive, even tedious sometimes considering that all you'll do is punching or shooting bad guys over and over again, just to level up, complete a mission, get a rare loot, gain Questionite or obtain the Mods you're looking for. But then we could argue over the fact that it's "essential" to any massively multiplayer online roleplaying game : Everquest, Ultima Online, Lineage, Dark Age of Camelot, Perfect World International, World of Warcraft, Allods Online, Aion, Tera... none of them has avoided that part. Even Firefall (quite an interesting MMO third-person shooter) couldn't dodge the bullet, but the game is still fun nonetheless.
One thing I personally appreciate nowadays with Champions Online is that you can get everything for free. Really, no trap there but you'll need to invest a bit of yourself and your free time into it if you want to gain something. Remember this Questionite I mentioned quickly earlier? If you get enough of it, you can trade it on the in-game Market for Zen points, and said currency can be used to purchase things in the Zen Store such as costume packs, travel powers, new Archetypes to play with and (for the absolute zealot or masochist) even the mighty Freeform Slot.
But what is a Freeform you may ask? Simple : it's a character who has access to all the powers available to players in the game, and can combine them as they see fit. Of course, many veterans will claim that "Freeform > Archetypes" but believe me when I claim that I've seen some horribly designed Freeform characters and even made my own mistakes when I first tried. A Freeform character is only extremely powerful if you intent to design it this way, and some Archetypes can still beat you if the player knows what he / she's doing. You could try for example to challenge Fleur@Augusti to a duel : this guy plays a Blade Archetype, and has probably taken down more Freeform in a month than myself in a year.
To conclude : this game has potential, and it's absolutely free as long as you want it to be. You can spend your money if you want to reward Cryptic Studios (and the newly created Cryptic North) for the few improvements they brought to the game, or you can start farming the Questionite if you happen to be some kind of grumpy Uncle Scrooge because one single Zen point is worth 225 to 250 Refined Questionite Ores on the Market. It's definitely not a ground-breaking game that will strike your mind as astonishingly beautiful, original or even just flawless... but some people may see there an Eldorado where the player can become King if they find the energy to climb their way to the top, while some artists would find a tool to unleash their creativity and try out their ideas.

I really wanted to like this game. The character art is good, the story isn't breaking any new ground but it's fairly competently executed, and I thought the idea of a JRPG set in a single building and grounds, where you kept getting new exploration tools to open up secrets metroidvania-style, was kind of interesting.
Unfortunately, the combat is a drag -- the enemies are almost never threatening and the strategy involved was about as shallow as possible. It felt like the combat was just there because RPGs usually have combat and wasn't doing much that was interesting or useful. Making the monsters scarier and more threatening, or spending a little more time on the combat, or even just taking it out entirely would have been better.
Overall the game seemed to lack polish -- I ran into a lot of layering errors, events that repeated when they obviously weren't supposed to, and kept spotting typos in things like monster ability names where they should have been easy to catch. Some of the environments felt sparse, with acres of blank floor, and I felt like the atmosphere could have been really improved with more little details like stuff to look at (I kept checking barrels and bookcases for interesting tidbits or items, but to no avail), more flavorful equipment, and more movement and reactions from characters in cutscenes rather than just text box after text box.
Ultimately, I hit a game-ending bug and couldn't continue. I might email the dev for a fix at some point (since apparently it SHOULD be fixed by now?) but I'm not so excited about the game that I feel absolutely compelled to take extra steps to reach the ending.
All in all it seems to have the foundation of a great game but fails to follow through.

I really liked this game.  I have a lot of RPG Maker type games, and this one managed to stand out.
The whole Lovecraft vibe is very well presented and is one of my favorite things about this game.  Creepy ancient monastery, weird characters with weird quirks, eerie sound effects- they all pull together to keep the mood slightly horrifying.
As others have noted, there is a lot of backtracking and searching for items you missed or places that you couldn't access before, but that is part of the fun.  The levels tend to be maze-like and the backtracking helps to keep the map in your head.
The monsters and battle system are standard- more there to keep the danger vibe than to offer any real challenge.  This game is definitely story oriented rather than action oriented.
There were times that I needed to look up the location of certain items, because they aren't always noticeable.  There is a little sparkle in interactive places, but sometimes you need to be standing in exactly the right spot to notice.  It only happened 3 or 4 times, so it didn't really affect my gameplay.
For replayabilty- There are two different endings you can get and achievements to unlock. For this type of game,  I usually wait a while before playing it again so I can be startled all over again and  find secrets that I had forgotten, but it is a game that I'll be playing again.
You should be able to finish the game in a day.  I recommend a rainy, dreary, quiet day when you feel like playing something dark and moody, but still casual.

All in all, loved it.

After spending hours trying to find the upgrade that made the gameplay fun and interesting, and combing through a walkthrough, I was dismayed to learn no such upgrade exists.
I gave this game way too many opportunities to redeem itself, and it never did. I saw it in the store, and it looked nice. A friend got it and played it. Told me it wasn't worth my money. So that wouls have been the end of it, but I think I ended up with a copy froma  Humble Bundle or something. It sat in my library for about a year, until, bored one day, I fired it up.
It starts out in the standard manner for this sort of game - you start with one direction of movement, then unlock the others. Cheesy, but the earliest games were reestricted to lateral movement and the like, so I was game. Up until you pick up the transition from grayscale to 16 colors. The grayscale setup was a bit of a stretch, since graphics never really worked that way for early games (not counting  handhelds), but I was being lenient. 16 color made it clear that the designers had never really looked at the graphics for anyhting earlier than Playstation era. Even if the system could handle so many colors on a single sprite, it means the main character permanently occupies half the available pallette of the world. (Fun fact: Mega Man had to be composed of two sprites to support his whopping total of 5 colors).
Clearly, the developers were aware of how much they messed up 16 colors, because they jumped to 256 colors almost immediately. As noted above, though, they never did the same for the gameplay. In fact, they actively made the gameplay worse than the old games they claim to emulate - as part of a cheap gimmick, you get an upgrade that unbinds you from the grid. While that should be a good thing, it means you're out of alignment with enemies more often than not. And 95% of the game still uses a grid, so you're not getting much benefit from it. Up to and including gaps between trees like the cute barrier they put in place for you to bypass - nearly indistinguishable from the normal grid barriers, and exceedingly rare.
Problems like this pop up so often that it becomes clear that the immediate jump from 16 colors to 256 wasn't any sort of self-awareness; they want the game to be "pretty" as fast as possible. They take way too long to add a health bar to progress beyong 1 hit = death. They add a "Loading" screen that costs 5000 GP to get rid of - from random fights that drop 100-200 GP each (not that there's much worthwhile to spend your money on, but it's still a stupid aproach).
Things start to get some hope when they drop you into a Diablo-style section, but that's msotly padding and an excuse for cheap jokes - back to the status quo after that. With one exception - you get a combo chain ability (because we all know that Diablo invented the combo chain).
All in all, it starts off with some promise, but the hope for it to get better gradually fades. On top of that, 2/3 of the way through the game, you've unlocked pretty much eveything, and from that point on, it may as well be called "Spinal Clam SE: Heaven". Except that still gives too much credit to the story writing.

-The Appeal-
Awesomenauts appeal comes from its fastpace gameplay, colorful graphics, and great soundtrack (I recommend you buy the OST if you dig the game). It's clean and open movement allow alot to work with. Matches don't last long so your not stuck losing, however there is still a good enough chance to turn the game in your favor even if losing. While waiting for matches you can watch your previous games (even your friends matches), watch games currently in progress or play that super secret minigame. You don't need to be the biggest moba fan to play. I never have and will likely never play another moba and I love this game.

I've been playing for years so I've been though the rough spots of this games history and I can say the 4.0 update has done alot for the better. They've still got a few thing that need to be worked out but Awesomenauts is sitting in a good spot. I started this game with zero knowledge of anything other than the music is amazing, did terrible and worked my way up to the point I can call myself a good player. Sometimes I wish I could stop playing this game, but nothing else offers anything like Awesomenauts.

Probably the best game by the late Cryptic studios now has been ruined by region locking and unbalanced f2p features. Do not bother buying it. In fact - do not buy any games bought and ruined by Perfect World.
That said - there are two things that every mmo should try to emulate in future:
1) You can create completely custom characters with abilities from any class. You could easily make magic based character with some perks from tanky tech based character. You can paint all of your abilities in different colors. You can change every piece of cloth, weapon or gadget.
2) Each character can grab two different methods of travel - for example superspeed and flight. Or ice-path and super jump. Teleportation and flight on a piece of earth. Each type of travel has its perks and downsides, they can also be customized with different effects and colours.
Everything else is pretty much standard for mmo's - grinding, questing, instancing, group events. Unfortunately developers quickly run out of ideas and predictably were forced to make it f2p.

This game had a lot of potential.  I played all the way back into late alpha testing, when some of the forum goers were allowed to join the tests.  It was a great game back then.  The problem was, that the part of the community that yelled the loudest, always got their way.  "The squeaky wheel gets the oil."  Well, the truth was, that if 15 people said something one way, and 3 said it another way, but those 3 kept ranting and raving while the 15 said "forget this, these people are just flaming everyone" then the 3 got their way.  Strange, but true.
So, the game got hammered with stupid changes that made the average player unable to play at all.  This gave the game a bad start, but those things got fixed.  Over time, the bad start took it's toll financially, and Cryptic Studios had to switch publishers.  The new publisher, Perfect World Entertainment, is notorious for the garbage they make.  What's more, is regardless of what the devs may say, it's pretty obvious that the direction of the game changed pretty fast.  More half-nude women, lockboxes, pay to win style upgrades and boosts, and more made their way into the game.  Currently, the most powerful opponent the players can face is Gravitar, a women that epitomizes both the ditz and the... female dog... in every way they can.  That means that instead of someone like Dr. Destroyer, we get a sexual icon for a villain now.  This is just the tip of the iceberg, but it's one of many reasons why this game has gone down the drain.
If you want a good superhero MMORPG, you're probably out of luck.  City of Heroes was killed by NCSoft's desire for more money.  DCUO is great, if you want to be a sidekick.  Marvel Heroes is a Diablo II clone, if you like that sort of thing.  And Champions Online?  Well, if you avoid lockboxes, boosts, alerts, vehicles, and anything put in after PWE took over, then it's actually a good game.  Most people won't play that way though, which means I can't recommend this game.  I still have my lifetime subscription that I got myself suckered into buying, though, so I'll still come back from time to time, just to have a change of pace.  After all, I haven't spent a cent on this game since launch, and I still have full VIP features still.  For anyone new, though, watch out.  This one had potential, but it was squandered by a few really bad decisions, and now it's just another pay to win style "free to play".
Oh, and if you do play, make sure you study hard on the powers.  Get the wrong power combinations, and you've just become the Super Wimp.  So much for roleplay.  =/

This is the first game hailing from Warfare Studios that I got my hands on to play, and reading many a good reviews about the developer in Aldorlea forums beforehand, I had decent expectations to begin with. All it's pros and cons gathered to make a last call,
is a good RPGMaker game, yet not a good RPG.
It all begins during a heavy rainstorm, at the ruined tower halls of a forsaken monastery. We witness a battle for life and death between a Victorian gentleman, and... An undead priest and a pretty nun??!?! As the scene changes, we meet Lecia - or rather Elecia, who is a prim and proper lady with a chemistry degree. Through her diary, we learn that Lecia's husband, Lesnar left to search for an expedition arranged by the university, for the forsaken Vermillion Monastery. Said researchers haven't been heard from since and Lecia hasn't heard a thing from Lesnar thereon either. As the story starts, Lecia dreams of Lesnar calling for help and decides to go investigate the matter herself. What she will discover shortly after, is beyond her most foul nightmares.
Okay, okay. Pretty yet smart girl, lost relative, someone calling for help to an obviously dangerous place and as the protagonist follows, a dreadful occult catastrophe threatening to end the world occurs? Yup, we have seen this one many, many times before. It's the baseline of all HOG and most RPGMaker games out there anyhow + even some Hollywood movies. Yet, what makes
notice worthy among others?
First of all, I should say that the game presents one of the better uses of RPGMaker out there. Environment design isn't terribly rich, yet it is gathered into a logical and consistent collection to present you a really, really big dungeon crawl and a decent enough atmosphere. The original midi soundtrack is pretty and the setting in enriched with even proper sound effects. The story itself is a bit lame though, but characters are enacted properly with appropriate personality undertones to make them somewhat memorable. Their story interactions are well-written. It is very much Henry James meets Arkham Horror out there.
As an RPG though, it is pretty much a straight railroad on a dungeon crawl. You recruit a party as you play, adorn them with items, defeat monsters for the experience; etc. I didn't notice any level cap, but I ended the story with my characters around level 20, and I am quite sure there was nothing else left to slay within the huge main map. If you have an idea about the prime function of any and all JRPGs, battles will become boringly easy within half an hour, and character skills are not various enough to challenge you into battle strategies. Monsters do not differ that much in their abilities either. Thus, you play for the story.
Well, there are 2 distinct endings - one happy, one not so happy - for you to discover according to your actions nearing the end. I'd say the whole thing packs 7-8 hours or gameplay if you don't mind grinding a bit and visiting the same areas within a huge map to collect loot and experience. Oh, and it has also achievements.
Last verdict? It's nothing brilliant, but a decent time kill with a story for a day. It depends on your mood. It was a bit fluffy on the "Old Ones" concept if you ask me, but who am I to judge? Overall, the game is not bad at all. Don't forget to fetch it on a sale! Good day, and good gaming to you!

Black Home is a turn-based RPG about a woman who teams up with a group of travellers to find her missing husband. The characters are pretty interesting and have unique dialogues, but the story is pretty generic (blah blah evil cult etc). It was an interesting idea to have the entire game set in one building and its grounds.
The game isn't bad really but it could have used a bit more polish. There are a few typos in the dialogue. The battle system is functional but it was never really clear to me whether various elemental attacks actually had different effects or not so I always ended up just spamming the highest level skill I had rather than using them strategically. Additionally, it was kind of annoying that there was no way to see how much health an enemy has left, so it was hard to know whether to use a skill that used up a lot of SP or not, and you didn't know how far through a boss battle you were. Music was okay but the looping clips were very short so if you were really exploring an area it could get annoying pretty quickly.
Many items that you can interact with are indicated by a little star, but some are not, so sometimes progression would halt for a bit because I didn't have an object that I didn't know I could pick up. Also in some areas it's hard to tell if the edge of the room is a transition to another area or just a wall.
Enemies are visible on the map so they're avoidable if you don't want to fight them at that moment (though it's a little weird that all enemies use the same 3 or 4 sprites) and enemies don't respawn when they're killed, which makes exploration a little more bearable. You will be backtracking over areas as you acquire equipment that makes new areas accessible so this is definitely a good thing.

Lecia Coy is trying to find her husband who is missing in an abandoned monastery. Unfortunately, this monastery is home to a number of secrets. She'll have to team up with several other people who have come here for different reasons to try and find her husband.
Black Home is an around 6-7 hour RPG that also features multiple endings. I'm not quite sure how you trigger the different endings though as I only got one. The entire game takes place within the monastery though the areas look different enough that it doesn't start to feel too dull to always be in the same place. There's only one set of collectibles to find, chess pieces, and you'll have to do a lot of digging and searching to try and find them all.
While Black Home might not be something to write home about in the end, it is an interesting game. Most of the game is fairly straightforward - I only got lost once while trying to find what I needed to progress. Some parts may make you think a bit, and as long as you don't mind that the AI of enemies trying to chase you can be a tad shaky at times, then check out Black Home.

A game with a bit of difference, but still of the 16-bit style, Black Home is an absorbing and exciting tale that takes place in an ominous old and supposedly long deserted monastery that was previously being explored by the main protagonist's (Lecia) husband who is now missing/lost within the walls of the menacing old building.
So she bravely goes in alone, and finds herself in a huge, maze-like, and (not entirely) deserted assortment of rooms, corridors, hallways, secret passageways, etc. looking for her missing loved one. And, of course, she will find strange companions (a priest, a raider, she herself is an alchemist), mysterious items, apparitions, hidden places, and spooky monsters of all sorts as she searches.
It appears that the game takes place entirely within and on the grounds of the monastery which adds to the story by confining the action to the goal of discovering all of the secrets the place has to reveal.
Artwork and graphics are very well done, especially the monsters to fight. And the monsters are visible, and sometimes appear with eerie sound effects.
And the sound effects throughout genuinely add to the creepiness of the game.
The story's pacing is very well handled as just enough information, weapons, and supplies are made available as you go ---- but you must look everywhere very carefully to discover all the secrets.
Although it is fairly linear in the overall layout, you must still stay alert so as to not bypass or overlook items or places that are important.
It's a little different, but no less fun or exciting and still keeps the 16-bit rpg flavor that I enjoy so much. Story is exceptional, and I would certainly recommend adding this one to any library. Great fun here.

On one hand, the references to Zelda and Final Fantasy are humorous if you've played them, particularly FF7, but otherwise, you won't understand the simple nods towards the two series. The throwback to the 80's, I believe, is interesting. It really makes you appreciate the progress that has happened in the last few decades. Honestly, it was eye-opening, as I didn't grow up in that era. It was fun seeing the game itself grow.
Still, despite the humor and nostalgia, Evoland doesn't really offer anything new. The story is rather short and can be completed in 3-4 hours. I honestly do not remember the story. What I do remember is that I went through dungeons, found the hastily created boss, beat him once, then again in another form. The combat is boring; it's either slash, drop a bomb, or try to aim at moving enemies. There's nothing original about it. Combat in 3D mode is LoZ while open-world combat is classic FF mixed with 3D character models. It's basic, to sum it up.
All in all, I suppose I'd recommend it. The Steam achievements are fairly easy to 100%, and if you're stuck, there are 3 wonderful guides to finding everything. However, it is rather short. Get it on sale if you're bored and have a few dollars lying around.

Evoland is an enjoyable, well-designed game for the short time you play it, filled with references that gaming veterans will easily pick up on and appreciate. However, the incredibly short playtime and some weak and ineffectual, forgettable sequences downgrade what is a good game into something that really is not worth paying for.
Gameplay wise, Evoland does what it advertises; in the beginning you start with not much at all in the way of gameplay options, even directional buttons need to be unlocked. Slowly but surely, however, the game is built around you as you play in a clever merging of gameplay and ideas. The graphics are charming throughout and as a kind of 'museum' of RPG tropes over gaming's history, the game succeeds in the showcasing aspect.
For the short amount of time you do play the game, it has a decent package; the gameplay is as you'd expect, the story does its best despite being restricted to parody territory as a result of the design ethos the game was going for, the sound is enjoyable if not exactly memorable, but sends up classic soundtracks of the genre in a recognisable way. and the graphics, in addition with how they merge with gameplay in a memorable mid-game puzzle sequence, are charming and work for their purpose in showcasing the history of the RPG genre.
However, while these ideas work to some degree, once you get past the initial impression, the game's elements all fall down as you start to look for something deeper. The storyline is basically just trope descriptors and script-reading in its most literal sense, the gameplay has some memorable and interesting moments, but over time specific elements become unenjoyable. For example, the random encounter system becomes infuriating, not least because the game's battle systems are just skin-deep at best. Combat in this game is not enjoyable and it is not deep; it's 'servicable' enough and works for the purpose of a showcase, but it really is a shame that the gameplay was not expanded upon to an extent to make Evoland worthwhile as a game in its own right. The world-building is restricted to a point it appears lazy and the sound is, as mentioned before, not memorable in its own right.
In addition to the game elements described, the length of Evoland is a cause for concern; other Steam viewers can see how many hours I've put into this game: two, to be more precise. Within two hours, I had beaten the game, and the feel of reward for beating the game any further just wasn't there for me. The game is not deep in the slightest so I had no motivation to dig any deeper as I had finished, because what I had found thus far was not valuable enough as a game to keep me coming back to try to find all of the secrets in the game.
Because of the creative ideas behind Evoland, it is a shame I am writing a negative review of this game. Evoland is, for all intents and purposes, a collection of decent ideas. It is unfortunate, then, that these ideas are never expanded upon except in the most rudimentary sense.
In conclusion, while Evoland succeeds in a small sense that it is a sometimes-humorous and appreciable showcase of the RPG genre, the incredibly small number of hours of very shallow gameplay that Evoland provides is not satisfying enough to really make it successful as a game. I would not recommend this game because it is simply not good value and a big disappointment considering how this game never lived up to its potential to be something truly interesting.

Having enjoyed the Mass Effect trilogy and Dragon Age Origins, I was looking forward to playing this. Several friends had lavished praise on this earlier Bioware game and suggested I give it a go.
I felt this was a very well realised RPG. It contains many of the trademark elements of later Bioware games, and benefits immensely from utilising the rich and wonderful mythos of Star Wars as the foundations of its story. In my view, the game has stood the test of time, with only the graphics betraying its age. I recommend KOTOR to anyone who likes RPGs, and especially those who have enjoyed Bioware's more recent offerings.
My highlights:
- Good voice acting (especially love the alien-speak!)
- Authentic star wars universe, true to the spirit of the films
- Great light side/dark side dialogue choices, some of which made me laugh out loud
- Enjoyable plot
- A large game that doesn't outstay it's welcome
- Great cut scenes
- Superb star wars-eque soundtrack
- Fantastic sound effects that are true to the movie
- Satisfying finale
Things I would love to see improved:
- Some of the playable characters were not as compelling as hoped
- Some RPG side-missions were a little tedious
- Graphics showing their age (although perfectly serviceable)
- Far too many NPCs have the same voice and face
- I experienced some bugs (e.g. certain light side/dark side options were not made available to me as a result)
- (minor) I couldn't get this playing on full screen at 1080p  via basic Steam release
All in all, loved it.

Reassembly, at first glance and without watching the trailer/gameplay, seems like a Captain Forever (i think that's what it's called) rip-off. It's not. You aren't limited to trying to destroy the enemy core ASAP to save it's pieces so you can upgrade your ship, although you pretty much have to kill in order to upgrade your ship in the first place in Reassembly. It's pretty much just Asteroids but with badass looking ships instead of a dinky triangle. It's kinda hard to explain, but basically there are multiple factions, around 15 at the time of me writing this review, and you only get to be in one at the start. To get in others, you have to kill giant murder machines from other factions to unlock them. There's also a weird credits and resource system, you gain resource (called R in-game) by either farming or murdering other factions, and you get credits (called C in-game) by dropping off your resource at stations or ships with a factory on it, and then those stations/ships can use your resource you dropped off to make more ships, possibly a ship with a factory on it, making a weird cycle.
Also, pro-tip for newbies, GET THE FARMER FACE (faction 2) AS FAST AS POSSIBLE.
It's pretty much better than all of the other factions, because they can farm with ease because they can attach plants to themselves so you can essentially farm on the go, which, as previously stated, gives you resource.
All in all, if you like ship building and somewhat intense space battles, Reassembly is for you. A solid 10/10.

I picked this game up during the Endless sale, when Endless Space 2 was about to release. Due to the sale I got the game and all DLC for about $30 so, not bad.
On the positive side, this game looks stunning. Great particle effects, great detail and with a great HD monitor and rig this game is beautiful. There's so much to see on the screen that it's visually pleasing.. at first. Here lies one issue I had with the game though - there is too damn much going on, on the screen. There were times I literally couldn't find my army without hotkeys because there were so many other 'anomolies' and terrain effects. And if your unit is engaged in a seige the hotkeys don't work, so, you now have to hunt for your armies, next to a city, buried in terrain details. Damn the beauty, where's my army! I basically had to go into my military screen and locate my armies from a menu. It works but dammit I shouldn't have to search and click around like this.
How about the game? Well it's Endless so, the pre-made factions are not stellar. Only now they come with a faction-required trait that you're stuck with. So you waste up to 25 trait points on a crappy trait you can't get rid of. Some of them aren't bad, others just suck and aren't worth the wasted points. Still, the customs work fairly well, and the preset ones are semi-functional. And they have decent stories so, they're actually interesting. Be warned though, a couple of the faction quests are questionable; I played through with Vaulters and got the Domination victory in 225 turns without ever being able to get past the 3rd part of the main quest. So basically, I killed everything, but the quest said I still had to kill things.. ehhh not the best.
There are also in-game "deeds" kind of like wonders, once someone gets them, they're unavailable to everyone else. This isn't bad but, several early ones are military based, so if you play a peaceful game, or play militarily weak faction, kiss those early deeds goodbye to the other players. I tried to restart to see if they were random but they never changed so, unless you plan on some early fighting, you're going to miss out. And if you're an indirect-war faction, you may gimp yourself going for them unless you're careful. It isn't horrible but it does add increased difficulty to certain factions.
Game play itself is... another mixed bag. It wasn't totally boring but.. I didn't find myself getting that "just one more turn" feeling. Heroes and their abilities were interesting. But you only get 3 or 4 units until late game and by then you don't need super-elemental-units.. at all. I found myself having to make armies to wander around to check ruins and grab pearls that would spawn in my territory.. this amounted to mindless busy-work. The AI doesn't appear to play smarter at higher difficulties, it simply seems to be more aggresive and get a resource boost which feels kind of cheesey.

All in all, was it fun? Kind of, but I was never really engaged or connected with the game. Will I play it through again? Probably not. I still have Civ 5 still waiting to be played (yeah, yeah, I know lol). Would I recommend the game, even on deep discount? I would have to say no. No, I would not. May as well save the $30 for Endless Space 2, or a Civilization game.
All in all, it isn't bad. I'd give it 6/10, and only if it's on sale.

Character and Power customization = 10/10
Everything else = 5/10
Overall rating = 7,5
Shame that this game lacks in content after you've run through everything a couple of times (other than farming and collecting), because the character creator is amazing and very versatile, the best I've seen in any MMO. The power customization is excellent as well, given you pay for the subscription. The game is worth it just for its' ability to create exactly the character you want, down to the tiniest detail. At least it is to me.
It's F2P, and you can essentially play a character from level 1 to 40 while paying nothing. But it does suffer from being a F2P game in the sense that there's a lot of fluff to buy, including some of the best items locked behind gamble-boxes, and most of the content coming out is quickly consumed. No new zones, no new long quest lines ending with epic villains, no major updates/bugfixes to outdated systems (PvP is dead and rewards useless, Nemesis content is bugged to hell and has been for years). It has gotten better with the new devs, but I wouldn't expect major updates or expansions in that direction any time soon.
Since this game went FTP, if you take away the content relating to gamble-boxes, quickly consumed content(alerts and the like), becomes (toggle-ables where you become a different monster/character, most of them (only) useful if you're not a subscriber), and vehicles (essentially also becomes), you're left with costume items, new gear, and other collectibles, as well as some power updates, updates of a couple of systems and a few bug fixes. This might look like a lot written down, but compared to the fact that this game is over four years old, it isn't that impressive. Go to the website and look at the patch notes for this game and compare it to so many other games, it'll give you an idea of the pace this game is moving at.
So once you get bored of sitting on your pile of shinies, there's not much to do but run a character through the same stuff all over again, blasting through Westside so many times you could point out every little pixel blindfolded. But having the power to create just the character you want, and thinking up your own story as you go along, somewhat makes up for running through the same content a million times. Luckily this won't be a problem until you've been playing the game for a while.
If you have a good imagination, and you're not bothered by repetitive content, you'll have hours upon hours of fun. I certainly keep coming back.

This was my first point and click game, and really it made me like the genre.
The story is very interesting from start to finish.  You play as Horatio Nullbuilt version 5.  A robot sort of obsessed with fixing things, building things and correcting problems.  He lives aboard his ship with his creation Crispin Horatiobuilt version 1.  They live in the middle of a wasteland aboard the UNNIIC, a crashed ship with a long lasting power source.  That and the nearby scrap gives them all they need to survive.  A problem arises when that power source is stolen from them though and they have to find a way to get it back before they run out of juice and are shut down forever.
The story just gets more interesting from there as you meet more and more interesting, very well written I should add, characters and solve some very interesting puzzles and problems.
None of the puzzles are overly difficult, with each having a sensible solution.  Nothing like I had always heard point and click games can be, with solutions that are so removed from reality you pretty much have to have a walkthrough to beat it unless you are supremely patient.
the fact that there is several endings as well as a way to alter the best ending slightly by how you play is quite wonderful.
All told the game shouldnt take you very long.   4-5 hours give or take allowing for some time to get stuck on what to do next I think.  Shorter if you are really fast, with some replayability in terms of endings and getting the achievements.
If you like well written stories give it a go.
Personally this rates very high with me and I look forward to whatever this dev puts out in future.
