As someone who is extremely casual about this genre and has really only dipped his toes into it a few times (Civ5, Galciv2, and a lot of Ck2), I still feel like the strengths of this game are very apparent from almost right out the gate, and they set some high bars for the rest of the genre.
-Tutorial is boring, slow, and kind of necessary. The interface and mechanics are just different enough from other staples of the 4x genre that it's helpful to know how to get your army out of the city, why you can't just settle anywhere, and a few other things you think you know already.
-Preeeeeeeeeety.
-Reigons are a great twist, forcing you to plan where to settle based on what you give up. Patrolling your borders is made easy thanks to a pulsing state line.
-Every action has an obvious effect, making it very simple to understand what you should and should not do to meet your goals.
-There is no tech tree. Tech items are grouped into eras, so you can research weapons all game without once having to research animal husbandry. Need something? Research it. Bam. The benefits of each item are immediately felt, too.
The bottom line is that you never feel like you are tasked with stupid busywork, and still have the strategic depth that all the greats have. Mechanics make more sense, and makes it all that much easier to stick around for more turns than you wanted to.

Fun fact: If you never knew why they're called 4X games it stands for explore, expand, exploit, exterminate.
Endless Legend does an incredible job of innovating the 3rd "X"; exploit.  Your faction colonizes territories and immediately you begin exploiting the area around you.  Harmlessly at first.  Then you realize you can assimilate minor factions in your provice in a number of ways.  Who doesn't love getting a little bonus and then pacifying and gaining the ability to recruit some creepy looking worm people, two headed dog warriors, or a flying demon that looks straight out of Diablo?
Beyond that you start exploiting different naturally occuring deposits as your research makes them available.  As you and the other inhabitants of the world exploit more and more, the winters get longer and longer.  "Maybe this is bad for the planet?" you may ask, but then you get distracted by shiny pearls that are just ASKING to be harvested.  Let's face it, you NEED them to help build structures that negate winter's affect on your exploitations.  Plus you can make pearl armor, weapons, and chic trinkets to accessorize your heroes with.  My archer lady looks great in pearls.
To get to the point, you can really get lost in this title.  I've found the normal difficulty is great for the standard 4X player (aka me).  The game doesn't feel like it's cheating against you as I've felt with other games in the same genre.  The one major city per province mechanic allows city building to feel less like a race and more like a reflection of the progression of your empire.
The quests can give you plenty to do, the roaming minor faction armies make you keep pace with your military, and I've rarely gotten to the point in a game where an AI opponent rolls in three armies just cause they can and wipes me out.  The diplomatic measures are balanced, the factions are unique, the setting is eye candy, and you can spend hours and hours of your life hitting that 3rd X super hard and building the empire that you never could in those other games.
The game works great with the Steam Controller.
My only negative: Running this on a Mac OS leads to the occasional crash about every 25-50 turns

I've played Champions Online since it first came out. Having come from the grindfest and overall nightmare that was City of Heroes I feel that Champions Onilne was a great way to do the super hero genre as an MMO.
The simple fact that you can build a hero the way you want from the ground up, start to finish, is nothing short of amazing. The powers and costume combinations that you can build allow you to recreate almost any hero that has existed in comic books to date, or create your own version of what you think a hero is.
The only downsides to this game are the lack of an ability to play anything other than a hero, the generic power selections, and the feel of the game.
I like playing a hero in a super hero game...I mean that's the whole point, but it gets boring after a while to always be the good guy especially when you have powers that let you animate the dead or poison people or set people on fire. The power selections that are available to choose from scream for a villain side of the game. Yes you can make an "anti-hero" but he's still doing the same heroic deeds and stopping the same bad guys that every other hero is. There isn't any depth to the game in that respect. It's "Help! Someone stole/robbed/broke-into/kidnapped/is about destroy, this person/place/thing! Please stop them!"
Rinse and repeat.
The powers in the game are great for what they are. Each style has mutliple variations on how that power should function, but they are all still very generic and aside from some minor color changes you can make, you're still not going to see powers like you want them to be. They will be mere facades, posing as a cosmic blast, but being a kinetic blast of force in actuality.
The combat in the game is good, but it's not very engaging. I don't feel like the hero so much as a person controlling the hero. It's a very "stand back and watch me blast this guy" type of gameplay, even for the melee archetypes. Just bland.
Overall it's a very solid game even after Perfect World took over it's come out with some nifty little enhancements to make the game a little better than it was. The worst part of the game however is the C-Store and the purchases that can be made within. I highly suggest that if you intend to purchase anything from the store, you don't purchase the cosmic keys or participate in the lockbox sceme at all. If you intend to spend that kind of money on the game, then purchase the lifetime subscription instead and reap it's rewards, but stay away from the keys and lockboxes.

C'mon, the game is a DOLLAR! Do you really need to be reading a review to tell you if that dollar is worth it?
It's a game that is fun for a while on your own and more fun playing against others. You pick from a handful of humourous looking, albeit generic characters (i.e. old guy, foreigner, fat buy, etc) and put them into insult matches with each other. Throughout the course of play you can unlock several additional characters, including H.P. Lovecraft, Lo Wang (from Shadow Warrior) and Serious Sam (from the games of the same name).
You 'battle' in several scenarios which range from a pet store with a dead parrot (Monty Pyton FTW) all the way up to the afterlife debating a god-like figure over the meaning of life. You engage in battle by constructing an insult from a list of randomly chosen words, along with two extras only you can use, along with two more available by drinking tea. Plus each character has weaknesses you can exploit, and if you mention the same thing multiple times (Your mother, you, your sense of style, etc) you can get a combo.
Sometimes you might get something stupid like "Your mother acts like your son!" or "This pet store has more hair then your math teacher!" But through practice, you can craft some beautiful insults like "Your father moves like a pregnant yak!" or "Your mother is silly and full of eels!"
Like I said, its less then a dollar, its loads of fun, and its simple to play. Just go buy it, you dim-witted dullard!

Spurned forth from the success of Evoland Classic that won the 24th Ludum Dare, Evoland is like a short love letter to gaming history. Giving plenty of nods to well known classic games that set the bar for games of their time, like Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, and Diablo. If you've been a long time gamer, and looking for a trip down memory lane, then look no further than this series... Though I have heard that the sequel to this game does it better.
Sadly, for as innovative as the game itself is, there's not much in terms of Story. You play as Clink, who is one of the few remaining members of the Order of the Dragon Knights, a group who roams the world aiding those in need and vanquishing evil. As things have been peaceful, there's not been much for the Order to do.
But, with a uprising evil, and monsters flourishing in the world, there's once again need for a hero. And, being named after two already well known heroes, it's obvious who's going to fit the bill here.
So sadly, it's a pretty cut-and-dry formula. Even their sort of plot twist near the ending kinda didn't come off that surprising, given who the two main characters are kinda named after. Still, they at least get a two for trying to have some semblance of a story here, as opposed to having none.
This is, yet another area that is unfortunately lacking. Aside from what's typically on the screen, such as health (once you unlock it) and swapping weapons (again, once it's unlocked) there's literally not much you're going to do with it. They have a sort of stats and item menu, but there's not much you can even do with it. Still, as lacking as it is, it's at least there. Granted, I can't really name a game where you have no sort of interface to work with...
Ahh yes, one of two of the main boasting points of the game. The gameplay, if you're a long time gamer, will definitely seem very nostalgic, as it starts off in a playstyle very akin to the old 2D Legend of Zelda games. And through advancements and progression, eventually upgrades to a older Final Fantasy RPG style, before advancing to a 3D action adventure feel, with the overworld being that of a Final Fantasy 7 styled RPG combat system with a single area being reserved for a original Diablo style of combat.
And while, it doesn't bring anything overly new in those styles, It manages all of this while managing to be fully functional in each playstyle
in the same game at that. Which, getting all those functions to work smoothly in one game is impressive alone. Not only that, there are a few puzzles that use switching between 2D and 3D to overcome, which is a pretty neat idea that was executed fairly well.
Like the gameplay, this was another selling point of the game. Not because the graphics are like, next generation or anything like that. But because the game improves the graphics through progression. Starting out as a black-and-green LCD-esque display a la Gameboy, and later on advancing to that of 3D chibi-ish graphics akin to, but not up to the standard of the Final Fantasy DS remakes.
And, just like the game play, the graphics are done well, and seem to have been seamlessly integrated in to the same game, and even switching between 2D and 3D is managed well with only little delay. Which, is quite impressive on it's own.
The music isn't anything that would be the kind you'd be listening long after you played the game, but it doesn't downright suck either... But, it's also clear what games' tracks they're parodying as well. But given it also advances as you go through the game, and from what I remember, it compliments the Atmosphere of the game as well, it at least deserves a even score.
It's basically your typical RPG Atmosphere. There's forests, grasslands, caves, deserts, and places where you know just from the look of things, that intense stuff's going to go down. Sadly, there's no nice snowy lands to see in this game. Which is a shame, as I'd have loved to see how they would have handled it. But, from what I recall, the music supports the atmospheres pretty nicely.
Innovative idea that was pulled off fairly well.
Various gameplay styles integrated well in to a singular game.
Atmospheres are done decently, with music and tone to match setting.
The entire game is primarily made to appeal to one's nostalgia of older games.
There is a LOT of parody content, even the main characters are parodies.
Graphics and Music improve with game progress.
A LOT of things to collect up.

While not shy from flaunting its inspiration, Evoland does a great job of being original with all the stylistic elements and tropes it emulates. A love letter to the entire history of Japanese-style role-playing games, Evoland honors and pokes a bit of fun at its progenitors simultaneously.
The visual evolution of Evoland is the biggest and most obvious selling point, but the way they keep the items, UI, controls, music, and everything else evolving alongside this is perfect. The story feels a bit hollow and derivative at points, but that's clearly the objective, so there's only so much one can complain. There's a bit of grinding thrown in as well, but you expect that sort of thing from a jRPG, so that also works.
If there's anything that I could say bothered me, it's that the final battle pops up a bit earlier than expected (I figured I had at least another half an hour of game), and it feels phoned in compared to the rest of the game, along with the ending. After a lot of other cute twists on expectation, I was hoping for a bit more. Stll, great game, and if you're familiar with the jRPG genre or just down for a cute time, absolutely snag Evoland.

Honestly, it's hard to take this game seriously. Sure, you begin said game with fairly easy-to-use controls and ship construction, but it turns into...well... Imagine a ship which spits out more ships which destroy ships so that the first ship could gain the resources to build more ships. See where I'm going with this? It becomes a matter of power and dominance, and eventually the AI simply cannot keep up with your Ingenuity. I built a ship that was precisely what I described. Sure, by itself, it wasn't ever going to last, but when the ship has reached a maximum of around 500 drones (fighters) and a full fleet of 70 entry-level skiffs, not so much. The point is that, in this game, one can gain absurd levels of power that they can used to destroy other absurd levels of power. Anyway, if anyone wonders what the game is all about and is happening to be reading my review, then allow me to enlighten you: You begin the game with a default ship in a default faction which can be used to capture stations (spawn locations), destroy other ships, or scavenge to gain the resources to level up to allow for more stuff to be packed onto your ship or gain more stuff to pack onto your ship. Such stuff usually consists of weapons, shielding, thrusters, drone launchers, factories, harvestors, generators, etc. which become harder to place on your ship if you don't level up or don't use enough power generators to use such stuff. Once you have the upgrades you need and you have the level, you have free reign to place as many of that item on your ship as you want for ****ing free, and that is what leads to gradually overpowered ships. My advice, just fly around in a custom ship equiped with default thrusters for days and capture every single station you can. As they are mostly unguarded, it's pretty easy to rank up doing that.

Albedo: Eyes from Outer Space is a hard game for me to come to terms with. It has a lot that I love and a lot that I absolutely hate, but no one can really say it's a "bad game".
Most of what's wrong with it is wrong at the very core of it, and is only wrong considering what people expect from it.
It's a pure adventure game, like the older point n' clicks with some very wild solutions to puzzles. It does have some other problems, mostly related to how it conveys important information, but those problems would be minor in any other genre.
The game has several levels, each being a more of less self contained puzzle. But the puzzles don't follow a pattern or a type. They're completely different from one another, which can be very... alienating (pun intended).
There was a level where you had to (SPOILERS!) melt wax into a padlock to see its pattern, and figure out the number code to open it.
That's stretching waaaay too far out of what the player expects. I'd also like to mention that it doesn't seem to be an actual method of "breaking" locks -- at leat a quick Google search didn't find anything.
There are other puzzles with some quite clever solutions, as they're all very physical, in a sense. It's the kind of improvised solutions that a human being might try, if he were actually there.
Unfortunately, this is a video-game, where things don't quite work as well as one would expect, and it's very, very easy to miss crucial aspects of a given puzzle.
There are guides for that, if you want. I'd recommend, if you're in the game to experience its setting.
Which is what I love. It's pure old sci-fi. The kind of suspenseful from movies, with a very characteristic soundtrack to go along with it. It's awesome!
I really love what it's trying to do, clearly being a game that stands on its own. It's not dictacted by fun or what players want, it's clearly a very personal project, and I commend it for it!
If that's what you're looking for, definitely give it a go!
There are some other problems, especially with the brightness levels not being very clear. That game doesn't have a gauge (something like "increase brightness until you can barely see the darkest image"), so I didn't want to push it too high. As a result, there were some items that were completely obscured, at some points. Not ideal.
Another big problem is the camera. First Person puzzle game tend to give me A LOT of motion sickness. This is no exception. At times it was physically painful. The camera is very wanky, contantly moving a lot to the sides. It's especially annoying in the shooting sections.
One last thing is how the interface is rather clunky, but bearable.
As a conclusion -- it's not perfect. Not even close. It has some very frustrating moments, mostly because the player didn't get the right information, or, in a particular level, the controls were incredibly dodgy. But, if you can withstand it, there's an incredibly unique game in this, with a nice twist at the end.
If you're a fan of old sci-fi, I recommend it!

With the complete failure that is RollerCoaster Tycoon World, this remains as one of the top two entries in the RollerCoaster Tycoon series (the other contender being RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, also available on steam). This Platinum Edition includes both the Soaked! Expansion (which allows for waterparks) and the Wild! Expansion (which allows for animal exhibits, ala Busch Gardens). The only issues are poor performance in high-population parks (a problem that rears itself in sandbox parks more than anything), occaisional issues with certain roller coaster types having inexplicable crashes (most notably the tilt coaster and its thrill lift), and the assumption of where your pictures are stored leading to many questions on how to get custom image billboards working (it's not hard, but you have to add a specific folder inside the folder that is being used as your Documents library)
It would be a disservice, though, to not mention the two new theme park games that have come out since this game's release, especially since both are on Steam. First, currently still in Early Access, is Parkitect, has a similar look-and-feel to this game but has more depth and, important for some people, actual modding support for custom rides. Second, recently released, is Planet Coaster, generally accepted as the true sequel from Frontier, the dev team behind this game. If you like this kind of game, do check those out as well.

Event[0] is a first person game where you are in the shoes of a spacefarer on a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa (this is the second game I saw with a story revolving around Europa, other being The Turing Test). The game starts with a written narrative about describing your past and also gives you some basic choices about your gender, background and your ideals, meanwhile continuing the narrative.
You participate in humanity’s latest effort on Europa, the Europa-11 mission when everything goes haywire. The facility’s AI declares an emergency and encourages everyone to evacuate but no one except you survives the incident. You are marooned in space for a while before encountering a previously unknown human ship. The ship, named Nautilus, pulls you in and you realize no one is aboard, except an AI called Kaizen, or in short KZ.
You have to type to interact with Kaizen. It means there are no pre-defined choices when you speak with him, you have to LITERALLY type whatever you want to say like you talk to an ordinary friend of yours. You have to ask him to open doors, play something, turn on the lights to get things going, there is no button to push, no lever to pull, nothing to interact except Kaizen’s terminals throughout the entire game.
This is where the game stands out. Kaizen is very distrustful and skeptical at you first, like a normal human being when you first meet them. It is your actions and responses towards Kaizen will shape your relationship with him. Asking him politely instead of ordering him to do something and thanking him after he does something for you will greatly improve your relationship while acting vice versa will strain it and this WILL AFFECT how the game ends.
All of the interactions you perform with Kaizen are over various terminals scattered across the starship. You can ask him to open different doors, elevate beds and even play some music/TV in certain rooms. You can also access the terminal’s logs if you ask him politely and these logs are essential to figure out what happened to the ship.
Of course, the AI is far from perfect game-wise, like he can sometimes reply irrelevantly to your queries if you are not clear enough. For example, if you talk about some certain individual at some point, asking him to clarify or enrich his story without the usage of the person’s name but with a pronoun (like he/she) may sometimes confuse the AI and either he will ask you to clarify your inquiry or present an irrelevant answer. This does not happen often but when it does, you may change the words you use.
Naturally, the AI is also far from being all out open to you about everything and this is not a bug but an intention. If you want to treat him like a pet, promptly order him around, be quite rude and call him names, think again, because if you remember what I said above, this guy controls the ship’s doors and airlocks and you have to ask him by typing to open the doors. This means he CAN shut the airlock while you are outside in space and leave you to suffocate out there when you ask him to get back in. If you treat him nicely, he will usually give you clues about solving some puzzles, he shares his knowledge generously about what happened in the backstory and the whereabouts of things you are looking for.
I really liked the visuals of this game. Space is not a hard place to depict but you can clearly see the Jupiter with its animated storms and also Europa while you look out of a window or go outside, which is eerily calm and quiet in a soundless environment. Interiors are designed well too, there are several color palettes chosen for each different room or hall which radiate the room’s purpose, like living room having vivid, yellowish, cozy colors while the abandoned halls have darker, blueish tones.
Sounds are pretty much what you can expect from a game like this, airlock and no vacuum sounds are fine but it is the music track that is quite fascinating. The game has one signature track “Hey Judy” playing in various different places and it fits quite well to the game’s atmosphere and storyline.
By the way, game’s atmosphere is quite immersive. You feel the loneliness of being stranded in a desolate spaceship, accompanied by an AI only who talks to you via terminals.
Overall, I believe this game is a brave attempt because of the way you interact with the side protagonist, since it employs you actually type what you want to say instead of presenting you with different and limited options to speak. This unbound ability also has some flaws in some ways, like the AI having difficulty in understanding and responding you but this is not a very common occurrence throughout the game. And I believe, character development of Kaizen is pretty interesting and solid at the same time, it is not very easy to achieve this in every game with a character you have no mimics or clear voice to rely upon.
Also I have to underline that, this is not an “AI-gone-rogue” game. The AI is not evil but he’s not good either. He is just a software trying to achieve what is best for his programming. No one in this game is particularly good or evil, everyone is right and everyone is wrong at some point and that makes this game stand apart from all other games where the lines between good and evil are drawn unmistakably.
The game has four different endings with some of them having minor, some of them having major differences between each other. Minor differences may not warrant a replay for some but treating Kaizen very differently will change the game's overall course substantially, including the ending.
This is a pretty solid game and a must play for everyone who can type and chat in a comprehensible manner in English language in my opinion. Hats off to the developer for their braveness to realize such a concept to a sturdy piece of art.

My first impressions. I love roguelike-inspired games such as Spelunky or Binding of Isaac but I'm not impressed with this one's gameplay so far. To its credit, its technical and artistic realization seems flawless. Haven't encountered a single bug yet, and the game's gorgeous.
But before I get to the pros and cons, information time for people who are new to the genre. This is not a true roguelike. Those are turn-based, have true permadeath (no permanent progression) and typically have unidentified items with sometimes dangerous properties. They do share procedural generation and random item and monster apparition with Full Mojo Rampage and other "roguelites".
Examples of true, very fun, free roguelikes:
This said roguelikes have inspired a lot of real-time games, starting with Diablo. From now on we'll just call this game a roguelike because it's just more handy.
Cons:
- The first level of the first mission, which you're gonna replay a lot of times, is boring with only two enemy types plus the occasional bigger version, healer or miniboss. You need to explore the whole thing to get all the chests and special locations, but it feels empty and uninteresting.
****HERE'S A NOTE TO ROGUELIKE DESIGNERS: PUT MOST OF THE VARIETY IN THE EARLIER LEVELS, WE'RE GONNA PLAY THEM THE MOST****
- Huge difficulty spike in the second level with the apparition of kamikazes and direct shooters, aggro a few too many monsters and you're completely overwhelmed. Then to have a chance to get used to it you must replay the first boring level.
- Grindy. Because of the permanent leveling and permanently upgradeable unlocks, the aforementioned second level is gonna get easier, but only after you restart the game several times. But then, the first level is gonna be even more boring because it presents even less of a challenge. Contrast that to Spelunky and Binding of Isaac where you can never let your guard down even in early levels.
****SECOND NOTE TO ROGUELIKE DESIGNERS: PERMANENT STATS PROGRESSION MAKES YOUR GAME GRINDY, STICK TO UNLOCKING NEW STUFF TO FIND WITHIN RUNS.****
- Your max range is not well-defined, at its edge it can look like projectiles hit enemies but they don't. Thankfully there's always a sound for successful hits.
- The items that change how you shoot are limited-use. That means you'll be shooting the same boring projectile most of the time. You can't even save them for when you really need them, as they instantly replace your default shot.
- You get lots of items but they don't have the same impact as in Binding of Isaac or Spelunky, most give you either 5 to 10% passive buffs or one-use effects.
- System for combining items sounds interesting at first, but it simply puts the characteristics of two items on one. So no Shin Megami Tensei demon combining here, it just means backtracking to free up an inventory slot: boring.
- Enemies spawn as you move, and if you're moving towards the bottom of the screen, that means super close to you. Good luck if those are kamikazes. At least there's a sound to warn you of it, but I think the game would've been better with a Torchlight/Diablo-like enemy placement.
Pros:
+ Great music
+ Good controls, I like the mouse-driven shooting
+ Nice graphics and theme
+ Classes (gods) play very differently
+ Many items to find and unlock
+ From an initial look, good variety of environments and bosses
+ The effects of items can be creative and funny: giant chicken, disco ball and so on.
+ Daily generated dungeon which you can try and then compare your score to the community.
I'll revise my evaluation if I play it again and it feels more fun, but so far I don't feel like going back to it... bad sign.

This is a really difficult game to recommend. If you take a gander at the negative reviews you will see the same sentiment echoed over and over "I wanted to like this game." And, I did want to actually like this game too, but there are some heavy flaws that get in the way of the experience. I think what it comes down to is that I am recommending this game because I think it was frustrating in the right ways more than the wrong. I will always appreciate a game that tries do something more or different and fails over one that suceeds at doing what every other game already did.
Albedo: Eyes from Outer Space is meant to be a first person adventure game. In that sense it has puzzles, action and storytelling all done in real time, first person. Think of it like a point and click (Walking Dead, Monkey Island, etc.) meets a rather nonviolent first person shooter. The meat of the game comes from solving puzzles to move on to the next area with small bits of action here and there. I play a lot of games in general, but as someone who plays both point and clicks, and puzzle games, these puzzles are arduous. I absolutely needed to use a guide to help me ge through the more demanding areas, even on easy mode. Difficulty is just a hard thing to measure. Games like Super Meat Boy. Hotline Miami, or IWBTG! make me think there is no such thing as too difficult, but I know that even those gems can turn off some players (I didn't dare waste more than 10 minutes on the opening level of IWBTG! before I moved on). But, if a developer makes a game too easy, players will get bored. So, while Albedo's puzzles can be incredibly hard, I think the solution aspect of the puzzles is fair and challenging. It's the execution that causes puzzles to be frustrating.
The inventory system, controls, and interface of the game are far from intuitive. As someone who uses a trackpad mostly, I can deal with a lot of wonky controls in games, but even Albedo made it unnecessarily difficult to do something simple like equip the right item for a solution I already knew. Some of the more classic point and clicks used to be frustrating because you would have multiple actions that could be attached to a large variety of items in your inventroy, making for a large number of combinations that could easily make progression nigh impossible. Thankfully, Albedo limits itself to a few per item and does not attach every action to each item. However, even with this saving grace, I still had struggle to combine item A with B many times.
Outside of mechanics, the game some great aesthetics. The style of the game is interesting and fits with the sci-fi feel. The aliens are wacky and the enviroments all look great and easy to tell apart. The ambient noises are a nice touch, and the soundtrack does well enough, but there might be a lack of theremin to help conjure up that 60s sci-fi b-movie vibe.
Overall, this is a really tough recommendation. The puzzles are challenging, clever and have some good variety (number sequences, multifaceted pipe arranging, picking locks etc.). However, the demanding puzzles come with the clunky controls that can get in the way. Those hoping for an even split between action and puzzles will find that there is more focus on puzzles than action sequences: they pop up more often, there is more variety, and they feel more rewarding.
This game is ultimately not the champion we needed to bridge the gap between first person shooters and point and click games, but I think it is still a game worth checking out. For those of you that want a film comparison, this is more
than
. If you think you are up to the challenge, or are willing to swallow your pride and take just a quick peek at a guide, this is a strange and fascinating experience, and I hope to see more games like it.

This is a generally fun adventure game, where you have to find hidden objects in various scenes to progress through the story.  It's about a treasure hunt for five different treasures, and each has about 5 or 6 locations you visit.  The game doesn't involve much more than finding the hidden objects, but often some objects requiring additional actions to be performed before you can locate them.  This can mean brushing away dust, breaking things open, or lighting things on fire to clear them.  There are also at least a few puzzles to solve along the way, and a special unnamed geocahce item in each location.  If you get stuck, there's more of a cheat system than a hint system -- an object finder will locate things for you (with a cool-down period after each use) as long as they're visible and don't require additional actions before you can access them, and I don't think it works on geocaches.  I would have liked a hint system I could use first, that would, for example, show an outline of the object so I knew what I was looking for, because some objects are ambiguous (e.g., "fan" -- is that a folding paper one or an electric one?).  The overall difficulty of finding the hidden objects isn't too high, so you shouldn't get stuck for too long, and there's always the item finder.  In terms of replay value, there is some but not a lot.  After initially clearing each scene, they game will hide another set of objects in it for you to find.  So you can go back to clear the locations 100%, either as a second run from start to finish or in each scene as you go along.  But once you finish the story, there isn't much left.  The geocaches you find are all put into a room where you can see them, like a trophy case.  Unfortunately, that's all it is.  I was hoping for more information about the items or history or something once the geocaches were found and stored, but that's not the case.  The story is nice and develops as you find each treasure, so it helps keep the game moving along.  Overall, it was an enjoyable way to spend ~5 hours (and I did all locations twice, to 100% clear them), and I'd recommend the game to those who like these types of point-and-click find-the-hidden-object games.

I liked it, and spent money on it as it wasn't like pretty much every other MOBA out there, and with full offline play, with local co-op, and online Steam user invites (when online), I could always play it, with who I wanted to play it with. Now it's trying to be like pretty much every other online PvP MOBA out there.
I played it, and spent money on it as unlike pretty much every of MOBA out there, it was a purchased game, that functioned just fine offline (so you never had to worry about it being shut down), and it didn't force you to play with a bunch of random people, so you could avoid the usual drama, and rudeness of the online MOBA community, as well as the potential connection lag between them. It was still very samey, so I could only play it now, and then, but then along came ways to adjust game play settings, so it would play somewhat differently, plus more recently, the ability to make, and share your own game maps for custom mode, which also improved things somewhat. Custom mode also always allowed me to level up my game profile, so I could play how I wanted, with who I wanted, and get rewarded for it by the game. In fact, since custom mode was the only way to use the relatively newly added mod maps feature, and other options, you could say it was even encouraging players to use custom mode to play.
Problem is after years of doing things one way, once they went to the F2P (Free to Play) model they made it so you needed to play online, or play an older version of the game offline, that is only partially functional (won't record your stats, and won't let you play with others except in local co-op, when we used to be able to invite other Steam users). Then if you opted to play the new F2P version, if you play custom you can no long advance your profile, or nauts (which is required to unlock your skill upgrades when playing), your games don't advance your stats, you don't get the new in-game currency, and at least some achievements don't seem to work, which also means custom game maps have quickly been devalued after adding them in the last game update not too many months ago. To make any form of progression, unless you can bring in enough other people for co-op vs bots, you now need to play with the typical online MOBA community the game has, with potential connection issues between them, and wait for the match maker to find people, especially if you want to do PvP. Now pretty much everything that made Awesomenauts special to me, and helped separate it from other MOBAs, has been flushed down the toilet.
They currently say a permanent solution to offline play is coming, although that's as much as they've said on the matter since announcing it almost a month ago. Also the fact they were even surprised at the backlash when they made these changes, and largely gutted offline play shows they don't understand the whole of their player base very well, which does not bode well for the future. The people that have been playing this like every other online PvP MOBA out there seem happy about this F2P change, but at least many of the rest of us are less impressed. Then they announced server changes recently to prepare for the huge number of players they were expecting, they got about 2k concurrent players on the first day. They get about that many, or more when releasing various big updates, holding free periods, and such, then during its first free period in Sept. 2013, it peeked at over 12k players, so right now the F2P launch seems to be rather underwhelming, and doesn't look very encouraging in regards to the future of the game.

Champions Online is one of those MMOs that comes around once in a blue moon. It is quite unique in the sense that it's one of the few superhero MMOs still remaining. WIth the fall of City of Heroes a while ago, the only other alternative is DC Universe Online, which I can't say I have an unbiased view towards. One of the game's foremost features is its costume creator, which is one of the biggest and most creative I've seen in the customization department. With this, many people have created heroes (and villains if you're into the roleplaying area) of varying shapes, sizes and colours, way more inventive than DCUO's.
Champions is a most colourful game with a lot of places to visit, lots of enemies to beat the snot out of, and fun to be had with it. Unlike most MMOs, the combat is fast and intuitive. While you might get a little bored with it after a while, trying out the different Archetypes or spending a dime on becoming a Gold player for access to the Freeform layout (/don't/ waste your $50 on buying the Freeform slot if you're a free player, it can only end in tears, trust me), the game opens up a slew of new opportunities.
Its most unique feature, however, is its roleplaying community. As a steadfast member of said RP community, I can safely say this is one of the biggest I've ever seen in a video game, especially for an MMO. Of course, the community is evenly split between roleplayers and non-roleplayers, and further split between good roleplayers and the scum of the earth, it is none the less one of the strongest communities I've ever seen. With the game's dwindling support ever since Cryptic, the developers, were brought by Perfect World, some members of the community will not stop fighting for it, until Champions gets the support it needs - and other Cryptic-made games, such as Star Trek Online or Neverwinter - deserve.
9/10 in total - five for the gameplay, four for the community. Bravo, Champions Online. Bravo.
Oh, and watch out for the demon werewolf succubus cosmic god roleplayers. You know that scum of the earth I mentioned? Yeah. Stay away from Club Caprice if you really want to keep your eyeballs.

Upon first purchasing this game during one of its sales, I was unsure what it would bring or how it would be. So I sat down, booted it up and jumped in. For a day or two it seemed a little confusing, despite having played the Civilization games in the past, as well as many different RTS games, I was completely blown away by how much more in-depth this game is. After a good bit of practice, it has become one of my top favorite games of all time. Easily something you can play for days and weeks without end and not get bored with. The faction system is truly unique, with each faction holding enough diversity that you would have to play them just to get a solid grasp as to their abilities. The rank system is superb, making losing a unit you've been cultivating for a long time all the more painful. Quest systems make this so that you are never bored or reaching a point where nothing seems interesting anymore. The diplomacy is something like I haven't seen before. You have to actually work to ally up with friends in multiplayer, and it actually costs you to do things. So you aren't just able to group up with no risk and alliances as well as betrayal are truly investments in this game. The map system and winter are also an amazing part to this game, as the maps are very unique in their generation and the winter system is something that, depending on how well prepared you are, can be a prosperus event or a truly harrowing disaster to your empire.
TL;DR This game is highly reccomended, replayability is through the roof and it easily rivals if not beats most other turn based strategy games. 100 out of 10.

Not played the original on XBone but from what I can see it's a very good port over to PC. Graphics are some of the best I've seen on the PC given that my rig is only halfway to being a powerhouse gaming machine.
The game itself plays alot like the Batman:Arkham games, has a decent (if a little short), well scripted and acted story. The character animation especially the faces of the main roman characters is amazing and the controls (I played on a Steam Controller) are intuitive. The fighting is satisfying to do and the executions are imaginitie at times although it'd have been nice if you could have more control over which one you were about to perform considering you can seemingly unlock quite a few but you seem to execute the same half a dozen or so each time.
Co-op is a fun deal, there are 5 mode types with a decent amount of scenarios and settings to choose from and co-op executions are cool when you've cleared the chaff and isolated a Boss type character and pull one off.
My only gripe is that the DLC was limited to character and arena skins. It would have been cool to have some extension to the main story, even if it had been backstory filler for Marius to show his road to joining his first legion or a seperate story arc for Vitalus and the 14th.
The story mode wont be what draws people back to play the game but there's enough in multiplayer to keep you coming back for a while.
Overal a decent buy for some gory fun!

It really pains me to write a negative review for this game; it's got tons of style and great ideas, and it's clearly a labor of love for its creators; but as an experiment in how to do a first person graphic adventure, it unfortunately misses more than it hits.
Halfway through I had to start using walkthroughs. A little bit further, I got absolutely stuck even though I knew exactly what I needed to do, and ended up giving up on the game. The game's weird interface causes lots of problems and makes it almost impossible to figure things out at times - even when the underlying puzzle is solid (for example, there is a lovely puzzle involving building a ladder out of tube parts that is renderd too obscure by its execution). There is very little clarity, very little consistency in how interaction works, and it's not helped by very fiddly or clunky sections.
Oh, and there are time-sensitive puzzles and parts where you are attacked by unbeatable monsters.
All of this is a huge shame, because as said before, there is a lot of love and imagination in the game, and when it works, it can be pretty great. It's worth trying and supporting, just be aware of what you're getting into first.

So, it's pretty obvious how much of an influence Sierra and Lucas Art adventure games inspired this (infact, make sure to keep looking at the tentacles...). It clearly tries to be as notoriously difficult as those games, but in some ways that doesn't work in its favor. Often times though, it does. The puzzles can be pretty esoteric, but none worse than some of those games. The controls are clunky. Not "clunky at times" just flat out clunky. But, they get the job done.
I really do like this game. The asthetic is perfect, and while I don't like the controls, I like the general idea and most of its execution. I want more first person "infinite pockets, use every item on everything" adventure games, and I think this a great place to start from.
Story is good and simple like those games as well, fits the atmosphere entirely.
Honestly, if you think you might like it, you probably will.

I will open as several other reviews do:
I really wanted to like this game.
I must echo what I see as the dominant issue with the game:
The inventory system is absolutely dreadful. I want to say it'd be fitting on a mobile device (as in perfect for swiping); it's NOTHING but annoying here.
I shan't criticize the puzzles, as I'm glad to see another vague first-person puzzler (Kairo, FRACT OSC, Ilamentia, Antichamber, etc.) that isn't grounded strictly in the abstract (
). All I can say is, if you're stuck, go back and pick up every object that seems of some interest. Upon entering a room, most interactions with them will be Observe and Drop/Throw. Once you get a step closer to progress, make the rounds again to find that you can now Use some objects.

No words can describe my stupidity. I misunderstood the controls in the Options (rebind-ed them). For some reason, the "Previous Action/Next Action" at the top threw me off.
I made it to the fourth room, found some shears, Longy commented on another eyeball (it wasn't hostile before then). I decided to Fight with the Shears; a few spams of the mouse button (after selecting the Fight action from the interface, which was a pain - one must wait a certain amount of time before the game decides to register the action you dragged to) and the shears flew out of my hands. Eyeball seems to have escaped.
EDIT: Shears flew out of my hand because no words can describe my stupidity.
Monster didn't escape; another story with actual Eyeball.
I have to assume that the issues with the game are because the dev wanted it to be as "realistic/immersive" as possible, taking cues from those games that did away with "intrusive" interfaces. For example, games like Montague's Mount, Dream, and ASAMU don't allow the player to actually pick up pages, only to zoom in ever so slightly.
That vision of realistic/immersive impedes the accessibility and intuitive-ness, making the game little more than infuriating.
The story and atmosphere necessitate that I leave a Positive recommendation... The game itself gets in the way of that, though (and not in the way one would assume (i.e. puzzles)), so I must do what I did.
Know that the point of the *Thumbs Down* is more to get the attention of the dev, rather'n to dissuade you from buying/playing it. MAYBE it simply comes down to getting used to the interface; thus far, when I've thought I've gotten it down, it acts unresponsively ("one must wait a certain amount of time before the game decides to register the action you dragged to") - I get discouraged from slogging any further into the game.
EDIT: I would have turned this review positive because I cited an issue that furthered my case in DownVoting the game that wasn't an issue with the game at all, but with mine own intelligence. However, I made it to the fifth room and am still having to wrestle with the mechanics just as much as with the big and hostile Eyeball residing therein.
I hope (and actually expect) to turn this review positive, if I can beat the game.
Not to end up saying "Psh, it wasn't that bad, I can recommend this game because I beat it, though I couldn't while I was in the prcoess of beating it."
It's to say - as I said - that the premise and atmosphere is very alluring; should the story ultimately satisfy, the "slog" will have been worth it, contrary to what I said.

I had, at first, a little smile on my face while playing this game because the idea wrapping it seemed great at first.
A game where you travel through gaming history while revisiting some of the most recognizable games of all time ( Zelda, Final Fantasy, Diablo ),
a game where the gameplay itself evolve during your walk through the adventure, a game where...
The game stops innovating passed the first hour and starts to be redondant and to be constitute of random fights every 5 seconds;
and that's the whole problem surrounding this game. The synopsis and publicity makes you think they took the best of the games it was inspired of, but it's false...
- The idea being original and meta.
- The graphics evolution, from "black and white/2D/80's" graphics to pre-rendered backgrounds and 3D fights.
- Some jokes and allusions may be funny...
- But the majority of them are just cringe worthy and could've been written by a 12 years old.
- Talking about the writting, the story is absolutely.. I DON'T EVEN KNOW WHAT IT IS, BECAUSE IT'S NOT THERE!
- You can basically buy two usable items ( potions and phoenix down ), a couple of swords and armors, two cards and... that's all. So much content.
- Your crew will be composed of you ( a fighter ), and a mage who's only magic is heal and crystal..
- The music is horrible. The composer tried to copy/use FF as an influence but it's poorly done and you'll end up muting the game while listening to some Migos/Future, because these trash rappers will be candies for your ears compared to this sh*t.
- The hitboxes and 3D gameplay are poorly coded, I'm pretty sure my character should've died from blunt trauma considering the number of times he took a tree right in the face..
- Lack of innovation after the first hour. Lack of an envy to live too.
- The random encounters. Every 5 seconds. A fight. Against the same 7 ennemies. Doing the same 2 actions. Earning the same amount of XP. The same amount of Glis ( Yes, they named the currency "Glis"... ). I swear to god, those random encounters are more frequents than homeless people in big cities.
- THEY NAMED THE F***IN' MONEY GLIS MAN. GLIS. I WANNA DIE, I KNOW I WANNA DIE NOW!
It's cute for about an hour and then becomes a tedious slog of a game.

With fully customizable character creation, you can spend hours just making a character. The free account allows you two characters, but you can purchase additional 'slots' if you need more. Its FREE to play, so give it a try, you may like it!

Reassembly is a beautiful, enthralling top-down spaceship-builder/space combat game with sturdy mechanics and an intuitive building system that deserves the praise it has recieved.
The basic building blocks are two-dimensional shapes (guns, hull blocks, engines, and so on,) which are a joy to connect and shape into fighters, freighters, capital ships and stations. As the player becomes more experienced, new shapes unlock, leading to some truly impressive creations. What's more, the fleets that other players have made are imported onto the map as 'Agents', meaning that, in addition to the various types of standard enemies, the player has to go up against the creations of fellow players - controlled by the AI, but built by humans. Some of the are quite brilliant.
Unlocking the most expensive pieces can be a grind, and the game doesn't tutorialise nearly as well as it should (there is a fair bit of advice online), but after many hours I still find plenty to keep me busy.
And if you ever encounter one of my capital ships, here's a tip: keep astern. For the life of me, I can't seem to design a ship with a decent turning speed.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a small chapter that serves to tie up the MGS: Peace Walker storyline and acts as a bridge between Peace Walker and MGSV: Phantom Pain.
It plays like a mission from Peace Walker, but the graphical and game play improvements make it feel much more like MGS4. Honestly I would have said that it is basically a tech demo of what Peace Walker might have been like if they had designed it for a full fledged console instead of the portable handheld system. The dialogue and information that you hear from the tapes is deeper and darker than most of Metal Gear has been so far, Big Boss and Kaz are much colder and less caring than they were in Peace Walker. Certain other returning characters are portrayed differently than they were in PW.
The Ground Zeroes map is rather small when you compare it to some of the older games, but it was never meant to be a full game…and there is a lot to keep you busy on this one single map. There is the initial story play through, and when you finish the main story mission there are a whole bunch of bonus missions with different objectives. Finally there are two unlockable bonus missions (there are normally one each for Xbox and Playstation but PC got both of them) which are fun missions that are mostly fan service referencing older games in the series.
Overall it handles and feels like a properly done Peace Walker, but the modifications to the tranquilizer gun and the new reflex system have significantly changed things. The tranquilizer gun while having a permanent silencer has lost a vast amount of range and the 3rd person targeting system for it has also become a bit more complicated. You have to get much closer to enemies for the tranquilizer dart to work and you start off with a very limited amount of ammunition. Now that MGSV is out you should get this if you want to fully understand the story. It is a decent (but short) offramp which introduces MGSV.

Quick review: nice premise, poor execution.
Longer review
This first caught my eye a while back and I liked central idea behind it - a game where collectables really do advance things. So, having seen it in a bundle the other day I snapped it up.
Up until hitting the first dungeon I thought it was interesting and could pass-off the ropeyness as part of the charm and/or the intention of trying to mimic the games of the time. After hitting that first 3D dungeon though my goodwill evaporated. Awful collision-detection and hit boxes were the primary reasons but moreover none of the mechanics were well implemented.
I know some folks are saying it's a parody (except it isn't funny at all), some say it is a homage (except it doesn't really do any of the games it is aping any justice); I consider it an experiment, something backed-up by the fact that the sequel is about 15-20 hours I believe. Unfortunately I find it to be a failed experiment, with the Diablo-esque segment feeling most out of place.
There's no polish here; there's no depth to any of the sections, the narrative is clumsy and wafer-thing and it doesn't really chart an evolution as much as it thinks it does. I actually think it looks its best right at the start; the 3D in particular is horrible to look at.  And that final boss is awful - relying on the dodgy collision-detection again and a ridiculously small timing window for part of it - urgh.
I had the sequel on my wishlist but no more; the fact that this failed to entertain me in my 3 or so hours playtime means I don't have any confidence that an extended playtime would be any more fun.

Okay, I will admit that there will be a little bias to this review, as I have successfully played through this game about seven times and have not had the oppurtunity to play any of the Bulder Gates games, but I would say that this is Bioware at its pinnicle.
Anyone will notice right away, the game has a strong emphasis on story, and its excellent. There are characters to fall in love with, characters you will grow to dispise, and characters that you don't know whether to trust or not. It gives a great feel and can keep any RPG fan coming back.
The graphics are also something to be praised. Many licensed games have the unfortune to not have much money put into them; KOTOR immediatly shows that it is the exception, having (for its time) some really nice textures, animations, and visuals.
The pros to the game is that it is the first real feel to be both a jedi and a sith. I mean really, there is no better feeling than saving the galaxy, or if you have darker inclinations, slicing some guy up because he looked at you funny. While the combat is not exactly balanced or the most stategic, it is still fun. There are some really cool animations, like jumping in the air and coming down with your sword, and one must still consider weaknesses and strengths of enemies and party characters.

Reassembly is a game that has grown on me.
I helped back it in it's early alpha days, giving its kickstarter my $30 donation. I liked the look of it. Sandboxish, procedural generation, top-down arcade feel. I played the very early alpha version and was entertained for a few hours. I soon lost interest, and the game became stale to me.
Since then I've come back to the game again and again. It's one of those games you'll get pumped about and think about all day only to come home from work and play it till you drop. It's enjoyment for me comes in short bursts.
Recently I've made a discovery. The game does not play itself. People complain about how tedious it is to capture systems and hold them. They say something along the lines of "Once you capture it there is no point. Your ships don't spawn there and you get no resources." Now listen here, that is where you are wrong.
You can build space stations that bristle with defenses and hold their own agains enemy capital ships. Alternatively, that space station can be covered in solar arrays to slowly farm you resources. Recently one of my favorite things to do is populate enemy territory with little "Outpost" stations via a factory on one of my ships. I then spend time fighting on the front line with my fleet to push the enemy out. This game is all about how you play it.
In summary, Reassembly is a great game. It's hard to find anything else out there even close to it (I think of S.P.A.Z. as the only other game that resembles it, another great by the way). Keep giving it a chance and you'll get a lot of replayability out of it. If you enter with a closed mind you'll get a closed off experiance. I highly recommend it.

There is one main story mission and then a variety of shorter challenge missions.  In addition to those missions there are various challenges in those missions that a player can attempt as well, along with additional difficulty levels.

Your mileage on this game may vary, if challenging your self for better scores is something that doesn't appeal to you, than find the game at discount and enjoy the few missions in the game there is. Primordia is a sci-fi, futuristic, post-apocalyptic story where you play as a robot named Horatio. In the world of Primordia robots run the planet; "Man" is but long forgotten and a thing only of legend. The puzzles are decently hard but not overbearing. Some puzzles actually have multiple solutions and the game has multiple endings. There is a built in hint system that you have the option of using. The hints gently nudge you in the correct direction but do not give obvious answers. I liked how the story pokes fun/satirizes modern day society and its views on religion without making it overly obvious. It was done subtley and in good taste. The story is just really well done; it is one of my favorites and certainly memorable. Primordia isn't just a well designed game; it is also beautiful, sad, and poetic. Overall, definitely another great title from Wadjet Eye.
Side note - There is an option to turn on commentary from the writers. I highly recommend turning on the commentary if you are enjoying the game - it provides a ton of context and for me made the experience even more so enjoyable.

Superhero stories. Who wouldn't have seen, or at least heard about any of them? Superman, Spiderman, Batman and I could continue the list of them.
Now, how about playing as them? Doesn't sound bad right? Now, let me ask you another question: how about, if you can make your own hero with unique superpowers, and (probably the most importantly) unique costume? No, I'm not talking about something like in most MMOs, that you can choose from some templates (or colors also, if you are lucky), but to completely make your very own, unique-looking hero. Well, Champions Online offers a total cutomization for all of your characters (you can also change your look later on, it's not locked forever, after creating the character), with millions of choices, and even to write their background stories.
I've played Champions Online nonsteam, downloaded from the official website. I've found myself playing it for countless of hours with my free-to-play account.
Let's see where to begin... first of all, I've never been addicted to superhero stories. A friend recommended this game to me, and I wasn't really impressed by the idea. Well in the end, I still took my time to register, download, and finally to launch the game.
The first positive impression came, when I begun to create my first character: I could completely customize it to my taste. Quite felt myself as playing with a "Barbie Doll Cool 'n Epic Edition". Yes, I actually spent around 30 mins if not more, of creating my character.
Then, the Tutorial begun. During the Tutorial, we only have 2 abilities, but they still look cool for that time. It's good enough to make the players learn the basics, and is not like a training course you can find in most games. Even the tutorial itself connects to the game's story, making it to feel even better completing.
After the tutorial, you get your next ability, and more importantly: your first travel power. Geez, how cool to select a spectacular way, we want to go from point A to point B. There are not just flying or running.
Now you are about to explore the first map: Millenium City. Complete your missions, and I'd recommend you to wait at least until lv20 when you are beginning to queve for "Alert" missions, which helps you get a rather huge amount of EXP, Resources (the in-game money), and Items that help you improve your stats. (Must mention, that this game is still action-rpg, and you must take care of you environment too)
I would like to talk about the game's leveling system. In CO, you can reach the highest level (40) quite fast. You don't need to grind for months (or years). In fact, if you are a maniac, you will definitely reach it in 2 weeks after creating your character. However, this doesn't mean, that the game would be unreplayable. Even if you are lv40, life doesn't stop. In fact, the game only begins to be the most fun, so you just better doing those Alert missions.
Oh, one more thing: did I mention, that when you reach lv25, you will be able to create your character's Nemesis, who is also totally customizable? Well, someone doesn't like, that you have beaten them, instead of kicking other villains' back parts.
Pros:
+ Total customizating opportunity to our characters, that other games doesn't provide.
+ The terms "Spectacular" and "Fun" really meets in here.
+ Good stories and introductions for each maps.
+ Leveling is easy, even if you are a loner player.
+ Regular maintenance/updates, and ever-growing content.
+ Item drop system is balanced, not allowing others to steal your loot, if it is dropped for you.
Cons:
- Poor voice actings: sometimes I feel, they should have only stayed at the comic-style speechbubbles.
- Time-stealing: Loading screen until you are respawned in front of a interactable door, then "interacting-line"-loading, then another loading screen. You have to wait this all (expect this a lot, when you are playing a certain type of Alert).
- Freeform characters are cool, but may be look unfair towards for free-to-play/archetype characters (well, there are some really badly designed Freeforms, so Archetypes are still not handycapped).
- Same for vehicles, especially in race-missions.
Summary:
Even if you aren't into superhero stories, you must give this one a try. I think, you won't regret.

It took a while for me to have Full Mojo Rampage sink in, but when it did I was completely sold. It's a rogue-light, or whatever you want to call it, playable in co-op. You're a voodoo priest in diapers and a silly mask ...
Well, I can't explain the diapers, but TF2 has Hats™ so I guess masks is next big thing(?). There are no saves, but the quests you play can be completed in under an hour. Everything you pick up during that quest is gone if you die or when you've completed the quest. Your character progression and permenant buffs however are saved.
So it's a isometric ARPG by mechanics, where you play levels where you usually have to complete a couple of objectives and then get out. A quest is made up of several levels. After you've completed the objective(s) you can also walk around and explore the place, but of course there's the risk of you... you know... dying. You'll find mojos (temporary buffs for that quest), temporary weapons (when the ammo is gone your back to your default) and you might find a god. Gods live in caves and offer you buffs, but sometimes (and this is one of the parts I love about FMR) they want something in return. So they can offer you double damage, but you'll have to give away a quarter of your max health. That's a painful decision to make.
For me, personally, this game is at its' best in co-op, even though there's actually no direct use for it in the game mechanics, but it's always more fun to play a game in co-op than single player IMHO. It's a fun and challenging (oh yes it is!) rogue-light ARPG with cool music and funky graphics. If that's how you want your voodoo doll to hang then this is a game for you... go get collecting 'em masks!

I've logged in many hours into this game, so I figured that it's time to make a "fair" review. **Please understand that this is only just an opinion, so don't let this dictate your decision of playing or not.**
Pros:
-Easy to learn the basic game controls
-Multiple game modes to chose from
-Customizable "skins"
-Fun holiday events that allow players to obtain "devices" which can temporarily transform another player into something holiday themed
Cons:
-Pay to win game, tons of microtransactions
-Difficult for un-maxed evolution and un-maxed equipment players to obtain the top positions
-Unbalanced competitive mode (partially due to loss of player base)
-Updates do not resolve bugs
-Lack of administrators in-game and out of game
-Coin "farming" through various game modes AND through guild war season rewards
-Inability to distribute guild coins (from season rewards) based on guild statistics from last season
-Small changes are not announced to the player base, leaving players having to guess what changed in-game
Since this is a pay to win game, only maxed level and max gear players can "enjoy" this game the most, as under leveled players have very little chance against higher leveled players with maxed gear. Players who have played this game for a while continue to notice that bugs are not being fixed. The admins fail to respond to player requests, but say that they "acknowlege them." Okay, sure, the majority of the player base are kids, but please respond to bug fix requests. Bug fixes should be a top priority, as well as the security of player accounts.
Even though there are a ton of negatives, I still enjoy transforming players into pumpkins or snowmen. Okay, maybe that's just me. This game still manages to suck many hours out of my week, so there must be some sort of fun factor to it.  I tried not to go into specifics, as that would extend this review by too much.
Enjoy~

Primordia is a beautifully crafted science fiction adventure game in the spirit of Lucas Arts' The Dig. The melancholic mystery of the lovingly rendered post-apocalyptic setting is off-set by often light-hearted dialogue and cleverly ironic story elements (Freud's ego, id and superego populate an enormous defunct robot's skull at one point). The gameplay is deceptively simple, but my actions and choices had consequences, as I learned on my second play-through, which surprised and thrilled me. Like The Dig, Primordia's adventure game format ultimately serves as a vehicle to tell a subtle and poignant sci-fi fable. I highly recommend this game.

This game is so amazing it actually pains me to delete it from my computer. It was an amazing experience and I URGE any and all of you to try it out. I am thus writing a review to leave my mark.
Gameplay : the puzzles are sometimes a bit contrived, but satisfying overall. It's all a matter of investigating the area and DON'T FORGET YOU CAN USE CRISPIN. He's essential to many puzzles and I got stumped because I didn't know I could use him as an item! Otherwise, despite being occasionnaly frustrating, the mechanics are very well implemented and its a joy to interact with the game's world.
Graphics : All the graphics in this game are simply GORGEOUS. You can tell the makers put their heart into the art (pun intended), despite there being not all that much since the game is a bit short. But you can tell from the screenshots that this game really shines visually.
Audio : The real beauty of this game : the voice-over. The voice actor for Bastion's Narrator is the main character here, and he doesn't disappoint! And neither do the other characters! Each and every robot has a unique personality, and I loved just examining every little detail just for more of the voice talent. There's even a robot that only speaks in rhyming riddles! And the music, simply entrancing. When you play this, be sure to put up the volume!
Story : As usual, you are an amnesiac and you live with your faithful companion Crispin. While short, the adventure is really gripping, and charming- despite the post-apocalyptic setting. Similar to Machinarium, the world is only populated by robots, and they live in a big city of lights! There's two main sections to the story : exploring the desert, discovering various different areas, and exploring the city, which sadly wasn't that big. Unlike the desert, which had a map with a few area markers you could jump to, the city was only a few connected screens, which blocked you with puzzles. Despite the city being a bit small and the story short, it ends (according to the good ending) on a good note and offers the possibility of a sequel.
At least... I hope...
I give this game a 9/10, with frustrating puzzles as the only negative point. Try it out! Don't worry, there's plenty of comic relief thanks to Crispin :)
If anyone is looking for a good old-fashioned point-and-click game with a beautiful environment, a interesting storyline, and puzzles with multiple solutions, Primordia has all of those and more.

This game isn't nearly as cute as it thinks it is.
One of the devs must have wrote an exhaustive list of every cliche in video games, and then put every single one in a checkbox, to use once and then ignore. Pushbutton switches? Okay, walk over one and then never see one again. An enemy you defeat by bumping into a hole instead of attacking? Great, you've got it, moving on now...
Evoland never does anything interesting with any of the mechanics it shows you; it just points out that they exist and then hurries you on to the next mini-achievement or lame fourth-wall-breaking gag. I suspect the developers do this because they realize the gimmick of the game runs thin fast, and they're just trying to get you through it mercifully quickly. Hopefully, they reason, you'll be too distracted by the next flashy graphical effect to realize the game is all smirking irreverence and no substance.
This attitude reveals that the devs don't understand why the games they're aping are great. People didn't like Zelda becuase it had 8-bit graphics, a sword that you can cut bushes with, and  the ability to move from one tiny corridor and cramped room to the next. They liked it because the world was expansive and interesting, the combat was challenging but fair, there were actual puzzles where the solution wasn't immediately obvious (because, haha, the JOKE is that the solution is obvious, get it? Isn't this a fun way to spend your time? Haha!)
Evoland isn't a good game, and it's not even a good homage to actually good games, because it merely mimicks the surface of classic gaming. This game is the kind of mass-produced soulless single-severing Nostalgia™ that you see on ThinkGeek or LootCrate. Don't support this.

Albedo: Eyes from Outer Space is a first person action puzzle sci-fi game. Where you play a man trying to escape a lab during what seems to be an alien invasion.
This game is just gorgeous looking. I've only played a few hours so far but according to the most recent update you can play through the full game now.
You move back and forth through a beautifully designed world picking up items, solving puzzles, and occasionally killing some giant eyeballed aliens!
Albedo is a well designed, fun experience. The music direction is great you always feel tense, never knowing when an alien may decide to ruin your escape. The puzzles are challenging and executed well.
My only gripe with Albedo may be the awkward control scheme. I found myself dropping items accidentally. A minor annoyance more then anything.
It's the best sci-fi atmosphere in a first person game, maybe, ever. It has a feel of 'Mars Attacks meets Half-Life'. This could be a point and click adventure and I'd enjoy the hell out of just the environments.

Wow, did I ever want to like this game. The clips I saw of gameplay footage were just amazing. I thought it was going to be like watching the lovechild of Half Life and Bioshock. Then I actually start playing, and I can't even get outside of the stupid cellar I'm holed up in. Now I can sort of relate with the game creator, games like Call of Duty can only be appreciated by small-minded gamers that want their gameplay experiences like they want their rides at Universal Studios, easy and completely laid out for effortless progress. Games like Resident Evil also insult my intelligence with how little effort is put into the puzzle-solving aspects.
This, however, is completely on the other side of the spectrum. It's like the game requires you to be Sci-fi McGuyver in order to even get out of the first room. There is a huge monster pounding on the door, and I can only assume the game wants me to make use of a brick, a broken valve, a rope, and a used rat trap to somehow kill this thing when it breaks in, and I'm just not understanding what the game wants from me. Even games like Testament of Sherlock Holmes at least give you some context on what exactly you need to accomplish, without outright telling you how to do it. I mean why not just have the monster break in within like 30 seconds, and you kill it by pulling the cable from a circuit breaker and electricuting the thing to death? It'd be clever, interesting, and not make me dwell so much on a moldy cellar.
I really want to see how much potential this game really has. But at this moment, there are only two words I'd use to describe it: Boring and Confusing.

"ZAT" is a brilliant return to what I loved about older games: It revolves around basic play mechanics and careful tuning of balance. With those two elements in place, a large number of very fun challenges can be cooked up. The difficulty curve matches beautifully with the "novelty" curve: Just like a "Mario" game, you gradually encounter new enemies and environmental conditions, and these are mixed together in different ways to create problems for you to solve. Because the bedrock mechanics are so solid, even the tough problems avoid a feeling of being arbitrary or "cheap."
The basic shooting is okay, but the sniping is where things really get in the groove. The zombies' jerky, rolling gait makes them "just challenging enough" to headshot, which creates a real sense of satisfaciton in marksmanship. A normal human tends to hold their head still, but the undead are much tougher to predict - and this makes even the basic enemies a real factor. Even if all you're facing are simple "walkers," you have to think about what you're doing. Further, the way the common enemies synergize with the other zombie types provides lots of ways to get through an encounter. Sure, you could take out that suicide zombie at longer range...but he'll blow up when he dies, and look! There's a whole bunch of "regulars" all clustered together over there. If you time it just right, then -
BOOM! :)
Another excellent piece of design is how terrain and timing work together. Especially in the late game it becomes critical to have a feel for how fast the enemies move, how they tend to path to your position, and how to take shortcuts through the level. Your sense of all that is built incrementally throughout the game, with the end of the experience being a hard-but-fair final test.
Of course, I would be remiss if I didn't mention the overall feel of the game world. Although it's all definitely gory and gruesome, there's a certain aspect to it all that I can only describe as being "understated." That's pretty ironic to say, especially with all the Doom-esque imagery you'll encounter. The best way I can put it is that, unlike lots of other titles, this game is its own setpiece. Yes, you get into big engagements with all kinds of chaos going on, but none of it seems gratuitous, contrived, or scripted. Everything in the world feels like it belongs there, and there's an excellent sense of mystery. Not everything is shown to you or explained, and it doesn't really have to be. There are little side-story vignettes that glue things together a bit as they "trickle out" in bits and pieces, and the developers tend to let your own imagination do most of the knife-twisting there.
"Zombie Army Trilogy" is a tour-de-force in how a few elements, each invididually polished and then carefully fit together, can create a long and saisfying experience that never tires the player. I think it says a lot that I consider this title a must-have, and I generally consider the whole "zombie thing" to be overdone and tired. The developers of this game have really hit a home run.
