Primordia is a must for anyone who is a fan of old-school point & click adventures.
The tale follows robot Horatio and his floating companion Crispin as they try to retrieve a power core stolen from them by a boxy robot with lasers in a post-apocalyptic style world - however, the story is much more than this basic premise. One of the central questions the player wants answered is what exactly happened to the humans who presumably once inhabited this Earth and created the robots left behind. Added to this is a tapestry of moral and philosopical themes such as the meaning and existence of free will, individuality, progress, and what constitutes the 'greater good'. These sometimes rather heavy themes are pulled off through excellent writing, and are offset by a quirky humour that runs through the whole game. This off-beat humour and occasional breaking of the fourth wall are reminiscent of some of my favourite, genuinely old-school games such as Simon the Sorcerer, and I think anyone who was playing this kind of thing in the early 90's will appreciate it. The worldbuilding and background detail is fantastic - my one gripe is that the game just doesn't go far enough. There are hints of exciting other locations that we don't get to visit, and the larger philosophical themes are never fully explored.
As this is a game and not just a visual novel, I should probably mention a bit about the gameplay - it's pretty much standard of point & click games, and uses the traditional inventory system. Nothing stood out as unique, but equally nothing was inconvenient or jarring. The puzzles are not particularly challenging, and there's plenty of hints on hand from Crispin if one chooses to press him for them (it's also pretty fun to hear him getting annoyed and snarky when you try and use him too many times). I prefer simpler puzzles so the flow of the story doesn't stall, but others might find this game too easy.
In terms of visuals, the pixel art is gorgeous, and the colour palette of browns, rusts and muted golds perfectly realizes the dusty, disued world. The audio content is also great, from the music to the voice acting. Even minor characters are voiced, and the robot voice effects are pretty cool.
Overall an 9/10 for this game. The presentation is beautiful both visually and aurally, and beneath this is a solid story rooted in a world that feels like it really could be our future. Horatio and Crispin are likeable and memorable characters to journey through this tale with, and their easy banter creates the emotional anchor to this crumbling planet. Points are lost for the sense that the game could have been bigger both in terms of the number of locations, and the philosophical ideas that never seem to be explored quite as far as you hope. Regardless, 'Primordia' is highly recommended!

Have you ever played a game with spaceships and wanted to tweak the design a little?  "Why did they build it THAT way?" you wonder.  Well, now you can find out if you have what it takes to be a (fictional) spaceship designer.  You've got to grow your faction to control the galaxy, and you do it by building up a fleet of custom designed ships of every conceivable size.  Seven playable factions use different components and combat styles.  Another interesting twist is that there are "agents," special ships that are player-designed that get shared over the net when you go through a wormhole.  Beware the agents, for they are deadly!
Reassembly is a fascinating mix of cerebral ship design and combat strategy, mixed with arcade shooter action as you put those designs to work.  I recommend you read one of the game guides to get a feel for the game and get started on the right foot.

Only took about 5 hours to complete but a pretty enjoyable experience.
It's sort of a mix of God of War, Rome, 300, Saving Private Ryan and 13th Warrior put in an alternative history package for the soldier Gaius to hack and slash his way to revenge.
-The story is pretty standard fair with the usually discrepancies present in such stories but it works well enough. Any twists you'll see coming a long way off.
-The combat is visceral and pretty satisfying, relying on an Arkham Asylum system though a bit less polished and while it has visual queues for certain attacks it can sometimes be hard to see them. Gaius can also sometimes have wonky targeting for certain enemies making it much harder to finish someone off. I may have been doing it wrong but some of the boss fights are a bit of a slog towards the end. Executions allow you to gain health, focus, XP and temporary damage boost and are wonderfully bloody. Also don't penalize you too much if you fail to hit the right button.
-The visuals are stunning and some cutscenes were damn high quality and put more impact on the meh story. Scenery and locals have some loving details added to them making it feel pretty alive for the rather narrow lanes you go down. However, some executions on certain maps would suddenly make my game start stuttering so there are limits.
-Gameplay is the hack and slash combat, unit commanding where you'll join or command troops as you take or defend various objectives and mounted gun segments. While the first is the most common the other two help spice things up. There are various things to collect though I only found a few since that isn't my main draw to the game. There is also a multiplayer bit that I never tried but I'm pretty sure it's dead.
Over all I'd give it a 7/10 but I still had a great time and I'd recommend checking it out if you're in the mood for this sort of game.

Something I should mention from the start is that this game is pretty niche. The concept of "handling the logistics of a mass infrastructural transportation network" is, from what I can imagine, not a lot of people's idea of a fun time. For those out there, however, who find that sorta stuff really fascinating, this game does a fantastic job at satiating that.
Yeah, the UI isn't the prettiest. It's handled a bit like RollerCoaster Tycoon's, only with even more miscellaneous window management and vague controls. That being said, it's not nearly as bad as a lot of people in the reviews say it is. After using the in-game help section and fiddling about with menus, it took me maybe an hour or so to get my little company off the ground and start transporting stuff.
Once you get past that hurdle, you're rewarded with a really solid and in-depth management game that's sure to last you many hours if you devote yourself to it. Grab yourself a coffee and give it a go for an hour or two, you might just like it.

Death is pounding its way through the door to get at you. By the looks it ain't gonna hold much longer. A whole other mess of horrors whose only desire is to turn you inside out are at your back, slaughtering themselves on the energy barrier you erected to cover that approach, but if experience has taught you anything it's that now that things look like they couldn't get any worse the power's likely gonna cut out and, if you're real unlucky, it'll happen the same time the horde at the door breaks in. Adrenalin is doing what it should, heightening your senses, stretching every second, and your pounding pulse is almost drowning out the bleating of your assault rifle telling you your ammo is critically low.
You just gotta hold on a little longer, you tell yourself. The automated sentry you're working feverishly to power up will be a notch in your favour come crunch time, but it's no guarantee of escape. Luckily your squadmates are working their way towards you, trying to give you an out. Then it hits you. The video feed in the corner of your head-up is broadcasting static. While you were covering your own sorry♥♥♥♥♥no-one was covering theirs. They're already bug food.
There's nothing else for it then. The only way out is through.
The sentry completes its boot cycle and so you figure there's no time like the present. You punch the door release and hose the corridor beyond with bullets. This ain't the time or place for short, controlled bursts. The sentry overhead starts raining shell casings down your back and you welcome the pain. Pain means you're still living. As long as bullets are flying and the blood in your ears is still pounding there's a chance you can make it to the reactor, disable the coolants and let the whole infested mess blow itself straight back to hell. Preferably after you've kicked off your boots and lit up a celebratory stogie in the escape capsule home.
The reactor room is a mess of bug parts. Looks like your comrades put up one hell of a fight. The coolant safeties are just beyond the protective barrier you swear is taking hours for the automation to lift clear. The bugs' assault is relentless. Surely they gotta go extinct sometime soon.
It's just after you get the first of the coolant safeties shut down that the power shorts out. Then the ammo runs dry. And, as the final insult, your suit battery pips out and you lose the high beams.
At last you're alone in the skittering dark, making peace with the feeling  you're about to be enjoying that stogie with your buddies in the afterlife.
Feels a lot like "Chris Sawyer's Locomotion".

I feel a lot of people will pass this game over, but it's shaping up to be one of the most enjoyable Roguelike games I've played.  With a good progression capability (You do level up, but so do the levels), games are broken down into quests in which you need to complete a couple of randomly generated levels and then fight a final boss.  Along the way, you have inventories of usable items as well as trinkets that affect your abilities.  Sometimes they are 100% good, other times you are sacrificing one stat for another.  As well, at the start of the game you can alter your loadout a bit to increase stats, increase gold find, add inventory space, etc.
There is also coop in the game as well, but I haven't tried it out yet so can't speak about it.  Sounds very promising though.
For a Early Access game, this is very polished and playable.  It sounds like they mainly want to add new quests during the period, which I'm totally okay with.  If you are a fan of games like Rogue Legacy and Risk of Rain, you'll want to check this out.

It is very rare that a game can have me hooked, even in such an early stage of development. Full Mojo Rampage (FMR) has a certain quality to it that is so incredible. It may be the art style, which is very dark, yet very cartoony. It is composed of very gloomy blues, greens, dark reds, and purples for it's backgrounds, but pops with bright and electric colors on it's foreground. It feels very mystical, and is reminiscint of the environment in the Secret of Monkey Island. It plays almost like a twin-stick shoother, but with the core gameplay feeling like an ARPG, such as Diablo, or Torchlight. It also has an ALMOST perma-death, with levels and certain stats carrying over, but nothing else.
You will die time and time again, but be excited to start over. It is incredible how simple and yet how fun this game is, and it is only in it's alpha.
I would reccomend anyone who enjoys Diablo-like games to try this game out, and for any roguelike fans to give it a shot as well.

Rather, I think the game's "stage" is too small. Overall great game, there is some good and bad however. First let me say that I've played quite a bit offline, so my experianc in game is a little more than the 10 hours I'm clocked at.
I'll start with the bad.
Each race has race traits, some good, some bad. Howevr, these can not be changed. I would personally like more freedom with this, but I got over that fairly quickly.
Second there is not tutorial, not one that I found anyway. The gameplay is great and all but you're basically thrown on an alian world and thats about it. My first game I was wandering arround until I came across some creature and I was killed.
My second game I somehow randomely learned to build a city and then I died.
My fourth game I finally figured out how to use the race traits and build troops then I died.
My fifth game I actually know enough about the game to play it.
I dont like to go online and research how to do stuff, but if you're new to this game then you may have to do that. I've played a few similar games and the controls are very different from anything I've played.
Now for the Pros.
This game is absolutely wonderful, once you learn how to play it. It is very in depth and each race has a story that you can choose to follow or just ignore.
The other players (NPC's) are actually in depth. They all have unique personalities. The aggressive ones will actually be aggressive, and the peaceful ones will actually be peaceful. You dont have to be militaristic to win this game. And it isnt boring if you decide to follow another path, it doesnt take more effort, and it's just as rewarding. In the CIV games you cant win by being solely militaristic or economic, you have to be extremely scientific, it forces you into a corner. No matter how much money you have or how powerful your military is you will allways be outdone by someone that is more scientifically advance than you. In this game you dont have to worry about that, you can be strictly military, strictly economic, or strictly religious, or whatever.
Each race is very in depth, with its own story line and own backstory. It's actutaly quite amazing in how in depth it is and how unique each race is and the play style of each race. I dont like that some races have their own play style that you have to abide to, but I get over that considering how awesom the designs for the races and their stories are.
Overall I love the game I would give it an 85/100.

Been playing Civilization for a while (II and V mostly with a side of SMAC and Colonization) but this is a pretty great game with a nice breath of fresh air for someone looking for a 4X game that's about on equal footing with Civ games as far as difficulty goes.
-> Really strong thematically with an expansive and interesting backstory with relatively unique theming for factions
-> Quests to give you something to do and can also be story-based
-> Game encourages you to play wide instead of tall (like in Civ V)
-> Summer/Winter mechanic
-> Hero units complete with special abilities and RPG-style leveling
-> Turn-based combat in specialized instances turn battles into something where you have to think. Being clever about fighting can often nullify having numerically weaker units
-> Unit design/customization like in SMAC?!
-> Elevation like in SMAC?!
-> Really good art direction and music/sound
-> Super-friendly and elegant UI. I figured out most stuff without even playing the tutorial.
-> Doesn't look like♥♥♥♥♥♥on lower settings and loads MUCH quicker than Civ V
There are some downsides, however. The game sometimes closes all of a sudden (luckily autosaves make this more of an annoyance), the diplomacy is kind of eh, and the AI is prone to let you mostly walk all over them in lower difficulties (which is fine when you're learning the ropes but can get boring quick)
Overall, I'm really impressed! If you want a change from Civ-style 4X this is where to scratch that itch. With its extremely strong premise, art direction, and theme (not to mention sharing some game elements) it's much more of a successor to SMAC than Beyond Earth will ever be. Yet it's different enough from Civ games to stand on its own. I definitely want to see where Amplitude will go next.

First off I want to say that I am giving it a recommended rating because I nabbed it on sale for $4.75 and had I paid $20 I would have been disappointed. If you can grab it for $5 or less than I think it could be worth it to you. It was for me.
Pros:
Decent story - Not amazing but better than a lot of other games I've played
Reasonable good performance
Good graphics
Satisfying combat - At least initially. Several different combat mechanics that help break up rather medicore swordplay
High fun to dollar ratio when purchased on sale
Cons:
Short - Don't expect a long epic game with a plot that weaves between story arcs. About a 6 to 7 hour campaign.
Repetitive Combat - The combat throughout the game isn't horrible but the boss fights are pretty repetitive and boring. I feel like they should have spent more time refining the bosses and focused on making those fights fun and interesting because they certainly aren't a challenge.
Stutter in fullscreen mode - I had to run the game in borderless windowed mode. It ran fine in that mode without any perceived performance issues but I shouldn't have had to search a forum to fiind the answer to my stuttering. The game has been out for quite some time now and this issue should have been addressed.
Ultimately, it's a pretty fun game at $5 or less. Don't buy it more than that. Go into it expecting a short game with a decent story, by game standards, satisfying combat, boring bosses, well animated cut scenes and little replay value.
If you can pick it up cheap it's a very pretty, satisfyingly violent game. The campaign is very short but very enjoyable. Don't expect huge amounts of depth, it's linear as heck.

Ryse might just be the most forgettable game ever made. I should probably point out that I did not finish the game, though from what I gather I got very close. That this took an insulting three  hours is damning enough, that I couldn’t muster the enthusiasm to spend an extra half hour with the game should give you some indication of just how limp and lifeless the whole affair is.
You play Marius Titus, your standard forgettable scowling stubbled white guy and yes I did have to google his name. You move from arena to tepid arena fighting barbarians for about four hours and then the game ends. There’s so little to grab the attention here that it just about provides the bare minimum to be described as a game, albeit a pretty one. You’ve got the basics of Batman combat with God of War finishers, and that’s your lot. I hope you like ramping, as every single one of the hundreds of enemies you kill has one of about five pre-canned animations as a finisher. While they might be numerous enemy variety is pitiful, their most interesting characteristic being that they all hail from the North of England (you can tell because they all eat gravy and chips out of a flat cap on the back of a whippet). Occasionally you fight a quick time event poorly masquerading as a boss battle. That the developers thought that this would cut it (even as a launch game for a new console) speaks to either delusion or a seriously troubled development.
The other, depressing conclusion is that the developers were hoping the story would carry the game, a flaccid sub-Gladiator affair with a leaden script and cliché bingo. The cast of English jobbing actors actually do a sterling job with the material, and occasionally almost threaten to inject a modicum of life into proceedings.
There is nothing here worth your time, energy or money. Even this half-hearted shrug of a review is more than it deserves.

This review is for the single-player content.
When playing this game I kept thinking about why this was made.
Did it bring something new to battle systems that we haven't seen before or had some interesting take on it? No. It was mostly hacking, some blocking and dodging with the focus ability to slow time, then some QTE executions and boss fights where you have to learn their patterns and push buttons accordingly. Fighting was pretty repeating but satisying enough to continue on. It was nothing I haven't seen before or what haven't done better in other games. It was also pretty unsatisying that you couldn't use focus on boss fights at all.
Was it for history buffs? I would imagine that would be a niche market so no and besides the story throws history out of the window pretty quickly and it never manages to climb back up. There aren't that many games set in ancient Rome where you can hack and slash your way in, so if the setting intrigues you, this might satisfy it to some extent.
Did the story bring something new to the table? No, it was a cliché festival and it clearly had gotten influence from the Gladiator-movie. The story did get better towards the end, but it wasn't a story about romans or britons, it was a story about violent vengeance and those we already have plenty in the gaming world.
So why was the game made? I guess it was made that there would be something pretty to play on Xbox One and it is a pretty game, the graphics are on point.
Why I gave thumbs up after complaining this much? Because I got it from sale (5-7 dollars, can't remember) and for that price it gave me few hours of entertainment and fun. Anymore though and my head would have exploded from the clichéd story and the repetitiveness of the combat. I wouldn't pay the full price for this, it's mediocre, but when on sale it can be a good deal.

The main gameplay in FMR is probably best described as a bullet hell style top down shooter, with random rogue-like and rpg elements. The solo and coop game modes are quest based, of which there are currently (as of Alpha 5) 3 quests and 1 survival quest. The quests themselves are randomly generated sequences of random dungeon-like levels and bosses, with other random surprises mixed in. When starting a quest, one starts on a fresh character, so all items and equipment (called relics in FMR) are only kept during this quest. If one dies in the quest, they cannot continue onward and lose all items / relics found during that run. However, players get experience towards level-ups which remain throughout all quest runs, and there are certain stat increasing items called pins that also remain. In this way, many have described it in terms of similar games as a mixture of The Binding of Isaac gameplay with Rogue Legacy style leveling. In my experience so far, I would say the items found during a run are far more important than stat collections from pins and leveling up, so it leans a bit towards the rogue-like side. I'd say it has a nice balance.
As for game performance, I have had zero issues in single player; the graphics look great and I have had no frame drops. There was slight lag in online multiplayer coop gameplay, but I think dedicated multiplayer servers are likely in store for a future FMR build, so that may improve. That being the only negative aspect I've yet to encounter, I give this game a thumbs up.
Finally I should note the game development team is very active in the game forums, which is a plus.
Overall, it is quite a lot of fun in its current state and will probably continue seeing great improvements during its development.

The game breaker for me came with the fiddely controls. In order to do something, the game needs to detect that I am in the correct position to do it. For ex, grabbing a person without killing him so I can interrogate him, or placing an C4 on a AA gun. The problem is that the game mostly fails to detect that I am in the correct position. I have been killed in game many many times lying/sitting/standing next to the target I need to interrogate without being able to grab him. Im so close that I can't get any closer, yet I can not grab him. Of course he spots me, the alarm goes off and I'm dead.
I have also spent quite some time figuring out the best time and way to sneak up on an AA gun without being spotted on hard difficulty, Just to end up sitting next to the AA gun, surrounded by enemys who have not yet spotted me, with an C4 in my hand but without the game noticing that I should be able to place it on the AA gun. Thereby forcing me to circle around the AA gun with my nose scratching it - but still not being able to plant the C4. Of course, after a while someone spots me, the alarm is raised and I'm toast.
With this happening time and time again, i've grown tired of the game really fast. Bit of a shame, even if it's not a the full Metal Gear Solid V game. The thing is that the game has some replay value, but it's utterly ruined with the above mentioned problems.

Evoland is an interesting game, not for its look, but for its gameplay.
Much like the game "Life of Pixel", this game centers around evolving through different eras of video games. Unlike "Life of Pixel", this game is more Legend of Zelda/Final Fantasy/WoW in its RPG approach of gameplay (while LoP focuses on the aesthetic of specific video game consoles from the 70s-90s using platforming mechanics). Both games are great for nostalgia factor alone.
If there are any nitpicks, I was a little disappointed in how sparse the story felt, but I didn't let that keep me from enjoying the exploring. I didn't care about the villain, but I did care about the environment and the exploration.
When the game was first released, it was a little buggy, and some of the bosses' hitboxes didn't trigger, which made beating the game frustrating, but I am pretty sure that was resolved since I 100% this game a few months after. The act of collecting cards and playing a variation of FFVIII's Triple Triad card game is enough to get this. If not, then appreciate all the nods to your favorite retro games of yesteryear.
No matter how you look at it, Evoland is a fun game. Give it a go, then brace yourselves for Evoland II, because it looks like everything the first game is, but better.

I first heard about this game back in early 2009, while I was still heavily involved in CoH/CoV, and was overall pretty excited to see a new Superhero MMO in development. Naturally, I bought a Lifetime Sub a few months before the game launched and by now it's more than paid for itself. As I've been playing on and off ever since launch, I figured it was high time I wrote a quick review. So here goes nothing.
In Champions Online, you play as a superhero who begins their career helping the Champions (CO's the Avengers, basically) repel an alien invasion of Millennium City (essentially a rebuilt Detroit, Michigan). From there, you thwart a plot between the various gangs of the city and eventually move on to dealing with more global concerns as the different zones are opened up to you. Aside from Millenium City, the other main zones are the Southwestern Desert in Nevada, the far north of Canada, the aptly named Monster Island, the underwater Lemuria, and Vibora Bay, essentially a New Orleans analogue (voodoo and all). Each of these zones has its own distinct flavor, along with mission chains that take you through the various locales.
The overall tone of the game is somewhat on the silly side most of the time (though it does have its share of darker moments, especially with some of the Adventure Packs), and takes a lot of inspiration from American comic books and superheroes. Many of the game's characters and settings are based off of the Champions RPG, which is essentially a tabletop game where you play as a four color comic book hero.
PROS:
-Excellent Character Creation tool allows creation of countless possible characters
-Freeform Characters can select any powers, albeit with some tiered restrictions
-Free/Premium Archetype Characters are generally pretty solid and good for new players to learn the game mechanics
-Varied and interesting environments
-Fluid, though somewhat twitchy gameplay
-Nemesis system allows you to create villains for your hero to fight against
-Regular holiday events (Bloodmoon, etc.)
-Rotating Alerts/Rampages offer an alternative to running missions
CONS:
-Missions can get repetitive; there's not much variation in them, especially at earlier levels
-Freeform characters (the main draw of the game, IMHO) require a subscription or special character slots that run somewhere in the $50 ballpark last I checked
-Various other aspects of the game require a subscription (Premium Archetypes, Costume Sets, etc.)
-Lockboxes put you at the mercy of the cruel and heartless RNG Gods, and are the only way to acquire certain costume sets/vehicles
-No CoX/CoV style mission editor
-Nemesis system (another huge draw of the game) is no longer being updated
-PvP is essentially dead, aside from random duels
-Currently very little going on development-wise, aside from new purchasable costume sets and lockboxes
-Some potentially game-breaking bugs still exist
-Little to no communication from the devs to the player base
Unfortunately, the current state of the game isn't super great. The last major update was back in September 2014, which added a new archetype, a couple of powers (to be unlocked for freeform characters by leveling said archetype to 40), and about 4-5 hours worth of in-game content. There hasn't been much communication from the developers on what the plans for CO's future are, but the game still limps on despite being largely forgotten.
That being said, I've sunk countless hours into playing this game (I have several freeform characters at max level), and every now and then I feel the alt-itis kick in and get the urge to roll up a new character. While the game is not without its flaws, it's definitely worth playing if you haven't tried it yet.

I first heard about this game back in early 2009, while I was still heavily involved in CoH/CoV, and was overall pretty excited to see a new Superhero MMO in development. Naturally, I bought a Lifetime Sub a few months before the game launched and by now it's more than paid for itself. As I've been playing on and off ever since launch, I figured it was high time I wrote a quick review. So here goes nothing.
In Champions Online, you play as a superhero who begins their career helping the Champions (CO's the Avengers, basically) repel an alien invasion of Millennium City (essentially a rebuilt Detroit, Michigan). From there, you thwart a plot between the various gangs of the city and eventually move on to dealing with more global concerns as the different zones are opened up to you. Aside from Millenium City, the other main zones are the Southwestern Desert in Nevada, the far north of Canada, the aptly named Monster Island, the underwater Lemuria, and Vibora Bay, essentially a New Orleans analogue (voodoo and all). Each of these zones has its own distinct flavor, along with mission chains that take you through the various locales.
The overall tone of the game is somewhat on the silly side most of the time (though it does have its share of darker moments, especially with some of the Adventure Packs), and takes a lot of inspiration from American comic books and superheroes. Many of the game's characters and settings are based off of the Champions RPG, which is essentially a tabletop game where you play as a four color comic book hero.
PROS:
-Excellent Character Creation tool allows creation of countless possible characters
-Freeform Characters can select any powers, albeit with some tiered restrictions
-Free/Premium Archetype Characters are generally pretty solid and good for new players to learn the game mechanics
-Varied and interesting environments
-Fluid, though somewhat twitchy gameplay
-Nemesis system allows you to create villains for your hero to fight against
-Regular holiday events (Bloodmoon, etc.)
-Rotating Alerts/Rampages offer an alternative to running missions
CONS:
-Missions can get repetitive; there's not much variation in them, especially at earlier levels
-Freeform characters (the main draw of the game, IMHO) require a subscription or special character slots that run somewhere in the $50 ballpark last I checked
-Various other aspects of the game require a subscription (Premium Archetypes, Costume Sets, etc.)
-Lockboxes put you at the mercy of the cruel and heartless RNG Gods, and are the only way to acquire certain costume sets/vehicles
-No CoX/CoV style mission editor
-Nemesis system (another huge draw of the game) is no longer being updated
-PvP is essentially dead, aside from random duels
-Currently very little going on development-wise, aside from new purchasable costume sets and lockboxes
-Some potentially game-breaking bugs still exist
-Little to no communication from the devs to the player base
Unfortunately, the current state of the game isn't super great. The last major update was back in September 2014, which added a new archetype, a couple of powers (to be unlocked for freeform characters by leveling said archetype to 40), and about 4-5 hours worth of in-game content. There hasn't been much communication from the developers on what the plans for CO's future are, but the game still limps on despite being largely forgotten.
That being said, I've sunk countless hours into playing this game (I have several freeform characters at max level), and every now and then I feel the alt-itis kick in and get the urge to roll up a new character. While the game is not without its flaws, it's definitely worth playing if you haven't tried it yet.

If you like superhero games with a friendly membership, GREAT customization, a comicbook look, and powers beyond imagining, even in the free to play Archetypes, this game is for you. Really fun Superhero MMO for all gamers.

I've been playing this on and off for years. For people who enjoy complex simulations and managing finances, this game is just incredible. The downside is it can be so complex that you'd need to invest many, many hours just learning the mechanics, and even more so to master the nuances involved in running a transportation empire.
The logistics of making sure that passengers and goods are transported in the most efficient way possible is daunting enough. But understanding the tools you use to make this possible is near excruciating when you're just starting out. I recommend spending a lot of time with a small map following a tutorial and experimenting. Otherwise, you will always just lose in ways that are mysterious to you.
That being said, the skill, effort, and meticulous balancing can be extremely rewarding when you pull if off. But it's not for everyone. This game is for people who look at a balance sheet and become satisfied at a healthy profit margin and who are challenged most of all by inefficiency. If you prefer a lot more excitement, this game is not for you.
Finally, the interface is ancient and in some cases obscure. Many actions are unnecessarily difficult, such as organizing the stops for a line. The graphics cannot be described as retro—it is more accurately described as aged, dysfunctional, and lacking. It is also so small that putting down stops and arranging roads can be an agonizing process. The game itself is also prone to crashes and the occasional glitch.
Ultimately, the game is rich is simulation and this is a must-try for those who enjoy deep simulation and making complex systems work. But the aged interface and graphics as well as the steep learning curve will turn some players off, regardless of how impressed they are of the mechanics.
The game is free, and I recommend everyone try it. But more importantly I recommend everyone give it their best try, tutorial reading and groans of annoyace and head bashing on the wall and all. This may be the best and only way for you to know if the game is sufficiently rewarding for you. It is for me.

fantastic, each game is different and can be as in depth and involved or as surface and mindless as you want for a turn based strategy. The lore is also fascinating and you learn more about each faction with each game.

I love the combat system. You move armies around the map like normal units, but when a battle starts you move into a sort of battlefied-level strategic interface that lets you arrange the units of the army and move them individually. This allows all sorts of strategy from flanking to stalling to wait for reinforcements to arrive. At the same time, while you can do some work to acquire a few additional base units, most unit upgrades in the game come in the form of you re-outfitting a base unit with new technologies and resources. That means that you essentially customize the design of each unit type in the game over time which is also a huge strategic factor. Overall, it makes the Civilization series combat/military seem like child's play.
However, at the same time, I found the complexity sometimes getting in the way. The game uses a lot of invented words/culture which makes for an initial learning curve to know what is what (e.g. money is "dust" and all of the strategic resources are things I've never heard of). In a game that has a lot of concepts, I didn't seem to be able to find any in-game help that explains how everything works. I did play the tutorial and the tooltips are pretty well populated, but, for example, I had to go online twice to learn how unit healing works. The first time, nothing seemed to happen so I went online and found a lot of vague responses that said essentially that you heal automatically over time based on various metrics. Cool. Then I played another game and found that my units weren't healing and apparently the civiliztion perk "can buy citizens with dust" (which is money remember) implied that units of that civilization can only heal by using dust. But don't do that for all army units because your army will likely be mixed with minor faction units that heal on their own like usual. ... See how this starts to get pretty complicated? Better in game help would go a long way toward understanding these things in the first place, but in some cases it just seems needlessly complex even after you get to know it.
The interface is mixed. I love the consistency of the pop-ups/windows (you can minimize or dismiss anything and right clicking on the background always takes you back). Allocating workers in a city has clever little interface as do some other areas. But then there are some annoying issues. The interface overall feels too "busy". I find a lot of times I'll overlook a unit on the map because of how busy/detailed the graphics are. There is no way to rotate your view which means sometimes you're looking at inconvenient angles. The actual battle controls seem to require a lot of extra clicking when I'm trying to micromanage. So, the interface is definitely good and bad, frustrating at times.
Despite all its complexity, there are a few areas the game takes a simpler approach than many others. The world make is kind of like the game Risk in that its divided into predefined region settling/taking a city anywhere in that region gives you total control of that region. This eliminates a lot of the sense of the strategy of defining and growing your border or varying city density. Another area where it seems sadly simple is the navy. As far as I can tell there is no naval combat (nor air combat) which is a bit disappointing given how rich so much of the rest of the game is.
Overall, I recommend this game and I'll be putting in more time to learn it and enjoy it. It's certainly not perfect, but overall it does some interesting things and is fun and strategic.

Pro's:
-It's a flexible game, with many victory conditions from which you can choose
-Each race has a different way of being played, allowing the creation of varied strategies
-Because it's turn based it doesn't require a constant state of alert while playing
-The save/load function allows you to take a break of the game whenever you want and to restart from where you left it last time
-There is an auto-save function which really helps alot in case of a corrupted save file
Con's:
-Each "match" takes a really long time, in my case, consisting at least of 4 hours a match
-Because each race is played in a different way, if you don't know how to play it you might be in a huge disadvantage when you play a new race
-Even though it has tons of things to do, playing it alone might be a little boring, especially after having some hours into the game
To sum it up, I would give this game a rating of 3.7/5, though I would rate it higher if it had a story mode or the matches where shorter.

The first challange in Endless Legend is its absolutely awful load times (its long enough that even when I think about playing I often dont because I remember how long it takes) and once you get past that you will run smack dab into the wall which is this games learning curve.
This game is aggresively hard to understand for new players and 17 hours in, I still have only a vauge idea of what is going on.  I know Im winning, but I am not entirely sure why.
Most of the tech you can research seems pointless, anything but military upgrades will eventually see you getting overrun by some other group.  And the combat itself is confusing and poorly explained, again, seventeen hours in and I cant say for certain how the combat actually works.  I actually thought it was impossible to move characters for a while outside of the AI doing so and then found out that i could only recently, just as a proof of how confusing this is for the player.
Additionally, the combat itself lacks any real strategy or depth, at least as far as I can see.  Sure there are some posistioning things you can do, but in the end it basically comes down to who had the stronger troops at the start.  I am reminded of when Yahtzee said "It basically comes down to who started combat with the biggest boots" because that seems to be the only thing that matters.  In Starcraft II, with proper control, a small and theoretically weaker group of marines can outmaneuver and kill a larger and stronger group of zealots.  A battle will turn into a game of control and tactics where your abillity to think quickly is as important as your abillity to react quickly.  In Endless Legend, the stronger group will win without fail.
And to top it off, the game length and size is far smaller than I expected.  The game maps are small compared to something like Civilization, and the length of a game cant even compare.
Endless Legend plays around with some interesting ideas, but is brought down by massive issues in its execution.  I hesitate to call this a strategy game when the only viable strategy seems to be "build massive and well equipped army and smash"  Lack of any viable means to defend yourself if you try to take a peaceful route, combined with roaming monsters and the horrendous combat...  I know this is a well liked game, but I simply cant recommend it.

Really neat game. It absolutely excels at what it's meant to be, to emulate how a Snes game plays, feels, looks, moves and sounds. It's quite amazing and I've never played a game that does all of these things so well. More than that, the game also has the polish, level of detail and variety of a good, classic Snes game. I absolutely love this game.
Now, there is the fact that a lot of reviews here are about how the controls are "unresponsive" and people write stuff like "you can't shoot straight upwards". This has caused me to break my hand and forehead by way of a
, but now that I've returned from a lengthy, painful visit to the hospital, let me tell you people this: The controls are absolutely fine and simply not
at all - people who claim that have no idea what they're talking about. In fact, the controls are about as responsive and clear-cut as you can get with this type of game. You have complete freedom mid-air, the movement isn't slippery, your character only moves exactly as much as you press the direction button, there are no lost inputs, nothing like that. This is way easier to control than, say, Ghouls & Goblins, old Castlevania games, old Nes games that had weird momentum physics (the original Mario Bros. counting among them) and the like.
And you can do exactly as much as you need to do with your weapon. It's actually mind-boggling for me to read people writing stuff like "you can't shoot straight upwards" when there's really no place anywhere in the game where that would be useful.
I suggest anyone who has problems with the "controls" to put the game on Easy mode, get a turbo controller and also a Game Genie. You can easily beat this game on Normal in little more than an hour or so and not have any problem with the controls if you're not a dink.
So, I recommend this game if you like old Snes games and stuff like that and you're not a dink.

I had really high hopes for this game...
I really like RPG games, idea is awesome and it looks pretty nice...
I grew up in the 90s with many old RPG games, and I was very happy to play this one...
But, as a game... it sucks...
"Evolution" is very short... I thought that I will be able to play throughout the history of RPG games... But in 15 minutes, you are already playing in 3D... It would be nice to have more information about evolution steps (i.e. first game that implemented it, year, and such...), and to experience it for at least 15 minutes before going to another...
Aside from that, some "evolution" steps are without any sense... You got "Maze", at the entrance of said maze... And similar...
But, that is not the worst part... Worst part is that game is awfully dull... There are two types of combat; Real Time and Turn Based...
Turn based is stripped down version of JRPG combat. You are attacked randomly, and WAAAY to often... So, when you just want to explore the dungeon, you will spend 2/3 of the time just clicking attack... And don't try to explore the same area more then once... You will be attacked again, and again, and again...
Real time combat is somewhat better, but still boring, and unlike the turn based, there are some encounters that are pretty challenging... And if you die, prepare to return to the last checkpoint (save game)... And checkpoints are way too far aparat... This wouldn't be a problem (I am not so much of a fan of hard games, but don't have a problem with them), if the game and combat was actually fun to play.
Smaller problems would be;
- If your controller gets disconnected while in the game, you will have to exit it and launch again with controller turned on (a classic problem with many games).
- Extremely irritating sound when your health is low (ok, game is trying to simulate old games, and probably motherboard speaker, but it is not pleasant, especially since I already play in full 3D)
- 2 completely different forms of game, that are getting you confused (one on the "map", with random encounters and turn based combat, and one for the "levels" with visible enemies and real time combat)...
This game had SO much potential... It had a great idea to pay homage to the great history of cRPGs... But it failed miserably...
P.S. I played more than 0.2 hours... It appears that this game also have a problem with actually telling Steam that it is running...

Simutrans, is literally a "transportation simulation" game. (get it? SimTrans? Sigh.)  This is a surprisingly fun and deep game where you must connect materials to factories, products to stores, and people to their destinations.  Although there is a lot to learn and I've barely scratched the surface, I'm having a great time learning the systems and experimenting with different strategies.
PROS
+ TONS of settings to customize the game to your style
+ Random world generator with lots of options keeps replay value high
+ Multiple types of systems to implement or ignore (public trans, mail delivery, manufacturing supply chains)
+ Complex systems allow solutions to any type of challenge
+ Dynamic world keeps things fresh (technologies change, cities grow)
+ Ummm, FREE!
CONS
- Very steep learning curve (start simple: bus stations or single-chain train lines)
- Many buttons are not intuitive and require research
- Poor tutorial (didn't even work for me), confusing in-game guide, basic tooltips
- Old Old School graphics, sound, and interface
- Crashes occasionally (enable Auto Save!)

-When you get hit somewhere your health bar doesn't drop, you lose that part of your ship. Your thrusters got blown off and your only weapon faces forward? Sucks.
-Every faction truly plays differently. It's not a game of "What weapons am I gonna rambo with this time?" It's more like "These are my options, now what am I going to do with them?"
-The physics are great and really consider a lot of important factors such as center of mass and thruster location.
-The music is astounding. Gives a nice space-y feel and also compliments the actual gameplay quite well.
-Buildup from small to large ships doesn't feel grind-y and boring. It's just a different phase of the game, where instead of taking on giant death machines you go around activating stations and collecting resources from easier sources.
-Ships made by other players spawn in your world, so you get a lot of variety.
-The graphics are great. Frankly, I'm sick of repeated textures and copied/pasted environments. The basis on particles makes each game experience unique both visually and in regards to gameplay.
However, this game feels like it never left alpha/beta phase. There are insane numbers of holes in regards to instructions/development. A minor example (that still bugs me quite a bit) is part tool-tipping. Many have descriptions while even more have no real explanation whatsoever.  The number of typos is also embarrassing.
The number of general options is also a joke. Why do I have to turn autozoom off every time I start the game? And why do I have to deal with that stupid tutorial every time I start a new file? There's no skip option! And don't even get me started on those quests that never go away (why should I have to minimize the HUD just to sweep the pathetic tutorial under the rug?)
The biggest issue has got to be the bugs, though. So. Many. Bugs.
-The game crashes frequently during ship construction or even just flying around. Or sometimes it will freeze for 2 or 3 minutes just 'cause.
-Sometimes I catch allied ships desperately trying to kill themselves on asteroids. I mean, just slamming into them and then keeping thrusters full speed ahead until they finally explode.
-Sometimes the above happens to me and gives me no control over it. Even if I'm holding "X" to stop the freaking ship.
-Lag lag lag. I know this is a particle-based game, but come on. Going through Spiky Plant territory means sending the game into slow motion (about 1/2 time, maybe slower).
-Weird glitches regarding exploring. Sometimes my territory goes from my ownership to "unexplored" or no-ownership unexpectedly. Even if I'm sitting in the middle of that territory with a few stations and a fleet of 50 ships. There are other similar glitches, such as arrows pointing to stations that don't exist.
-Lots of glitchiness surrounding drones/missiles. Particularly during ship construction. Sometimes the parts just do really weird things like spawn a missile inside of the ship, which leads to all kinds of glitchiness. I once had a ship I was working on explode into a few pieces IN THE EDITOR because of a stray missile.
There are a few non-bug-related issues with the game IMO, but those are actually pretty minor. Compared to the bug issues, I often forget they're even issues at all.
I could go on and on about all the glitches in this game. It's insane and needs to be addressed more immediately. I love this game for the ideas/concepts and gameplay. It's really fun and has a lot of awesome mechanics. The brilliance and creativity that went into making this work of art are just enough to overlook the pile of crap that is the coding/attention-to-detail.

This game is an extremely bloody third person action game set in Roman times. You play as Marius, a... well he's a guy who does stuff and you'll learn who he is as you play through the game, should you buy it.
Graphics- The game's graphics are excellent for the year it was made in, thanks in part to Cryengine. The art style gives off an ancient Roman vibe and the cutscenes are solid, with great facial animations.
Sound- Good, some of the stabbing and cutting sounds begin to get lame though, after you've heard them literally 1000 times over.
Gameplay- Stale. The same generic barbarian enemies, the same weapon and shield, the same combos and blocks and finisher animations, the same Testudo formation sequences, the same balista sequences... and don't even get me started on having to use quicktime events for EVERY. SINGLE. EXECUTION. If you can't stand quicktime events, stay away from this game.
Story- Good. a tale about honor, war, the Gods, and corruption. Marius is recalling the battles and events that led up to the vault where him and Nero are hiding as the story progresses. The story is not life changing, though.
Optimization- Definitely a problem. My computer should be able to run a game from 2013 without an issue, especially when not on max settings. But this game says otherwise. I couldn't get the game to stay at a smooth 60 FPS even with the graphical settings tweaked to perfection and a GTX 760.
SHOULD YOU PLAY THIS GAME? - Maybe. If you are a fan of 3rd person action games or Roman times, it might be worth a go. But keep in mind the combat system and quicktime events and enemy types become very repetitive and mediocre-feeling. The game, in one word, is... decent. That's it. Nothing exceptional.

Fun roguelike game with randomly generated levels. You have lots of settings to configure to adapt the difficulty.
You're required to find and download a bunch data cores and ultimately find a reactor, disable all it's coolants and return back to the starting point.
You have the chance to gain random power ups when downloading those data cores.
You'll have to deal with random power and equipment failures, which means you'll have to keep track of the locations of circuit breakers, repair stations and armory stations to refill your supply.
There are also turrets you can activate to help you out.
Enemies will create breaches (spawn points) at random and spawn endlessly.
I wouldn't call it frightening or scary after playing a bit, but it's definitely thrilling and keeps you on your toes constantly on higher difficulties, which can be  extremely hard to beat.
The only things I don't like are the small variety of enemies, lack of player customization and that the Online multiplayer population is rather low at the current state. Aside from that and the rather cheesy name, this is a pretty fun game.

This game is the best kind of hard.  The controls are responsive and hit detection is very good.
I enjoy the way the game's mechanics play against you.  Enemies are ruthless and deadly; you're never more than a few moments from death.  As a result, you'll want to take your time as you move through the map.  As the mission drags on, however, not only do more enemies spawn, but more spawn points open up.  As your suit runs lower on energy you start to lose features.  Your flashlight dims, the ammo counter on your gun goes out, and eventually you're left standing in darkness
with no hud and no idea how much ammo you have left.
I also greatly enjoy that every time you start a new game your character is assigned a random name and when you die that character ends up in a list of fallen heros.  Presumably I'll get to keep using the same character for more than one mission if I ever manage to live longer than 3 minutes.

The flaws:  It's very short, lasting around 6 hours if you don't linger too much on the puzzles, which are sometimes (later on in the game) reliant on numbers and math to an extent that there was no way I wouldn't be pulling out a guide.  Worse, when I found the numbers needed to solve a puzzle, I wondered how the writers even arrived at that solution.  Evidently, I cannot math.  (Thankfully, though, plenty of other puzzles are subtle yet logical, and a pleasure to work out.)  Some of the dialogue here is pretty cornball, clashing with the dreary dystopian setting, but then again I suppose that fits with the tradition of this style of game.  Beyond these issues, Primordia enjoys an aesthetic drawing from Giger, Moebius, Dune, and probably a bit of Machinarium and/or Beneath a Steel Sky, with music that recalls Blade Runner and Kaiba.  The scope of the story and its setting suggests far more than the ground you actually cover, but just that it seems so sprawling is wonderful.  Primordia feels like a labor of love.

Cute series of winks to RPG developments in history. It's nice to see the game evolve visually as you unlock stuff, and there's a small puzzle element that requires you to switch environments.
The quality of the experience varies a lot though:
- They actually included annoying elements from the games they're parodying, such as no dungeon minimap, way too many random encounters and a stupidly hard boss battle.
- Controls are bad, directional pad not responding well using an Xbox360 pad
- 3d animations are bad
- All gameplay elements are hastily implemented and are worse than what they imitate... it can only be pardoned if you're here for the joke, but if you expect a serious RPG expect disappointment.
- The humor is so-so
Overall I kind of enjoyed it, but I got annoyed several times at the game and was about to quit just before they brought in a game-changing element. At least it's short, so it shouldn't overstay its welcome too much.
Oh yeah, and if you're into that you can backtrack once you're almost at the final boss to collect stars (useless) and cards (to play a minigame). I'll pass, but I appreciate that they put in the effort for those who like that.

I see the appeal of this game, but once a-freaking-gain, it's a title that shipped long before it was finished.
I LOVE these types of games. Build ship, gather resources, build bigger ship, smash enemies. That part of this game is fun. However, it's a broken PoS. Half the things don't work properly.
List of broken stuff:
-Drones fly off without reason into space and die.
-Missle targeting flys around in circles for no reason.
-Auto-target turrets don't auto-target 75% of the time. They sit there idling.
-Auto-fire doesn't auto-fire when enemies are nearby 75% of the time. They sit there idling (noticing a pattern here?).
-Ship re-building randomly doesn't work. Once, I was half-dead, went to allied territory and went to take a leak. Then I made a sandwich. Came back 5 minutes later and I still wasn't rebuilt. I had to exit and re-enter the game.
-Sheilds randomly malfunction . No, there was not an EMP, the sheilds simply didn't want to turn on so I had to go kill myself to get them to work again (even though dying in this game isn't much of a consequence, it's still annoying!).
-Thrusters on the side of the ship do jack-all. No matter what angle I put them at, strafing is a hundred times slower than going backward and forward. I put LITERALLY 10 times more thrusters on the sides of the ship than on the back of the ship, and no change. Barely any strafing at all. A thruster on the side of the ship does 1/100th the power of a thruster on the back/forward of the ship simply for the fact that it's on the side. I'm not sure if this is a glitch or if it's designed to be like that, either way, it's really damn annoying.
-Half the time, the ship I'm currently flying either wants to go forward, or turn. Never both at the same time, but one or the other, exclusively.
-Entering or exiting a menu resets the volume of the music to MAXIMUM. I play with my speakers pretty high up and turn most of the in-game volume down. This usually isn't a problem except in this game. Every time I go into the menu to change my ship, my fleet's ships, check the map, or pause the game, the volume for the music cranks all the way up to 100% for about a second, deafening me. This is more of a personal problem, but it's just another glitch that shows the game released too soon.
-Every third game, my base spawns in the middle of god damned no where. No enemies within a hundred miles. Just dead, deep space between me and them. At the beginning of the game, you're especially weak, so you rely on your allies to help significantly, but it's impossible in these games, so the best advice I have is to just remake it. Another annoyance.
-Every few minutes more I play this game I find another glitch/bug/thing I don't like.
Positives:
-Music is awesome. It gets my blood pumping at times and at others it makes me sit back and relax to the joys of the graphics.
-Looks awesome. The graphics of this game are amazing. Beautifully done.
-Ship building is simple, yet deceptively complex. You can't simply stick a massive shield on one side of the ship and have it work properly. You need to counter-balance it with another shield, or something with similar mass. Center of gravity of the ship actually matters and you can easily build a ship by accident that can only fly in circles. I love that!
-Individual part destruction. When a part gets hit, you lose it, simple as that. If you lose your left aft engines, then guess what, you're flying in circles 'till it regenerates buddy.
-Individual part regeneration. After a short period (dependant on the part), it regenerates, free of cost, without having to go back to a station to repair and refuel.
-Unlock a part and you can use it as many times as you like.
-Free ship re-design. Re-design your ship over and over and over aaaaaand oooooooveeeeeeer again all you want, it's free. You're gonna need those remakes to create a good one. You don't even have to enter a spaceport and whatnot.
Once again, I'd love to love this game, I really would. There's a lot of great features and design aspects of the game I really love, but it's just not finished. It's just yet another game released before its time.

Great open-world shoot-em-up with a fantastic modular ship design system. I could (and probably already have) spend hours just designing and testing out different ships. I've played it for hours and there are a number of things I really like, but I'm going to focus on the areas that need improvement for this review:
My biggest complaint is the lack of end-game goals. Once you reach the upper limits of ship size and amass a big fleet, there's pretty much nothing that can stand in your way and the game becomes trivial. At that point, even if there wa s a win condition, there's no real reason to keep playing.
One of the other areas I'd like to see improvement in is the various factions. The first faction, Terran, has a lot of different technology to play with, but most other factions only have a few different weapon types, etc. This made playing the factions I'd unlocked less fun than I had hoped.
Finally, the ship AI leaves a bit to be desired, specifically their ability (or lack thereof) to navigate around obstacles. For a game set in space, the world is densely populated, and I've frequently had issues with AI ships getting stuck behind asteroids or accidentally getting latched onto other ships (the more irregularly shaped ones). Even trying to turn your own ship around in similar situations can be difficult with the default control scheme (mouse rotates ship).

Reassembly is a game that won't let you go even after dozens of hours, keeping you busy building your own Death Star and then sending a fleet of those to ruin someone's day.
Reassembly is all about space and freedom of it. There are seven factions available, each with their own unique playstyle. You can peacefully grow plants and extract energy from solar panels, or you can set up your own fleet of doom and plunder the galaxy. You can take things down with precise lasers, continuous beams, play a pew-pew-em-up with plasma cannons and if that doesn't help - spam them with missiles until they die. For those who desire exotic methods of space annihilation, make your own sawblade of death. Choices are limitless.
There are just three resources in this game: R(esource), C(urrency) and P(ower), each made to limit or unbind your possibilities. The cycle seems to be simple - R is traded for C, C is spent on P, and P is how many hardware you can put into your ship to earn yourself more R. But it's harder than it sounds. You don't just buy hulls, glue cannons on them and go gunning things down. You build your own ship piece by piece, and that's where LEGO nostalgia hits. Space, energy and Power efficiency is what makes it hard and beautiful. You can put tons of armor and guns on your ship, but thrusters just won't carry such mass. You can be tanky and quick, but with little to no offense available. You can put powerful guns and quickly execute hit-and-run tactics, but two shots will annihilate your little scrap piece of death.
You'll find out soon enough.
So, you've made your bulky space cannon of extreme vengeful execution of space heretics and conquered the whole galaxy. And that's it? No, of course not. There are wormholes and agents.
Wormholes is what gives Reassembly infiniteness. When you approach a wormhole you're offered to either pass through to a newly generated galaxy, or to send your current fleet to other worlds in form of agents.
Agents are what slows you down. They are well-equipped fleets made by other players, and they are extremely hard to defeat. There are usually 6-8 fleets on the galaxy map, and they're moving towards you. Slowly. But when they reach you, they start plundering your stations and ships. Until they are defeated, they'll find you and destroy you. But the reward for killing them is worth the trouble.
Well then, recently there had been added Steam Workshop support. Test out all the new player ships and factions, unleash their power on others or get wrecked by their overpoweredness. I'd say that the choice is yours, but you don't really have any choice. The galaxy's cruel.

Killing Floor meets Slender, Aliens VS Predator's Marine campaign and modern Rogue-lites. It's hard to judge this game by the screenshots or videos. You have to experience it by yourself.
You find yourself in the middle of a spaceship/station. Your goal is to download and retrieve info from datacores which may also offer some upgrades such us infravision, visual upgrades to your HUD or reduced dowload times. Then you must overload the main core and escape. All this while a enormous amount of xenomorphs and facehuggers try to hunt you, crawling in the walls and opening breaches. One single hit from a xenomorph and you are dead.
Teamwork and strategy are crucial. The game doesn't only depend on your aim. You can use doors, laser fences and sentries to create improvised labyrinths for your enemy while you find supplies or repare your gear.
Graphics can look a bit outdated (maybe Unreal Engine 2 style), but the atmosphere and the lightning are superb. The dynamic music and sound effects only makes the tension even bigger.
You really don't want to find yourself in a situation in which you think you have everything under control and a power failure happens. Everything goes dark, the sentries and traps you activated stop working. Your flashlight runs out of energy and you must restore the power back while your motion sensor blips with hundreds of dots. Your only source of light is your weapon.
All of this I have only experienced in single player. Playing with friends is a blast. Also, this game is a great example of how procedural generation should be used. So each single game is a different hell of corridors, immense rooms and mazes. And each game is highly customizable: size of the map you want to play, structure... I strongly recommend starting each game with power off.

Ultionus is a pretty fantastic game.  Likable main character, great graphics, familiar play mechanics.  The shmup sections are actually a bit more forgiving than some of the old school schmups I've played.  They are still challenging though.  The platforming sections are a lot of fun.   Much like old school games of this type, once you learn the bosses' patterns, victory is pretty much yours.  In the platform sections you'll have to decide when to avoid enemies and when to shoot them.  Most take a few shots to kill, so you might want to just leave them behind rather than kill them all.
This game encourages multiple playthroughs the old fashioned way, through hidden sections that you have to unlock to reach, including a true boss ending.  The kind of thing you might have bought a guide for in the old day.  Honestly, though, you'll probably end up coming back to this one after a stressful day at work when you just want to unwind, even after you've pretty much seen all the hidden sections.  (It's not an extremely long game, but I don't really have a problem with that.  Some long games end up just repeating the same levels a lot anyway.)
The story is a nice change of pace, being based on the concept of petty revenge rather than saving the universe from the bad guys.  The whole Spacebook thing is humorous, and kind of fun for a game with such a 90's aesthetic (when Serena would surely have been using Space Geocities instead, eh?).  Serena clearly owes a lot to pulpy comic book heroines along the lines of Barbarella or Taarna from the film Heavy Metal.  (Though her story more resembles the goofy Captain Sternn from Heavy Metal or maybe one of Leela's adventures on Futurama.)
Anyway, I'm recommending this to anyone I know who is currently drooling over a Retron 5, or is considering finally making that Ebay purchase of a turboExpress.  Basically if you like side-scrolling platformers, this purchase is a must!

Ultionus is a throwback platformer/shooter. A throwback to where? To this Amstrad game called Phantis. After a few play-throughs of this game I checked out some Phantis vids. The protag is wearing a space bikini, there's an alien planet, a couple 2D shooter stages, and dinosaur rides. Wow it's like I'm playing a next-gen sequel!...Well if next-gen was DOS.
That's mostly what this game reminds me of. Those good old days of shareware, dozens of action-platformers, and command prompts. For the most part this game is pretty decent. It's rough at first, since the heroine has a pitiful gun and a measly three hit-points. Checkpoints are fairly frequent but the bosses are pretty brutal(pattern memorization is a must). Most of the time the trick to getting around is to simply jump a lot and fire downwards. It's a higher rate of fire, and should keep the screen fairly clear. The game can get overwhelming though, since regular enemies adhere to the Ninja Gaiden school of design. They respawn constantly and whenever you move so much as an inch off-screen. It's frustrating but hey, that's how it goes sometimes.
Ultionus strikes an odd balance between old-school hardcore and what we take for granted today. There are unlimited continues, saves, and extra-lives are fairly frequent. Everything else though is a lesson in pain. The hit-box is large, so Serena takes damage whether it's a projectile to the gut or an alien that just grazes the soles of her boots. Enemies also love to hang out on cliffs or appear just when you're trying to make a jump. There are ways to make the game easier on yourself, but they're not terribly obvious. In fact in your first play-through you just might miss them entirely. Four of the seven stages offer hidden armor or weapon upgrades. Once you grab the rapid-fire you're pretty well set, though armor upgrades mean more damage can be taken(plus it's fashionable!). If you manage to beat this game without any upgrades, subsequent play-throughs are gonna be easy peasy fo' scheezy.
Less forgiving is that the Serena's ship is subject to inertia. Maybe that was a thing in older PC shmups but uhhhhh ehhhh ummm NO. Yeah sorry but when I stop moving my ship I want my ship to stop moving...INSTANTLY. The true final boss throws some bullets around and it makes those tight squeezes a bit too finicky. I'll throw this under nitpicking because I tend to get a little ornery about 2D shooters.
Oh and this game is short. Average play-through is about 30 minutes, 35 if you go for the good ending. That's in-line with Ultionus' inspiration, but it might not be enough for gamers today. I guess another one or two stages would have been nice. Perhaps these stages wouldn't be themed like the rest of the game. By that I mean Serena jumps and shoots through all too common environs. There's the Ice stage, fire stage, jungle stage, elevator stage, and you get the idea. On the other hand that extra stage could very well have turned out to be an underwater one, and that's just no bueno.

Okay, first off, let me get this out of the way.  This game is short.  If you are an old school platformer/shooter fan, someone who laughs at Ghouls and Ghosts or Ninja Gaiden, this adventure will take you about an hour.  If you are...less skilled, it will take many replays, cause while the game isn't as tough as those legendary titles, it is pretty damn tough.
That out of the way, this game friggin rocks.  The graphics are very pretty and the enemies have charm and are very large and detailed.  The combat is super simplistic, basically boiling down to platforming and shooting with a gun.  There is some variety in stages that feature auto scrolling or shooter elements, but the combat is pretty straightforward.  You go from point A to point B to get through zones, though there are bonus areas in each to improve your weapons, which you spend your high score on, which is also your money.
This game is worth it for the sound track alone, which is supremely awesome and actually features a fully voiced song at the end.  And, while story is pretty much just framing device, it does manage to be pretty amusing, especially the ending, which is sweeeeeeeet.
Problems with the game are enemies which respawn at a rapid rate, a very very weak weapon which you need to upgrade to even have a chance of finishing the game without a boatload of skill, you can only upgrade in the bonus areas, and some occassionally frustrating jumps.  Aside from that, it's a great ride.  Very pretty, great music, and the combat is kinda meh, but for an arcade-esque title like this, it works.
Is this game worth $7?  Well, I think so.  The soundtrack is fantastic and the graphics added to that make it worth the price of admission, I think.  Give it a shot.

The weapons aren't the most balanced (revolver and shotgun are clearly op) or the most varied. The game runs fine most of the time, however, I personally experienced significant lag in full matches whenever the carnage was high. This game feels like a watered down COD zombies with less variability than Left 4 Dead. If you are really into zombie horde games you might find some enjoyment here because it is by no means a terrible game, just suffers from a very low replay value. If you do plan on buying this game, get it on sale because it is not worth $44.99.

1.2 hours in: Enjoyed the quickly evolving graphics/playstyle as you run around. Hack and slash mechanics are fun, as are the turn based battles (makes me want to play some Final Fantasy games). I've gone through one dungeon and fought a boss. Wasn't difficult, more just figuring out the mechanics of the fight and doing the right thing at the right time. So far, enjoying the game and want to play more!
2 hours in: I've finished the story up to the last boss. Let's be honest here, not an amazing story. The time travelling section was more tedious than creative or tricky. I plan to collect all of the hidden items in the game, but I think that may wait as I just don't really feel like playing more at the moment. But I do want to 100% the game.
6 hours in (I admit some of that time was spent afk with the game open): Just got 100% completion on the game. Was definitely tricky to find some of the hidden stars/cards, but once you figure out where you need to go, you can usually find the ones you missed the first time around (hint: wall hugging is a good idea). Some of the end game areas were rather tricky with the time travelling mechanic, so that was nice. The final boss was actually quite perfect. Took me a few tries to understand how it worked, but once I did, I was able to down him quite easily.
Overall, I would say it's an enjoyable game. After the first hour, you've pretty much unlocked all of the visual and/or mechanic upgrades that you are going to get. That being said, I did enjoy playing through different game styles; it was definitely fun and brought back some great memories of other games. I don't think there is much replay-ability with this one.
I would say the game is worth at least half price. Definitely enjoyable, but gets a bit repetitive after the first hour when you are going back and hunting treasures. I think I physically played the game maybe four hours, so I would recommend, but only if it's on a sale.
