There's a lot of things I didn't like about this game but when it boils down to it, I enjoyed the presentation enough to overlook it's many pitfalls. This is a mini-series more than it is a game. Every level is a perfectly constructed stage. Every piece of action and each event is designed to keep pushing you forward at great pace. Every time the camera is out of your control whether in game or in cutscenes the directing and cinematography is perfectly framed. The actors, both digital and vocal, are amazing. The audio aspects are top notch. All of this keeps you engaged to the end. But you're stuck playing entirely on someone else's terms. You're merely a pawn of the video games Gods in this one.
The pace of the game was superb. Beyond the atrociously bad and repetitive boss fights you never had time to breathe. That only had one drawback because unlike other games in a similar vein you never felt encouraged to just take it all in. The environments and levels are meticulously filled with beauty but save for some very few uninteresting collectibles you have no desire to ever just admire and explore your surroundings. You're splashing headlong down an ever tightening funnel. Which is well and good as the pace builds adrenaline.
Adrenaline that you instantly dump upon getting into a battle. I can't imagine anything but using a controller on this one but combat basically amounts to the dreadful "timed button mashing". No combos, no skill required, no nuance. Just timing and patience. Dull dull patience. The only glimpses of satisfaction are quick-time event finishers... That get old fast. But those finishers are used to replenish health, or earn extra focus/damage/XP. So you have to do them like the pawn you are. Endlessly. I'd say I spent, conservatively guesstimating, at least thirty minutes of my five hours thirty minutes of playtime watching finishers. Gruesome and awesome finishers admittedly, but again, they got old. You can count the ultra-basic standard enemy types on one hand. And that same count is the amount of models you're presented with. No gear or clothes change ups, just endless barbarian clones for slaughter. The fat ones all have shields, the tall ones all have the same fur cloak, etc. Then the bosses... Oh the bosses. They're just drawn out versions of the standard hordes. But you can't be offensive. You just have to wait your turn to strike. Repeat with a block or dodge until your number is called, then strike. Only on their terms. Circle around and hit em from behind? Nope, they will have none of that! Afterall, you are but a pawn.
The story itself is average but engaging. With how much you have to turn your brain off for the combat anything more from the story would of made this more of a heartbreaking missed opportunity. So I was satisfied with the story. Especially with the very fitting ending. It was beyond appropriate for this game experience. But while the story serves as the force that keeps pushing the pace, its the visual experience that is all that you're after here. With any other aspect you have to keep your expectations reeled in quite tight. I enjoyed the parts where I was along for the ride, and trudged through the bad gameplay to get to the next part of the ride. Of course opportunities were missed and I definitely do wish the gameplay was more than it was.
I didn't like the menus, there's a technical complaint or two with how it ran on my toaster, I didn't even try keyboard and mouse, nor did I try multiplayer, and I'm sure something else is escaping me as well. And my recommendation is only if it is on sale for < $4.99USD or bundled. But. I do recommend it simply for the direction or cinematography or whatever you want to call it.

This review is a long ramble so to put a disclaimer right at the front the takeaway is this: It's a fun, tense, nailbiter of a game that's a little buggy, a little repetitive, and a bit too basic to justify it's steep Early Access price. But it's got it where it counts and if you can find someone to play with it becomes a really great experience overall, especially for fans of James Cameron's Aliens. Now on to the review, proper:
Space Beast Terror Fright is at it's core a very basic game. Move forward through a darkened derelect ship, collect data from computer terminals along the way, set the ship to explode and run yourself to safety before things go boom. Sounds simple enough...until you factor in the dificulty.
The titular Space Beats here are not your typical first person shooter fodder. The player doesn't run and gun their way through levels taking out legions of enemies without breaking a sweat, ala Serious Sam or Doom. Instead what the player finds themselves contending with is a more fearsome foe. At first they might be easy enough to kill with your rifle, machine gun, or shotgun but soon enough they'll horde up on you, crawling out of the walls, the ceiling, through doorways, from behind you, and if they get you...you're dead.
No matter what if the player allows the various space aliens, shrouded and darkness and moving just fast enough that it's almost impossible to get a good look at them without essentially committing suicide, to get anywhere near them they'll be mauled to instant death. This makes for a game less about speed and who's the tankiest player in the game, or who can exploit the best upgrades, and more about just trying to keep your enemy at bay long enough to accomplish a simple mission.
The intensity is what makes the game. It's rare that I've played a game that's genuinely got my blood pumping from the knowledge that every move could be my last and no matter what plans I may have laid out by myself or with a group of friends...death waits right around the corner and it cares not about my plans. At any moment a space beast could be just quick enough to get passed your firepower and in that one second you're a goner, and everything you've accomplished up to that point is out the window.
Ultimately where this game shines is in it's embracing of the one thing that most modern games - especially shooters with their tendancy to utlize spawn points that throw you right back into the middle of the fray as long as you have the points to continue playing - have been neglecting for years. Consequences. Death is a real thing in this game, and you really don't want to endure it. From this the game builds tension as the stakes ramp up and the players luck starts to run out. You'll jump at every sound because that sound could mean death is seconds away. Any shadow you think you see down a dark hallway could be the end of your play through. If you're being attacked fleeing might be the best option. All your senses are working overtime just to keep going and get to that next computer sentry or gun turrent that might provide the smallest bit of help against the unknown alien horde that wants to eat your face.
With the ambience and atmosphere the game builds, using tricks of lighting, sound, visual effects, and etc. to manipulate your emotions as you run through procedurally generated levels you're just as unfamiliar with as your player-character counterpart would be, the game becomes an exciting, starting, genuinely suspenseful experience worthy of the best roller coaster sci-fi horror flicks that Hollywood has had to offer.
In a world where video games have been homaging or just outright ripping off the film for years I'd say that in Space Beast Terror Fright fans of James Cameron's seminol 1986 classic "Aliens" finally have a game that lets them play through that experience. While not technically being a part of that franchise Space Beast wears it's love for it on it's sleave and on a surely miniscule budget have managed to capture the frenetic intensity and relentlessness of James Cameron's work. Even visually the game is perhaps the most evocative of the film of any I've seen.
The Multiplayer should be touched on as well, as that's really where this game shines. It's one thing to roam through these darkened corridors knowing that at any moment the unseen alien beasties might shut off all power to the ship and leave you straded alone in the pitch black of a dead ship. It's quite another to manuver your way through those halls with friends, trying to plan and strategize your way through victory knowing at any moment you may be the last member of your party standing and the last hope of stopping the Alien infestation. There's something oddly satisfying as watching your buddy's screen go black as a monster eats his face.
The game does have it's flaws. Now and then a Space Beast would seemingly spawn out of nowhere to insta-kill me, and that was frustrating in the cheap and irritating way that an enemy camping at the edge of a platform in Castlevania used to be. It's price point is also quite steep for a very basic indie game in early access on Steam. Fun as this experience is, it's not worth the 15 U.S. Dollars the game currently costs. That's especially true given the lack of variety within the game.
Overall if you can afford the price without issue I'd highly recommend the game. If however you look at the gameplay and find yourself thing "that looks fun but a little repretative..." then maybe you might want to hold off for some kind of sale.
If Call Of Duty really isn't your thing, and you're a little tired of the arena shoot-em up style of games like Doom (2016) and want something that presents a dramatic change in tone, pace, and difficult...Space Beast may well be the game for you.

This is a must have game for any post-L4D gamers and fans of coop shooters. It's really the only experience that matches that initial feeling that L4D players get before becoming jaded. Space Beast Terror Fright is what L4D should have been: shocking, scary, unpredictable. It would be fantastic if this was redone with AAA graphics and more content.

Aliens.  If you ever wanted a game to give you the same paranoia those marines had in the second installment of the Aliens franchise, this is probably the one to pull it off.
You have a near-dead space ship you need to nuke along with its unsightly wild alien infestation.
You have a number of datacores to access in order to unlock the reactor core so you can set the joint to nuke itself and take the skittery buggers with it.
Once you set the reactor to blow, you have a few seconds to get back to your ship so you don't go down with this one.
You have a gun. One. Of several. Try not to choose the wrong one. Not that you'll always know which that is beforehand. Heh.
You might have sentries.
If you're lucky, their bullets won't ricochet at you too often.
If you're luckier still, you'll have laser grids to seal corridors and make pretty lights when bugs zap themselves.
If you're lucky, you have backup.
If you're lucky, they have enough of a clue not to shoot you in the foot, leg, butt, back and face.
If you're really lucky, they'll be able to shoot the aliens rushing your rear while you shoot the aliens being more up-front about their intentions.
If you're really, really lucky, the power won't go out while you taunt a seething alien horde on the other side of a laser fence.
If you're really, really, really lucky, the power won't go out when your flashlight dies, leaving you to see by your own muzzleflare.
If you're good, you can check off all the boxes on your to-do list while you're there and get promoted.
The main game mode is Salvage (the stuff described immediately before this).
The short version of any given Salvage run:  Collect all datacores, proceed to reactor, set to blow, escape.  If you survive, you take your upgrades and ammo with you, making the next job a bit easier.  The map layout, settings and how you go about approaching those objectives while xenomorphs try to eat you are where the gameplay lies.
The game is procedurally generated. You can let the game choose a random seed, going in blind with no clue as to layout or what onboard defenses (turrets or laser fences) there may be for you to use. You can also specify a specific seed so that you can try a single map again and again, until you get it just right - this is where the leaderboards come in.
A lot of setting tweaks are also available, and seem to work both for explicit and randomly chosen seeds.  These allow you to specify certain aspects of game behavior: Only big aliens? Are turrets present? Frequency of alien spawns and/or blackouts? Do the aliens come in only from dead-ends, or can they break in anywhere at all? Are the walls covered in crunchy xenomorph resin (you know the stuff - the reactor area in Aliens) that covers up interactive objects, like turret control panels and circuit breakers?
You have a thankfully simple (I've never been a fan of including more than a dozen guns in a shooter) array of weapons to choose from:  The fastest firing SMG-type, a somewhat slower rifle, then the slower multi-projectile weapons.
Varying degrees of infravision and motion trackers are tools, too, but you'll need to find them first.
There are two types of aliens currently implemented - do not know if there are plans for more:
Beasts - the big ones.  Get caught by one and it's game over.
Astrocreeps - the little ones.  They kill you slowly. You can shoot them off yourself, but they damage your systems while they're still chewing on your face. No more systems left for them to go through? Game over.
Both varieties are quite happy crawling along the floors, ceilings and walls, causing occasional hilarious (multiplayer) and/or infuriating (solo mode) sentry ricochets. These ricochets can be accomplished by humans as well, for bonus hilaritorture, though the exquisite nearly 180 degree ricochet is largely relegated to sentry fire.
There is a deathmatch mode, but DM is not my thing. I've never felt compelled to play it, so I can't speak to it. It doesn't sound popular, from the modes I've seen people play in the online server listings and what I've read (may have actually been the result of player requests).
A new mode - Rescue - I've detailed in comments.
List time!
The pros:
+ Atmosphere is surprisingly good for what ought to be a fairly straightforward sort of game.
The music really helps set the mood.
+ Mechanics are fairly simple, so it's easy enough to pick up.
+ Procedural generation allows for map variety.
+ Roguelike aspect helps you be ok with dying since upgrades come easy. Levelling? Pah.
+ Not a lot of controls to remember or futz around with (see cons, too, though)
+ 4-player co-op & DM. Online and local.
Getting eaten/shot in the back with friends is almost always better. It also allows you to use split screen mode whether you're playing locally or not, so you can see what your teammates are doing, and once you die, you can hop from view to view as well.
+ Replay feature.
+ Leaderboards
+ Friendly fire is ON.
+ That moment a dozen aliens smash through your door.
+ Updates still coming, roughly monthly, from what I've seen, and the dev is active on the forums.
The cons which I expect can and will be addressed, but are not necessarily high priority either:
- Controls are not currently configurable.
The defaults don't seem weird or troublesome for me - WASD & left and right click - but other people may have different needs in this department.
- Resolution doesn't seem to be adjustable, and is a bit small.
I'd guess this runs at around 1024 x something, or maybe even smaller - it is still a widescreen resolution, though, by the looks of it. I play in 1280x720 windowed modes where I can, for streaming's sake.  This is still totally playable, at least, and fullscreen remains an option for anyone who doesn't have a need for windowed modes.
- Multiplayer progression.
You can survive a few missions in multiplayer mode, but if you leave online mode (you can leave the lobby safely) your progression currently will not save. Single player progression does save. Arguably incentive to go out with a bang.
The cons I think might be there a while, unless extra help is brought onboard with development or priority shifts:
- Environment.
While the environment doesn't look bad (tastes will vary), there is not a lot of variety either.  It sounds like this is dependant on the dev being able to afford more art assets, though, so I'm not sure how likely this is to change in short order. I do know there has been at least one addition of a tileset since it went public, but I can still see why people will say it looks samey.
- Gameplay structure is ultimately going to feel repetitive.
The primary mode of play is straightforward and unvarying in its defined objectives. Depending on how different you need gameplay to be to feel fresh, game settings tweaks may not be enough for you.
Grey area stuff:
- Default graphics are a motion sickness hazard.
The settings available do seem to help alleviate that problem, though. One friend was able to continue as normal after tweaking some in-game settings.
- Abundance of flashing lights (muzzleflare) are an epilepsy hazard.
- Two marines can block a corridor + no crouching.
I don't find it a problem, but some people may not want to allow for the thematic reality of giant suits of WH40K-style armor getting in the way of shooting forward past two teammates.
- Marine models are both threatening and goofy. They're big and bulky - except the face, which might make you giggle. You're not going to see it a lot, but it's still there. Whether that kills the mood is up to you.
- Some may want more gun variety.
- 3d game. 2d map layout. This helps with 2d planning maps in pre-game, but you might miss the vertical element.
- The online lobby is not a ghost town, but neither is it very busy. No current method of queueing for a spot.

This game really does have a special place in my heart. Now, I'm reviewing this on the stance that I have played the first two, and replayed them again and again before purchasing this game. Zombie Army Trilogy is a remake/sequel to the surprisingly successful Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army games. This game, while containing remade versions of the first two games, includes and entirely new third chapter. I shall go over the pros and cons, and the final virdict.
Pros~
- The graphics are VERY nice, and compliment the world and atmosphere greatly.
- The soundtrack is very likeable. It reminds me of those 80s horror films with the synth soundtracks.
- Gunplay is fantastic. This was a given with a Sniper Elite game.
- This is a fantastic co-op game. Team up with up to 4 of your friends to take down the zombie menace!
- Kill Hitler. Zombified. If that's not a selling point, I don't know what is.
- You can now, unlike the others, play as a female.
- For some reason, that I'm NOT complaining about, you can play as the Left 4 Dead characters. M'kay.
- Replayability. I went back and was constantly discovering things I didn't see.
- The brand new Horde mode. Fight of waves of the undead until your eventual downfall!
Cons ~

I recommend this game, but with a huge caveat. How much do you
enjoy retro platforming?
Everything about this game is very well done: graphics, the Heavy Metal magazine heroine, and the fantastic soundtrack. There's even a good bit of replay value, which isn't always the case for platformers. The gameplay is... well, "retro".
If you've never experienced actual older games, or you tend to forget how many of them actually sucked, I recommend watching a playthrough of a game called Phantis, which this game is basically a remake or spiritual sequel of. With some exceptions, older platforming games often had slow, sluggish protagonists, with fast, incessantly spawning enemies, with awkward jumping and shooting controls. This game is no exception.
Serena walks slowly. She has to stand still to shoot. There's a small delay both before and after firing the actual projectile. She can only shoot up at a shallow angle (perhaps 30 degrees), but not straight up. You get hurt from touching a robot's toe or a wizard's robe. Additionally, the delay in firing means that if you try shooting just before you land, you won't fire. Even her ship takes a moment to accelerate to full speed when moving up or down. None of these would be a huge problem by themselves, but combined, it can lead to some very frustrating moments.
Everything else about Ultionus is improved over the older games; why not tighten up the gameplay too? There are also plenty of other "retro" games that actually have really great controls.
As I'm sure most can agree, it's more fun to challenge the game, not its controls. But if you love punishing gameplay, repetition until perfection, or just love all platforming games, then it's hard to do wrong by Ultionus. Even better, it's very inexpensive.

Awesome graphics, awesome music, awesome concept. Could be an awesome game. But it isn't.
Because it's too hard, and all the difficulty is caused by the worst of all possible reasons: sluggish, awkward, unresponsive controls. Which means it's impossible for you, the player, to get better.
The game is just barely functional enough to tease me into thinking "maybe I could pull this off with enough practice," but I'm not willing to suffer through that much frustration.

In many ways, Ultionus is something like an old Amiga game; it's got the lush pixel art and bangin' chip tunes you'd expect when stepping into Commodore territory, yet it is also unfortunately plagued with the god-awful gameplay that would forever prevent the euro school of home computing from ever obtaining the prestige its Japanese console competitors rightfully earned.
First off, the controls: they just feel sluggish and unresponsive, which is only made more problematic by the game's enemies which move erratically and are generated with no real rhyme or reason. Most of the time I just find myself running past everything, hoping those three hit points will get me to the next checkpoint. Everything seems to spawn faster than you can shoot so why even try to fight back? That just puts you at risk of getting killed by the soldier or alien behind the one you just gunned down, or perhaps an entirely different direction all together.
The boss fights are equally as mindless, providing nothing more than a basic memory game but without the proper animation tells to give you an idea of the pattern before you've blown through all your miserable lives. Clearly uninspired and phoned-in as an afterthought.
Not all of Ultionus's problems relate directly to its gameplay; in my hour or so of playtime I found myself encountering a number of bugs, everything ranging from incidentally gaining the ability to walk in the air (harmless) to losing functionality of my d-pad after respawning requiring a client restart to fix (game-breaking). The game also suffers from framerate issues which, while one might construe this as intentional given the nostalgia factor, it apparently isn't according to the developer and his purported fix (disable gamepad support) doesn't do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥to help. The more likely reason is that Ultionus is built on the garbage-tier system that is GameMaker which to my recollection is known to be problematic for everyone involved on the distributive end.
All-in-all, Ultionus is a perfect example of why some game design mantras are much better left in the past because when it comes down to it, there's a pretty big difference between classic and dated and if Ultionus were an actual retro game? It'd fall squarely in the latter, no questions asked.

Evoland is a game that takes you - quite literally - through the history of video games. Start with low-rez circa '93 graphics, and unlock (via chests) various upgrades until you reach the third dimension. Calling it a standard LoZ clone would be selling it fairly short, as I think the game has more merit than simply, "Check out what we used to play!".
You start as a little 8 bit boy with the ability to move right. That's it. You unlock left movement, music, sound effects, and various graphical upgrades throughout the game. It starts off very much like old-school LoZ, and filters back and forth between turn-based combat (a la Final Fantasy) as the chronology dictates. There are subtle (and mostly not-so-subtle) homages to classic games strewn throughout the story, and despite it's linearity, it remains charming and interesting all the way through.

Evoland is as much a small parody as it is a game of it's own. It borrows heavily from other RPG games and classics (such as Final fantasy and Zelda), meaning mostly that it mocks them in that loving parody way. The game story is pretty... simple. Big evil destroying world, you must go and defeat it. Along the way, you evolve... not in power, though you do get to level up.

The selling point of Evoland is the "RPG through the ages" bits. You start off as a pixelated character in a plain world with no enemies, and as you find chests, you start earning things. Such as enemies, the ability to level up, town citizens, pixels, and yes, 3D with nothing, then textures, and finally HD definitions. Combat is both action based and turn based; during world map encounters you will have turns, and during dungeons you will be fighting real time.
The game also has one card minigame for your enjoyment. While the story is nothing to call home about, the evolving aspect of the game is fun. The graphics, even when you're just playing your pixel form, are really quite cute and very well done. The world is nice too, although the puzzles/level design/secrets are not really too difficult and everything was far too visible. I don't think they were meant to be difficult, though. The music I was not a fan of, however, it evolves as you do as well and seems to match the game perfectly, so thumbs up on that. The story is also very short and the replay value is really null unless you want to go back and do 100% achievements (which are also not terribly hard to get, but I frankly couldn't be bothered to go search for them).
The parody aspect also makes it fun if you love these type of games and have a good sense of humor (see quote above and on image below for an idea of the type of humor). Actually, this was the one thing that made me rate it so high - I had great fun discovering all the chests that made the land evolve and gave me things that had funny captions, or talking to townies and seeing what they would say.
I do have to say though, the battles do get a bit annoying after a while, and once you've unlocked everything and seen all the world has to offer, there's really little reason to keep playing, too.
There's not much else to say about this game.
Did I have fun? Yes! Exploring was fun, fighting was meh (there's really not much you can do, just attack and heal). I will full on admit I quit halfway through the last boss not so much out of frustration, but because there was really little else to do but beat him.
Does it get boring if you take it seriously? Also yes. Don't even bother grinding your levels, it will not make a difference.
Is it worth full price? Don't think so.
Finally, if you like this type of game and get it on sale, it might be a fun little game to spend some time on for a funny, nostalgic ride into the past. Otherwise, I would recommend you pass.

This is a niche game with a significant learning curve, but it has impressive complexity and really rewards effort. With a bit of creativity you can use this to accurately simulate any transport network in the world. If you want to get inspiration for what can be done, check out the New York City scenario that comes with the base game, or some of the projects that people have made on the Simutrans forum.
The game is highly customisable and it's easy to make new graphical elements and worldmaps with relatively little knowledge or skill. There's also an active Experimental development branch which adds extra features and greater realism.
Lots of people have noted that this is similar to OTTD. Both games are obviously inspired by the classic Transport Tycoon, but they've been in separate development for a very long time. The difference that originally attracted me to Simutrans was that each passenger in Simutrans has a specific destination in mind, rather than simply going where you take them. That was a while ago though so I'm not sure if things have changed with OTTD.
In summary: if the idea of simulating networks and infrastructure is interesting to you, this is definitely worth a look.

So, Simutrans is a game about shipping goods from one place to another. There are several thousand random maps you can play, or you can play on a height map. There are also scenarios, and, I must say, they are rather confusing for me, since I had never even known that this game existed until its Steam release. I think that the tutorial can be improved quite a bit, since I'm not able to place anything in it. Also, I have trouble connecting to online servers, but I think that this may be do to A) My OS (Windows XP SP3), B) My processor (Intel Pentium 4), or C) The game itself. There are a total of 8 (I believe) scenarios, ranging from making a successful bus system in New York City to advertising your formerly abandoned complex to the people of the 4 cities. One of the things I love about this is that there is NOTHING TO PAY FOR! You also can't 'win' in this game, since you don't have any Victory screen, at least not that I've seen. The advancement is pretty cool, since one year you THINK you can transport the most coal possible in that tractor trailor, and the next a big dump truck is introduced that can carry (I think) 180t Bulk, compared to that measly 35t Bulk. Also, the Railroad Schedule, Boat Schedule, and Airplane Schedule, unfortunately, doesn't possess the 'Copy Backwards' feature, unlike the Road Schedule. (I haven't attempted to do anything with Monorails, Trams, Molotovs, or Narrowgauges.) Also, what is the purpose of the Geothermal Power Plants and Solar Power Plants if you can't do anything with them? After all, there are no Consumers/Producers to ship things to/from things related to the Geothermal and Solar plants. There are simple chains, such as the Coal-Fired Power Plant, which only needs Coal. There are also complex ones, like the Car Dealerships, which need a Car Assembly Plant, which need Steel Mills, which in turn need Coal Mines and Iron Mines, and the Car Assembly Plant also requires a Refinery, which requires Oil Fields, which tend to be scattered around the map. Also,  the Waste Incinerator should need Coal, since it should require fuel to burn the Waste. And, all the while, you have to worry about going bankrupt (unless you are in Freeplay mode). There are also upgrades to the roads and railroad tracks that appear over time, the highest of which, I believe, are the [/s] 400 km/h Grey Ballast Express Track and the 200 km/h Barrier Freeway [s]. There are also... Airports and Shipyards! Boats are tricky to use, as you must know how to get things from the Sea to the Land (Yes, this is a reference the Fishery industry). Also, I REALLY hope that there are updates that allow even FASTER transportation, and even MORE diversity between vehicles! Also, I think that there should be Local and Private Servers. In a Local Server, you can invite people that are in your general vicinity. With a Private Server, (this is Global) anyone can join, provided that they know the password. At the very beginning, you are just thrown into a world with $500,000 dollars to your name that your grandparents gave you. You are expected to raise a transportation monopoly, starting with transporting small things, like Coal. Later on, you start working for Supermarkets, Dairies, and Gas Stations, all the while hoping that your money doesn't die off. If you are in the negatives for three straight months, you are declared BANKRUPT! Although I have never experienced it, I think that bankruptcy is this games' version of a game over. I will add to this review when the next update comes out.

There are many games on Steam, but there are few masterpieces. Gaming is one of the biggest markets among kids, teens, adults and even seniors. There are games pouring out each and every day, but there are so many choices. This game is the only choice you should have to make, My Best Friends: Cats & Dogs is a masterpiece. From the second I entered the game, my body tingled with excitement as if it was my 8th Christmas. You're met with the amazing music, so delightful you could've sworn  it was composed by Beethoven. Never have I seen such good graphics, it's as if I was playing it in real life. This game is the definition of immersion. You get the choice of being a boy and girl, and I chose the boy. I got a choice of about 5 entire outfits, it's just like real life. My eyes started tearing as I hit that green "Ok" button to advance forward in what shall soon be known as "GAMING". This game is all you need. I picked the cute brown dog, I got to name it whatever I wanted and it still amazes me to this day how there are so many choices, so much to explore. The possiblities are endless, should I name my dog Henry, or perhaps Sylvia? All I know is that this game has changed my life, before I woke up every day as a boy, but since I have played Cats & Dogs: Best Friends. I have woken as a MAN. This game is not a game, it is an experience, a religious one at that. You get to scrub the dirt off your dog in a bath, you get to feed it a choice of either basic food or oily and healthy food, you get to let it sleep for THREE or SIX hours or even a day! After your dog feels happy, you get to take it outside and suddenly the game turns into a top down perspective, wow! I am amazed! This game does it all! I walked myself over and begun teaching my dog tricks, I taught him to stand, lay down and EVEN ROLL OVER! I was shaking with excitement as my heart pounded. I was delighted. I advanced to "catch", where it turned into a side scroller! WOW! I threw the ball very far and this dog ran vigorously and hard through the dirt and grass and caught that ball, he was tired afterwards though, so we teleported home and went to sleep. As I explored all the activities, I was just amazed. This game must of taken years to develop. This was when I realized that this isn't an experience. It is art.
My Best Friends: Cats & Dogs is the best game I have ever played, the graphics are beautiful, there is so much immersion, tons of activities and tons of happiness. Games are sometimes re released as "Game of the Year" edition.

This is a good game! The first thing you may have noticed is the visuals, which look great in videos but are flat-out gorgeous running natively and fullscreened. It's super lush, and really evokes a 32-bit style, which is my personal favorite. And just like in a classic game, the enemy sprites are way better than the player sprite. Honestly the whole game feels really nostalgic; the controls are stiff like Castlevania or Ghosts 'n Goblins but way more responsive, letting you control your jump in midair and all that. It's a good blend of old and new. It also manages to fix a lot of old-school gripes: you don't get pushed back when hit, pits aren't bottomless, and the continue system is infinite, with the extra lives mostly there to give you more chances to figure out a boss (or on hardcore, to retry a checkpoint with full health). Enemies wander around aimlessly respawning; everything wants to kill you. The music may be the best part though, done by the great Jake "virt" Kaufman it's in a super nostalgic style that you just don't hear anymore in modern games. The soundtrack is free on his website by the way so go check it out.
I can't really endorse the level or boss design, however. The game mostly comes down to navigating the mazes looking for any secrets you can find on your way to the boss, which you'll soon find out are only the shop key, the shop itself, and your buddy Balzac. It's pretty much the same thing over and over, with only a few new ideas and some autoscrollers mixed in. The bosses are also pretty weak; they look great but they come down completely to memorization. While it is satisfying when you can clear it without taking a hit, bosses that have a movepool that they draw from randomly with a bit more of a telegraph have always been cooler to me. The worst the game has to offer though is the upgrade system: for one, none of the upgrades are very tangible, usually they're just a basic shot or health up. But how you buy them is really bad: you spend your points that you've earned from killing enemies. That's not inherently bad but with no time system in place score is essentially infinite, which means very often you'll have to grind against infinitely respawning enemies until you have enough to buy it with. Why it wasn't a simple "pick one" is beyond me...I guess the balancing of score with spending it on items and clear time could make for interesting speed runs, but that's really the only reasoning I could see for it.
The game doesn't really start until you've beaten it, though. That's when you start working on achievements, which aren't too unlike other games but are still a lot of fun to plan and work through. The game is especially great on hardcore, as it doesn't just arbitrarily increase enemy strength but instead manipulates some of the established game elements like checkpoints and lives. It's really cool. I am convinced that it's impossible to beat the game on hardcore with certain upgrade paths so you may have to play it through a lot to 100%, but it's a pretty rewarding experience in the end.
tl;dr: Play for the nostalgia, stay for the post-game achievement layer. The game itself is nothing special but that's ok.

This game has some really great ideas, and the concept of playing through the evolution of action-adventure games was really, really fun. Seriously, seeing the graphics evolve from the chunky pixels of the 8-bit era to smooth, 32-bit graphics, was really cool.
That being said, there were so many issues with this game that I wouldn't suggest buying it unless you, like me, are a huge fan of classic RPG games.
First of all: the way the game spreads out the different upgrades is really bad. In the beginning, things move fast. It feels cool, but it's also kind of disappointing that you don't get a bit more from the early stages. Then, towards the end, it basically stops changing altogether, giving you plenty of time to get sick of the last stage. I really do wish the stages were spread out more evenly. It sucks that you have to deal with the 3D graphics stage for so long, yet it upgrades from primitive 3D graphics, to textured graphics, to HD textures, in just ten minutes. More time with each stage would have kept things fresh and maintained a nice feeling of momentum. And, for the record, rewarding progress with better graphics, sound, and gameplay mechanics is such a great feeling, despite my complaints, you're still going to have a lot of fun.
This game is fun, especially early on. As it progresses, it gets less fun and more irritating. The gameplay mechanics are, understandable, the bare essentials. So, when you get turn-based combat, you only ever get one partner and a couple of moves. There's very little strategy to it. That's not a problem, it's really not. I'm ok with that. What I'm not ok with is the fact that the random battles occurred SO frequently. The leveling up mechanic wasn't fun at all and was basically useless, there wasn't enough to buy to justify a lot of grinding, and none of the battles were fun, so WHY did there have to be so many?
This is also how I feel about the dungeon crawling. That's a bit better than the terrible random battles, but some of the platforming and combat was just so clunky and irritating that I don't understand why there had to be so much of it. It all felt like weak filler, and I hated it. Towards the end of the game, there were so many random battles that I dreaded being out of town. I've always been a fan of classic RPGs, and turn-based combat has always been something I love about them. I just want to make clear that the problem isn't that this game features that stuff: it's that it is executed SO poorly.
Now, the graphics, I love. The pixel-art is absolutely fantastic, and even the 3D graphics look really good, despite the low polygon count. The textures are wonderful, the pre-rendered backgrounds are wonderful, --I could go on and on here. But you know what isn't wonderful? Lag. Now, it pisses me off when people complain about lag and the response is "uhh your PC is too slow sorry pal". Dude, no. If somebody's computer is capable of playing Skyrim or basically any other modern 3D game, they should be able to play a game replicating PS1 / PS2 era graphics. But, without spoiling anything, there is a segment in this game in which the framerate is downright ATROCIOUS. Borderline unplayable. It is an almost complete rip-off of one of my favorite game series from my youth: Game Over / Phantis, that in turn is based on Milo Manara's space opera comics, as well as Barbarella.
Almost complete because it has (good) music, some scarcely animated backgrounds, is colorful (opposite to the almost-16-color-grayscale from the original) and the gameplay is faster and *WORSE* than that of the original Phantis.
After playing this game for ~15 minutes, I went back to the original 256k MSX version emulated on a MSX2+ and played the full game only to compare.
Phantis was slower in earlier machines, but enemies would need only ONE shot to kill. Then in machines with Turbo (overclock) capabilities (MSX2), the speed and gameplay from the original game was just... perfect. Fast and precise.
The need to fire 2 shots to kill most enemies is just plain bad. Then, I've never cared to find all powerups. Got disgusted enough with the blatant rip-off and worse gameplay at first sight.
If the authors wanted to actually improve gameplay (Instead of make it worse as they made), it would be better to insert a charging-shot 1HitKo when full from the start. Instead of the clumsy 25degree diagonal shots, that are somewhat useless and make the game less fun and less precise (Vide MEGAMAN!) than the Original game (That PLAYED more like MEGAMAN! When speeded up!)
But... Just for being a Phantis rip off, this game is somewhat special and worth it. To take a look at it, get filled with nostalgy, and then go find the 256k Phantis release to play on some emulator, with turbo on, and with a good playlist on my media player.

This game has a lot of issues, enemies spawn without rhyme of reason, trying to kill them at any point is suicide most of the time, they spawn continuosly so trying to confront them is slow and tedious. Instead you must avoid them, but that sorts of defeats the player's ability to explore the levels which have multiple paths, because you are constantly jumping around avoiding everything around you. By the way, these enemies have no AI, the moment they spawn they have a path, and they just follow said path.
The bosses though, are an enjoyable experience, they act in pretty much the same way as the enemies, they have a pattern and they follow it without considering the player, but in thi case this decision makes much more sense as bosses usually confine you on a close space, multiple lives makes learning the patterns an accessible challenge and over all theymake a good job of teaching you how to defeat them.
The game has another huge problem though, it crashes very frequently, on my first 20 minutes playing, it crashed twice.
All that being said, the game's art is GORGEOUS, the levels feel very unique, there's a crazy amount of detail on everything, and the animations are great, nothing too complex, but not too shabby in any way either. Last dimension seems to come from a guy with experience in the industry, that is trying to go at it on his own. I can appreciate his efforts, however, his specialty, 2D pixel art, is still at this point his only forte, as far as this game shows me.
Last Dimension needs a dedicated Programmer and/or Game designer, either that, or maybe it just needed this, in my opinion, failed experiment in order to get feedback and experience for a following project. Either way, while I cannot recommend this game, I can certainly recommend following Las Dimension's next efforts. The art alone is that good.

Great, great, GREAT concept. Fantastic art, decent music, decent gameplay. This game does not do anything that you haven't seen before... and still manages to be original.
However, the game is a bit short (4 hours, 6 if you want full completion). It also suffers from a sometimes questionable level design, and a repetitive soundtrack.
Finally, Evoland suffers from a pretty major pacing problem. Early on, you will keep on noting how clever the mechanics are, how cool the nods and references to videogames tropes feel, and how the world is evolving with you. However by mid-game, this sensation will be gone - not because you get used to it, but simply because the game stops throwing anything your way. It just becomes a barebone version of existing games, and by the end you may find yourself thinking you'd rather play the masterpieces Evoland references rather than Evoland itself.
Evoland is a brilliant idea, and an absolutely cute game which loves to take advantage of your gamer instincts and reflexes.
Sadly besides its concept, the game itself is a bit stale, if not repetitive. I didn't think I'd say this one day, but I wish the game held your hand more, because this is where the game shines. Evoland starts off strong, and ends rather weakly. The games has tones of potential, and for the prices, it is definitely worth getting a look at, but don't expect too much out of it.
With all that said, I am extremely excited for the upcoming sequel. Evoland is a rough diamond and with enough polish, could be a BRILLIANT game. Wait and see...

I've played many, many hours of this in the years before it appeared on Steam and let's get one thing out of the way straight off the bat... it's not a looker.  Simutrans originally came to life way back in 1997 (making it the same age as Fallout, Age of Empires and Goldeneye, to name a few utterly unrelated games that it really can't be compared to in any meaningful way) and the graphics were nothing to write home about even back then, so don't be expecting pretty pictures.
However, its lumpy graphics and clunky interface conceal a very complex, very deep game that has been under continual development and tweaking since it was turned over to its community of players more than 10 years ago.
As its name suggests, it's a transportation simulator.  Specifically, it generates a map and puts you in charge of a transport company whose goal is to organise transportation of goods and passengers from wherever they are being produced to wherever they need to go.  Every industry on the map will have specific suppliers that it will accept resources from, and everything that the industry produces will need to be shipped off to the next part of the chain.  You need to buy vehicles to do the actual transportation, build roads, rail or waterways for the vehicles to use, and ensure that no part of your industry chain runs out of materials so that everything keeps running.
As one example, if you decide to make beer (and, really, who wouldn't) you will need to provide glass and grain to a brewery.  The glass will have to come from a glassworks, which will need to be provided with coal and sand in order to produce any glass.  The grain will come from a farm.  The beer will then need to be shipped off to its destination.  If the glassworks runs out of coal or sand it will not produce any more glass.  If there is no more demand for glass (i.e. if the brewery already has plenty) it will not produce any more glass, and will stop accepting coal and sand.  Your fleets of trucks for carrying coal, sand and glass will queue up at the depots and (if you're me) will back up onto main roads and cause massive gridlock that bring any other industries using the same roads grinding to a halt and bankrupt your company while you are afk.
It's very easy to fail at making profit, without resorting to exploiting silly things that haven't been very well balanced (in some variants, for example, great profit can be made by using huge freight planes/trains to transport milk from a farm to a dairy), but very satisfying when you get things right.  It's also a glacially slow game at default settings, although the configuration options allow you to alter pretty much any part of the economic, landscape and time settings, so it's possible to set the game up in more ways that any one lifetime would allow you to explore.
I suspect that there's a very, very small subset of gamers who enjoy games like this.  If you're one of them, and can see past the ancient look of the isometric map and the ridiculously obscure and wilfully difficult to use interface (honestly, a tutorial or even an up-to-date manual would have been nice!) then give it a go.  If you're not one of those people then don't go anywhere near it - it will drive you demented.

This game is stupidly fun, especially with friends, that I'm shocked to see it isn't 10x more popular than it already is. Let me bulletpoint some awesome mechanics this game has:
* Couch co-op, on PC, for up to 4 players. This is so rare in games these days, it needs to be highlighted.
* Firing your weapon basically blinds you. Therefore you have two choices: spray and pray, or do short and controlled bursts, which take longer to kill creatures and are thus significantly less effective. Both have legitimate uses but the tradeoffs always make the decision intense.
* Bigger aliens kill you basically in one pounce (instakill), while smaller ones chew away at your suit systems until you die. Each smaller hit you take disables a critical suit system, ie flashlight, radar, ammo counter, leaving you more and more vulnerable with every hit you take. The only solution: don't get hit.
* Friendly fire means you must keep an awareness of your allies (aided by the radar) or you will end up hurting your buddies.
* The music system is intelligent and dynamic and is really, REALLY good at building/releasing tension in a cycle.
* The game is very easy to pick up and play, and for every mission you finish you retain the upgrades you got during the last mission, so you just want to keep going and going and going. It's very addictive.
* Basically every aspect of the game is well-thought out and entertaining. Nothing is slap-dashed here.
As for cons? There aren't many...
* There ARE only two game modes: Salvage (co-op) and Deathmatch. I haven't tried the latter, and the former always has the same mission structure, which does get a little old after a while. But then again: the game is just $10 (at least right now). You get what you pay for (though it is worth every single penny, and then some)
* The character models aren't perfect and some of the UVs for the textures are a bit janky, but when everything is in motion it actually does look nice.
But, one final great thing about this game that offsets these cons is that it is the kind of early access game where THE DEV ACTUALLY UPDATES ON A CONSISTENT BASIS!
So, go buy a copy of this game right now and support the dev and this awesome game. The matches are fast so you will be able to get several dozen in and form an opinion before you decide whether or not this is the game for you. BUY IT BUY IT BUY IT. Can't stress it enough.

"Oh Sir!" is, at heart, intended as a party game; something you play with others. It has a rather clever set-up - two twee Brits politely exchanging insults over some inconsequential difference - and its retro-art is charming... in a retro-art sort of way. But as a game it is sorely lacking in content and game-play.
As a single-player game, it really doesn't stand up on its own merits. The gameplay is too minimal and too dependent on chance to be much fun. It also has a disturbing lack of content; with a mere handful of characters and locations, it doesn't take too long before you start hearing the same insults (or segments thereof) again and again. The gameplay itself is clever - each round, both players have a limited - and shared - pool of words with which to create their insult, and the game is as much as building your own zinger as preventing your opponent from doing the same. Unfortunately the end result - a point value assigned based on how insulting your creation is - seems random and non-coherent. The different characters have certain weaknesses (for instance, insults against their social status, parentage or country may grant bonus points) but even this isn't certain. Even as a party game, played against friends, the game is limited. The insults are too nonsensical, and the charm of the game's weirdness lasts about ten minutes. After that, people quickly start looking for greater depth - and there just isn't any to be found.
According to Steam, I got 66 minutes of gameplay out of this title, and that was only by really, really trying; I think most people will move on after half an hour, and never return. It's just to thin on content and concept to stick with it otherwise.

If this is your first foray into 4x, I'd suggest Civ 5, which gets you way more hours and is usually cheaper and deeper. Most things are not intuitive, so you're sort of left floundering about hoping to find the combination that works... or just to zerg your opponent. The game is really good, with some flaws. I'm only about 30 hours in, which is not much for a 4X, but I think I've got a handle on what I like and dislike about it.
First of all the pros.
The game is beautifully done in so many ways. In terms of aesthetics: the story is bare but a cool concept, the factions are really cool and beautifully depicted, the graphics are about the level of Civ 5, the music is awesome (really cool if you listen to it but fades into the background when you want to concentrate).
The game play is pretty deep. Most notably the combat system is a little bit deeper and more fleshed out than Civ, although it has its drawbacks as I will detail in the cons section. The factions play differently without feeling too gimmicky - if anything I think they could have taken some of the factions further in terms of their uniqueness (Vaulters, Wild Walkers, and Drakken all play pretty "standard"). I haven't messed around with Diplomacy too much yet, but it seems like it will be interesting, and I do enjoy the use of "Warnings" and the like. By warning or complimenting another civilization, you can reduce or increase the cost of declaring war on them later (among other things of course). Quests and ruins, though the quests can be flawed as well, give you an interesting use for units when you are not using them for war. Minor factions (which give empire boosts, new units, and population) are also a neat addition.
It has a few flaws.
My main gripe is that it is not easy to determine in-game what X you need to do Y. Requirements can be a bit fuzzy at times and it makes you really miss the encyclopedia that sits behind all of the Civ mechanics. All of the information is out there but until you know most of it you will be doing a lot of alt-tabbing to your browser. I recommend reading about a faction fully before you start using them, or you might end up playing a whole game without using your faction's most important mechanics.
The combat can be frustrating at times, and mostly it stems from one design decision: you set your units move/attack targets at the beginning of each round of combat. This can lead to some useless wandering around at best and some major tactical blunders at worst. Most of the time it works fine but it's that one time when you needed this guy to move here so that he could block the other dude, and he just didn't and now you're loading your game to get a redo.
The Expansions:
I have picked up two expansions but only really delved into the new mechanics of one of them: Shifters. Shifters gives you some control over the Winter, which in the base game is just a gigantic bummer that blows over your empire every once in a while. In Shifters you can now collect Pearls (which give your non-fighting armies another thing to do) and use those Pearls to get empire bonuses, etc, and to in effect choose which effects winter has. There are also special quests and buildings that can only be fulfilled/built by one empire, similar to how Wonders work in Civ. For the price ($3 on sale!) it was a great boost to the mechanics and I wholeheartedly recommend.

Beautiful, vibrant pixel art and fleshed out backgrounds that seem to go back forever. Awesome monsters and huge-frantic boss battles. Every inch of screen is full of charm and polish.
Excellent FM-Synthesis-esque soundtrack (reminds me of Later DOS games) really brings everything together.
The level design is straightforward, but there appears to be multiple paths.
The dev probably needs to work on conveying game mechanics a little better, as it stands there are some things that aren't ever made clear or even mentioned in game. I got an achievement for beating the game without upgrading, and I didn't even know I could upgrade! Additionally, there are some "S" coins littered throughout the game that I still don't know what purpose they serve. I'd RTFM, if one was even included.  The achievements menu seems to convey more about the smaller mechanics than the game does itself.
The game is pretty tough, you'll probably die a lot more than you think you would based on the screenshots. I felt like this arbitrarily increased the games lenth a bit.
That last point being key because the game is very, very short. 7 stages, as it says on the tin. I've only played on easy mode thus far, but my total game time from first boot to completion was 55 minutes. I assume higher difficulty levels will increase this dramatically as easy mode has infinite lives. I'll be going back into the game's normal mode momentarily.
That being said, the game's actual quality is top notch, it's a ton of fun to play and look at. I see a lot of concerns about the "meme culture" in the trailer but rest assured it's mostly just for marketing purposes, I've yet to see any troll faces or anything of the sort in game. Only one Doge reference in the achievements menu, and I don't mind.
People afraid of or disgusted by images of well endowed women should already know this game isn't for them from the cover art. I for one, have no problem there. Looking in the forums however, it would appear that this portion of the game did not filter out a large quantity of progressive type people.
It's definitely worth a play. 7$ is a bit steep for a single playthrough, but multiple difficulty mode, good and bad engings and so on makes this 7$ well spent. Recommended.

After playing 1 playthrough of the game's campaign and multiple matches in the gladiator mode, i feel i can make a just and deserving review of this game.
Ryse Son of Rome's Campaign is without a shadow of a doubt;
.
The way the story is told, the plot behind the story, the immersion you have as fighting as a roman centurion/Leader, it truely is a story where you will remember after playing it.
There were many moments in the story where you feel like the lead character; Marius and just want to yell " COHORT, MOVE FORWARD " or "I AM MARIUSSSSSS", truely some adreniline pumping moments.
The campaign is averagely sized, you could possibly do it all in a 24h period or less, but for the average gamer, playing about 2h of this game at a time for example; you will have plenty of fun for the story side of things.
All in all a great story to play with a Masterful Plotline.
The Gladiator mode is also great to play. When i first heard of it when i was looking on the store page i thought of the Spartacus Blood and Sand Series, And it does deliver that sort of feeling but only to a certain extent.
You play as your gladiator; with an array of swords, sheilds and armor to unlock and wear; Fighting for the roman crowd in a collisium that changes its arena by 'loading' different battlefields such as the temple or forest setting.
You fight barbarian hordes; either solo or with a partner online.
Personally; i find the arena 'Loading' a setting fun, but a bit immersion breaking, they could have put in a simple 1v1 dueling mode where you just fight another gladiator, but still its a good game mode to play.
Players still play online for partnered matches but you may be waiting a while to be matchmade.
Without a doubt yes.
The Campaign is a quality piece of work that you will get immersed in and enjoy.
The Gladiator mode is good; if lacking in immersion slightly; that again you will enjoy.
All in all; a quality game with a masterful story, a good multiplayer mode, that you could and should pay for when its on offer, or if you want a great roman era game; pay full price for.
9/10 - with just the 1 point lost for the gladiator 'Loading' arena's.

INTRODUCTION:
Ryse: Son of Rome is a third-person action-adventure game developed by Crytek (known for games such as Crysis) and, surprisingly enough, not published by EA games. It was originally an Xbox One exclusive title but was later ported to the PC. The PC release has since been praised as a superior version to its console counter part boasting better framerates, better graphical fidelity, free bundled dlcs and no micro-transactions.
PLOT (No Spoilers):
The player takes on the role of Marius Titus, a Roman Legionary who's on a mission to avenge the death of his family (Gladiator movie 2000). Son of a legendary Roman General, he quickly rises through the Legion ranks searching for the people behind his family's murder while, at the same time, fighting for Rome, a superpower, against an inferior rebel group. (Call of Duty: Roman Warfare).
PROS:
+ Graphically and Visually MAGNIFICENT
+ Great Animation
+ Quality sounds and voice acting
+ Refreshing new setting (Ancient Rome)
+ Intense action packed combat
+ Fun and entertaining execution moves (though a bit repetitive)
+ No Microtransactions
+ Surprisingly good
+ Story is acceptable at least, its easy to understand and ties up the plot nicely
+ Has potential (if they develop the plot and combat mechanics more)
CONS:
- Very Short (I personally completed it within 7-8 hours on Hard 'Centurion' difficulty)
- Too many (and some unnecessary) turret sections
- Camera can sometimes be dodgy
- Repetitive combat with little variation in attack moves
- Quick Time Event (QTE) based execution moves
- A bit to easy even in Hard difficulty (But challenging in LEGENDARY Mode)
- Wish the game could have added a desert setting or a snowy terrain
- Too restrictive map with no room to explore
- Could have done better with a few more RPG elements
- Co-op maps sometimes glitch out and event triggers does not activate

A lot of people believe that if your food (especially soup) has become too salty, then an easy fix is to add potatoes because they apparently soak in the salty flavor. Well, that's just not true, as potatoes aren't sponges.
Robert Wolke, professor emeritus of chemistry at the University of Pittsburgh and the author of What Einstein Told His Cook: Kitchen Science Explained, tells Real Simple that it just won't work:
"This is an attractive idea, but it doesn't work because potatoes are not particularly absorbent," says Wolke, who conducted his own soup-and-potato experiment for his book. "There is no reason they would attract salt."
Solution: The last time we asked you, you had some good ideas (including the old potato trick), but what works best is re-adjusting portions so the salt is balanced. So if it's salty soup or stew, remove some of the liquid and add fresh, unsalted broth or stock. Similarly, for salty pasta or rice, remove some and add in unsalted bits.
Wolke adds that a little bit of vinegar or sugar can cancel out the saltiness by giving your taste buds competing flavors.

Pros:
-Appealing art style

-Endless possibilities of ship design

-Moddable factions with steam workshop support
-Moddable ship parts, potential for completely custom ships

-Interesting AI differences in factions, some npc ships will actually salvage parts from downed enemies and use them to upgrade their own ship.
-A sandbox mode where you can simulate battles, take control of ships you spawn, and write scripts. Great for testing your custom factions and ships.
Cons/Suggestions to devs:
-The ship editor lacks a symmetry mode, which would make ship building a bit more streamlined
-When you run into stuff, you take damage. I feel like there should be an option to disable this for new players, however this feature grants the ability to create ships that ram when in combat, which is always fun as hell.
-There needs to be a better way to quickly check how damaged your ship is. Perhaps a bar on the hud that shows what percentage of your ship is damaged. Sometimes the screen gets so busy you can't see how much of your ship is left and when it would be a good idea to turn tail and flee if things get too hairy.
-Sometimes it's hard to travel quickly from one place to another because you can't see far enough in front of your ship to see obstacles like asteroids and stations. Space high ways or warp gates would be an excellent addition to the game.
-There is currently no way to tell how much of your shields are left. A way to monitor that would be very convenient.
-The sandbox mode lacks a tutorial on how to use the command line.
-An interesting addition would be factions that have more than just 2 colors in their color scheme. I sometimes feel limited when attempting to create more flashy and appealing ships. Maybe the ability to paint your ship or add decals would work.

Reassembly...a game where you can build you very own fleet piece by piece.  A very interesting and fun game that I would reccomend to anyone and that I think anyone could get a kick out of. The only thing is how long you'll stick with it. Now, I've only played this game for about 9 hours, so this is more of a first impressions, so take everything Isay witha grain of salt if you wish.
This game is certainly an interesting idea that was executed rather well. They made the building system rather intuitive, but it is a bit difficult to master.  I did enjoy when I had my fleet and I was just cutting a warpath through my first world until I got to the wormhole and sent my fleet to other worlds and logged off for the night. It's a game you think you'll for an hour or 2, only to find yourself walking out your door screaming "WHAT YEAR IS IT!?!?" However, my only real problem with it is that is all you can do. To me it feels like a game that will get repetitive instantly.
Again, only played for 9 hours myself, so take what I say with a grain of salt. I would reccomend this game to anyone to give it a go. It is certainly worth the 20 dollars, especially if you get real into it.

I've always been a sucker for customization and Reassembly offers the second best ship-building experience that I have ever had. I think that I spent more time perfecting and refining my ship designs than I did fighting. Seven playable factions each with their own unique weapons and playstyles. Depending on your combat preference, some factions are easier to play than others. You kill things, buy new components and increase the point limit for your ships. I consider a faction finished when you've bought all upgrades and built an 8000 point Superdreadnaught that is pretty much unstoppable.
I bought this game during a sale but after playing it I can say that, for me at least, I would have been happy to pay full price.
The only things that I would change in this game would be an option to disable tutorials when you start a new faction and perhaps a few more components for some of the factions that only have two different types of weapons.

Been playing this game for a long time period, it's one of those games I go back to, start a game and find it hard to stop until I finish it. Then I will leave it sitting for a while and do it all again.
That isn't a bad reflection on the game at all, it keeps drawing me in time and again. (might be a bad reflection on my games stock :/ lol)
Now as to the game, honestly it's hard to explain and can be daunting starting off. There are some features that aren't explained in the tutorial but after a game or two you will pick it up.
Each faction operates differently in the way their 'economy' works. Each city produces  -food, production, science, dust, influence. Some of these aren't used by some of the factions(One nation has to buy their technologies for example, one doesn't use food etc etc)
Then you have global strategic resources, and 'luxury' resources.
All heroes and units can be equipped with better weapons (like armour/weapons/helm/boots/accessories) once the suitable research has been completed or an item is obtained through one of the many mini-quests.
Range of victory types, similar to other games in the genre, but race has a unique 'quest' victory condition which follows the strength of that race.
I've personally found that the expansions for the game have always added nice new interesting content, though the base game was always really solid so if you want to try it out you don't NEED the expansions.
Combat is carried out in an auto or mini-battle screen where you don't directly have control over your units as such, more just give them orders and watch it play out.
Comparisons to other titles of this genre? Well Civ is going to be the obvious one, I've played so many hours of every civ game and I don't regret whenever I play Endless Legend, it is different enough and it always hooks me when I turn it on until that final turn.
I think it's worth full price, but if in doubt wait till a sale. They happen often enough. I would recommend this to a friend, and have happily brought it for a friend knowing it wouldn't disappoint.

The authentic controls can present a bit of a challenge if you're more used to modern tight-handling games, but the implementation appears to have been well thought-out; there's no situation in the game that can't be handled with some finesse.

There's a lot to like about Ultonions: the bright retro graphics, the chip'ish music and even the sexuliased 80s heroine.  But... The gameplay is not quite bad but the design aimed for retro and ended up with unresponsive instead.
You can aim in only 4 directions, left, diagonal left/up. right and diagonal right/up.  It would have been better as an 8-way scheme.  Or even just up - I want to shoot up.
You can shoot or walk, not both.  And you walk slowly.  This may be a side effect but quickly swinging round to shoot and swinging back again seem to stick.  This is incredibly annoying when dealing with fast moving flying enemies.
The crouch animation is unusually long, you must wait for it to finish before firing or walking again.  Popping down to shoot and popping back up to jump and dodge stuff is not going to happen.
About a fifth of your view is obscured on the left and right by the decorative interface.  This makes the dino-riding stage particularly vexing as you can't see what's coming.
I cramped my thumb trying shoot fast - I haven't managed that since I had a Commodore 64.  Not sure if this is a good or bad point.
I'm not recommending this but is a weak non-recommendation.  Learning from your mistakes is big part of the game and that's good reto but not having the space to see or control responsiveness to react is bad retro.  Games like Thundercats, Mask and Turrican all got this right 30 years ago - Ultonious really should have too.

However, that's not to say it's a
game by any means. The Quick Time Event (QTE) based combat can be a bit of a slog, but I find that it's not as bad as it could be. It's very hack and slash based, but there
several enemies that require precise timing to defeat in combat.
Now, as a game I would only give it a 6.5/10. The graphics are delightful and while the mechanics of the game are very simplistic, they aren't necessarily bad.
However! I would not recommend going into Ryse: Son of Rome with the mindset that it's a game. I would instead suggest you go into it under the belief that it's an interactive movie. In terms of storytelling, I give it a 9/10. It isn't the end-all-be-all story by any means, but at the end of it all I found myself whispering "Holy crap, that was amazing."
It's short and the QTE based combat can be off-putting, but if nothing else I would recommend this game for the story alone. Don't get it all full price, but if you can grab it for 50% off or more, I highly recommend you do so.

Having played The Agency of Anomalies: Mystic Hospital years ago, it had always been one of my favorite HOGs.  When it mysteriously appeared in the New Releases here on Steam, I knew without a doubt I needed to play it again.  However, as I booted up this classic, I questioned just what was it about the game that left such a mark on my memory; the artwork is good, but it’s nothing that stands out among others in the genre (or even the series itself), and the gameplay is your typical HOPA-fare.  But as I stepped into the agency investigator’s shoes yet again, this time with a few years of HOG-playing experience under my belt, I was better equipped to pick out all the things that make this title one of the best the genre has to offer.
Set in the post WWI era, the Agency of Anomalies has been contacted by one Dr. Oliver Orvos, a German doctor, scientist, and the sole survivor of a horrific incident that occurred 10 years prior at a top secret military hospital.  Recent events lead him to believe that a dimensional vortex may surface at the abandoned installation, and he’s in desperate need of someone to investigate and deter this paranormal phenomenon before it risks tearing apart the very fabric of existence itself!  As the Agency’s top investigator, you must uncover the hospital’s secrets in order to prevent a world-ending cataclysm.  Nope, this isn’t your typical HOG story, but that’s one of the things I enjoy so much about it.  One can only take so many haunted houses and magical fantasy worlds before boredom sets in.   Traversing this abandoned military facility is a welcome divergence from the stereotypically colorful settings that fill the genre these days.
Gameplay itself is pretty standard “adventure lite” fare, but it’s the little details that make it stand out.  The addition of secret animations that play on certain clicked items breathe life and atmosphere into the empty world, even if they’re only tricks of the Agent’s mind.   I also appreciate the era appropriate items in the hidden object scenes which help immerse the player in the time period.  The scenes themselves are well composed with plenty of objects to search through, but nothing so obscured as to feel unfairly hidden, that is as long as one has enough patience to look carefully.  The item that is to be added to your inventory is the final one to appear on your list after all others are found, which makes it feel as if there’s a purpose to searching through all that junk.  Although it’s such a little thing, it adds a lot.
But above all else, it’s the writing that distinguishes Mystic Hospital from the rest.  The main character is written so well, his personality oozes from the commentary and journal entries.  You can tell this is a guy who’s seen it all, nothing phases him, and he’s gonna finish the job no matter what it takes.  He’s witty and sarcastic and dangit, I wish he had a name, but I’ll just have to settle for Agent.
Then there’s the patient files which are narrated by the good doctor, giving us an interesting glimpse into the experiments performed on the hospital patients which ultimately lead to catastrophe.  The voice actor does a wonderful job of describing the events that took place without hamming it up with the usual HOG camp.  The inclusion of beautifully painted, sepia-colored art pieces serve as a pleasing complement, and contrast, to the grittiness of the rest of the game's graphics.
As much as I loved the main adventure, it pains me to note how disappointing the bonus chapter was.   Usually these extra snippets give additional background into the plot and characters, but it merely included a few documents hinting at the sequel, and not much beyond that.  This would have been fine should the gameplay have been engaging enough, but the additional play time was padded with so many hidden object scenes that even I had grown weary of them towards the end.  I still recommend playing through it, because why not?  But I really wish we would’ve been given more information on the hospital, the villain, or even the protagonist himself.
Small grievances aside, Mystic Hospital remains one of the best HOGs I’ve played.  Perhaps the artwork and premise may not appeal to those used to more brightly painted titles, but the gameplay, atmosphere and writing is truly some of the best I’ve come across in the genre.  I certainly hope the rest of the series makes it over, as I cannot wait to experience more of this Agent’s paranormal adventures.
Bottom Line: Highly Recommended.

Coming again to review this game, I can only speak against it, even with nearly 1000 hours and still playing it (Or trying to do so, to be honest). I've stated before my problems with it, but I'll resume older reviews in some simple points:
-
The game uses a P2P system to host the matches, when one player (the one with the best ping) acts as a host and the other ones connect with him. This usually leads to lags spikes, which happens a lot less in game with dedicated servers.
-
Usually you're teamed with players of other Leagues, due to the low playerbase, but that isn't the worst of it. The MM is hosted in a separete server, under the name of Galactron. It gathers all the players and launches matches every 3 to 5 minutes, making you wait a fixed time. If by any chance you miss the game, no matter if there are players or not, you've to wait for the next. even if you're kicked out the match due to another player disconnects in Naut selection. Besides of that, the game makes you pass 4 checks of connection availability: To Steam, to the server with your profile data, to Galactron and to the chat server. This constant checking acts as a DDOS attack to your computer, overloading it when you have slow internet and making you COMPLETELY UNABLE of playing a MM game. This only last the MM phase, as you can play fine in a Custom game. Also, this has been addressed to Ronimo many times, with their only answer being that the user must check his net configuration and pastfowards ports on the router (Which doesn't fix the problem).
-
There are Nauts so OP they're broken and others completely useless. Of course, the game results depends of the player's skill, but given two players with a top tier Naut and a low tier one, the most OP wins, simply based in dmg input and movility. This is more obvious after new Nauts are released, most of times so OP one wonders if they have been tested at all. There are frequent nerfs and rebalance patches, but this leads to character still being OP or utterly trash, needing a buff in posterior patches. The full balance is never accomplished.
I generally like the game, or I would have just stopped playing. But you make it hard, Ronimo, no player should have to deal with this only to enjoy a 15-20 min game. And as most people will not stay for it, I can't recommend other people to keep trying. Go for other games, they will give you a lot less of headaches.
