On the surface Evoland seems like a brilliant idea. Thats it's main problem though, its only real lure is on the surface. The gimmic of making a game that showcases many different eras of action/adventure games is a great idea for a game, but this execution of it leaves much to be desired. The (so called) story is incredibly predictable and linear, the money system is useless, the random encounters that pay homage to final fantasy type game only serve to capture the most annoying parts (0nly really use item, heal, and attack), overly simplistic puzzles, and the list goes on. If you really want to see the evolution of videogames, save yourself the 10$ and just google history of action/adventure videogames, It'll be more entertaining and about as difficult to complete.

Seeing the “evolution” of RPGs is done fairly well in terms of graphics, music, and UI, but there's not much else to Evoland. There’s no actual exploration. What you do is walk towards wherever the game points, tediously fighting the same handful of monsters again and again. The few puzzles in the game are explained to you beforehand, further ensuring that you never experience any kind of challenge. There’s nothing to care about at all because the devs were preoccupied with trying to make you nostalgic for Final Fantasy and Zelda.
This kind of gimmick can go in two directions: It can serve as the basis for a new type of gameplay in a legitimate RPG, or it can be an excuse to make shameless references to older games and call it a day. Evoland took the latter route. Recommended to anyone who posts about having been a ‘90s kid.

Cons:
-Odd Pacing, felt like I was flying through the beginning with the evolutions, only to peter-out about 20 mins in. I felt they could have spent more time by putting more classic content in the beginning stages of the game.
-Zero replay-ability
-Extremely short (knocked out 85% in 3 hours, and I probably won't chase the last 15)
-Near the end of the game, combat gets pretty basic/ repetitive (Hit, Heal)
-$9.99? Lol. Catch that bad boy on sale (I did). There's cheaper options to kill 3 hours.
Overall:
I'd recommend it. Playing this game really reminded me what I loved and loathed about the classic titles it pays homage to. As I said, I would catch it when its on sale. This would be a better value at $2.99 - $4.99 range. But if you got some extra cash, its a good experience.

Evoland is a game which takes a lot of traits from series like Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy. In the later part of the game you can also feel some of Diablo's gameplay.
Story in Evoland is as basic as it can get. One could argue that it's even less because ideas for characters and plot are straight stolen from abovementioned games.
When it comes to presentation this game is neat. Music and graphics evolve as you collect chests with upgrades to them. You are acquainted with typical look and sound of consoles from third to sixth generation (so Gameboy, SNES, Gamecube etc.).
I have to admit that I really liked some of the music tracks used in the game - they were adequate, familiar and pleasant to listen to.
Gameplaywise Evoland offers some variety but every "game mode" presented is bare-bones. Turn-based combat is less than satisfying, inventory in the game is a joke (quite literally), hack'n'slash combat lacks skills, puzzles are repetitive etc. Random encounters get annoying very quickly and boredom is guaranteed when trying to 100% the game. Additionally, Evoland is a very short game (took me about 4 hours to finish it and 6 hours to complete it) and has very little replay value.
Something that I really want to mention is this game's approach. It knows what it is and tries to be funny. In that regard, it succeeds, I had an honest laugh few times. Additionally, I had a blast trying to find every reference to video gaming in the game (Mario was quite obvious but I think I found The Elder Scrolls Morrowind as well).
My score for this game is 6/10. It's unique, funny, quite diverse but offers very basic gameplay.

Space Beast Terror Fright at first caught me off guard with it's name, Halo esque assault rifle with iron sights pointing into a screen, and Warhammer 40k looking Space Marines. After watching some gameplay, though, it definitely got my attention and I ended up buying it soon after. SBTF is an awesome little Horror indie gem and an absolute blast to play with friends. As soon as I got in game I realized the videos I watched really didn't do this game justice in terms of visual quality and overal atmosphere. The game runs really well, has very little bugs, and easy to pick up controls.
SBFT nails atmosphere, audio, and visuals to create a really scary and intense experience as you fight your way through various space stations to activate data cores and escape. Taking damage will effect your suits systems and disable many different features such as your ammo counter, mini map, station system alerts, and other various HUD elements or the HUD entirely. Collecting data cores and progressing, however, can earn experience and unlock new suit systems such as battery recharge rates, motion detectors, and mini map upgrades. Unlocked upgrades and experience will be kept if you survive but everything will be lost on death.
SBFT can be played solo or it can be played 4 player local splitscreen or 4 player online splitscreen. Yep, online splitscreen. You have a few options while playing online. You can choose to see your screen only, your screen and other players screens as small monitors on the right edge of your screen, or classic splitscreen. This gives you the ability to keep track of your allies as you wander through the darkness and mazelike corridors. The maps can be generated at random with a variety of modifiers or can be created using specific seeds that can create some pretty unique experiences.
Space Beast Terror Fright is an incredibly fun and intense Indie game that really shines when played cooperatively. It's very difficult but very fun and has a lot of repayability between the map generation tools and the incentive to continue after you finally survive and get to keep all the progress you made. I definitely recommend this game if you've been looking for a coop rogue-lite horror game to die hundreds of times with friends or want something to do before Space Hulk

Very nearly didn't puchase this game, but I'm glad I did. It's incredibly fun, unique, and will definitely get your adrenaline going in the right moments. It's interesting in that its strengths are executed perfectly, but it does suffer from a number of weaknesses...
Pros:
- Randomly generated maps are done incredibly well. It puts you in unique situations and you'll be forced to work strategically with your partner in order to survive.
- Many suspenseful moments to induce panic but each with a solution if you can remain calm. (Alien swarm too large/fast to gun down, doors breaking down at strategic points, power outages, running low on ammunition, becoming damaged and having to fight without parts of your hud)
- The simple gameplay is incredibly fun and easy to get into with your friends.
- The environment, hub, sounds, and effects make for an incredible environment that really pulls you into the game.
Cons:
- Not fun to play alone
- Small community mostly occupied in private lobbies. SBTF is very much a game that is improved dramatically by company. Solo play feels overwhelming and unfair, If you don't have friends lined up to play the game you'll have to look towards randoms to team up with. Most players set their lobbies to private however and many of the public lobbies will still kick you if you join. Finding a game to join during peak hours is possible with patience, but at odd times of day/night is pretty much not possible.
- Lacks the finer aspects. (Crouch, zoom, run(manually))
- Bulky marines are fun, but it went too far. It's virtually impossible to shoot down a hallway past someone without hitting them.
Overall, I absolutely recomend this game to anyone who is looking for a fast, fun, run & gun of the horror variety.  What the game sets out to do, it does incredibly well.

Reassembly is a space combat game, in which you build your own ship, and can also design all the ships your faction spawns.
The ultimate goal is to conquer the galaxy, eliminating all other factions (I've never managed).
It's got a great atmosphere, the galaxy really feels alive, with plants shooting their spores from one asteroid to another, all the different factions doing their business, battles raging, quiet stretches of space littered with the remains of destroyed ships, asteroid fields and wormholes.
It also has a sandbox mode (with command line and all), and a tournament mode, where you can organize battling championships.
All in all, it's a great game! As you can see (or not, depending on when you are reading the review), I sank over 92 hours into this game in two weeks. That's quite a lot - and for good reason, it's super addictive. It felt quick because I sank so many hours into it in a short time, I think, but it's got great replayability, I still play it occasionally.
Slightly dissapointed with some unlockable factions, and the UI isn't great (no way to save individual ship weapon bindings?), but I don't regret buying the game at all, it was (and still is, to be honest) a blast.
[EDIT (Feb 2016)] - Binding issue seems to be fixed! Devs are still fixing bugs and facilitating modding! :D
Most people should be comfortable with full price, it's not an expensive game at all.
Go ahead and buy it! :D

Metal Gear Solid V: Gound Zeroes
First off I want to state that you are not going to get the story-saturated, lore-driven deliciousness that the Metal Gear franchise is notoriously known for. The game is set up like a television show with a series of episodes in a season. Where one mission in the game would be one episode. When you start up the game you go through the main story and then in less than thirty minutes, it's already over. Whereas with other Metal Gear games, you are given a butt-load of lore, story and gameplay in advancing the game. Then in order to satisfy your hunger for more Metal Gear, the game gives you side missions that don't really expand on the world you're limited to exploring; like filler episodes in a show. The base this game is set at gets boring after a while, even when doing the other side missions that are supposed to appease. Overall, the game is okay. The gameplay is incredible and the story is amazing, but what holds it back is its limit. Everything is just too little. After finishing, it feels more like a demo than an actual and complete game. It's a good introduction for people trying to get into the Metal Gear franchise, but for others who want to actually play a full "Metal Gear" and enrich themselves within the massive world that the series has expanded upon for over twenty-five years? You would have a better experience playing Phantom Pain than this.

Been playing this game for a long time period, it's one of those games I go back to, start a game and find it hard to stop until I finish it. Then I will leave it sitting for a while and do it all again.
That isn't a bad reflection on the game at all, it keeps drawing me in time and again. (might be a bad reflection on my games stock :/ lol)
Now as to the game, honestly it's hard to explain and can be daunting starting off. There are some features that aren't explained in the tutorial but after a game or two you will pick it up.
Each faction operates differently in the way their 'economy' works. Each city produces  -food, production, science, dust, influence. Some of these aren't used by some of the factions(One nation has to buy their technologies for example, one doesn't use food etc etc)
Then you have global strategic resources, and 'luxury' resources.
All heroes and units can be equipped with better weapons (like armour/weapons/helm/boots/accessories) once the suitable research has been completed or an item is obtained through one of the many mini-quests.
Range of victory types, similar to other games in the genre, but race has a unique 'quest' victory condition which follows the strength of that race.
I've personally found that the expansions for the game have always added nice new interesting content, though the base game was always really solid so if you want to try it out you don't NEED the expansions.
Combat is carried out in an auto or mini-battle screen where you don't directly have control over your units as such, more just give them orders and watch it play out.
Comparisons to other titles of this genre? Well Civ is going to be the obvious one, I've played so many hours of every civ game and I don't regret whenever I play Endless Legend, it is different enough and it always hooks me when I turn it on until that final turn.
I think it's worth full price, but if in doubt wait till a sale. They happen often enough. I would recommend this to a friend, and have happily brought it for a friend knowing it wouldn't disappoint.

A hilarious fighting game style similator where you put together insult phrases to hurt your opponent. You can perform combos, use certain words against your opponents weaknesses and more. It's really funny and a lot of fun. Also has online play and multiple game modes, as well as some newer guest characters (like H.P. Lovecraft) with their own unique insults.

Imagine a turn based 2D fighting game. Except instead of slinging special moves and uppercuts you're insulting your opponent's fashion sense and insinuating some unsavoury things about their familial relations. Wrap it around some Monty Python style skits and some wonderful satirical humour. Then charge less than a cup of coffee at Starbucks.
The game itself is relatively simple. Each round presents you with a collection of words and phrases, and you and your opponent take it in turns to select words to build an insult designed to bring your opponent to their knees. Each player also has two private cards only they can use (which can be reshuffled once during each round).
There's some nice strategy in picking those insults though - each character has vulnerabilities to certain topics and chaining together insults on the same subject applies a multiplier. There's also some interesting decisions when it comes to picking words - both players can see the insult being built by their opponent, so sometimes it's possible to effectively block them by removing a word they need, assuming you can build it into your own insult. These add some surprising depth to the game given the price.

TL;DR:  Retro-styled in looks, sound, and difficulty, this sidescrolling run-and-gun platformer with some shmup stages will slap you around a bit, but will still play fair.
I'll preface this by saying I got this in the Groupees Be Mine 11 bundle.  And this is probably the first time I've gotten a game, downloaded it, played it, AND beat it all in the span of maybe a couple of days.  So with that said...
Ultionus is the story of a woman, her robot head partner, and a social networking comment that leads to a crash landing and a lot of things to kill.  As you can tell by the screenshots, it's a "retraux" game, a modern game made with retro-inspired graphics and gameplay.  You actually don't have a gun at the very start, so you need to rely on your bouncing robot head partner to destroy the enemies as you move to the left, and then you get a gun and can start blasting everything to death.  This threw me off at first, but that's what experimentation is for, right?
I thought this game was pretty hard on Normal, but it wasn't unfair about it.  Our heroine can only take so many hits before she explodes in a shower of cartoon hearts and respawns at the last checkpoint or stage entrance.  You get restored to full health when you pass a checkpoint the first time or find a red heart 1UP.  Controls are fairly tight, though Serena is a little slow on the ground and especially while firing since she stops altogether.  You'll be spending most of your time in the air, and thankfully this game doesn't fall into "Castlevania 1 jumping" where you can't change directions mid-air.  Hitboxes seemed pretty accurate and there aren't really any fancy controls.  For the 360 controller, A could be tapped or held to change the height you jump, X and B fire your ray gun, Y doesn't seem to do anything, and the d-pad and stick both can be used for movement.  No movement faster than a leisurely walk, no sliding, no wall-jumping...simple stuff.
There are upgrades, but you not only have to find a special coin in each level, but also get to the merchant's door.  I'd also add "and have enough money to buy the upgrades" but you get money by killing everything you see, and you'll be doing that anyway.  You have to choose between offense and defense, and you can only pick one per stage.  If you find the coin and door that is.  There are multiple routes through each normal platforming stage, and the auto-scrolling vehicle ones obviously only have one route.  Get to the end of the level and you fight a giant enemy thing.  Die and you start the fight all over again.  Learn the boss patterns or you'll eat through your stock of lives (on Normal and Hardcore; Easy gives you infinite).
I would honestly suggest trying this on Easy first.  It takes the pressure off of playing well and it'll allow you to go through stages by different routes and learn boss routines, even though running out of lives merely gives you a prompt to start the level over with 9 lives and all of your money, or exit the game.  I started on Normal, and I honestly game overed twice, though I didn't get the best ending (the bad ending spells out what you need to do to avert it though).  The dev has said on the Steam forum that playing on harder difficulties will unlock achievements for that and the difficulty level(s) below it.  So if you get the best ending on Normal, you get the Easy achievement too, for example.  There aren't many achievements but they're actually something to work towards.  Without trying, I got two for winning on Normal with the bad ending and watching the credits all the way through.
Graphics are really colorful and the animations are quite nice.  You can pretty easily tell what would hurt you and what won't, and there's quite a bit of detail work done here.  You don't really notice the big border after a while.  I didn't really feel like I'd do better if I didn't see it at all.  The music's pretty catchy and I kinda wish there was a sound test option (or maybe there is one and I just haven't unlocked it yet).  I don't really have much to say about the sound effects.  They're there.
I won't do my usual "I liked/disliked this" sections since there's not much to say.  I had fun.  My heart raced, I cursed, and I'm not only glad this is on Steam, but I'm glad I gave this game a chance.  It's short, but there's a little bit of replay value, and I can see myself giving this game a few more hours.  I've forgotten what it's like to actually
to learn patterns and get penalized by starting boss fights over when I don't.

The Positives:
- You can create pretty much any PBR material procedurally.
- It has tons of content including alphas, generators, environments, Filters, Materials and so on. You can get more from Substance Share for free or get paid ones by subscribing to Substance Live. If you so desire, you can upload your own substances to Substance Share.
- Texture baking is fast and you can change resolutions on the go. Designer will recalculate all the nodes giving you a true resolution scale instead of an upscale or downscale.
- Export in various formats or Substance Files which are compatible with almost all 3d softwares or Game Engines. You can check out the plugins on the website for the software or game engine you use.
- Works seamlessly with both Substance Painter and B2M.
- You get standalone licenses even if you buy through steam. Just sync your steam account with allegorithmic.
- Support is really Good.
Negatives:
- Still has a bunch of bugs especially in the 3D View. I have reported a few myself. It does improve over time with updates but has to be mentioned.
- It has a really steep learning curve. Allegorithmic does have a lot of training videos on its Youtube Channel and Twitch but I still feel it needs a proper Beginner Course.
- No Blender Plugin !!!
Verdict:
I highly recommend this Software for its price. I would also suggest looking into Substance Indie Pack which gives you all 3 Substance Softwares at a lower price than buying them individually.

GAMEPLAY: 5/5
Defense Clicker is a simple blend of tower defense and idle game.
Gameplay consists of placing towers to defend against enemy waves and purchasing upgrades. The 'idle' segment of the game consists of persistent resources and upgrades that remain after you lose all lives, also knows as resets. Resets happen often but as you upgrade, you will survive longer each time.
As for the early access aspect of the game, the dev has many improvements planned for the game and updates daily. For such a low price I did not find the early access state of the game discouraging me from purchasing as it normally does.
GRAPHICS AND AUDIO: 2/5
Graphically the game could use some improvement. The particle effects are nice but the tower visual designs and general level design could use some improvement, I feel the scattered trees look more clutter than the forest it seems to be trying to be, and the UI blend with the terrain is a good move, it is a little too simplistic and could use a little more texture.
Sound and music definitely need some improvement but due to the genre they have minimal impact on my enjoyment of the game, as the inclusion of the mostly automatic 'farming mode' may have you muting them to let it do its thing in the background until you return to the active play mode.
SUMMARY:
All in all, despite the current flaws of the game, the gameplay itself is enough to warrant my positive recommendation. I have enjoyed my experience so far and look forward to whatever improvements the dev has for the game when they arrive.

Wow... took me quite a while to actually write something... Not very handy at reviews I'm afraid.
Amplitude Studios always has had a knack for their games. They might be one of the most underrated studios out there, both on their costumer support and how they allow their fanbase to voice how they want their games to proceed forward; to the amazing quality and polish of their games.
Endless Legend is a new game on their Endless Series, a continuum of games interconnected on world lore and events some way or another. A departure from Endless Space sci-fi genre, Endless Legend focuses on a more fantastical approach in which several races fight for supremacy on one way or another in the planet Auriga. Ever since the game's first iteration, the core mechanics of 4x (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit and eXterminate) were solid, being more and more improved as the expansions and extra free content were added. The game is very streamlined, teaching you step by step when you first start out the nuances of it's content and UI. Some things of course, are better learned on your own, as any good game leaves a couple of surprises.
That said, everytime you pick a race, you are given a sort of a main quest, a guideline to send you on your way that allows you to both grasp how they function and what drives them. It's not just a question of stats and numbers, as the way it's presented helps you immerse on the lore of who you guide, aswell as the world itself: from the sites and artifacts you gather, to the heroes that join your cause, to the minor factions you encounter; Auriga is full of mysteries and things to learn.
Some core systems where improved with expansions, Guardians went forward with Ancient ones that count as super units, if you fight them or control them.. aswell as giving players means to work together or fight each over over legendary monuments and objectives. Shadows gave us a new race, focusing on espionage as well as fleshing out those systems... no longer you can sit content on building things and sorting armies, when everything you fought so hard for can be undermined with a smart spy network. Shifters gave a sense of the changes in Auriga, the difference between spring and winter and how deeply it can affect the various races... including the one added that is attuned to those said changes. Finally, Tempest, the new expansion, adds a race focused on a system that was lacking... naval battles and sea events... expanding the scope of the game even more with extra threats and things to explore... I'll be honest that I haven't dwelved as much into Tempest, but I will when I get time.
Lost Tales Dlc adds a lot more tales based on lore and events that happened that led Auriga to the state it is, very recommended if you enjoy more of this world and how it came to be. Finally Echoes of Auriga adds more songs to the game, which itself boasts a magnificent and immersive soundtrack by the ever so talented FlybyNo. From haunting to relaxing tunes... every race and season has their song to enthrall you in this magnificent world.
All in all Endless Legend is a gem of a game, that hooked me from the moment I started playing it, and I can't wait till I get my decent desktop to play it in its full potential, as all this was experienced from a very old laptop.
So do yourself a favor, either full price or on sale, give Endless Legend a go if you are a fan of 4x and fantasy, for Auriga awaits for the ones that can master her secrets.

Having finally put more hours and multiple games into Endless Legend, I can now comfortably say that it is just as fun, if not slightly more so, than the other game we've probably all played - Civilization 5.
The comparison between the two games basically ends at "4x game" and "Empire building/management." Beyond that, the games play very differently as its core mechanics are similar, yet different.
The best thing about Endless Legend is in its Endless Universe - an original, story-rich environment that spans all of their games; In fact, people who played Endless Space will recognize that Endless Legend takes place on a unique planet that spawns in that game -- Auriga.
Expanding on this is the fact that the factions are not only diverse, but are actually very different from each other, with their own strengths and weaknesses; More than I can say about the relatively 'bland' Civs from Civ5.
In Civ5, the best things about the various Civs were in their individual character; They represent known leaders from history, and their dialogue and actions strive to align with their personalities. However, ultimately, every Civ boiled down to a couple bonuses here and there, with one unique ability to prevent them from being exactly the same as each other. Unfortunately, I felt most of these Unique Abilities were simply an extension of a fairly simple bonus - More Culture, or Production, or Science, etc. Occasionally you had ones that affected other systems, such as stealing technology, or annexing City-States, which were a bit more unique.
In Endless Legend, the factions' mechanics themselves are functionally different from each other, much more than simple bonuses and penalties. Do not misunderstand -- there is still a system of bonuses and penalties (such as +1 science per tile, -1 Food per tile, etc.) but each faction's UA causes these to have different amounts of value to the player. For example, there is one faction (Broken Lords) who doesn't need any Food at all - Imagine the options available when you can outright completely ignore one of the basic resources! Another faction (Necrophages) instead generates extra Food through slaughter with their armies; Imagine if Civ5's Zulus were aggressive because killing things was how they grew their cities, instead of just being needlessly aggressive because that's what they liked doing.
Unfortunately, the diplomatic game leaves much to be desired. It's functional, but the interactions simply aren't as 'fun' as those in Civ5 where, again, the best thing about the Civs were their individual characters, which are flaunted quite proudly in their diplomatic interaction screens (even if the diplomatic logic was flawed, but then that goes for both games.)
In the end, I find both games fun and "one more turn"-ish, but they cater to different 'games' and requiring different strategies. To that end, I do recommend Endless Legend, not as a replacement, but as a change of pace from Civ5, and switching between the two depending on my playstyle mood.
Finally, just as with Civ5, pick up the expansions/DLC. Civ5 is quite boring without Brave New World, and I feel Endless Legend is a bit basic without Guardians (for World/National Wonders,) Shifters (for new Winter mechanics,) Tempest (for Naval play,) and Shadows (for the Espionage system.)

With stunning visuals, smooth gameplay and a hauntingly awesome soundtrack, Endless Legend is one of a kind. Its unique gameplay with a multitude of factions, characters and troops allows for a fun and diverse experience. With the ability to customize factions and the importance of interacting with minor factions, EL stands out as a 4X game. Each expansion pack adds satisfactory QOL changes, but it doesn't feel like I'm missing out for not having one. They're also released sporadically, so I don't have to break bank to get them all in one go.
My only complaint is the long loading time as each world is being generated. In multiplayer, if one person disconnects, it isn't like Age of Wonders III, for example, where the game can still run smoothly and can rejoin. It's worth the wait every single time, though. Also, the fighting system can be a little challening to get used to at first with the way movement works, but once you understand it, it's quite simple and fun!

This game has a beautiful style, including everything from the very detailed map to the UI.  The variety to this game is incredible, with each race having truly unique qualities that require different playstyles, which adds an incredible amount of replayablility on top of what a typical 4X game provides, which is usually a lot.
There are a few noteworthy problems, though.  The lack of an in-game encyclopedia of sorts similar to what most other 4X games have is my primary complaint.  Finding explanations for many things is a bit too hard, and sometimes requires resorting to trial and error.  The battle system is a bit difficult to get the hang of, but it's not as bad as most seem to think.  If you don't like it, you could always bypass it by choosing auto and it would be no different that most other 4X games.
Overall, if you like 4X games, this is a unique gem that I highly recommend.  Even if you don't like all aspects of it, I'm confident that it will make a memorable impact on you, and that you will get your money's worth.  If your new to 4X games, this is a fine game to start with, but just keep in mind that it does things quite differently and probably has a learning curve that is a bit steeper than others.

To be completely honest, I didn't expect much from Evoland. I got it during the Winter Sale, and thought it was going to be a straightforward RPG.
To a certain extent, I was wrong.
Evoland takes you through the history of the RPG genre: through Zelda, Pokemon, Diablo, and many more classics. While the gameplay itself isn't stellar, the parodying of RPG classics, along with a beatiful representation of the RPG timeline, definitely makes this game a worthwhile buy.
It is rather short, and doesn't have much replayability. Furthermore, the game does get a bit "grindy" at times, a la Diablo. Nevertheless, it's worth it, as you explore a beautifully animated world, and changing the medium that you look at the world.
I'm not trying to say this game provides Skyrim-depth plot, replayability, or graphics: but for 9.99, it's a great steal for several hours of fun! Definitely would recommend for a casual game.

First, let me just start by saying that I would not recommend buying this game at the list price.  However, it's a solid choice for a Steam sale.  The game is around five to six hours long on the initial playthrough and, unless you want to find all the collectibles, there isn't really any replay value.
That said, it was enjoyable enough and didn't overstay its welcome.  The game is gorgeous, which I guess is to be expected from what was the Xbox One's flagship launch exclusive.  Everything from the armor to the enviroments to the lighting effects looks great, and there is quite a bit of variety to the levels as well, ranging from bright forests filled with aqueducts to the streets of Rome to dark, spooky woods and mountains at the edge of the world, and more besides.
The story was better than I expected as well.  It's a relatively simple and predictable tale of revenge.  Marius, a Roman soldier, witnesses the murder of his family and then travels to Brittania to seek vengeance on the barbarians that killed them.  As expected, there is more to the story, and while I won't spoil it here you can basically predict exactly where the game is going from the moment it begins.  We've seen this tale before.  But again, it was enjoyably told, and the voice acting was generally pretty good.  The Roman gods play a role as well, which adds a bit of uniqueness to an otherwise pretty run-of-the-mill story.
The cut-scenes, of which there are few early on and quite a few more as the game progresses, are all well-directed and stylish.  The words I would use to describe Ryse are "set-piece gaming."  It's a game where you move from one set-piece to another, almost more spectator than player at times.  However, when the game looks as good as Ryse does, you almost don't mind sometimes.  There are plenty of memorable set-pieces too, from the Saving Private Ryan-esque beach assault early in the game to the massive battle with war elephants and a horde of barbarians toward the end.
The main weakness to Ryse, unfortunately, is the gameplay itself.  It's sort of similar to the Arkham games and Shadow of Mordor with its combat style, although not nearly as deep or fun.  It's simplification personified.  You have an attack button, a shield bash that knocks back enemies, a counter, and a roll.  Unlike the Arkham games, though, this one doesn't give you a notification when enemies are about to attack you, which makes the combat clunkier than it probably should be at times.  Some enemies also have heavy attacks where they glow red for a brief moment, but often they don't glow red soon enough for you to counter it, especially in the midst of a crowded fight.  It's just not great game design, really.  There are times when everything clicks and the combat is fun for a time, but for the most part you're just going through the motions and using the same moves to kill the same few enemies over and over and over again.
The only saving grace to the combat is that it looks awesome.  Even when the gameplay itself is uninspired, you can't help but enjoy watching the combat unfold.  The finishers, which are glorified quicktime events (although there's no real punishment for failing them), show Marius absolutely decimating his foes in a variety of incredibly over-the-top and gory ways.  You do end up seeing the same handful over and over again for the most part, and the health regen finishers are by far the most practical later in the game, but it never stops being pretty.
And that's kind of Ryse in a nutshell.  It's a very pretty game without a lot of depth to back up the visuals.  Would I recommend it for sixty bucks?  Hell no.  Would I recommend it for twenty?  Eh...not really.  But if you see it on sale for five or ten bucks and want a pretty, mostly mindless six hour thrill ride?  Sure, why not.

Reassembly is a 2D vector graphics based space shooter where the only objective is to conquer and destroy everything else. You start in a small ship in your own faction with only one station to your name. You gain resources by destroying enemy faction ships, collecting resources from nearby asteroids, and expanding your territory by activating unused stations. Once you have enough resources, you can design your very own ships to the fullest degree as they are no mandatory templates or spaceship hulls to work off of. You can build ships that can build other ships on the fly and command a fleet of your custom made ships. All the blocks that make up a ship must be researched first, and the only way to gain blocks to your "datastore" is to destroy enemy ships with said block.
*** Pros ***
Vector graphics and particle effects mean zero load times and small game size (~100 MB)
Custom build all ships from movement to weapon systems
Extensive tutorial to teach the games mechanics
High replayability as you can unlock other factions ships
Good soundtrack and sound effects
*** Cons ***
Large battles can get confusing because of particle effects

This is a simple sandboxxy space combat game.  Focus is on design and some very arcade style combat.
NOTE: I haven't played past the first 'race' - and the playstyle of other races are different - but in a limited sense.
In theory you could do economy building, but you only control one ship (effectively) so actually building a economy to produce masses of ships appears a distant dream.
Complaints about the balance are justified.  Ships designed by other players will inhabit your world, and they run the gammut from harmless to ... very challenging.
I'm continuously annoyed by 3 things.
1 - Economic development is unmanageable, and resource farms are often eradicated by combat.  It's not merely a re-seed problem - you can actually destroy asteroids - the 'ground' on which you plant farms.  Only one faction can effectively generate farms. Humans can push asteroids around and then hope that seeds spawn before the plants / asteroids are destroyed by combat.
2 - The blocks aren't quite standardized.  The slight differences in size and connection point locations are amazingly frustrating.  75% of my ship design time is spent trying to find a way of connecting blocks that are off by a few pixels.
As a bonus sometimes the order in which you assemble the exact same shape can allow or disallow a connection.
3 - Progression is very shallow.  You can spend your 'money' on:
- new weapons / modules (but nothing outside your faction and there is no 'tree' or research time, just a list of items and prices).
- AI ships (like one of your faction's ships?, you could make one or just buy it)
- Size limit increases. (your personal ship is 'free')
'Size limit' is the only thing that prevents you from making collossal ships at the start.  Modules and Weapons (but not hull) have a complexity cost, and your complexity limit starts at 300.  You simply spend 'money' to buy a larger limit, and 2000 appears to be a good target for a good combat design.
You also have resources which are used to produce new ships.  You can trade resources for 'money' by dropping them off at a station.
Overall:
If you want a sandbox for designing blaster ships, this game isn't bad.
Advanced stuff isn't possible due to the AI and mechanics. (AI can swarm - but you can't)
The game quickly devolves into a deathball mopping up the galaxy - which becomes a chore awfully fast.

This game suffers from severe identity crisis; one minute you'll be playing a Legend of Zelda-style knockoff, the next you're  fighting enemies in a turn-based format like in Final Fantasy (even the characters are explicitly copied from FFVII)! There's even a section that's reminiscient to Diablo. The problem isn't that it emulates these games; the problem is that it emulates these games pretty badly and doesn't tie the vastly different gameplay styles together very well. During these 3 hours you're going to wish that you spent your money elsewhere and/or that you were playing the very games Evoland tries to pay tribute to.
Evoland is a good concept at its heart, but it's simply too tedious and tries too many styles at once to be enjoyable.

It's bascially an "Evolution of Dance" Dance for video games. On its own its really lacking and is really only entertaining with a full suite of cultural knowledge. Even then its bascially a compilation of video game references - I'm sure the devs are really passionate about their baby, but it feels like a gimic :/
To be fair I only played an hour of it, up to the point where your first companion ditches you temporarily in the second, beat up town. But after that I just completely lost interest
This game was absolutely amazing. The progression through different styles of games and RPGs was fantastic. You will enjoy every minute of this game.

Short version: I'm being snobby and wanted more of a deconstruction of classic games and less straight nostalgia.
Evoland draws inspiration from old school RPGs, primarily the Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy franchises. There is nothing inherently wrong with this, but it makes several gameplay mechanic choices that imitate limitations without considering why those limitations existed. In the action RPG (Zelda) sections where you directly control attack and movement, you are limited to only 1 active weapon and need to pause to switch between the sword, bomb, and bow. The original Zelda game had about a dozen useable items, but only 4 non-directional buttons to assign them to, hence the pause and switch mechanic. Evoland's implementation is mostly just an incovenience.
For FF-style turn-based random combat (which, oddly, skips actual turn-based combat like the NES games used and goes straight to the Active Time Battle system of the SNES and PS era games), is pretty much devoid of options. Sure, old RPGs mainly just involved repeatedly selecting attack, but Evoland's protagonist has virtually no other options. There is a special attack that I still haven't unlocked over an hour into the game, and items, but I've only seen potions and phoenix down, which you rarely need as the enemies do almost insignificant damage. You gain an magic-using ally not too far in, who knows heal. About an hour in, she learns a basic magic attack. No elemental spells to exploit enemy weaknesses, no status effects, just boring vanilla damage. This spell makes her basic attack obsolete, as there is no MP stat, magic is free.
Another issue I have with the game is that the FF-style inventory menu is completely non-interactive. You can't cast spells, look at a map, detailed character stats, or even look at item descriptions (much less use items). You don't even equip the weapons and armor you buy/find, it just automatically applies.
Final gripe: in the town that first mimics Play Station era graphics, there is a disc loading delay between screens in the town as a little joking reference to the time. This joke quickly wears thin as the screen is about 2 seconds long, happens between EVERY screen in town, and then the game sends you on a fetch quest in town, repeatedly running from one end to the other. There is an in-game item you can buy to reduce the loading-screen, but I'm only assuming that because it costs more money than I had. I would have had to spend time grinding random battles, which would have taken longer than the time saved from the item.

Interesting concept, sections of it are a bit frustrating, but that's more because I'm not the biggest fan of this style of RPG. I like the additions to the game as you go through and it's a nice little interactive history of RPG games, but it does feel a little empty at times.
I'd recommend giving it a go. It's nothing phenomenal but it's a solid concept and definitely worth a look.

I'd give this game a 7.5/10.

It took me a few hours to get the hang of the game, as it is somewhat different from what I was used to in Civilization 5. First of all, you are punished significantly more by having more cities, so if you want to expand all over the map, you would probably need to build a specific faction to do so. This brings me to the 2nd large difference: You can create your own faction by mixing and matching traits from the different factions, and boy are those different! In my 56 hours of game time I haven't even tried out all factions yet, but in contrast to Civilization, I am very much inclined to. This is simply because of the large differences between them, which keeps it all fresh and interesting. The combat system is very different from what I was used to as well. It really takes planning: You try to give your units orders to the best of your abilities, and then the combat round plays out in its entirety all at once. I love the tactical planning this requires. All in all, I definitely got the 'one more turn' feeling from this game, and would heartily recommend it to any 4x fan!

After having spent hundreds of hours in Civilization V, I still found Endless Legend to be refreshing. It goes for a more fantasy perspective, compared to Civ V's historical one. Endless Legend manages to provide a compelling and unique story for each faction. It has more in-depth mechanics, and a combat system I actually prefer compared to Civ V.  Its tie-in to the story of Endless Space (another great game from Amplitude) is an added bonus.
This game gets my vote for 'The “Just 5 More Minutes” Award'.

Endless Legend has only been around since 2014 but its rewards for the ardent 4X gamer are “timeless.” It is certainly one of the most beautiful and evocative realms in all of PC gaming and the Amplitude development team deserves, that’s right, unending praise for their accomplishment. Wonderfully, they continue to support and build on that accomplishment, as their latest “Tempest” expansion proves, opening up the boundless seas of Auriga’s world for exploration, new modes of combat, rare minerals, a new race,  and new capabilities with which to build’s one world.
As a “seasoned gamer” of 60+ years, I especially appreciate the game’s  cerebral challenge, especially its  customization choices, world-building, questing, and hero-building. Combat is not the high point for the real treat in Endless Legend is the infinitely replayable gameworld itself, shimmering and shining with colorful terrain and plentiful resources and vasty continents and seas to be explored. If there is any flaw in the game design it is that the “recurring winter” syndrome becomes a bit tiresome and the mid to end game could be spruced with more random events and surprises.
Let’s hope Amplitude holds on tight and never lets Auriga go.

basically, this game does what it does best very well.  i don't think that many people saw Kill Bill because they wanted a legitimate history lesson on ninjas.  please don't play this game and expect to be accurately educated on how things went down in Rome's extensive military expansion and conquest of the nations.  but then again, i wasn't there.  maybe this is actually how it went down.  i'm just asking, are you playing this game for a history lesson or to be entertained?
which segues nicely into my second point: is this entertaining to you... the brutal decapitation and gutting and de-limbing of countless foes in slow-time sequences?  the gameplay is at once both frantic and meticulously detail-oriented... some of the best i've seen since shadows of mordor.  not as refined, in my opinion, but certainly wonderfully magnificent in it's own right.  now, to be clear, i played shadows of mordor on the ps4 with a controller and this game on PC via keyboard and mouse... they are two very different experiences, but the essence of combat remains the same: you better be on point and bring your A game if you seek a challenge.
these games, today, can be so astonishingly different based simply upon the level of difficulty one chooses to approach them with.  when playing a game on easy, i feel that we tend to be more focused on storyline and graphics, etc.  when playing on higher levels of difficulty it's very easy to focus on how brutal the mechanics are, and how un/rewarding the loot system or levelling progression systems are.
allow me to summarize:  this game is amazing.  having played nearly everything from pong on up, this is my verdict:  one can't simply choose a game today based solely upon it's theme or content.  the bottom line is that you have to ask yourself "what do i truly enjoy"?
if it's gratuitous and wildly reckless violence with incredible graphic detail, then this is definitely a game for you to examine.  additionally, if you enjoy the complexity of near-perfectly-timed combos and strategic real-time positioning, then this also is a game worthy of your consideration.  the levelling system felt rewarding to me, the finishing moves and loot are affordable and significant, and it was a clearly well-thought-out production worth the value of full price, but absolutely a steal at the 5 dollar purchasing price which i acquired it for.
so here's the verdict:  i don't recommend this game because it's violent and disgusting and brutal.  that being said, it's got some touching elements of redemption and honor and justice.  it's just that the good does not outweigh the bad.  in fairness to the developers, it appears that they certainly TRIED to offset those scales... there are certainly more than a couple of memorable moments where it seems as if humanity is creeping into the story line...  but then gore and blood and revenge jump right back into the picture.  again, if this does not bother you, then it really only serves to add to the value of the story and gameplay.
i hope that i have said enough.  basically, you're a big boy/girl.  if you don't mind violence in excess, this is an amazing game because the mechanics and graphics take it to a whole new level.  if you prefer simplicity in your fighting games and don't embrace brutal depictions of human suffering, you might want to try something else.  i'm not complaining at the purchase price, but i wonder if i might not be better off for not having cutting off so many arms of people who opposed my personal viewpoint.
end of the review:
gameplay was amazing, yet violent.  there are many other games out there without violence, but if you don't mind it, this one is AMAZING.  i played it, regardless of my disdain for excessive violence, primarly because the graphics were so brilliant but also because the combat system was so rewarding and fun to master.
do you, boo.  play it or don't, i simply hope that my two cents helped you to make and informed decision.

The game I've been looking for. Reassembly is easy to understand, rough to master, with multiple different ship construction strategies that may or may not work, whether alone or together.
Your objective is to collect resources to upgrade and build your ship(s), eventually providing your ship with a factory block that can spawn a fleet for you. Enemies are generated off of other players' designs, copied through the use of wormholes, keeping you however from ever encountering real players, just AI versions of their fleets.
Pros:
-No frame drops, I've rarely been lowered in video quality throughout my time playing
-Expansive maps, plenty of sectors generated swiftly with new stations to capture and factions to fight
-Comfortable building interface, with useful tools like mirror and copy and paste to make everything much faster to build, putting you in the fight sooner, plus a lot of weapons and tools to make specialized ships like drone swarm spawners, rocket carronades, snipers, etc.
-Nice artstyle. Very minimalistic, but it is still nonetheless fun to watch your ships "reassemble" as the new parts are traced and come to life in the middle of a battle
-No loading screens. Literally none.
-Test feature, which pits your newly made ship against another of the same value to test its strength in a real battle, before you try and fly a space dumpster into a battle and waste time
Cons:
-Slightly repetitive soundtrack. Good music, but it seems to loop a lot. Maybe I'm just playing too much :P
-Instructions and controls must be looked up a couple times to learn how to do everything (ie Toggle hud, commision fleet ships, set child cycles for your fleet's ships, etc)
-My biggest problem: Ship control. Most games like this have the WASD keys stay in a locked position of North, West, South, East. This game, however, orients control around your crosshair, meaning you have to constantly check which way your shape is facing and reorient yourself to fly properly. Very hard to get used to.
All in all, I'm giving it a 8/10. Fantastic game, and I highly recommend it, I would just like to see some new features implemented and that movement control thing given a second option.
Things I want to See Implemented:
-Co-op multiplayer. Allow a friend to join you in your faction and grow alongside you. Perhaps a combining force of an intelligent gunship and bot spawning mother-ship, I thought this would make a fantastic duo.
-New music
-New weapons and hull parts/utillity pieces, some ideas are:
> Repair drone. Accelerates rebuild speed.
> Cloaking system
> Repulsion/Attraction blocks, for pulling in enemies into short range weapons or pushing them away from a long range ship
> Kamikazee drones. Name says it all
> Barrier construction. Some kind of attachment that uses resources to build walls for defense, or maybe even dispense some kind of acid or magma to ward off pursuers.
> Parasite drone. A drone that embeds into the core of a ship and changes its faction, rebuilding it and putting it in your fleet, maybe even copying the schematic into your inventory
So those are my ideas and reviews of the game, hope it helped and you agree!

If you're a sucker for design-it-and-fail kind of games (like I am), then this game will be the crack to your addiction. The simplistic parts that you get to design your ship with is all you need to create the coolest looking space-ships this side of the galaxy. It's not as simple as "plug the device on and go", you need to build your ship CORRECTLY or it won't maneuver through space! Don't have enough retro-thrusters? You better hope you can back off the enemy fast enough by turning (and not dying from losing your back end). Didn't think you needed thrusters to turn? Guess you're going in one direction infinitely. It's a constant failure zone, and I just LOVE IT!
It's a very grindy game, so if you don't like grinding, I would certainly stay away. And the sandbox mode isn't very intuitive either. I tried to build something in the constructor (in the sandbox mode), and I didn't even get things to build with. Don't get fooled with sandbox mode, it isn't a free build-any-ship-for-free mode @.@ If you don't mind grinding as you play different factions (have to unlock them), then you'll find HOURS upon HOURS trying new designs and seeing if they stack up with the best.
This game is even better!  Again the game is grindy, but the different factions (without mods) force you to build your ships in different patterns. Have a good design for faction 1 (Terrans)? You're not using it on Faction 4 because there are no long-triangle blocks! The only downside with ship-building, is when you test your ship against others' you need to fight these really cheap min-maxed ships that do nothing but fly backwards when your ship catches up with every default ship in the game; actually it's the CPU attacking the other ships, but it's still cheap tactics that win.
Also, the sandbox mode isn't as convoluted as I first thought. I can create any ship I want with the right commands, and even see the default ship palettes for each faction. Unfortunately this isn't explained very well and you need a tutorial outside of the game to understand which commands do what (and that Faction 1 is actually Faction 8 for example). You can still build any ship you want in your save game, but the sandbox is very misleading (not much of a sandbox :/ More of a programmer's blank sheet of paper). I'm still getting my money's worth out of the game; Time to conquer the galaxy!

Counter-Strike Nexon: Zombies is a MMO reinterpretation of the old but gold original Counter-Strike with many game modes for you to try.
Counter-Strike Nexon: Zombies (CSN:Z for short) is a readaptation of the old acclaimed original Counter-Strike (mostly known as CS 1.6) with some MMO elements put into it.
It's like Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, but for a different targer audience. Same as CS:GO, CSN:Z also has an inventory section where you manage your items, a rank system and basically all CS:GO has, though designed inside CS's Goldsource engine with a zombie sidestory attached to it.
I've always being a fan of the original CS and its mods (same goes for Half-life too), so this game brings me a lot of nostalgia. You'll find many kinds of game modes to play, some better than others in my opinion (basically, for instance, because some modes lack maps).
Community is like any other MMO nowadays: some people are nice and others are complete douches, that's the regular stuff and its none different here.
Because it's a Goldsource game, it's not safe from its glitches. Often you'll find yourself within a glitch effect.
Its MMO standards added to this game microtransactions to keep up with it's glory. Though, of course, who is willing to expend money on it has some advantage, those who preffer to stay free-to-play can get access to premium weaponry through mileage decoders that are given to the player for free after each hour of gameplay, with a cap of three per day. So, with some luck, you can acquire very high level weaponry without having to put cash into this game, if that's your wish.
Sometimes you may think that some weapons makes the game unbalanced (yep, I'm talking about the AK-47 Paladin and M4A1 Dark Knight). Even if they really are a bit overpowered in comparision with other weapons, I don't think that's game breaking. Not that many people put their hands on them and, with teamwork, zombies can take down people wielding them. Problem is, however, that zombies team almost never play as a team, so that gives the feeling that the Paladin or Dark Knight are game-breaking, but it's actually because you're pretty much trying to take them out on your on.
I think if you're a fan of modded CS gameplay fun and considering that this game is free, it's worth a shot. At the very least, you will not waste any money.

If you're looking for a turn-based strategy game with more depth than Civilization, but without the learning cliff of Paradox strategy games, look no further than Endless Legend. Well worth a look for fans of turn-based strategy.
This was the type of game that I found myself playing at 2 in the morning without noticing that I've wasted the night wanting to go to the next turn.

By far one of the best turn based strategy games I've played in a long while. Lately we are seeing a lot of the old classics fade to the backround (compare this to the public assumed heavyweight champion Civilization) while newcomers continue to not only show some excellent ways in how to enhance the formula, but in some cases surpass and even show those devs "Hey, this is the game you should have created." Such is the case with Endless Legend. Amplitude Studios stacked the deck with beautiful and artistic graphics, easy to understand UI, storytelling (via quests), variable ways to win & gave the players what Expansions are supposed to be. Not just extra hours of content, but creative ways to evolve the core game with pre-established systems that were already capable (Subterfuge, Winter, Sea). I can only insist to try the game, like it and get all the expansions or introduce them one by one while you try the new mechanics out piece by piece because the devs clearly put thought into each one.
That isn't to say Endless Legend is 100% original in it's mechanics. Rather it draws inspiration of things that have worked in the past and successfully blends things together in one solid game. Some can argue there are some strategies that overpower others (war? lol) or have unfair advantages (Drakken political power) but honestly that's more a reason to evolve your strategy when facing these odds. Should you focus military early to take out your aggressive neighbor? Should you join the political scheme and rise with the Drakken or maybe you should scheme to betray them later because you yourself think a victory by war is the only way.
Art/Music/Writing:
Again the artwork is beautiful. The music has a wide range and is equally pleasant to listen to as the game carries on into turn 60 and beyond. The writing for the quests makes the world feel alive with history, of which there is the world quests, quests specific to each race and lesser faction quests. A few typos still exist but nothing that could possibly ruin the gameplay.
Races:
The varied races (of the 9 at this time with all expansions) have a way to them that is refreshing from the usual 1000 nations to choose from that have little to no difference between them. The game tells you their preferred win style when you choose a race but that doesn't mean that is the only way for them. I've been a warmonger with the Drakken who are easily the best with the political scheme. Some races are better at sea while others excel with spies. To my knowledge this game can suit any playstyle.
-I mentioned the lesser factions earlier and just want to say I love that they're not just there as fodder. Incorporating them into your empire has static effects that stack based on how many of the lesser faction camps you have control of. Such as increased movement on the map, initiative, industry (for building)
Heroes:
Aside from your starting hero you can research a tech to open up the market and employ more. Some are better suited for city management and others to keep in charge of an army. You'll learn which ones are better or just check out some tips from others when you want to refine your skills. However you do it, there is a wide range of heroes to choose from and the game refreshes these as time goes on. These heroes level up and at such time you can choose to put points into abilities that enhance combat, city management and even some that enhance their ability with subterfuge. Personally I think they could expand more on making heroes more individual but as it is, it works well.
Units:
Every race has strengths and the game never puts you in a jam you can't counter. That warmongering neighbor of yours building a bunch of Mounted units? Edit your own to have the Cavalry Slayer ability and send them packing.
-Equipment: Speaking of editing your units for the better, this game doesn't over do the "Edit your unit" menu like a few other games I've played. You got a weapon slot, a few armor slots and finally a few accessory slots. Heroes also get these of course. When you edit a unit you can also rename it and make another of the same type with a different layout. Like having a budget army (Fodder! YAY!) and the elite army (DIE DIE DIE DIE DIE!!!!) that consumes the Strategic Resources in the game.
Difficulty:
Based entirely on you. Set it 1 on 1. Throw 8 factions onto the map for a battle royale. Adjust the difficulty of the map itself. Want an island world? Go for it. Don't like a specific win condition? Turn it off. Want winter to last forever? Turn it to Harsh.
Anyhow, lovely game. Good fun. If I convinced a single person to play it, great! Hope you enjoy it as much as I do.

This game is an excellent addition to the 4x genre. It is innovative and extremely well-polished. Ever since it came out, and with every DLC, I haven't had any bugs or issues. While in many 4x games races feel very similar, in Endless Legend, each race feels unique and distinct with significant strengths, weaknesses, and unit types that change how you play. Diplomacy is more predictable than it is in other 4x games, and while a resource-based diplomacy is a bit prohibitive at times, it makes diplomacy feel more like a wothwhile investment because you know what you're getting for that investment, and what you can and can't afford to do.
Combat is handled by isolating a portion of the map around your army, and using that as the field for a tactical turn-based combat. The elevation changes, forests, cities, and oceans on the map become important features in combat. In this combat you don't control your troops directly, but instead give them general orders that they will do their best to uphold as a turn plays out. This system poses a bit of a learning curve to understand exactly what each command results in, but makes combat a bit more streamlined.
Science is not a single techtree, but a series of tiers. You can research any tech in any tier available to you, but you often don't research every tech in a given tier. This results in your choices of research more meaningful than in a game like the Civ series where you wind up having the same techs as everyone else eventually.
Overall, in Endless Legend, it feels like you have a lot of options when it comes to playing the game, and it feels like the descisions you make are important, impactful decisions. This is a welcome addition to a genre where games can really start to feel like they may as well run themselves.

Oh I do love it when Devs take a great concept and simplify it, just to prove a point.
As in this case: Awesomenauts. I mean look at it... It's League Of Legends In 2D, isn't it?
It's a money maker, sure, but there's room for free-2-players too, and I, for one, approve of that.
Granted the hardcore gamers can wipe the floor with us, I've no doubt, but who cares? - I mean, play it - You'll get it. It's easy to understand, there's no REAL backstory you need to familiarize yo'self with, and best of all, once you get into it, it's good ol' fashioned, clean fun!
There's no real downside to botmatching your way to feeling good on a sickday or a slow weekend. And if you're feeling ballsy, you can throw down with players in ranked matches? - And, what best of all, some Dev did something I VERY MUCH APPROVE OF, probably just to prove a point... - You can buy your way to all the nice stuff, sure. You can be the most hardcore gamer on the server but luck can still step on your toes and Teamwork can, and will, trumph individual skill and pre-purchased powerups.
I, myself, spent 10+ matches winning, winning, winning and doing some more winning, thinking... "Ok, I'm not that good... Is this game just that easy?" - Hell to the no! - I experimented with the different characters and found one I liked playing and I STILL got owned, along with two other, (I thought) VERY skilled players. Why? The other team worked together. That's it. So there...
So the game... Well: The music, the graphics, the controls, all of that is just fine, but it's the culmination of it all that really matters! - The FUN! It's simple to master, easy to grasp, hard to be consistently good at and to let go of. Its a nice and easy little game with lots and lots of content you don't really need or have to have to have fun with the game... - Its just there if you want it.
All that being said, there is  a big FAT Con that I almost didn't mention. And for once, it ain't even the Dev's fault. It's just a little warning...  It's the players (Don't crucify me guys, I'm just being honest here,) or, to be more fair and precise: It's the fellows who like to spam "creative" things in the chat. Once upon a time, years back, when I was playing other games where there were chats (MMORPGS and what-have-yous) a world, trade, community or whatever-chat was a fun, friendly and/or practical place to be. These days, though, it's more of a competion of who knows the most code-words for offensive terms. I don't really mind it, but I don't really care to participate in it anymore, either. I don't really care how many ways there are to incorporate "creative web-slang" and I don't care to learn. I'll stick to playing the game and ignoring any idiots spamming the chat. I'm not a puritan and I don't really care that you have or use the right to free speech, but let's be honest. I neither have to, nor want to listen to you if and when you do.
Right then, now that the rant is outta the way, I'll just say to the Devs: Good Game. Lots of Fun. Could use More Content. Keep at it.

So basically you play as red-hating blue guys who want to eliminate the lame red guys while fighting on rooftops because the breeze is nicer than indoors. Champions Online: Free For All is a MMO based around a city which is full of super heroes (and villains). There are several large maps you can switch between as you level up which keeps things fresh and interesting.

The community itself is still generally thriving and while there aren't as many people playing as there have been in the past, the numbers are fairly steady and will probably grow as it's almost summer and lots of extra spare time will be available. Now would be a good time to join.

9/10

- Not a TON of items to build with, though he'll probably add more over time.

Arcade-style graphics.
Design your own ships.  The part shapes are just occasionally odd enough that getting things to line up becomes part of the fun.
Test designs by letting them autopilot versus random other designs.  Center of gravity and healing rate are important.  Some ships are practically a huge gun with a seat and thrusters strapped onto it!
I spent hours not even playing - just designing a ship and watching it play against other designs in the test phase.
Once you are happy with a design (or just want to shoot something yourself) go in and harvest resources where the bad guys are, which also allows building up a fleet to team up against opponents.  Building a fleet is pretty cool - although they are something like a herd of cows...  not too smart and they get stuck in the weeds sometimes.  Playing the fleet dynamics is a whole game by itself!
The flight is very space-like where you have to oppose thrust to slow down, which makes it feel very swimmy (I think why they say welcome to the tide-pool).  In that regard it feels a little like Spore's bacterial stage, only flying takes much more concentration.
Replay value is sky-high, as optimizing ship designs at all size allowances allows starting over and trying new ideas.
Also, the game feels very different than other games because you have complete control how your ship handles (although once it's damaged and your engines have fallen off it will handle very differently until it heals again over several seconds, relatively fast).  Trying to control a damaged ship reminds me of Robocraft, though this game is much more twitchy.
TLDR:
If I had to pick a favorite game so far in 2015, this might be it.  The gameplay is straightforward.  There are always more things to want to try out, which takes time to get there and try them.  And Space feels alive.  This is more of a tadpole simulator than a space game.

What can you say about Ground Zeroes that hasn't been already said. It's a great introduction to the MSG world, a beautiful open level stealth game that will challenge you and make you ogle Snakes bum.
One of the best things about this game is the replayability, the amount content that you unlock after completing the Ground Zeroes campaign, you'll be at 7% complete, this is really worth the money spent as it will unlock additional missions. I played through all the missions and managed to achieve an "S" rank for all the missions, I got all the tapes, all the patches, and I am still at 95% complete. The only thing left to do is fine tune my gameplay and replay and complete the trials.
The game is set in Cuba, 1975 at a U.S. military base that is operating without oversite from the goverment. Someone wants a place to interrogate POW's that won't fall under Cuban, American, UN law. It's really like what has (is) happening in the world today, minus the Miley Cyrus nipple flashes, although... nevermind.
Playing as Snake you'll crawl and crouch your way through the base, either knocking out the soldiers or killing and hiding the bodies, I would knock them out and then throw them into the sea so that they wouldn't wake up and be a bunch of jerks. I really like the CQC aspect and the animations that Snake does and the animations of the soldiers as they crashed head first into a wall or me slamming their pathetic American asses into ground, yeah that makes me smile.
The graphics are just so beautiful, the dust, rain, and night and day changes are really well done. I played through the extract the classified intel mission and found that I was sneaking through the entire level on my stomach, crawling through the grass and quietly sneak past the guards and cameras, just like I do at work. Up close the weeds show some low resoluton but that's ok.
The Stealth aspect is so well done that I wished that more designers would take clues on how to do stealth right. Sneaking around the large open level was an absolute blast. Knowing that I held some dumb♥♥♥♥♥American soldier's life in my hand made me feel like a god, or at least a high powered super soldier. The animations are very well done, for Snake and the soldiers. In the day light, you can really see what the soldiers look like, nice textures and sound make it very immersive.
As I wait for payday to buy The Phantom Pain, Ground Zeroes is keeping me busy. Collecting all the agents, and prisoners so that I can import them into TPP when I get it. Play it, be Snake.

this is a stratagy game with a twist. you begin on the legendary world of aurgia a world that once was home to the long lost endless race that conquered the starts. you start the game a long time after the fall of the endless in charge of one of the many factions that have survived the wilds.
The world itself is sectioned into regions with each regon housing a minor race that can be pacified. as the master of your own faction you can build cities (one per region) to claim the regions and expand your empire. each faction has a distinctive game play style that changes how you play the game completely resulting in a game with a lot of replayability value.
to add a new level to the game augria is dying and so it has harsh winters. as the game progresses the winters get longer and cause harsh penalties on all factions. in short this is a fun game that can be enjoyed again and again

To make a long story short, Evoland is a hands-down thumbs-up fingers-crossed interactive documentary about the early history of the action adventure game genre. The game intentionally starts out lame and progressively improves in gameplay and graphics the further you press on, giving players a history of how action adventure started from side-scrollers to top-down hack-and-slash to turn-based action to puzzler to tactical turn-based combat to horde hack-and-slash.
Veteran gamers might not get much more than a nostalgia-induced parody, but this is a good introduction for kids to the world of retro action adventure games.

I have played Evoland from start to finish for a few hours that I really enjoyed. The game is a simple RPG game which, through its story takes the player through various fazes of gaming history from black and white and 2d and no sound to beautiful 3d with textures, music and effects and all sorts of nice little add-ons like inventories that you collect.  I really liked the idea of the changing of the gaming genre which kept me up one night thinking about it. I also really liked how a chest which for me in an RPG used to mean a new item here was a new texture or camera angle, or all sorts of interface improvements. Loved it. I loved the the story, fun tone, the way the game transformed and developed and I really enjoyd this game which really got me hooked from the start to the finish. Thank you developers. Waiting for Evoland 2 :). I really, really loved and love this game. :).

Save points are too far between - I understand that the idea is to progress through the history of console RPGs, but mimicing one of the most panned and unnecessary characteristics seems rather sadistic on the part of the developer.  It's just poor design to stump you on a boss battle and then make you jump through hoops just to get back to that battle.  That exact combination is why I'm moving on to another game, and the extent of my remaining use of this game will be to run it at the title screen while I watch TV to collect the cards (if and only if I am ineligible for a refund).

Feeling nostalgic? This new game feels like an old friend as it walks through different stages of game technology and progresses as you move through the story. Graphically, some areas maintain a SNES-like appearance, while others move into textured, but cartoonish 3D. The overall story is simple, though it resembles a Legend of Zelda game, to which Evoland pays homage. It's doesn't take long to push through the entire game, and even though it has some tricky sections, it's not frustratingly difficult. Achievements are achievable, and some might have you scratching your head without the aid of a walkthrough. There are multiple types of battles (turn-based and real time.) Boss battles are a mix of skill and strategy, and the game plays easily on a laptop keyboard. If you're looking for a fun, but new walk through memory lane, Evoland is woth a download.
Excelent tribute to the early gaming history! Even more fun if you are familiar with Zelda and Final Fantasy!

To give it a go, I received this game when it still was in beta.
Despite what other reviews told me until now, I do have to agree that this is not battlefield, CoD or one of the other high-end video games etc. However, what this game does offer is a great adventure throught the life of students just like you and me.
This game shows a clear view on how school-life looks like and what it actually is to be a student again. Besides, I've played the game for hours and hours and to be honest the bugs have been fixed for like 80% compared to the first time I tested this game. There are indeed some issues leftover, and knowing the developer and his test-team I can be sure these will also be fixed as soon as possible. Besides, I've checked the graphics of this game and as I said one cannot compare this to the high-end games on the market simply because those games have a way higher budget and a way higher teamperformance. But seen the circumstances this game scored a clear 10 for Graphics on my gradinglist and therefore I have to admit i was surprised how good the game looks, how clear the game runs and how smooth it works on every device!
To wrap thing up,
This game indeed needs a little bit more bug fixing, I do understand making these things is hard since I do it myself too. All in all the game looks gorgeous and has a clear goal. This simulator will give you the exact satisfying results you expect. It gave me an amazing view of what it looks like to be a student and above all this game was capable of entertaining someone like me for hours. I really enjoyed testing/playing this game and I hope you continue creating this kind of good stuff.

It's evening, and a group of hostiles chase me guns blazing up into one of the wooden guard towers. I choose to prone on the wooden floor which my enemies somehow fail to penetrate even after 30 seconds of constant firing.
