As it is custom with big licenses, Star Wars had many video games offsprings, and amongst them, KotOR still stands out.
It captures well the atmosphere of the universe and, even if the plot is not that deep (while there is a moral dilemma related to the Force, a big and nicely crafted one, most of the game is like a treasure chase to find something long forgotten).
The gameplay is solid, with a D&D-like system for the stats and combat, dialogues are mostly well written, som characters are pure platinum (HK-47, you exquisite sociopath assassin droïd !), there are loads of fun...
But while I adore this game and would strongly recommend it for any Star Wars fan, I think it a bit too much lauded, moreso when KotOR II did everything better.
So if you are tempted, I'd warn you about some real weaknesses of the game ; how much they weigh in the balance is up to you.
- On the technical domain, it shows its age. Nothing horrid but be prepared for some atrocious eyeballs and clothes (like someone just sprayed paint on a mannequin), aliens of a same species looking all the same except for some color swap, and a lot, lot of clones. Be prepared to see Bob the human many a time.
- The level cap is low (20, combining your pre-jedi class and your jedi-class) meaning that you'll probably reach it way before the final... And it can be frustratring to keep slaughtering enemies in such a gain, when you don't gain anything anymore out of it.
- Related to that, the game is too easy. The beginning, pre-Jedi, can be a little tricky at times, but after Taris you will seldom face tough encounters. HK-47 is a beast in combat and a trio of Jedis is quite formidable too. And unfortunately, the final boss is pathetic.
- The game can be at times a little... Goofy. Sometimes it's because of the dialogues (the "impossiiiiiiiible" from the trial on the aquatic planet is magical), sometimes because of the karma system (light side/ dark side). It, well, lacks of subtelty. Chase off kids tormenting a Ithorian, give him a medkit ? Light side points. Slaughter Tuskens ? Dark side points. Quite manichean.
Worse : near the end, you can make a decision cleaning off the slab, towards dark or light side, don't mind that you acted on the polar opposite all along.
- Carth whines so much you might want to impale him with a lightsaber.
All in all it shouldn't deter you, but my humble feeling is that it's quite enough to makes KoTOr fall from a position of excellence. Still, even factoring all this, it's worth playing it, would it be only to be prepared for KoTOr II !

If you have the original Frozen Synapse, don't get this game unless you're willing to drop $25 on a nice graphics. I got this in a bundle, so I pretty much bypassed the  $25 price tag.
On to the game itself, it plays just like the original game. You issue orders to your dudes, such as run here, look in the direction as you walk, crouch, etc. Then you press play and watch your plan act out as your opponent(AI or player) acts out their pre-made plan at the same time. Team with the last man standing wins.
Unlike most people, I like the new graphics, and also unlike them I liked the keyboard controls, and actually prefer it over the original game. The controller support is perfect, with all the right mapping to make the experience smooth. There's more feedback on what the various map, game mode, and team setup do, and easier to mess around with. There's plenty of interesting pre-made maps and scenarios to screw with, plus the map generator and campaign.
So the game is definitely fun, with nice controls and graphics, BUT it's a reskin of the original but with more polish. I would not get this if you don't think what I mentioned above is worth it. Even if you do want this, I suggest waiting for a price drop/sale.

A lot of people seem to have forgotten how to feel nostalgia for the sake of itself.
Evoland is an absolute steal at this price (currently $2.49 at the time of this review).
Evoland does a remarkable job of illustrating, in both sound and design, as well as function, the evolution of gaming from its inception on upwards. The only thing it does not illustrate is the brief period of time when graphics weren't even a thing, but very few of us would remember that era anyways, as it didn't last long.
From the smallest of things as only moving in one direction, to transitioning to 8bit, 16bit, 32bit, 3D, etc graphics and beyond, it's like getting a history lesson in the most amusing way possible.
The gameplay itself is reminiscent of Zelda, Final Fantasy, even a hint of CCG thrown in (there's a full-fledged miniature card game within the game itself once you reach a certain town). There are hidden items to find along the way, and the combat system changes with time as well. There are also a lot of interesting puzzles.
I wouldn't call this game something you'll enjoy if you're looking for a huge challenge, or something incredibly fast paced or modern. This game was so obviously primarily designed to harken to days of old, so whether you're a younger individual who just wants to know or see what life was like while you were a toddler or not even born yet, or a seasoned game veteran looking for a nostalgia kick, this will be for you guys.
And come on, who the ♥♥♥♥ complains about a $2.49 game?! I bought it back when it was $4.99 and the only reason I don't have more hours into it is because I have a backlog of waayyyyyy too many games to play (see Steam account, 90%+ of those aren't played fully, hah, but they are still worth every penny!).

One-line review: Space Beast is a fantastic indie game that lets you experience what it is to be a Space Marine in Aliens. It's not a walk in the park! :)
-----
In an age of flabby, overproduced AAA titles, Space Beast Terror Fright is a perfect fusion of focused game design, moody atmospherics, palpable tension and heart-stopping jump scares. When SBTF popped up in my game recommendations, its quirky title caught my eye. But the gameplay videos looked cool as hell. After watching a couple Let's Plays on YouTube, I was sold.
Since then I've put over 50 hours in this game. I've also gotten a few friends to buy it, and it's been a blast. I'm definitely going to be coaxing more of my friends and coworkers to take the plunge.
I have a library of 100+ Steam games and for the last couple of weeks SBTF has been my favorite gaming experience, especially when played with friends online.
EDIT: I've now played this game for about 160 hours and can confirm it is still holding my interest. I mostly play it with friends at lunch or after work, and it's so rewarding to work as a tightly-knit team and survive a grueling level. There's something oddly intimate about knowing your teammates so well you know what each of you will do when entering a new room, without saying a word. Makes me grasp (in some small way) the comraderie which develops in combat between soldiers. You think I'm being melodramatic? Try the game yourself, you'll see. This game is the most fun I've had in years, especially with friends.
Every time I introduce a new player to this game they always say something like "this is the best Aliens game ever!" It really is that good.

(Written after playing the release version 1.02 for 20 hours or so).
For me, a good 4x Fantasy-based game has always been something of a Holy Grail. I was hooked by "Masters of Magic" and this sort of game is my favorite. Of all of the countless fantasy games I've tried, this one is among the best. Be forewarned, I'm biased because I've looked for this type of game for so long, but I'll try to give it a thoughtful review.
The Good:
-Strategically, the game gives you a hard time. The AI takes a dim view of your success, and likes to declare war when you look weak or dangerous. It feels right at that level.
-Many game design choices were made correctly. I love the tactical combat system with fungible starting spots (and with the option to skip tactical and instantly resolve a dull fight). The tactical map isn't just a window-dressing either. Both the tactical and strategic maps are detailed, and the units interact in interesting ways. Terrain matters, and even the layout of the province you're fighting over is a factor. All of this a great source of variety and fun.
-Lots of Fantasy fiddly-bits are everywhere. The world does feel alive, not just like some kind of random number generator gone mad. Nations have unique provinces--all of them do. This is excellent for immersion and a sense of exploration.
-Many key elements on the strategic level resemble games like Europa Universalis. It feels like a good version of that kind of game--less number crunching and more immersive.
-There are many settings, which I haven't explored all of, to set up the game you want to have. That's great design right there.
-The dev(s) seem to be into fixing things. That's always needed when a new game is launched, and that's happening here.
The So-So:
-The price isn't rock-bottom, and the game itself is a work in progress. It's very playable, and I've only had it crash once in 20+ hours of play. But still, this is an unpolished gem.
-The game doesn't explain itself very well. This was an issue for me, and even after seeking out wiki-type info, I was left with gaps. For example, I believed for my first few days of play that the unit production queue was a QUEUE, building one unit at a time. This is not the case. I eventually figured out the game builds all the units in the queue at the same time.
-The tutorial, as the brits say "is dodgy" and actually seems to evade comprehension. After a point is made, you are forced to click "next" or "Okay" literally dozens of times to get it to  g
The Grim:
-The interface is clearly unfinished. It works--barely--but there are plenty of problems. Just try to find out how you cancel a trade deal with another nation... or what will happen if you do.
-Lots of things are printed with tiny print, or with incomprehensible miniscule Icons. This reminds me of the early hearts of Iron games--but it's worse here.
-There are a number of mouse-focus bugs. For example, you can run your mouse over various provinces and the game will give you an informatational card which talks about that particular item
-There are highly exploitable imbalances in the game at the tactical level. For example, missile units do more damage to units that are fresh--too much damage. Skirmish units can rip up big lumbering standards in melee.
In short, the game has great feel, a good heart, and it's fun to play. There are distractions and errors everywhere,e however, and it's up to you to ignore them.

Awesomenauts is a very fun and addicting game that has it's pros and cons. Starting with pros, the game is a solid 3v3 experience which can be fun for anyone. The soundtrack in my opinion is amazing and nothing else. The wide selection of heroes results in new things to be learnt everytime you play a new match. A very nice feature is the countdown which tells you the amount of time you have before the game starts. The community is pretty good and rarely do I see offensive things being said. Now for the cons. My main problem with the game is the amount of times that it lags while I am playing which results in the experience being ruined and a gamer becoming very upset. There should also be other ways to obtain skins rather than just ALWAYS paying. At least maybe 10 that you can earn for performing certain tasks. This game is... weird. I am recommending it based on the great graphics and art, and on the fact that I really like the theme of Ancient Rome - that said, Ryse: Son of Rome is very far from being historically accurate. And I really mean it.
The combat, not being out of this world, is interesting enough to keep you going. I particularly enjoyed the possibility of being part of an attacking testudo, protecting my unit from missiles and throwing pila. As far as the combat itself, I confess that I was delighted with the graphs and execution animations. Getting to know the combat system will take you some time, but once you get the hold of it, it's easy enough (I played normal difficulty, I believe it's called Soldier).
The storyline is a cliché about revenge. Some pathos involved made me take pity on a few characters, and I liked a few details, but the story itself is somewhat bland.
The weird part of the game lies where you mix storyline and History: strange stuff happens. I don't want to leave any spoilers here, but imagine the following: you have a peaceful meeting with a barbarian that doesn't go well, and all of a sudden the Roman fort is being sieged by thousands and thousands of barbarians that weren't there in the first place. Or imagine that Rome is attacked by barbarians, which just invade the city without any warning or siege.
I mean, at times it feels like whoever put the plot together was a child telling make-believe stories. I'm fine when a game attempts to make an alternative historical approach, but less when the pieces of the puzzle just don't fit.
At this point, I didn't play multiplayer, but I am feeling tempted to try it.
All in all, recommended with a good pinch of salt.

As it is custom with big licenses, Star Wars had many video games offsprings, and amongst them, KotOR still stands out.
It captures well the atmosphere of the universe and, even if the plot is not that deep (while there is a moral dilemma related to the Force, a big and nicely crafted one, most of the game is like a treasure chase to find something long forgotten).
The gameplay is solid, with a D&D-like system for the stats and combat, dialogues are mostly well written, som characters are pure platinum (HK-47, you exquisite sociopath assassin droïd !), there are loads of fun...
But while I adore this game and would strongly recommend it for any Star Wars fan, I think it a bit too much lauded, moreso when KotOR II did everything better.
So if you are tempted, I'd warn you about some real weaknesses of the game ; how much they weigh in the balance is up to you.
- On the technical domain, it shows its age. Nothing horrid but be prepared for some atrocious eyeballs and clothes (like someone just sprayed paint on a mannequin), aliens of a same species looking all the same except for some color swap, and a lot, lot of clones. Be prepared to see Bob the human many a time.
- The level cap is low (20, combining your pre-jedi class and your jedi-class) meaning that you'll probably reach it way before the final... And it can be frustratring to keep slaughtering enemies in such a gain, when you don't gain anything anymore out of it.
- Related to that, the game is too easy. The beginning, pre-Jedi, can be a little tricky at times, but after Taris you will seldom face tough encounters. HK-47 is a beast in combat and a trio of Jedis is quite formidable too. And unfortunately, the final boss is pathetic.
- The game can be at times a little... Goofy. Sometimes it's because of the dialogues (the "impossiiiiiiiible" from the trial on the aquatic planet is magical), sometimes because of the karma system (light side/ dark side). It, well, lacks of subtelty. Chase off kids tormenting a Ithorian, give him a medkit ? Light side points. Slaughter Tuskens ? Dark side points. Quite manichean.
Worse : near the end, you can make a decision cleaning off the slab, towards dark or light side, don't mind that you acted on the polar opposite all along.
- Carth whines so much you might want to impale him with a lightsaber.
All in all it shouldn't deter you, but my humble feeling is that it's quite enough to makes KoTOr fall from a position of excellence. Still, even factoring all this, it's worth playing it, would it be only to be prepared for KoTOr II !

I love this game. Spent hours, no days building and optimizing spaceship designs. This is a designer's game.
Pros:
-The controls are flexable so you can fly however you want, a very welcome feature in these top down 2D games.
-The attention to detail in physics is incredible, e.g. if your ship has no off-axis thrusters, it turns really slowly.
-Open ended - no one strategy to dominate. You can go for speed, armor, shields, range, or build cost. Or you can just be a farmer or a gatherer.
-Multiple races - just when you think you've optimized a ship series for a particular race, you can play a different race with different abilities and different parts!
-Really pretty
-Self-building ships: the trouble with other building games (e.g. StarMade) is that you always have to rebuild your ship after a battle. In this game you don't worry about that, although there are design strategies for having your ship regenerate faster.
-Good combat AI, so you're not frustrated with the AI pilots being idiotic which breaks many other games.
-Ability to customize the build sequence of allied ships and stations
Would like to see:
Fleet vs fleet battles with the asynchronous mulitplayer! There are ways to do this with the sandbox but it's not very accessible.
Better (maybe customizable) combat AI: e.g. turning the ship to hide damaged armor or shields from enemy fire while it regenerates, or maybe being able to specify a preferred range of engagement.
Better non-combat AI: Having AI ships being more exploratory would be nice, otherwise they exhaust their local resources and just end up sitting around.
My dream is to build an agent fleet that can go into someone else's universe, replicate like crazy and be hugely successful, and completely take it over. Muhahahaha.

I really can't recommend this... (TL;DR below)
At first I found the game enjoyable, and I liked the things that set it apart from the glut of RPGMaker games on Steam (specifically, the "Battle Ready" mechanic).  Several hours in, though, the game has become a boring slog that I really can't see myself finishing.  After the initial enjoyment was long gone, I still wanted to complete the game (that's how I roll) and ALSO get the last 2 Achievments.  I literally don't think I'll be able to bring myself to load this one up, ever again...
The other reviews here have really hit on just about every point I could hope to... but I do want to reiterate just a few points, and bring up a few complaints of my own.
1) The writing of this game is just absolutely ABYSSMAL.  In the beginning of the game, it was fine if not inspired, but it becomes abundantly clear they just ran out of steam and had a "let's get this f*ckin thing finished" mindset.  It seems the devs wanted "to make a RPG" -- NOT that they had a story they wanted to tell.
2) The characters are unrelatable at best, and obnoxious at worst.  I'd been playing this game pretty frequently (as my in-game time should demonstrate) up until the last week or so (when it became too much to bare) ... and I *literally* cannot think of but *TWO* of their names aside from Xen herself (Will and Markus -- so inspired!)...
3) There are spelling and grammar errors CONSTANTLY.  I wouldn't go so far as to say that a few small errors here and there would ruin the game or anything (hell, even some of the Square classics had 'em) -- but when it's a constant thing it is a HUGE hurdle to immersion.  The script seems to have never been proofread in the least, and the game itself most likely never legitimately play-tested.  The nature of some of the errors leads me to believe the (text file format) script was run through spellcheck and called good... ("you'll FREE to death"?!)
4) The title screen -- THE FIRST THING PEOPLE SEE WHEN THEY BOOT UP THE GAME -- is so bland and uninspired I can't wrap my head around it.  It's like... a (stolen?) cropped image of a pseudo-Medieval European cityscape, run through a filter, with "Victim of Xen" in plain ol' text in the middle.  This actually didn't occur to me until after I started to realize how totally sh*t the game is.  WHAT DOES THIS TITLE SCREEN HAVE TO DO WITH THE GAME?!  WHY COULD YOU NOT DRAW, *SOME* SORT OF SIMPLISTIC LOGO OR INCLUDE *SOMETHING* WITH *ANY* RELEVANCE TO THE GAME?!  Oh, I know why... because the devs DID NOT CARE about this game at all.  Again... "get this f*ckin thing done" mindset is my only answer.
5) The world map is tiny, cluttered, and cliche... and does not loop around on itself.  Literally, you get to the edges of the world map and there are invisible walls.  There is no in-game lore explaining any of this, either.
6) And, really, there is just NO IN-GAME LORE OR WORLD-BUILDING *AT ALL*.   If the devs don't care, how could expect the players to?
I could go on and on, about how the art assets are stolen, most likely the music as well... and how there are MUCH better games on Steam in somewhat similar mold that are FREE... but all of that has been said, and I'd just never finish!
So yeah... great job Smolders... you "made a RPG"... which seems to have been your ONLY goal with this project.  Thankfully these devs have not released anything since... and God willing they WON'T.
TL;DR: Go download "Eternal Senia" instead if you want a game that uses generic RPGMaker tiles and scavenged art assets.  What's the difference, you ask?  Well.. that game is FREE... and HAS A STORY TO TELL... and IT IS FUN.  FUN is something the developers of "VOX" seem to have *entirely* glossed over on their bullet-pointed "Things To Include In The Game" list.

OTHAFA is a kinetic novel (no choices) with many appealing factors which led me to recommending it. First of all, props to WarGirl Games to creating such a well polished game for their first title. When I saw OTHAFA I was immediately intrigued by the peculiar visuals and made a guess that this will not be your common visual novel on steam with sexual themes plastered all over the place (not saying that's automatically bad).
The beginning of the novel captured my attention with Mai's playful antics and it just gets better from there. There are many visual novels I've read where the humor seems forced or the dialogue between the characters feel awkward. Fortunately OTHAFA keeps those moments to a minimum and brings you a well written story which seeks to provoke certain emotions from its readers. It did damn good job in doing that.
The setting is unique for a visual novel, and the author takes advantage of that by weaving it into the characters' backgrounds providing explanations for the characters' actions and feelings. The UI is well made as it does not distract you when you're reading the text. The black bars blended into the background also provide a theater like experience. Another particularly strong point is the music which is well composed and blends well with the intentions of the scenes and artworks.
The only downside is that I feel OTHAFA is fairly short for its asking price, but I also feel the strength of the other parts of the game make up for this loss. If your looking for something different and worth your time, pick this up and definitely pick it up when it's on sale.

Endless Legend is my favorit 4X game beside the Civ series. It's biggest strength is it's variety: It has lots of different ressources, anomalies, biomes and what not. The playable races have distinctive mechanics, each plays a totally different way. You can annex many different minor races to gain special units and boni. Units are costumizable and upgradable in the likes of a RPG equipment system, so they can fulfill different roles. There are heros (with skilltrees and loadout) that can manage your settlements or lead an army. The technology progression is non-linear. There's a plethora of quests that can be triggered and give you goals beyond simple building and conquering. Seasons play a big role as the planet tumbles into an ice age as the game proceedes. Last but not least this game is absolutely beautiful, probalby the best art direction in any 4X game.
Now quickly for some quasi contras: The combat system is unusual and a little weird; not  bad, but it takes some time to get used to it. If you expand a lot the settlement management can become somewhat of a chore, but that's not unique in this genre... and if you hate that, the game features a race that is limited to it's starting settlement.
The base game has already a good amount of content, but the following is added via payed DLC:
- three unique and interesting playable races
- an espionage system
- a second technology system that depends on a ressource that can only be harvested in the winter season
- marine warfare
- epic units
- more quests and loadout

Endless Legend (and Endless Space) are essentially our go-to games for multiplayer. Tactical, fun, and with a ton of replayability - it ticks all the boxes for us.
Both the graphical style and music are amazing, and the map is simply beautiful in both summer and winter transitions. Each race is so thematically different there really is a style of play for everyone. Also, when you get bored of the standard races, you can go ahead and create your own custom race too, albeit with the main traits of the existing factions. Still, the fact this is even an option is great.
The only fly in an otherwise perfect ointment is that occasionally the game goes a bit squiffy (technical term) when hosting a previous multiplayer save and won't load in at the start without one of us bombing out, so we have to either roll back to a previous autosave or just start again. To be honest it's not the end of the world for us if it happens, as early game is where a lot of the fun resides anyway, and if you got boned on the starting location in the previous game you can hopefully get something nicer from the RNG gods this time round! Note that I don't get this issue in single player at all, so that experience has been pretty bug free for me at least.
All in all great game, and if you can get it in a sale then even better. So far I have bought all the main DLCs as soon as they are released for this game as I want to support the devs, and in truth there's not many games I will do that for.

That aside, the game has some decent ideas that are interesting (the combat system), but it's neither in-depth enough or simple enough in my opinion. Birthright: The Gorgon's Alliance which was released in 1997, still runs on every computer I have like a charm and is far better in every respect (diplomacy, combat system, unique factions, magic, paths to victory, interesting if fewer unit types, magic equipment, heroes, etc). Do you love it when a plan comes together? If so Frozen Synapse Prime is the game you want to try.
Image a world where you command mindless soldiers that do -Exactly- what you tell them to do.
Walk forward to a doorway, quickly sweep in front of it, now check behind you to make sure no one is there, quickly step out the door, duck behind this cover and keep moving.
Forget to check somewhere or plan for something, a detail left unaccounted for, that troop might die. A lot of Frozen Synapse is just spent in between turns going over and over that single turns plan, trying to account for every possible scenario and picking the best one. It sounds tedious and maybe it is to some extent but when you get a full map all quickly and efficiently doing what you told them to do and it works even better than you planned, its an amazing feeling. That feeling of knowing you used your brain and got the best possible outcome because of it is what makes this game good.
Frozen Synapse Prime is a remake, sure, but its done well. Graphics are actually good now compared to the original, SFX, game balancing and a few other changes to make the story a shorter and more enjoyable experience. The first one had gameplay at its heart but several things kept me from really enjoying it. This version, Prime, takes care of those and is the gem that the developers truly intended.

A very generous friend gifted this game to me, and I was interested to try it out because I enjoy tactical turn-based games. I was satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like tactical turn-based games, strategy, and futuristic, sci-fi themes, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are decent - the character models and amount of detail in the levels are average, however, the assets (character models, level design) are extremely repetitive and can get stale quickly. The music and sounds are good and add a relaxing feel to the game, although I muted the music in favor of my own after half an hour. The story is good, but nothing special - you act as a member of a rebel organization trying to break the hierarchy of power and oppression in a futuristic world. There is a lot of optional lore you can go through in the form of character dialogues.
The controls are slightly complex and can take a bit of getting used to if you are not experienced with tactical turn-based games. There is a set of tutorial missions that will help you get a feel for the gameplay. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with this genre. Characters die with one hit, so micromanaging every single step and action is critical to success (ex: check every corner and angle as you move).
Gameplay consists of you planning out moves for each of your units each turn, then executing it once you are ready (this counts as one round). You can experiment with potential enemy movements to help you better plan out your strategies, which is something I thought was interesting. There is no fog of war, so you can always see the entire map, including enemy locations without having to first spot them. In a way, this makes the game more challenging because it can bias you to consider too many possibilities (ex: every possible way an enemy can move), when a fog of war/line-of-sight mechanic helps slow you down and only use intel you actually have.
When you have queued your actions for each of your units, you can "prime" (end turn) to move to the execution phase. Here, it will move all characters, providing you with a slow-motion replay whenever characters shoot each other and/or die. You cannot undo turns, but you can cancel any orders you have queued when you move on to the next round (you will always be prompted if you want to keep your queued actions or clear them). Enemy reinforcements may appear if it is part of the story, however, you will always start with all your units for each level. Sometimes, you may have uncontrollable allies or non-player civilians present.
Units have a circle dial of actions that include, crouch/stand, aim (focus on an area and have faster reaction time), sweep (scan an area during movement), etc. When you command a unit to move, you are able to add waypoints to the route and can even manipulate it as much as you want (ex: you can turn a mostly straight, tight right-turn into a wide, erratic route). You can also add actions to each waypoint you place - this is useful if you want to make your units scan each corner/angle as they move to a flanking position. Compared to other games like Breach & Clear, I felt that Frozen Synapse Prime's action set was a bit easier and user-friendly, however, I personally preferred B&C's. Frozen Synapse is definitely an easier tactical turn-based game to sink into if you are inexperienced with the genre.
There is a story, online, and skirmish mode available to play. The skirmish mode has all units unlocked to use, while the story mode requires progression before you have access to all unit types.
Overall, the game plays very well and is reasonably challenging, and anyone interested in the tactical turn-based genre should check it out. I always try not to mention price in my reviews if I feel it is unnecessary, however, I do think that people should wait for this game to be fairly discounted unless they are dying to play it.
Recommend!

Header: I've played the original for 82 hours here on steam but only played this new version 1.5 hours. So while my review isn't 'well founded' it adresses the issues I see and how this game relates to the original.
Summary: All in all I'd say I recommend the previous title. This is a mobile version of the game, it has bigger buttons than the old mobile version. I'd wager it's better because of that. This title doesn't seem to have all that much life but that's also true for the previous game. In this game they've adressed this to some degree by letting you post game setups on a matchmaking board where people can grab them. Rather than having to be logged in and wait for someone to take your game like the previous game did. Huge plus. But frankly with the way this game is played you don't need a massive player activity. You can go into the previous game, open it in windowed mode, start a "find a game" search. Have it succeed and play your game later. But now there's mostly hardcore players left and newer players might struggle. Either way purchasing this game is a gamble I feel. Hopefully it's better on mobile. But reading some of the reviews on the android version I'm having trouble believing that now. I don't know what happened. But Double eleven seems to be doing this game as opposed to mode7 who made the original. But if awards is something to go on Double Eleven seems to be doing ok. So why does this suck?
Details:
There's problems. The UI is clunky and is definetively a step back from the original. This game crashes. Ridding you of all your careful planning and enrages you to no end. It's clear there was an attempt at expanding to the mobile market here. That's the UI. It's almost entirely focused on being touch screen based, only PC-specific feature i've seen is that we have hotkeys for actions. But these actions are only accessible once you've entred into a menu (command wheel) via X or right click. So they're completely unessesary. The default keybindings are all the keybindings you have, you can't change them. And infuriatingly almost every action needs some form of confirmation step. For instance if you set a wait command you will have to hit E to confirm you're done. Unlike the previous game where you'd place your actions on the timeline directly you're now restricted to 0.1 second increments for your actions. Which may seem like a sensible gameplay change due to the amount of milisecond micromanagement that might very well have gotten you the advantage in the previous game but all it really does is introduce more randomness. You can't plan for very specific things and you might find yourself having to use waypoint tweaking to delay your actions instead. So if it's intentionally restrictive for gameplay purpouses (and not to support mobile better in some way) it's poorly implemented since all it does is change where you delay your actions.
For whatever reason the intro screens presenting the game technologies and the game company are now unskippable. Which is a very big deal for me since it really shaves away those precious seconds I have to jump in - play a turn - jump out. And the game decides that it's absolutely vital you're reminded that there's an autosave feature in the game. Except there really isn't. Because the game ♥♥♥♥ing crashes and erases your turn when you submit it and the only restorable state is before you've done any planning. You'd expect they'd actually have autosaving implemented since they're so keen on advertising it.
Yet dispite all of this it's a great game at its core. I recommend this for a mobile platform. I had performance issues with the previous Frozen Synapse on my phone (not surprising considering how cheap that tablet was) but if this runs better on your phone/tablet than it did on mine then I highly recommend it there. The UI in the old game was pretty much this situation but in reverse, you had the PC interface on the phone. Which wasn't too bad considering. It did take more time I feel and they've definetively increased the size of every element on the screen in this game so I can only imagine it's better. The confirmation steps are also nice on a mobile platform because it's not rare you accidentally touch the screen.
Only gameplay differences I've noticed is that double kill (stalemates, units can 'trade' killing both of them) is enabled by default. You can no longer rapidly switch view direction, something I'm a bit torn about if I like or not but I do see the problems it wishes to alleviate.
The graphical 'improvements' are purely technical. I much prefer the older aesthetic. It didn't need more in that department. It was stylistic and now it feels kinda bland. You don't really like looking at the characters in this game, they're not well made enough that you would like them. The only graphical improvement I really enjoy is the fact that they show LOS now. So you can tell exactly what's been "cleared" in dark mode. Which is nice. But you usually could figure that out just due to the simplicity of the playing field many times along with your ability to draw lines using the aiming markers.
It's regrettable that due to marketing reasons this would have to be a new release becuase that's the best way to catch peoples attention apparently. I really really wish all the focus would have been on extending the gameplay rather than visual trinkets. Sortof like Red did. The shield guys were amazing, open up so many possibilities and interesting gameplay. Along with Upload that really drove it home as an expansion with me. But this game doesn't do anything like that. The best feature of this game is room selection. But even that isn't that important. The old mobile version had something very similar with areas you could draw and have enemies be ignored if they were in them and that was way better because it increases the granularity. Here it becomes a very niche feature rather than something you'd actually consider using.

First off I would just like to say... HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥!!!! And now that I have that out of my system... I just am sooo amazed at HOW much this game has changed (for the better) with the playstyle and game mechanics. The creators at Kojima Productions REALLY outdid their selves and thsi is only a VERY small taste of what's to come in The Phantom Pain. Although the story is very short, I think that the replay value is VERY high for this. Going back ot try to get better ranks, Shave time of your fastest run, find all the little "secrets" (if you wanna call them that), and finding things you didnt find the last time you played. This is an AWESOME introductory to not only the gameplay mechanics but the story for what is driving Big Boss in The Phantom Pain. This picks up I belive aproximately 1 year after the events of Peace Walker and it does an awesome job of picking up RIGHT where that left off. I can just keep saying all the good things about this game. It looks just as beautiful as it plays. the controlls are VERY SMOOTH (Minus the Sniper Rifle when it's zoomed teh whole way in, but that's able to be worked around). I am a VERY long time Metal Gear fan and it's literaly my favorite game SERIES of all time and if this is any inclination of what The Phantom Pain is to bring us... I am VERY hopefull for it (And TPP has also recieved 6 different scores of 10/10 at the time of writing this, which is less than 24 hours to TPP launch). One thing that I have done in preperation before playing this was to go back and play the games that come before this STORY wise. The games release order was NOT, I repeat was NOT, the correct storry order (see below) Anyone new to the series could VERY easily jump into the game and kinda pick up on what's going on. But if you TRULY want to know EVERYTHING, each and every last little detail, I VERY VERY much suggest you play though (Or even watch the multitude of either Lets Play's and Game Movies that are availible online to catch up on the story so far).
I would just suggest someone COMPLETELY new  to teh series play them in CHRONOLOGICAL order instead of release order. Only because some poeple coudl be confused by who Big Boss is and who SOLID Snake is. When I was younger and played the first couple Metal Gear Solid Games back in 1998 and I think it was 2002 for MGS2: Sons of Liberty, I was still kinda confused about some things they talked about that happened in Metal Gear and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (Older games from the MSX from the late 80's). Playing the games in chronological order to the STORY makes more sense to me That way some poeple may not know if they are talking about Big Boss or Solid Snake. If that's the case and you ARE new. I'd play them in the following order, just as I played the first couple getting ready for this game and The Phantom Pain (which at the time of writing this comes out in less than 24 hours)
Metal Gear Solid: 3: Snake Eater
Metal Gear Sold: Peace Walker
Metal Gear Sold 5: Ground Zeroes
Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain
Metal Gear (VERY first game to be released in the series BEFORE the PSX game
Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake
Metal Gear Solid (First game on the PSX from 1998)
Metal Gear Sold 2: Sons of Liberty
Metal Gear Sold 4: Guns of the Patriots
and if you want to count it (I don't)
Metal Gear Rising at the end (follows Raiden after the events of MGS4 and not central to the story, i thought that game was GARBAGE but that was my opintion)

Okay, so I gave this a try and bought this package, and my review might not show the true colour of this game.
Overall, this will be "hit-and-miss" for me. One thing I'm sure, many people say it's hard to get people to join in your game. Well, IT IS NOT, I was worried at first but turns out it's not that hard for someone to join in your game. Just start up your own game, soon or later surelly someone will join you. I did host 3 games and within 5 minutes, all my 3 games are full of people. they constantly connect and disconnect though.
Back to the problem at hand, this game does not really pique my interest. I gave it a try but it just doesn't work for me. As a huge KF 2 fan, I thought this will be "almost" the same but well, it doesn't. the first problem is, who will pop zombie heads using sniper rifles? Sure one or two from a distance is awesome, but not if 700 zombies plunging themselves toward you. Using sniper rifles in those kind of situation is just "dull".
Secondly, if that still interests u, well, the control is damn wonky. I mean, super wonky. if you used to play KF 2, you know the control is smooth and when you stop moving your mouse, the crosshair will stop moving. not the case with this game. it gives you "after movement" even after you stop moving your mouse. maybe that's just the rebellion way of engine, i'm not sure. One thing I know, I don't like it.
Thirdly, how scarce the ammo is. This, might be hit or miss also. Some people love it because it gives extra pressure on the whole situation, but i like a game which will give u too much ammo to slay thousand zombies. the ammo in this game is damn scarce, and since i like to use my sidearms more than that wonky sniper rifle, it stressed me out.
Overall, I really wanted to explore all the storyline, they look nice, the graphic is also commendable, but the wonky engine (aiming), the ammo scarcity, and the idea for the sniper rifle (i tend to use shotgun/SMG/pistols more) really brings this game down, in my opinion.
If those things can be fixed, it will be one damn good alternative to KF2.

Sometimes, two children building spaceships out of LEGO will be in the same room and without adult supervision. They will probably start by dogfighting their plastic creations, but sooner or later they will be taking turns to throw each spaceship into the other. This is the game of those models.
Reassembly's ship creation is simple but pretty intricate in its outcome - you strap 2D weapons, components, inert hull pieces and engines to your command module until you're happy with the result. Ships can be any size, shape, scale (ships can be worth 50 points or 8000), tactical role and degree of effectiveness. You could build the Serenity, a Star Destroyer, a butterfly, a cartoon house with drone launchers in the windows, a space station shaped like Dover Castle or even a sniper rifle with a spinal death weapon for the barrel and a point defence laser for the trigger.
At any time during the customisation you can press the 'test' button, and the AI will fly the ship against available stock designs in a 1v1 arena battle. You can also use the tournament game mode to watch battles between selected designs from any of your save files, any of your friends' save files and any .lua files someone has shared elsewhere on the internet. The devs run occasional open tournaments for ship designs, as do some youtubers.
Single player is utterly devoid of story, it's basically a sandbox galaxy in which various mutually hostile factions hold territory. Kill things and provide R (the production resource) to your factory ships to gain C (research resource). Use C to increase your ship's build limit and unlock new components to play with, or to hire friendly ships to follow you around. Install a factory on your ship to be able to spend R on your custom escort ships, which you can release for more C. Conquer and comsume the galaxy, find a wormhole, travel to the next galaxy and start over. The visuals are pretty nice, the opposing factions are diverse and the fact that your escort ships are ones you yourself have designed makes the campaign feel more exclusive and personal in a 4X-ey sort fo way.
The 7 playable factions generally handle differently, which adds some replayability. Some factions have diamond or rhombus hull pieces, changing their look and design priorities. there's a faction with really cheap shield generators and sniper cannons that can spawn resource-generating space-plants, there's a faction with cheap high-damage weapons and deadly beam drones but very little effective armour, there's a faction whose only direct weapon is a spinal plasma launcher you build by stacking modular components on top of each other. There's one faction that gets nuke launchers and melee spikes.
On the downside though, some of the factions get their playstyle from a lack of versatlity and a poor choice of components. It's pretty demoralising to look at a new faction's full array of hardware and think 'is this it?' Tournaments can be dominated by Faction 4 (the modular plasma cannon one) and by 'spinny ships' (that exploit the AI's ability to lead targets, making them impossible to hit), the music is good but can be intrusive and gets repetitive after the first dozen hours or so. The campaign has almost no ships bigger than 3000P, meaning a player with the cap of 8000P gets to stomp everything with little effort or interesting events. They are small complaints but they do add up sometimes.
To finish, I'll say that Rassembly holds its players' attention not with a scripted or even emergent narrative, or with a great challenge, but with the promise of having something to tinker with. Working out the strengths of each weapon or design, using those extra 200P to give your flagship a little more punch, and reverse-engineering a design you saw on youtube that one time, are what contributes to an addictive and engaging experience that's well worth the £11 it asks for.

Great game, I'd even go as far as to call it superb. Basically you start as a small ship being part of a faction. You go around collecting resources and fighting enemy ships, bringing the resources back to your base or to motherships to be rewarded C (the "money" currency in the game). C is used to upgrade the max points you can spend on your ship, meaning you can create bigger ships with better guns and upgrades. C is also used to buy new weapons and things like shields you can put on your ships. You can recruit other ships also with C but it's a stupid thing to do since you won't really earn any C if you spend it on getting allies.
So you go around the galaxy, restoring your faction's stations and earning C and resources by doing so, destroying ships and their stations to enlarge your territory, but the enemy factions do the same thing to you. They destroy your stations and your hive ships and as you are expanding your territory in one direction, it's easy to lose your grip in another part of the galaxy meaning you have to upgrade all the ships in your faction as you unlock more total points to spend on ships, otherwise they will be too fragile when the enemies attack your base. You personally customize all the ships in your faction any way you want to, mixing functionality with design or just going flat out functionality with ugly ships.
After a while when you've earned a ton of C, upgrading the total points you can spend on ships, you start to build hive ships which can create new ships. You get to choose 4 ships that you can create but you can replace those ships whenever you want to without replacing the already built ships, meaning you can build 4 ships of a certain type then switch them out and build the next 4 while keeping the ones you already built so you can basically have a whole fleet of all the ships in your faction. This is when the game becomes fun for me because now, you're basically free to do whatever you want to. You started as a drone for your faction and now you have become a moving station, building ships from the resources you and the ships you produced gather for you, growing your fleet larger and larger all the time being able to take on more difficult enemy factions. Or you could just stay as a fighter ship if you're into that, collecting resources for your faction and letting it expand on its own.
Lots of fun!

Over the Hills and Far Away is an anime-style visual novel, and, I want to stress it - there is NO gameplay at all, the only thing you can expect from yourself - is to click through the whole story, there is no test to your skill, no interactive elements, nothing. So, if you never saw games of this type - that should warn you. Now, the anime part of the game was very pleasant for me, because I'm not a fan of those sometimes absolutely mad and hilarious scenes, that you see even in the most serious and dark Japanese anime creations - no, this one was far more European, with more detail to the character drawing and realism in storytelling. So, that's a definite plus for me, especially since the game touches a European historical theme of American Independence and British Imperialism, clashing together. Although, this is just a setting - don't expect to actually see any battles or historical events unfolding, or some kind of political context. On the contrary, the game shows us a story of two people, caught in the middle of conflict, and it focuses on their respective lives and interactions. The game has a rather nice soundtrack, well-written dialogues (I would compare the spirit of the story to something like "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn") and nice atmosphere. On the other hand, it is quite short. I felt that there are some missed opportunities here, which I will list in the negative section, but in overall, the game is absolutely worth the money, by all means. My recommendation.
+ Good story
+ Good soundtrack
+ Excellent artwork
+ Excellent narration
+ Atmosphere of a well-written book
+ A good balance between Japanese and European styles
+ A rather close-to-history look into relations between the natives and Europeans
- Characters aren't as complex, as they could have been.
- Not enough artwork, too many similar scenes - even for such a short game.
- A rather short game, especially since there is no gameplay - it should be a little longer.
- Absence of voice acting seems like a rather lost opportunity; I would really enjoy hearing the characters live.

text:
This is my first VN Review and in fact my first Steam Review in all these 11 years as an user.
Over The Hills and Far Away was a short and warm story, lasted only but 2 hours, yet it was warm enough to leave a good memory of it.
I typically avoid Visual Novels, and among my friends even bringing up their names are usually tagged with sexual content or the usual "hundreds of choices and hundreds of ends". This one was different, as I read from other review, as it required only the left click of your mouse button. Hence, it caught my interest.
*Soundtrack*. As I opened this story, I enjoyed the soundtrack immediately (and in fact bought the DLC). It brought me memories from Guild Wars I, a game I used to play a while ago. It gave life, taste and fragrance to what my eyes would muse on, and animate the artwork in front of me. There were no voices, but I could almost hear their tone shifting as the dialogue followed thanks to the flow of the melody. I could tell it was being repeated only but rarely on different scenarios, but not in the very same one. Hence, all the melodies were well reiused.
*Artwork*. You won me on the concept art for the girl. Her eyes, her clothes, her quiet personality and the expressions were unique to her like I've never seen before in any story. Trully, she is a one of a kind to this story and to all I've seen in anime over the past years. I wasn't that enchanted by the protagonist himself, but his story made him more interesting. I trully loved the artwork of the house with the rain outside. And in fact, they were really well executed to tell the story. Rich, vivid, it's the kind of art that gives you a starting point and with enough imagination you can write a movie out of it.
*Story*. Although the VN is left click only without options, the story splits nicely in about I think 3 different dimensions. There is a change of pace between slice of life, past, dream, etc that makes it dynamic enough to avoid boredoom. I wish there was more lore, however, past the end. All those menus and buttoms could have had just an artwork of a diary with logs, telling the story from different lens as you progressed in the story. It wouldn't demand much of sound, artwork, etc. just write up. I think that was the only point of improvement I would suggest to the devs. *e.g. he wanders quite a lot given the nature of the plot, we could have had those buttons being enabled with things he found along the way. Could be, again, just described in written form.
Also, the burning question, will be there a follow-up? Even text-only? I would gladly buy the book.
p.s.: I almost jumped out of my chair late night with the "War Girls" banner popping up and a "HA!!!!!!!" coming out of nowhere. Thats some memorable sound you got there tied to your group!

I'm a big fan of more 'experimental' games like visual novels and 'walking simulators'. That said, I simply can't recommend this game. I don't mind it being short, and I could even forgive the lack of any kind of choice to be made by the player, but the visual aspect of it was incredibly underwhelming and the writing too simplistic.
The visuals of the game consist of a handful (probably less than ten altogether) background images that accompany the text, with characters superimposed on them when the story calls for it - there isn't much more to it than what you can see in the preview.
Seeing all that, I hoped the writing would be this game's strongest point, but it's just not very well done. Aside from the aforementioned lack of choice - you literally go through the whole game without being to influence it - the characters are incredibly simplistic, and while there is an attempt to give them some kind of depth through their backstories, they just never come across as plausible human beings. They seem to exist only to serve the story, which also can't really decide what it wants to be: it starts out as a variation on the old 'war is hell' theme, and at the very last minute turns into a morality tale about religion and racism. I might be more receptive towards it if the writer had at least known how to write Mei's character, but it's hard to get emotionally involved with the game when the main two characters' dialogue is just so unrealistic: a 11-year girl for whom English is supposedly a second language fluently and eloquently talks to a supposedly  ruthless, adult English soldier who acts like a 15-year-old.
This is a cute short experience of a game if you don't think too much about it, and if you get it on sale, it's not too expensive either. However, don't expect it this 'visual novel' to go into any kind of depths; it's probably best suited for a younger audience.

Before purchising, please know that it's length is less than two hours long. I would wait for a sale before checking it out. As for the story itself, it's both heartwarming and heartbreaking, although it would have been more powerful if there was another hour of interactions and development. Very good, but should have been longer.

I only have 2 hours total play time so far (single player only), but I honestly have no complaints.  For $15,  you can't go wrong with Space Beast Terror Fright!

The game takes place on a single map where a realm and objectives (a storyline for that particular realm, or a conquest mode) are selected. The interface is quite average, making things like trading goods slightly more difficult than necessary. Provinces provide gold income that can be used to recruit troops or construct buildings. Special resources (like horses, wine, wool, crafts) are required to construct buildings and better units, so larger empires are heavily favored in the game. Armies consist of stacks of units (infantry, irregular, archer, cavalry, naval, or siege) of a set maximum quantity; gold income is plentiful enough to raise a large army quickly, but special resource restrictions inhibit the recruitment of better units by smaller empires. Research points can be used to unlock magic spells. Diplomatic options include trade, defensive treaties, alliances, declaring war, and espionage. Tactical battles are uninspired, while the AI seems to be a capable enough opponent. Sovereignty: Crown of Kings is a more simplified game than Dominions or Crusader Kings, and depth and replayability suffer because of that.

I must say: This game didn't have a very strong first impression, but I did perservere and made it to the end.
One big lasting note throughout the length of this game (which taking it generally at a medium pace took me less than six hours, which, is downright laughable for an RPG) is that most of the assets seemed to be taken from RPG Maker. Almost no custom work, but I guess that could be excused if the game had a strong story and RPG assets. Does it?
Ehhhh no, not at all... and I'll just break it down.
- THE STORY -
The story was probably the only thing that made me gather any remote interest in this game. Pretty much the story is about a (knight?) guy named William who basically gets to be in a game of body-juggling. On his mission to rid an imp in some elderly guy's basement he gets in the way of Xen, the witch in the kingdom of Opress. She gets annoyed of his friend and for some reason Xen zaps both of them (I honestly have no idea why, Will didn't taunt Xen in any way) changing Xen into a girl. The meat of the story is thrown in your face throughout the first half of the game: You are a girl and you want to be changed back. There's an underlying story of the war that should be stopped but honestly it's put in the background until the last hour of the game.
I don't recall playing RPGs where being a girl generates so much negative attention like in this game though. There are a good percent of people in the game that seem to just make sexist jokes towards you. Either way, most of the storyline is pretty cliche, and I honestly forgot most of it even after playing it. I honestly don't even remember most of your followers' names since they don't really garner any interest. There are people who seem to just get in your way for no reason and some of the plots actually never conclude (like the plot between William and his mother).
- THE COMBAT -
The combat is pretty bad... just laying that out there. I feel like the combat was just taked on for more length because in a game as short as this one, getting to level 10 is an achievement. Most of your partners share the same attacks so there's no variety. Swords are really the only useful weapons (because the five strongest weapons are SWORDS), and if you get the best piece of armour (for only 500 gold), you win.
Oh, and should I mention getting those best swords is so easy it's laughable? You can easily wipe through all the combat with one (I assume) missight if you go to the port town at the BEGINNING of the game, go to the wood shop, do the job there countlessly, and earn infinite gold. To put it clearly, I spent an hour doing the job, and earned enough to give my party the best armour and weapons AN HOUR into the game. This made all the combat pretty much pointless. It's bland enough anyway that I just kept hitting enter throughout most of the game and only lost like two battles.
One thing though, is you should get good weapons before going off to Unitem (or whatever it's called) because when you get to Oasis, you either need a lot of gold or strong weapons to defeat a boss on the island. I made the mistake of only getting armour to that point on the first playthrough and I was essentially stuck because there was no way to get better weapons and no way to earn gold. Had to start the game over.
Now, I know the majority of this review was negative, but it's honestly hard for me to remember any good points of the game. One good point I guess is that there's a lot of side quests (but they're almost all fetch quests that give you gold) and the dialogue is somewhat passible. Either way, I can list more flaws but I'd just rather play a better game in this genre because it's obviously taking roots from other, much better JRPGs like Final Fantasy or the Zeboyd games.
OVERALL RATING: 3/10
(If there's anything that I missed, feel free to notify me in any way. Keep in note that I write these reviews immediately after finishing the game.)

KotOR is probably my favorite game of all time, for quite a few reasons. I remember picking it up back in 2003 when I was 8, just because it had 'Star Wars' in the title. Ever since then, I have played this game through numerous times. The game regardless of how you play it, is just plain fun. The graphics are dated, yet they still look pretty decent. The gameplay is challenging and rewarding. The setting and locations in this game are stunning. From the urban cities of Taris, the deserts of Tatooine, to the oceans of Manaan, all of the locations are beautifully done. The characters you meet are diverse and likable. Most are pretty interesting, including npcs. There are plenty of opportunities to walk around and explore or talk to characters off of the beaten path. There are also mini games such as Pazaak and swoop races. The story is intriguing and has many turns. It also has a lot of replayability. There are different conversation choices, different endings, different classes, abilities, weapons, character party, and for the hardcore players no alien subtitles. There are plenty of customization options for the weapons you use, whether you want to be a calm and thoughtful Jedi using lightsabers and the force, or be the smooth talking smuggler using blasters and grenades, you are able to choose the way you want to play.
In conclusion, this is probably my favorite game. It has decent graphics that have aged somewhat well. The locations, characters, and story are all well made and great. There are many options for customization and replayability. Also the game is just plain fun. I'd highly recommend it to any Star Wars, sci-fi, or rpg fan.

Let me say this upfront: Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is NOT a full game. You can tell that it was initially a prologue level meant to be included WITH The Phantom Pain, but due to the need for (probably) more money for TPP's development, Konami forced it to be released as a separate title.
That being said, Ground Zeroes is not a BAD demo. The graphics are nothing short of fantastic, the gameplay is fluid, the enemy A.I. is intelligent and challenging, and the game runs superbly on almost all PC's. If you enjoy the stealth genre, this game will not disappoint you from a gameplay standpoint. Just be warned that if you're not a completionist, the main mission and accompanying "Side-Ops" can be completed in less than three hours. You can only truly get your money's worth out of this game if you take the time to complete the missions on higher difficulties, achieve the coveted "S-Rank" on each Op, collect all the cassette tapes, rescue all prisoners, and get all the achievements/XOF Patches. If those extra objectives interest you, then Ground Zeroes can take up many more hours of your time. I personally had a lot of fun replaying missions in this game, and I normally do not complete the games I play.

I have two main problems at the moment with FSP, aside from the painfully small player base, which I feel will grow eventually, those being the map generation system's lack of complexity since the days of FS, where you could alter the size of doorways, the width of walls, and so on, and the fact that FSP has textured walls means that this is a less viable option. I can also no longer see the actual numbers going into it, like the chance that a wall is destroyed or not instead of showing me the actual chance that it is destroyed it just shows me "Faultless" or "Destroyed", which is a large step back from the original where there were 51 different possibilities, each increasing in implements that even though small made a visible difference on the map created. My other main problem is the RGB colour editor. While it is great that this game has it in with sliders, you can only move the sliders one number at a time, rather than clicking and dragging. I also found that you can use arrow keys, but even if you hold down the key it only goes up or down by about five, over five seconds or so, then stops anyway. If I want to make my units red that should not take 510 key presses to get red to 255 and blue to 0. The sound options have this same problem, and when I am altering voice sound every single time I press the key it plays an annoying sound file, and it takes 100 key presses to mute it, and you will want to, with all of the ridiculous confirmation in the game. If I press "Aim here" then select somewhere to ♥♥♥♥ing aim then I don't want to be asked if I am "Really really really sure?" for the third time this round. And that is something which needs to be changed in the options menu, I want to disable these bad mecahnics, which do nothing other than slow me down. If I press spacebar to watch a video of what will happen in the next 5 seconds (it is always five seconds, no altering it for some reason) then when it is over can I not have to press spacebar again to get rid of it. If I try to make a change does it not realise that I no longer want it to be in video mode anymore? The amount of content missing in this game is atrocious, and the only notable differences seem to serve only to slow players down and make the game janky. I want to love this game, I really do, but if I have to press yes on the "Are you sure?"ometer one more ♥♥♥♥ing time I don't think I will be able to. With all of the mandatory instant replays on every single kill, the six man player limit, and a campaign that as far as I can tell is a literal copy-paste from the first, with slightly better map design at least, I just feel that as user-friendly that you have tried to make this you have failed. FS was all about being able to make complex plans in seconds, the thought of what you were going to do was always the complicated bit, but now I am being discouraged from using the wait command because the menu to just set up the goddamn thing takes 30 seconds, not three like in the original. To make this game playable and sellable to any veterans or fans of FS, or STBS at all for that matter, is to add the the options menu
A: Sliders for the colour bars
B: Turn off confirmations on commands
then add to the game-making menu
A: actual data for map creation, I don't care if in brackets you put (fractured) next to 0.5 on the chance that a wall will be broken for some context, just have the actual data so we have some more control over the maps we play
B: choices on turn length and limit, not just 5, 10, 20 turn games, I want an option for 3 turn games, or 2 turn games with minimal cover or walls, for a fast paced game, I want options to have more than 5 seconds a turn, 1 second turns were loads of fun in FS, if the other person was there, same for 30 second turns. I'm not asking to change the default, just have the options
C: More than 6 people aside please, that's pitiful, really.
Just make these five small changes, and seeing as how you copy-pasted the campaign you can copy-paste these from the base game, the coding ain't that hard people, and I swear that FS vets who loved the original will adore this game, honestly, I have several friends of mine who got this, and all were let down by the aforementioned problems. And please, whatever you do, don't lie to us like you did earlier this discussion thread in a reply to @THOMPSON, claiming that you had not taken these things out. Slowing down the game is in no way "User Friendly", and while I have no qualms with the radial menu perhaps just an option to replace it with the list functionality of FS would simmer people's nerves a bit. No matter what you do this will be compared to FS, and in it's current state it is just so janky and fragmented by kill cams and constant affirmations of your actions that has been weighed and found wanting.

There is no other interaction between the player and the game whatsoever. The only tracks are the background music, which is beautiful, and the sound effects. The art illustrates the scene we're reading about, or the characters' expressions and actions, in a very simple way. No fancy animations - just moving layers sometimes.

Artwork 10/10 - The artwork throughout the game was very beautiful and vibrant. If your interested, the developers provided a bonus section in the game with scenes, trial artwork, and backgrounds.

This was a tough one to review. As you can plainly see, I've got a healthy amount of hours invested into this game. I think I'm a little late reviewing this game, but hey, better late than never. Let's get in our droppod of choice, follow the solar trail, and crash straight into AWESOMENAUTS!
THE PRESENTATION: This game is absolutely oozing style. Colors. Animation. Artwork. Music. The whole package of AWESOME is included in this game. But first, let me contain myself, and start with the music. Now usually for a non-awesome game, I'd say something like "The music is good, and compliments the gameplay and story". But this game is a different monster. You see, AWESOMENAUTS is a 2D moba. So naturally, there's a lot of characters to play as. But it doesn't end there, oh no. Each character (32, and more upcoming) has their own theme song and killing spree song. Yep. That's 64 unique songs. And that isn't even counting the totally rad theme song, and other background music.The game is styled as a saturday morning cartoon, which is a stroke of genius. All the characters are unique in sound and design, and look like they came straight out of a comic. The graphics follow closely behind, as they too are beautifully drawn and hand crafted. Nothing, I repeat, NOTHING looks generic in this game. Not even the creeps. Overall, very impressive presentation and atmosphere. 3/3
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is the main attraction of this game, given it has really no story other than a reason to be fighting in space. The goal of the game is to defeat towers, kill enemy Awesomenauts, and destroy their drill, which, according to the lore, is used to drill out some stuff called SOLAR (it looks like urine, but that's just me). Solar is also the currency in the game, and you use it to purchase stuff in the shop. But wait, I'm getting ahead of myself. The game is two dimensional, so you jump around, point where to shoot, and generally try not to get yourself killed. Each awesomenaut controls swiftly, albiet varying in controllability depending on who you play. Some are heavy, and some are quick. Like other team based games, every 'naut has a certain role. Some are tanks, some are harassers, and others the ever-loathed support class. Furthermore, they all have an auto attack (hold left click and do damage) and 2 abilities. For the most part, each 'naut is balanced. Well, that's what I would say if the games themselves were actually fair. You may have noticed that many people flame this game for being unbalanced. This isn't because the 'nauts themselves are broken, it's because of the way the game is designed. You see, Awesomenauts is 3v3. Now hold up, that doesn't sound so bad. But wait, there's more. That's the ONLY gamemode. The only game here is 3v3 tower pushing. If one player isn't carrying their weight, you've pretty much lost. On the other hand, in a 6v6, one player could be struggling, but the impact is not as serious since you have 5 other players to carry them. This added to the fact that there are serious counters to some 'nauts makes it seem very unfair. Which it is. Also, the fact that you have to have offense on your team to win is also jarring,  since there are many nauts that pale in comparison to others in this regard. One bad team composition, and the odds will shift out of your favor. But overall, it controls well, and if you're a good player, you may be able to overcome these difficulties. 2/3
PROGRESSION: Now, what would a moba be without leveling? Yep, there's levels in this game. When you win, or get kills, after each game, you'll get experience for it. Every time you gain experience, you fill up two meters: your own player level, and the 'naut's level. Every time you reach a certain level, you'll unlock new stuff. These include new in-game items, awesomepoints to spend on new 'nauts, dropship parts to make new dropships, and badge slots to equip the wicked badges you've earned. The more 'nauts you unlock, the more freedom you feel like you'll have, and you'll be sure to play even more with their new abilities and techniques. Added to this is the league system, which functions like most other leagues in mobas. Do well, and you'll advance, playing against increasingly skilled players. Lose, and it's back to n00bville. But in all seriousness, some say it doesn't work, but that's really only due to the fact that there aren't enough players to help balance out the games. I personally never noticed it all that much, but perhaps it's only because I'm so used to it. But it'll at least give you a sense of how good you are at the game. I will say, though, that compared to other similar games, Awesomenauts is lacking in progression. There simply isn't enough stuff to spend your points on. It gets the job done, but certainly requires improvement. 2/3
THE TECHNICAL ANALYSIS: Uh oh. Looks like AWESOMENAUTS isn't looking too awesome anymore. Now, technically speaking, there are few glitches in this game other than some minor bugs; Ronimo is pretty good with that sort of thing. But then there's the connection issues. Wow. I guarantee you there will be a time when you could've sworn you were out of range of an attack, but it hit you. Unfortunately, laggers are common in the game. Not quite sure how this could be fixed, but it's a serious issue. I've seen people leave games because of laggers. I've even seen people take advantage of their own lag. Whether or not it's Ronimo's fault, I don't know. But it exists. And it will happen. 0.5/1
Alright, alright, I'll admit, this game isn't the most AWESOME game in existence, but really, what is? This game is super fun, and it's FREE. Even if you don't like mobas, give this one a try. It's casual, easy to learn, and is definitely a treat for the eyes and ears. So, Awesomenauts, lets join the fight. Take it star by star. Use your power, show your might. Win the cosmic war, THE AWESOMENAUTS!

This is my first Endless game and I'm in love. Let me start by saying I'm a huge fan of the Civ games. I've been playing them since the very first one and have put more hours into that series than any other. But after 10 hours into Endless Legend I might be ready to say that I like it more than any of the Civ games I've played (disclaimer: I haven't played Civ6 yet). This game is refreshingly different in a lot of ways.
Here are the highlights for me...
- Beautiful graphics:
Just an absolutely gorgeous game. By far the best looking strategy game I've ever played. And the sound effects
are amazing as well.
- Rich Lore:
Auriga, it's history, and it's inhabitants are very interesting.
- Diverse factions:
The only exception here being the Vaulters and Mizari. They're identical, just different skins. I've played as the Wind
Walkers and the Ardent Mages. I also have the Forgotten from the DLC but I haven't tried them yet.
- Quests:
Main faction quests and side quests that you pick up just from exploring add quite a bit of variety to each turn.
- Diverse Units:
At first I was a bit disappointed that each Faction only had four units. But assimilating a minor faction adds another
unit. And all units are editable and you can create entirely new units from existing templates. All of this together
makes up for the limited number of faction units.
- Passification/Assimilation:
Speaking of minor factions, each one can be passified for benefits. And you can choose one passified minor faction
to assimilate which, as I said above, allows you to train their unique units. A nice layer of strategy.
- Heroes:
I love the heroes. This adds an RPG element to the game with their skill points. And an interesting layer of strategy
as they can either serve as an army general or a governor of a city. These roles are interchangeable and offer unique
benefits.
I haven't tried the multiplayer yet as I'm still learning the mechanics and strategies. I have moved up from easy to normal difficulty. I'm also a fan of huge maps and slow games so I haven't been able to do much with diplomacy yet. But from the little bit I've experienced this seems to work well.
My only negative gripe is the occasional odd decisions my units make during a battle. A few times, after targeting an enemy unit, one of my melee units will move way out of range. I'm not sure if this is due to terrain or just poor AI. It hasn't happened too often and I've yet to lose a battle as a result. Although I have lost a unit as a result.
All in all, this game is fantastic. I'll update my review later if Endless Legend leads to the end of my marriage. Just...one...more...turn...dear.
