The recent years have been kind for us in regards to 4X games, and Endless Legend is no exception.
The word I'd pick to describe it would be "beautiful", I think. The soundtrack mostly isn't outstanding but serves as a mood-setter and not a distraction. Fascinating lore serves as an interesting sideline and provides insight into motivations of the races, which are highly diverse, even unusually so for a 4X game - where most games give you a unit set and calls it a day, EL only provides three unique units and instead, say, takes away the ability to wage war, research new technology, or farm. The shift to district-based approach as opposed to the classic Civilization-style single tile "hub" with buildings in it is interesting as well, and satisfies the Sim City fan in all of us.
The major downside of the game would be the combat, unfortunately, as orders are pre-queued at the start of each mini-turn, but executed in order of initiative, meaning that one often has to struggle with their own units' AI, trying to guess what they will do if their target dies or moves out of range beforehand. The approach to DLCs is also questionable, mostly introducing a new gameplay element (such as espionage) and also a race that excels at that element to the extent that it dominates it absolutely, but is not very interesting outside of that element (Forgotten). This makes it convenient to skip DLCs that introduce something you don't care for, as I did with Tempest, but also makes the whole lineup sound kind of piecemeal.
The AI is nothing to write home about, but that's not surprising, because we took many years to write a halfway decent AI for Go - a game with a very limited array of choices and zero hidden variables - and, as always, multiplayer is highly recommended, assuming you organize games with friends.
Overall, I highly recommend the game to anyone who's interested in 4X games and turn-based strategy in general.

TLDR Version:
"Sovereignty: Crown of Kings" is to "Birthright: The Gorgon's Alliance" what "Pandora: First Contact" is to "Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri."
Full Version:
Did you ever play Sierra's DnD: Birthright adaptation, "Birthright: The Gorgon's Alliance," from 1997?  I would bet good money that the makers of "Sovereignty: Crown of Kings" did.  Intentionally or not, this game captures some of the mechanical feel of that older title, though at the same time does not quite capture the personality exhibited by it's spiritual forebear.
First and foremost, "Sovereignty" is all about its field battles.  Take a look at the screenshots depicting armies arrayed in opposition to one another on a hex grid, and know that that is where most of your time will be spent with this one.  Unit abilities, terrain effects, and battle objectives are easy to understand, and the system is serviceable if you can accept the graphical abstraction of tokens-as-units.
Secondarily, every aspect of nation-building performed on the strategic-level world view is done in service to the field battles.  Your provinces dictate how many troops you can afford, and where they can be deployed.  Your realm magic is used to buff your troops or debuff enemy troops prior to battles.  Your diplomacy lets you attempt to control how many fronts you fight on.  Diplomacy/trading is also the primary means of obtaining access to resources (iron, wood, gems, stone, etc.) that don't occur naturally within the borders of your realm, which are needed to build your advanced troop types and province improvements.
The UI is clunky and the graphical clarity/organization leaves something to be desired, but "Sovereignty" has the potential to be a captivating turn-based, fantasy, grand-strategy experience, the likes of which we don't see much these days.  I hope this title continues to receive the polish it deserves: if it does, I'm confident I'll remember it as fondly twenty years from now as I do "Birthright" today.

This is another game I really wanted to like, but just can't.
By now you probably understand the game's primary allure: it's a turn-based grand strategy game in a custom-built fantasy setting.  The key difference between Sovreignty and a 4X game like, say, Civilization is that the game world is bespoke rather than procedurally generated.  Its replayability comes from the ability to play each of the prebuilt game-world's many different nations rather than having a randomly generated new world each game.  AFAIK this makes Sovreignty unique.
But the devil is in the details.  The game's concept is great; the implementation... not so much.  The interface is klunky, the AI is nonexistent, and many of the game's features seem completely unbalanced.  (Note that by "unbalanced" I'm not referring to the asymmetry between the different playable nations -- that's a *good* thing -- I mean that some basic gameplay mechanics are vastly OP while others are essentially useless.)  Not to mention that the game crashes -- a lot.  At least it doesn't take a long time to reload!
I'll keep playing because I want to finish at least one campaign, though at this point I'm certain it'll just be a monotonous grind.  I started playing my first game as a tiny "one-star" elven nation and in my first war easily whipped a much larger neighbor, then handily defeated a punitive coalition consisting of every single bordering nation, incluing the gameworld's #1 superpower.  I can't imagine the game presenting a more challenging scenario than that.  (I'm not bragging about my martial expertise here -- just pointing out that the AI is childishly easy to beat.)
I'd like to say that the game has potential, but that's like saying a farm tractor has the potential to win the Indy 500.  In theory, I guess -- but not without some serious rebuilding.

Als ich SW:KotoR zum ersten Mal auf der Xbox Classic gespielt hab, war ich ca. 10 Jahre alt.
Ich hab das Spiel damals immer und immer wieder durch gespielt ! Nach ca 10 Jahren sah ich das die Star Wars Collection im Angebot ist und hab natürlich zugeschlagen. In dieser Box war zu meinem Glück SW:KotoR 1 & 2 dabei und dachte mir sofort das ich sie unbedingt wieder spielen muss !
SW:KotoR 1 ist damals wie heute einfach ein RPG MEILENSTEIN, das Spiel hat eine wirklich sehr gut geschriebene Story die ein jedesmal von neuem fesselt egal wie oft man das Spiel durchspielt. Nach jedem Playthrough finde ich immer wieder Quests und Dialoge die ich noch nie gesehen hab.
So jetzt noch eine kurze erklärung vom Spielverlauf:
Man erstellt sich am Anfang vom Spiel ein Charackter. Man wählt die Klasse aus verteilt paar Talentpunkte, bestätigt und es folgt Star Wars typisch ein kleines Intro die, die Handlung vom Spiel kurz erklärt. Man startet auf einem Raumschiff das sozusagen als Tutoriallevel funktioniert, in dennen die Spielemechaniken erklärt werden.
Die Kämpfe sind Rundenbasiert wärend man sich auf Nah- oder Fernkampf spezialisieren kann. Dabei wird man immer mit 2 weiteren Charackteren begleitet die man im Verlauf des Spieles findet. In dem Spiel gibt es eine Gut-Böse Mechanik, sprich alles was man tut oder nicht tut hat Folgen auf den Verlauf des Spieles.
Nun folgt noch eine kleine Warnung:
Das Spiel ist frustrierend verbuggt auf Windows 7, ohne gewisse Einstellung und Fixes die man sich aus dem Internet zieht crasht das Spiel fast nach jedem neuen Level (Planet).
Deswegen möchte ich noch einmal einige Tipps mitgeben die mir beim spielen geholfen haben:
- Im SW:KotoR Ordner gibt es eine Datei die "seconfig.exe" heißt, dort müsst ihr unbedingt die Hardware-Maus deaktivieren.
Wenn bei euch das Spiel crasht wenn eigentlich eine Video abspielen sollte, müsst ihr leider die Videos deaktivieren.
- Im selben Ordner gibt es eine Datei die sich "swkotor.ini" nennt dort geht ihr unter "[Graphics Options]" und stellt "FullScreen=1" auf "FullScreen=0". Ausserdem fügt ihr "AllowWindowedMode=1" in der untersten Zeile von [Graphics Options] ein. Diese aktiviert den Fenster Modus des Spieles, da es im Fenstermodus weitaus stabiler läuft.
- Hier nochmal ein Video auf Englisch der das hier alles nochmal erklärt + einem Fix zum downloaden :
- Das alles fixt jedoch nicht eines der nervigsten Bugs im Spiel: nach einem Kampf kommt es vor das der Charackter sich nicht mehr bewegen kann. Das liegt daran der er noch im Angriffsmous steckt obwohl keine Gegner in der nähe sind.
Was dagegen hilft:
* Wenn du Glück hast ist noch ein Gegner in der Nähe die diesen Bug beheben können.
* Manchmal hilft es einfach mit einem Bgleiter kurz zu reden.
* Aber am effektivsten ist es einach zu speichern un neu zu laden.
Das sind wirklich die einzigen Bugs die man merkt und wer über sie hinwegsehen kann, dem erwartet ein grandioses Rollenspiel der bis zu 40 Stunden pro Spieldurchlauf fesselt.

I picked up the IndieGala "3rd Friday Special" bundle on a whim, figuring there had to be at least one or two good games in it. Victim of Xen was one of the games in the bundle, and I figured I'd give it a fair shot. In hindsight, I'm glad I didn't pay full price for the bundle, OR for this game.
Victim of Xen tries to present itself as having "a dynamic story set in a rich world" where the core of the plot has the protagonist arbitrarily gender-swapped by a witch.
In that quest for gender reversal, which took me all of six hours to fully finish, I went through a story line that felt like a scribbled bulleted list on a sticky note. Characters appear quickly, disappear just as quickly, are hardly given development or meaningful context, and engage in stereotypical themes.
For example, within two hours you're turned into a woman, thrown halfway around the tiny world map in various areas, sneak aboard a doomed ship, get sold into slavery in a desert labor camp, and so on.
RPGs can have awful stories but still be really fun. But VoX fails in this aspect too. The gameplay is so shallow it is non-existant. Battles feel tacked on just to give the "story" length, and never feel challenging or rewarding. End-game I was still only getting less than 50 experience per fight I was forced to do.
And money? The only good source of cash came from sidequests. One (doing something with wood) was infintely repeatable. 20 minutes of grinding later I had two of the best weapons in the game thanks to a nearby store, and the entirety of the game (Djinn on) was a cake walk. No challenge, no good structure, just poorly designed and implemented gameplay. Heck, the final two bosses took me two rounds each, using the same skills I'd been using since the start of the game.
All in all, Victim of Xen feels and plays like amateur's first RPG Maker project. Paying money for this, or playing this for anything more than achievements and cards, is a waste of time. I wasted 6+ of mine to end up with this review; you should do something better.

Leaving a review for awesomenauts is tricky... In short, it's a 2D platformer MOBA with a 3v3 setup.
This game has a couple of obvious downsides:
- The matchmaking is unstable during low hours.
- The netcode is peer-to-peer, which means that there are no dedicated servers. This leads to advantages for laggers.
- Apart from unlocking new characters, there is no late game content.
- Because of all these things, the playerbase has been shrinking. This has led to experienced players remaining with the influx of new players being too small to close the gap.
So, before buying the game you should consider these points. Nevertheless, I would recommend the game:
(- Let it be clear that this game is often on sale for -80% or -90%, which makes the cost ridiculously low.)
- The devs have done a very good job at balancing the game. Hear me out. Yes, some nauts feel completely overpowered. The problem with a 3v3 game is that there needs to be a balanced between how powerful the characters are and how slow the game can be. If the nauts are too weak, then nothing would happen. So, each naut carries a lot of power. To newcomers, this may be confusing, especially since they cannot practice with the nauts from the DLC. However, a lot of the OP-ness arises from inexperience with MOBAs. Once you get the hang of the general strategy (don't overextend, push droids, etc.), then no naut will be OP. Yes, some are better than others, but Ronimo has done a terrific job balancing all the nauts.
- The game is still fun during peak hours.
- The game offers games versus AI, which can be challenging and fun.
- The game offers custom game modes, which can definitely be fun (and also good practice).
- The game has a strong replay system, which allows you to look at players who were better and then better understand how they played so well.
One big problem with the game is the community. It has obtained a nasty way of fatalism. Some veterans are suggesting newbies to get a refund while they can, despite having bought the game during sale (i.e. it being 2 euros/dollars). If you think the game you play isn't worth 2 dollars, then just leave.
All in all, this game has given me plenty of fun moments. Like any MOBA, try to accept the fact that you can't always win. Mute players that you don't like, or just turn off the chat. There is so much to enjoy within Awesomenauts; it has given me fun for over a 1000 hours (smurfs combined), and I have gifted the game to many people who went on to invest hundreds of hours in it as well.
Trash. Peer-to-peer moba is the worst idea ever.

It's a cute idea, it really is, and as a longtime console RPG nerd I really wanted to enjoy this more, but the concept of evolving gameplay is much stronger than the actual implementation. The pacing of the evolutions is poor, leading to an early string of flashy improvements followed by long stretches of dull gameplay that would have failed to entertain back when final fantasy clones were a quasi-legitimate genre. When it comes to references, the game tries to stick its finger in far too many pies, with Mario Bros-themed monsters in one area and Diablo gameplay in the next. The game offers weak satire of some RPG gameplay tropes while remaining absolutely true to others, compromising the humor of the former and presenting itself as blind to the faults of the latter.
I mean, it's not a BAD game, it's just a highly inconsistent presentation that overstays its welcome. If the dungeons were a bit shorter, the combat just a bit flashier, and the writing a bit more clever, this would have been absolute gold. But as presented, this grab bag of references won't be much fun for anybody not looking to reminisce about a highly specific subset of console games from the 90s.

Idle Champions is a somewhat unconventional idle game. In addition to simply obtaining and upgrading units, you also have options regarding which of a characters' abilities you want to focus on, and though they seem somewhat scarce, alternative characters can appear.
The main factor in the game is positioning. Characters will have buffs applying under conditons such as being in front of or behind their target or working with a certain race, and optimizing positioning is a big deal. It's also nice to have separate "campaigns" to run, instead of a simple nondescript grind until things slow down, then ascenscion.
There are faults, however. You can't specify targets for characters, nor can you improve attack speed for individual characters from what I've seen, so you'll often lose a porentially vast amount of DPS to multiple attacks triggering on the same target, especially if the target is already at low HP. Clicking is basically useless for damage after the beginning of a run, instead applying a useful stun (which can be used to mitigate the previous issue), but also recieves no upgrades.
Losing a single party member (and it appears it will always be the one at the front of the party first) often ruins a formation so utterly, the time taken to be pushed back a level is wasted when idle. This is exacerbated by the first healing skill you get affecting a column also targeted by a DPS, and therefore requiring a massive DPS drop to heal the only characters taking damage.
Finally, while the chests are affordable and very helpful with scaling gold or character-specific items, doubles of items you have already feel pathetic, only improving the effect by .1%
Still, it's more engaging and accessible than many idle games, even if the starter packs seem far from being worth buying.

The way the story of this kinetic novel unfolds itself reminds me a bit of Planetarian. Great deal of the story is spent characters just chatting and building their relationship. In the very end of the story, there is a climax, which may (if you grew fond of the characters) leave you with tears in your eyes. Despite the emotional ending, I found the game a bit of…. boring. It is not a bad kinetic novel, but I just could not get interested in characters and I did not care very much what happened to them. The music and visual are however really well done and I especially enjoyed the soundtrack.
If someone were to ask me shoud they play the game, I would recommend it only if they like short, bittersweet stories, and do not mind a bit of amateurish writing. As such, I cannot recommend it for everybody.

TLDR;
Overall Score: 7.9/10
Despite it's short length compared to other visual novels in direct competition to it, Over the Hills and Far Away delivers a powerful narrative with relatable characters that make you feel emotionally invested. However, despite it's great story, the lack of choices and multiple endings leave much to be desired. I would recommend this game only if bought on a sale (It's like watching a short TV series except in novelized form).
---
Overall Score: 7.9/10
Gameplay: 7/10
(-3): Lack of choices, No multiple endings, engaging action events, nor unlockables that provide more useful background information on the characters (unlike the Fate/Stay Night VN and Clannad VN which has all)
Story: 9/10
(-1): Out of the many Visual Novels I have already read, I haven't come across any that have stories taking place in early America, let alone during the early establishment days. However, despite the uniqueness of the narrative, I feel like the characters could be more fleshed out. As it is, the story would make a great movie. However, I see wasted potential. I'm sure for many of you who have completed this novel, you probably want to know more about the characters... hell, see the two MC's grow up together. I'm dissapointed the developers haven't even considered a DLC to address this! Come onnnnn! :'(.
Art: 10/10
- Exactly what I'd expect from a Visual Novel's art style. Will age VERY well and likely looks good in any HD displays you may have.
- Very pleasing to the eyes. I absolutely love how the artists did the visual effects on the flashbacks.
Sound/Music: 10/10
- I personally feel the developers excelled greatly in the Music and sound department. I felt extremely immersed in the story with my headphones on when experiencing the story. The quality of the sound and music effects here demonstrate how a visual novel can make a novel EVEN better and more engaging.
Length: 6.5/10
- The story was way too short, especially for the price compared to other visual novels I feel are direct competition to it. Unless you buy this at a REALLY GOOD sale price like I did, you'll probably feel unhappy with how much you've paid versus the experience you'll get. The developer can solve this issue by either releasing a special edition that expands the story or provide a very affortable or free DLC that expands the length of the story.

Over The Hills and Far Away isn't really innovative in terms of gameplay; of course, that's to be expected. This is a sort of Visual Novel after all ( it doesn't even have choices!).
What this game (or rather "experience") does offer is a nice story that will distract from whatever thoughts or worries you may be preoccupied with in the present, and transport you to another world, in the backdrop of the War of 1812. This is a unique story. It's not a cinema, block-buster-esque storyline complete with explosions and giant robot testicles ( must have watched Transformers to appreciate this stupid joke).
It's more akin to a "slice of life" genre, which focuses on the more of the mundane and trivial aspects of life. Of course, the setting is uniquein itself, but the compelling aspect of the game is what I like to call the " intimacy of small moments".
Do you sometimes recall small, stupid memories of your "girlfriend" in middle school, that lame dance your sophomore year, that cute girl at the fair you had your first kiss with, and never saw again. Do you remember these moments at the most random times, maybe during your dead-end, god-awful job, and have to try to not to cry? Yeah, this game's kinda like that.
The beauty in those small, hidden stories that take place in the backgdrop of much larger events, that should overshadow that story. But in the end, there is still something very poignant about the small moments of joy and happiness that we are able to create in a world that sometimes feel too big as to being empty,
I won't give any spoilers, but if you want a simple game with gorgeous art, charming characters, enchanting music, and a premise that will make you wonder just exactly how many stories of lovers and friends, how many adventures and journies, how many small moments that really shouldn't matter but will make you cry like a baby - this game will not just tell you, but it will show you just how many of these transient moments happened in the war of 1812.
P.S. I know the girl is young, but... you know... like...,in the old days they didn't really think it was weird.... :) In fact, they encouraged it! Yeah! That's right! Don't you feel like the bigot now, jackass?! .... Plz don't arrest me

At first, you might get lost real easily by how the game starts out, dropping you in the middle of the game, letting you get your hands in the thick of it with no real instruction. EXPERIMENT! This game is literally endless, with no real, true penalties to stop you from doing whatever you want. From a few simple polygons, you clump it together slowly, piece by piece, and learn what YOU enjoy, and find to work, and improve off it. Not only that, but this game can conform to the way you wish to play easily, so there is NEVER any one, right way to play.
Wish to go in hard and heavy, with a giant, bulk-head cruiser? Go ahead, and charge at enemies with a hailstorm of laser beams. Or stay it safe, and strafe your enemies and snipe from afar with powerful missles and energy shots to obliterate the enemy. It is entirely put into the hand of the creator: You.
I bought this when it was at $30; I would do it again and again. I found it good enough to actually post a review for the FIRST TIME. This game rocks. It sucked me in completely for a couple of weeks. I'd look up at the clock and think omg it's been 6 hours! I'd go to work the next day on 5 hours sleep. It stirred my gamer blood! The ship building freedom is top notch. You build any kind of ship you want particle by particle and there are lots of smart, handy features in the ship building editor to save time. You can hold down the mouse and drag it across an area to select multiple components or you can just double click one piece and everything attached to it will be selected.
A quick ship building tip is to just build one side of the ship, say a wing, select all the pieces then hit c to copy. Move the cursor to a blank part of the screen and hit v to paste, then hit m to mirror (to invert the selection). Now you can just attach that perfectly mirrored section onto the opposite side of the ship if you need symmetry like for wings.
Symmetry is also important in placing your thrusters. You are in space so your ship isn't going to stop moving unless it crashes into something...or you put thrusters pointed in the opposite direction to the direction you're traveling in so you can break!
Also each different playable faction has some unique pieces to build with. Sometimes the minor differences aren't obvious, like where pieces don't have as much mass as other factions or they have slightly higher armor, but when you stack all those pieces together into a ship then the net values really make a difference in speed, toughness, or resource carrying capacity. You'll want to look at the stats on the ship pieces closely if you're into ship building.
If you're not into ship building there are premade ships available with each faction that you can use and just modify to your taste.
The game is beautiful to look at and very organic. To me it looks more like the world under a microscope filled with living, evolving organisms than it does a space frontier. Much like organisms, the ships actually create children. You can set a creation queue for yourself once you have a factory as part of your design. But you can also go into command mode by hitting tab and click on an allied vessel that has a factory and drag child designs into their queue so you begin to shape the future of your factions expansion without actually managing the execution. Just hit tab again to go back into pilot mode and go on your way. The allied ship you just programmed will now create what you set for it via the AI.
Once you've got your perfect fleet together you can find then fly into a wormhole. You will be given an option to follow it or stay. If you stay a parallel version of your fleet will upload to infect another player's galaxy through one of their wormholes while you remain where you're at with your original fleet. I just really wish there was some way of knowing how successful these invasions were, like a scoring system players could access to get some sense of how good your designs were.
The tournament mode doesn't pit you against other players. It just lets you test your own ships against your own designs and a small selection of premade designs. I would love to see a true tournament mode where you download player agents and test your ship against theirs with scoring. The game lacks true player interaction in real time but atleast we can see other player's creations as they come into our own galaxy as enemy agents controlled by the AI.
Unfortunately I do think there is a balance issue that needs to be addressed with faction 4. You will eventually find certain enemy agents that are typically oblong, travel at high speed, and shoot enormously long particle rays at you at range even from off of the screen! That's faction 4. They almost made me rage quit because they really get too many advantages, but I perservered and went back to the design editor. Their weakness is maneuverability. Their big bad weapon of choice is not turreted so the whole ship has to turn to target you with the death ray. This is not a huge disadvantage because their ships are inordinately fast but if you build a ship that can quickly side step their line of fire and either swarm them or ram them so that they can't turn into you then you can take them down...if you can catch them. Trapping them against asteroids is a typical ploy. Really though, no other faction gives nearly so much trouble...
The only other criticism I have is lag. No it's not really just a hardware issue. I play many other games where it's not an issue. The devs themselves have stated that they've worked really hard on the optimization but the fact is there comes a point where there are so many collisions going on in the galaxy that it can be taxing. I have an i5-4670, 8G ram, nvidia GTX 780 so my hardware is good. But I like faction 2 whose strength is cultivating resources and building up a fleet really quickly. Once I push out a bunch of ships that then create their own AI controlled child ships, the game has alot to track. The devs said to go into options and lower the physics updates per second value so I'll try tweaking that more. But it kind of makes me want to put the game aside now and come back later, maybe playing a different faction and not use a swarming strategy. If you get lag you can also follow a wormhole to a fresh universe, but that too can start to get repetitive.
The fresh content is really about fighting other player designs as enemy agents enter your galaxy. I hope the devs continue to work on the lag issue (maybe instancing parts of the playing field to lower the amount of AI activity needed as the game progresses). I'd also like to see them expand on player interaction by scoring invasions, and maybe add some simple tiered goals with rewards for flipping sections of your galaxy to your faction. I think those things would add alot to the game's longevity for me. Regardless, this is a really creative game. I love looking at it and playing it. It was worth every cent.

It could use some more parts admittedly, some factions have close to 40 while others have only 17 or 16, and it has a few factions that aren't playable at this point, both things I hope will be rectified in the future, but despite a few flaws, this game is undeniably a jewel, a unique and interesting concept.
In the end a Review is about one thing, is the game fun, and for me, and likely for those others who enjoy science-fiction and creativity tools, this game is definitely fun, prepare to sink hours into tweaking the designs for your fighters, capital ships, and stations.

“It’s like watching Battlestar Galactica through a kaleidoscope!”
This is one of my favorite 2D games at the moment and WHY I SAY THAT YOU MAY ASK? Let me start with the basics: Reassembly is an action oriented spaceship building game. Created by Anisoptera Games, an independent studio based in Los Angeles. Mainly inspirited in Lego and insect behavior in a world where everything is modular.
Reassembly
You start to build your very own ship piece by piece (ships are assigned a specific value based on their size) and most of the factions will cap out at 8,000P. Obviously it will take some time to get there ;). There are 7 factions in this universe and all of them play and work differently (insectoid, angley, squarish, plantlike or cristal like are some examples). One faction prioritizes high damage while other will get armor mostly. All of them have specific tactics and this will impact in their weapon choices.
You can also unlock most of the factions by killing large and valuable ships aligned to them. Once you destroy an specific amount (or, in other words, you make that faction lose an specific amount of value), you unlock that faction to play with.
Combat
Wield a wide variety of projectile and beam weapons, missiles, rockets and torpedoes, drones, and more against your enemies. Defend yourself with shields, armor, point defense systems, and pure maneuverability. The combat is a mix of skill, tactics, and preparation – an expertly piloted fighter can take down an enemy fleet, but having a well balanced arsenal helps. I can’t explain this better.
Art & environment
Maps are beautiful and the music flows with it. Procedural generated open living worlds where each faction fight for survival and evolution travelling though wormholes. There are usually a lot of “agents” (player fleets) spawning in the universe defending the sectors and spaceships, in Command mode you can pay them to join your fleet and seek you places to emerge. You need to conquer specifics zones to make spaceships emerge or grow your bases. But be careful, the big enemy fleet is looking these places to destroy them. Scavenge for resources, investigate disturbances, self repair, reproduce and take your fleet to the next stage.
Reassembly Reassembly
Reassembly Reassembly
Reassembly
Artificial Intelligence
AI is incredible. When you have a decent fleet of spaceships including your mother♥♥♥♥ing leadership… YOU WILL DIE… A LOT. AI ships can retreat if overwhelmed because they know how to measure the incoming attack. You need to plan how to attack and how to approach the battle and maybe take advantage of impromptu battles between rival factions to recover objectives, or run away after your opponent calls in reinforcements. In screen there can be around 150 ships in crossfire (it will run smoothly and at a decent framerate if you have nice hardware, otherwise you will be laggy).
You can only target 1 enemy at time with you entire fleet and that is a questionable design choice. A small system to target different ships would be nice in Command mode. The overall gameplay is very nice. Sometimes maneuvering big ships can be frustrating in places with a high amount of ships and planets, but is not that bad. We have three control types: Keyboard Only, Mouse and Keyboard, and Gamepad. This is very nice and completely user configurable, from colors to buttons, keys, even control schemes.
And well, we can’t have it all… No true multiplayer mode(can’t fight other players in real-time) the AI takes over other people’s ship designs and places them in your worlds. Obviously, you need to upload your fleet when you go through a wormhole. Last time a tried that Steam completely crashed, so some additional work towards multiplayer would be appreciated. PLEASE LET US PLAY IN REAL-TIME.

I have put several hours (80 +) into the first frozen synapse and i thoroughly enjoyed the first. It seemed to me a very strategic game of reading your oponents moves and trying to counter accordingly.
Frozen Synapse Prime isnt necessarily a sequel. I don't want to call it that. It is a graphical and UI update. The graphic update is whatever to me (it's nice), but the UI update is much needed. With the action command bar everything feels a little more smooth. They also implemented a UI update to the wait command which is very, very much needed. For example, in the first Frozen Synapse the wait command could get extremely cluttered really quick. When trying to use checks, and ducks, and aims, and stands all in the same wait command it got extremely clunky and cluttered. They changed that in this one expanding it so you can easily place and alter your commands within the wait timer and you can even isolate your wait command and play it out separately.
The multi-player is back yet they changed the multiplayer matchmaking a little. You no longer que and wait for an opponent. Instead you look for a match, and if none are open you create your own match (or two, or three, or four of your own), input your unit commands and come back later (if no one has joined yet) to follow up after someone has filled the seat of your oponent and input their own commands for their units.
They also gave the match creator more power in editing the type of match to create. Something that is lacking in the first Frozen Synapse. More power in adding/removing cover, adding/removing doors, how many rooms, what types of units. All is still randomly generated in the end but only within the parameters that you had already set.
I am a little disappointed in actual gameplay additions. They didn't really add any new content (except the campaign mode), units, features! They also removed the beloved shield dudes! It all just feels like an update. An update im more than happy to support since i love the series so much and i have a lot of fun proving my intellectual and tactical superiority. Frozen Synapse Prime isn’t so much a sequel to the original as it is a reboot. A new look with updated, swanky graphics, some more options for combat, giving you greater control over the outcomes; and a revamped multiplayer system. All together, there’s not that much new going on. The new commands now allow your units to ignore or focus on a particular room, and also allows them to focus on one particular point while moving, not exactly ground-breaking beyond the initial mechanics. While the graphics quite nice to look at, they’ve been implemented at a sacrifice to UI cleanness and clarity; and graphical smoothness. All the units move a little sluggishly, making the game feel less fast-paced, less tense.
The UI is nothing short of clunky. You can’t give a unit a move order while in the every-other-order dial, which requires a button to bring up and close. Space bar opens the turn predictor and closes while pause, fast forward and back have different keys again. The UI is clearly designed for the PS Vita touchscreen which doesn’t translate well to the PC.
Frozen Synapse Prime’s single player is pretty poor. The strength in the series is ultimately in its multiplayer. While adding an extra game mode and revamping the old ones, FSP wholly fails because of its multiplayer. Not that it’s doing anything too wrong, but more because there are just not enough players. FSP hasn’t got a large enough player-base to keep new players in the game. I played several matches against some European players (European a guess from their names), but most matches were never continued once the other player decided they were going to lose, a bit of a killjoy. I booted the game yesterday and there was only one player online… me, and zero matches waiting to be started.
I’m hoping I’m just a victim of the right game, wrong console. I imagine the game would actually be a lot smoother on the PS3 and PS Vita with more players online. Otherwise, despite the graphical upgrade, Frozen Synapse Prime isn’t really worth it, unless you can grab a group of friends to play with.

One of, if not the, best 4X games ever made, Endless Legend strikes a great balance between tried and true mechanics and experimentation.
Many tasks that would be tedious in another 4X, like worker management, are either abstracted or outright removed. In fact, the district system and linking of roads and trade routes was so well received they've shown up in a certain other 4X series.
Army sizes tend to remain smaller and more manageable than in most 4Xs, too, with an emphasis on elite troops with the best experience and equipment rather than huge stacks or map-carpeting single units. This helps the AI remain at least semi-competitive, since the tactical map stacks fight on is constrained enough to program robust routines for it. Sadly, while the AI is also good at the economic game, its grasp of war on the strategic map is too easily exploitable. If it's one of the best 4X AIs, that says as much about its competitors as about Endless Legend.
Instead of ever-expanding city micro, Endless Legend offers quests, ruins and minor factions to interact with. All more interesting, but they do eventually get repetitive. I also found the equipment system a rare downside, too fiddly for the scope of the game.
It's a beautiful game, though, with some of the best art design in the genre and high quality assets. Haunting music conveys the tone well, though it didn't stick with me enough for me to want the soundtrack.
Every faction plays differently, some, like the Cultists of the Eternal End (who can only have one city, but build it much larger than anyone else's), wildly so.
The DLC is also well worth your time. It introduces inventive new factions and mechanics (legendary structures, deeds and creatures) that fit nicely into the structure of the game.
I can't recommend this game enough

Ryse: Son of Rome is a Xbox One exclusive that made it's way to PC, so let's check it out.
In Ryse: Son of Rome you play as Marius. A roman soldier, who fights during the dark times in Romes history. The story begins with a siege on a palace and you as Marius fight your way through hordes of barbarians. You then save the emperor and lock him in a safe room and tell him your backstory and this is where the story begins.
I'll stop there to avoid spoilers. So lets get into the gameplay. The gameplay is a hack and slash game where you slash your way through enemy soldiers. To finish them off in gruesome finishers you need to enter an execution mode where you have to press buttons to defile enemies. It's fun enough to play, but it gets boring by the end of the game.
Graphically the game looks breathtaking. The environments look amazing and I didn't expect anything else from Crytek who make games which never look outdated. It's one of the best looking games I've played to date.
There is a multiplayer mode, but I didn't play it so I can't actually say anything about it.
The story is very engaging and it will take you 6 hours to finish all of it. After that there is no replay value, but there are survival maps and objective maps which do extend the game time.
There are a couple of bugs there and there like enemy corpses spazing out some times and some character model glitching.
Overall, I loved my time with Ryse, but I do however suggest you wait till a sale to get it as the short campaign doesn't take too long to finish.

Some games can be summarized in just a few words, Evoland is one of them. That doesn't mean it's a bad game by any stretch, but don't expect an epic journey that will last you for hours upon hours.
Evoland takes us through some of the gaming we remember from our past (or have seen on YouTube, if you're not old enough), of course it is rather quick to upgrade us from very, very simple combat and graphics to more clean-looking 3D with better combat options (but certainly still not good in any way for a prolonged period of time).
While people love to be nostalgic, who'd like to actually be stuck with something old?
There are some amusing puzzles if you're interested in gathering all of the stars and/or cards, but it could easily be more - and that's coming from someone who is absolutely braindead when it comes to puzzles in games. In addition they have a game within the game, which is simple, yet frustrating if you get stuck with the bad cards.
Overall, if you're just planning to rush through the game, you can probably do that in ~an hour (or less, I'm not sure), and as such the game might not be worth the money for you.
If you however is like me, and want that little bit of nostalgic feeling while taking your time to go through the game, find all the extra bits and just be very casual about it, I would highly recommend it.

If you are looking for a short, sweet and touching experience, look no further than this.
Despite the limited visual assets of the game and the short length, Over the Hills and Far Away took me by surprise in the best way possible. I couldn't have predicted that I'd get so emotionally attached to characters in such a compact story - I'll admit, I cried. T_T
Though I felt the story was somewhat predictable, it was immensely enjoyable, and I found myself smiling, admiring, and laughing very often at the little details and foibles that were lovingly woven into it. I loved the care and attention that went into the art and character designs, and I adored the soundtrack, which was breathtaking - I will definitely be buying the soundtrack.
This delightful Visual Novel ticks all of the right boxes for me, and I would heartily recommend it to anyone who appreciates authentic, heartfelt storytelling.
I may have been in the wrong mood or something but I found this story exceptionally boring. The art and music were very good but I literally fell asleep in my chair while playing it.

"When your time comes to die, be not like those whose hearts are filled with fear of death, so that when their time comes they weep and pray for a little more time to live their lives over again in a different way. Sing your death song, and die like a hero going home." - Tecumseh (qtd. in the beginning of the novel)
Over The Hills And Far Away is a kinetic novel, meaning there are no choices to be made. You simply either click or auto-progress through the story. It took me about two hours to read through, though I took a couple short breaks.
+ Great writing! The characters interact naturally, languages mix in in creative ways, and the pacing is just right.
+ Excellent art. The artwork is consistent stylistically and fits descriptions well. Only complaint here is that I wish there was a bit more.
+ Beautiful soundtrack. The orchestral score both built and melted tension as the story called for it. It layered with the writing without overpowering it. My only complaint sound-wise is that the bird call loop was a little too short and got a bit annoying in one of the sections.
It's an emotionally intense story that asks some serious questions of the reader. Set aside a couple hours and experience it in one shot if you can. It will be time well spent.
non-japanese visual novels aren't usually this good...

Over the Hills and Far Away isn't a war story, where you see a brave soldier who win a glorious battle and comes back home to his wife and kids. It's a story about a soldier who choose to live instead of dying on the battlefield, and a child who got sold into slavery and who dreams of coming back home to her village.
This is one of my favourite stories, and I'm actually a bit sad that I bought it during a -75% sale because it feels like I paid too little for something great. Everything about it is absolutely wonderful, the way the game is written, the lovely watercolour style and the characters.
Great music, somewhat culturally enriching, and all around solid writing and editing.

My biggest problem with this game, is that it forces me to experience this as a movie that I'm supposed to take serious. But it's not a good movie, and it's too ridiculous to take seriously. It feels like one long cutscenes interspliced with bits of gameplay. One thing that really irritates me in a game, is when I'm forced to watch a cutscene, then I get to "play" by moving my character forward 10 feet, and then it goes into another cutscene. This happens so much in this game, and it is so frustrating to me. I feel so disconnected from the character I'm supposed to be embodying. It's more like borrowing the character than actually playing as him.
This falls heavily within the "press forward to game"-category, where you're not really playing as much as you are moving a character from cutscene to cutscene, or from cutscene to QTE-based fights. It's a cinematic experience (I guess), so if you're into that sort of thing, try it out. If you want an actual game, then don't buy this.

This is a nice fantasy strategy conquest game that still needs to have some loose ends tied up.  This game still has a few bugs and there are some aspects of this game which still needs work.
The best thing about this game is the lore and history of all of the 35 provinces you can play.  On the default map there is a real storytelling about how the High Elves are forming alliances but the Night Elves don't think it's a good idea.  Meanwhile the Vessoi are looking for a few specific totems on the northern side of the map to wipe out all of the races south of them.  Just so much going on and I love every detail!
5 ways to play each province.  3 of them are always the same for each province, but there are 2 of them which are distinctly different that goes along with the story.  You will either complete the objectives set out for you for the province or simply wipe out your rival.
There are a lot of different units to choose from and each race will have a different unique unit.
In addition to have different units for each race, they will usually need different resources to create them.  This makes having a production of a certain resource invaluable (especially for trade!) However, once the game begins to get to the later stages, it doesn't necessarily become a problem.
Trading is limited by how many agents your specific province can have.  That means if you are playing a province who can only have 1 agent, you must do everything with that one guy which is good or bad depending on how you look at it but in the end it does prolong the game when you are winning.
As I said in the foreword there are a few things that this game needs to work on:
Auto battles.  Though you will normally use this when you are at an advantage and should technically win, it doesn't seem to separate your melee and missle ranged troops.  Often times, both will become hit by whatever is on the field.  Also my missle ranged units will stand in the front lines for some unknown reason and I cannot arrange them the way I like.
Tactical battles.  Obviously the AI does not do as well as a human player in this mode and you can pretty much outwit the AI even if they are supposed to win.
Game is a bit too easy to play.  The AI tends to make a bunch of the easy to kill units and doesn't mix their units up very well.  They will at times not attack you when you are weaker than they are.
Objectives aren't always clear.  I played as the Cloudfels and it says to take over a plains province, which I did but it still did not fulfill on my objectives that I did.
There are still a good bit of bugs.  UI bugs such as while scrolling through a list of names of provinces, they get stuck together.  From what I read there is a bug for a few of the province's objectives.
Overall a fun game to play with a lot of potential to become one of the better games in your steam library.  However this is still an unfinished game needing a lot more polish.

7 Hours. One sitting. And all I got was Gender Bender Quest RPGMaker Edition.
. Now, Victim of Xen isn't too bad of a game, rather it is the apotheosis of the run-of-the-mill collection of RPGMaker games.
The story itself kicks off at an admittedly gripping start, because the prospect of a fine gentleman (named Will(iam)) suddenly switching genders as the result of a laid back witch isn't something you'd see everyday. To the game's demise, however, the shock dwindles considerably due to plenty of stark blemishes in the gameplay, which will NOT go without mentioned. As you chase down Xen to, put it simply, smack the ♥♥♥♥♥, you will meet a couple of dashing characters. Unless dashing goes with negative connotation, perhaps I am being too flattering, because the game offers truly uninteresting charcaters with such banal personalities and ideals. No interest will be given to these characters also because no information or backstory about them is given to the player to make them hold any regard for them (
), which becomes frustrating when one character mentions a previous event the player has no background of, which happens so very frequently throughout the duration of this game. On the character notion, Victim of Xen is a moderately long game for the RPGM collection, yet the writers failed miserably to blossom any development in the characters other than MC's "don't be the plaything of fate" rubbish, let alone any chemistry between them. Instead, the writer(s) decided to make the characters here spit out vexatious one-liners that would make even the most jaded RPG fan cringe. Xen was probably the only one that was enjoyable watching. The nonchalant manner she presented herself in was fun, but very seldom you see her in action, though being
. Horrible is not quite the word to use for these characters, but they are so mindlessly colorless it will be one of the reasons one brings down the game greatly. The narrative is also brought down by it's sub-par plot pacing. The story that goes in an insane velocity becomes an unmitigated mess after the player's arrival at Opress Castle. Soon after Will is sent to the Oasis because *spoiler*, the story becomes sluggish as molasses and difficult to want to follow as a game people would think would be done in about three hours turns into a 8 hour expedition to "save the world". Also the ending sucks gargantuan balls, but it's practially suicide for me to discuss how disappointing it was.
Nothing is worse than a game with plodding gameplay, and this is absolutely Victim of Xen's first shortcoming, and this is seen most prominently in the first 2 hours or so of the game. You start off as the only member in your party and a very brittle-boned one at that, so if players don't play their cards diligently they will start smacking their desks in anguish. After Markus, party member #2 enters the stage, battles devolve to ones effortlessly simple, lacking in variety, and easily exploited once you acquire OP weapons as the game progresses. Most players won't need to waste time leveling up once you get possesion of some decent gear, so most of your battles from random encounters will consist of selecting the Escape option in the battle menu. Should you not choose to flee, the oher functions pertaining to the battle system are easily the most uninspired aspect of Victim of Xen. The developer did not even attempt to provide something different than the barebones template of gameplay of Attack-Defend-Item-Focus(Fancy word for Special Attacks, which are also not exciting). There is a reasonable amount of side missions, but most of them are fetch/delivery quests which will drain any entertainment you are garnering from the game at a faster rate.  It works for what it is, but in the abscence of remote substance in story is only rational to think other facets of the game will make-up for it. This is not the case whatsoever, and the game suffers from a dearth of these two crucial necessities as the game doesn't even have one of these things.
Functionality is important in a game, the most pivitol criteria at that, but they also need to go further in order to impress players and to warrant the purchase. You get what you pay for with this one. I payed 30 cents for a bundle including this, so that statement has an even more ponderous application for myself. Victim of Xen is akin to gazing at the clouds. Unless one spends time scrutinizing the small stuff until you find something worthwhile, it is just a mess of boring material.

It took me eleven years to get around to playing Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. I'm glad that I finally did. Because while it was released back in 2003, it still holds up today. The story is by far the best aspect of this game. Even though I already knew about the major plot twist (because, let's face it, after eleven years, what Star Wars fan doesn't?) it was enjoyable. Of course, the graphics are dated, but other than that, this game is solid. Of course it sounds exactly like Star Wars. From blasterfire to the soft humming of a lightsaber. Though I do feel it gets a bit too much praise at times. For instance, they give you a lot of options when it comes to fighting, but the fights themselves feel very distant. They never got really hard or engaging. There's  tons of force powers to acquire, but for me the fights usually boiled down to wailing on enemies with my lightsaber and healing every now and then. I tried different playing styles, but it always came down to that in the end. Not the strongest gameplay ever seen in an RPG, but the story more than makes up for it. What I also disliked, was the fact that there's one choice at the end, which can negate all of the choices you've made up until that point. I put 25 hours into an evil playthrough, only to (accidentally, because I thought killing a traitor was more evil than welcoming that traitor back onto the team) get a neutral ending. 25 hours of being evil, down the drain. That really left a sour taste in my mouth after what had been a very positive experience. Other than those two points of critique, the game is great. Any fan of Star Wars, or BioWare RPG's because their stamp is all over it, should give this a shot.

Evoland was the greatest barometer I could have ever had to let me know it was time for a new computer.
A love letter to RPGs of days past, Evoland tells a story that's not really too important.  Beginning with a silent, black and white, pixellated game, you will slowly unlock more and more gameplay mechanics.  Rapidly, you will gain sound, the use of a weapon, and then color, and then improved scrolling, and then better color, and on and on.  The true joy of Evoland is the anticipation of whatever's going to happen next.  With my last computer, my clunky processor ground itself to dust trying to handle the 3D graphics as soon as I unlocked them, rendering me unable to complete the game until I upgraded to a dedicated gaming rig.
You progress through a number of different gamestyles, and all of the familiar RPG tropes are lovingly shoehorned in.  There's Zelda-style dungeons, and areas featuring turn-based battles - even a Triple Triad-styled card game.
It's best not to expect a grand epic adventure - it's just not here.  The speed of your upgrades peaks really early and then kind of flatlines a bit - one of the biggest criticisms of the game is it gets boring once the upgrades have been seen.  That's a little true, but things pick up a bit in a late dungeon that involves time travel.
Also, this game is very short, which is a plus in this case - it's enough to give you a taste of what you came for in the first couple of hours or so, and then coasts to a pretty quick conclusion.
A lovely nostalgia trip.

No matter who wins or loses a war there is always pain left behind -for the victor, the vanquished, and even for those who try to remain neutral. Set in the War of 1812,
tells the story of a soldier and a little girl on the run in a harsh and unforgiving world. This game is a kinetic visual novel, meaning there are no choices to be made, the entire experience is reading. While this may not be everyone’s cup of tea the story itself is very much worth it as this is
In the game you follow an Englishman named William Aubrey, a redcoat who was conscripted into the British army and sent to fight in North America. While the game doesn’t require you to be an expert in American history it does require you understand the basics of the period. Aubrey, as the game refers to him, has abandoned his regiment due to its poor leadership and is now wounded, on the run from his own countrymen and American forces. Aubrey takes refuge in an old barn sharing the space with a young native girl.  Finding her name too hard to pronounce, he nicknames her “Mai”. What follows is a touching story of two people from different worlds trying to find the same thing- safety and happiness.
, a theme featured heavily in the game.
, the models are well done and really express each character’s personality. There aren’t many characters in the game as most of the time is spent with Aubrey and Mai and we rarely see much of Aubrey at all so a lot of the time you are stuck looking at just the background images while reading text. Thankfully, there are a few scattered cutscenes mixed in during certain plot points which add to the visual appeal of the game. The music is also enjoyable, fitting of the time period and location of the story. You can purchase the soundtrack separately as well.
The game is a visual novel and being as there are no choices to be made there is little in terms of gameplay here. The game runs well, all the menus are easy to read and you are given basic options that I feel any visual novel should have; mainly adjusting the text speed and the ability to put the text on autoplay. Since
, the autoplay feature allows you to sit back and relax while reading along. The game also has a gallery so that you can look at past cutscenes, concept art and background art at your leisure.
This is an outstanding piece of work, the story is rich and the characters are enjoyable and I found them easy to relate to as well. I enjoyed the historical background of the story, I even learned a few things as well.
has many different layers to it, the harshness of war, the treatment of native people, a person’s own struggle to find where they belong but it’s all told wonderfully in this visual novel format with great art and music to move along with the story.
that you can easily get by just playing through the story so that is also an added bonus. It may not be the happiest of stories, but most happy stories to come out of war are despite the war, not because of it.  It’s worth reading, so open yourself up to something new.

An interesting, albeit quite short (for a fast reader like myself) visual novel.
Interesting setting, well-defined characters, lush artwork, and a strong soundtrack carry the narrative, but I thought that the main narrative was a bit cliched. Overall, I enjoyed it, because I love colonial America and feel that it's a highly underused setting. I do, however, think that it could've been longer (as you can see by my play time, I didn't manage to rack up the hours other reviewers have), and more well-developed thematically (Mai's monologue at the end especially hinted at some interesting themes that could've been expanded). I also would've liked a bit more background about the characters to make the final confrontation a bit more satisfying. Alternate endings or routes likewise would've rounded out the experience.
Overall, it's one of the more enjoyable visual novels on Steam, and if you can catch it on sale (I wouldn't pay full price for something of this length), it's a good way to spend an afternoon.

The down sides that i've noticed include a couple of repetitive battles (same types of armies, using the same strategy keep smashing against my Strongholds). The AI isn't always perfect in the tactical battles but I can always use the simpler battle model to up the challenge level. I'll hold off for now because the AI still frequently makes an unexpectedly cleve move and the tactical simulation is simply more engaging.
All in all, this game is excellent (8/10) for early access. It might need some glossing. For example, better flavor text for the units instead of military-political quotes would go a long way to give life to an already fascinating world where history, politics and culture tie into game. I want to Re-Review Awesomenauts to hopefully clear some things up or at least explain things to new players, returning players, or people who just got this in some random humble bundle and never played it until seeing this brand new shiny update. TL;DR In short, I loved awesomenauts when it first came out and played probably 70 hours in the course of 3 months but since then the game has become irrelevant and dead- F2P will likely not fix this and the incorrect decisions are already being made.
When Awesomenauts came out it was a novel concept that dragged many people in, and the severs were well populated for a year plus. It was the first truly casual MOBA with sidescrolling elements- gone was the annoying shop where you have to study the metagame constantly to know what to buy, and in was unique items for each character that allowed diversity never before seen in one of these games. The maps had strange experimental elements to them like having to press buttons to release extra waves of minions and having large areas that would just pretty much instantly kill you at certain points of the map, making it more similar to a game like smash brothers than something like league of legends. Also it had multiple maps that would rotates whenever you played a new game, something that at the time was fresh and cool for the genre.
Time passed, and suddenly the game pretty much died overnight. Ronimo kept releasing huge patches and expansions to keep the game relevant, and while it worked for a few days after each patch, less people came every time. The expansions themselves had mixed reviews- if you bought one you got access to heroes that other people with just the base game couldn't play, so many people called them OP and paying to win.
Eventually, they straight up overhauled the way you level up in game and retooled the damage numbers. This sounds fairly standard in online game balancing, but this ended up totally busting the game. It made it so if you won the initial skirmish it was impossible to lose and you kept steamrolling due to the distribution of the EXP. This broke the game for almost a month and basically put a stake in the heart of the dedicated playerbase that was left. Not everyone decided to jump ship, but it divided an already measly playerbase and made matchmaking even longer.
A few months ago is when I last played Awesomenauts. Checking the patch notes, not enough has changed for me to say that I don't know how the game plays currently. The game will not benefit from a F2P patch at all and will only serve to make people angry that they paid for a game that is now going free (personally I'm completely fine with it, but I know others won't be). This is because of 2 main reasons, one because of the game itself and one because of the MOBA community as a whole:
1) Due to the game's lifespan, new players will get steamrolled. This sounds like an obvious thing to say, but it's especially relevant to Awesomenauts. Due to the long waits for each person to find a match as of recent years, the only people left playing the game regularly are people who are extremely dedicated. Thus you have a bunch of high prestige players who know every small nook and cranny of this game and how the meta works down to a tee slapping the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of players who are just learning the basic mechanics. When I played the free weekend a short while back, the matches were insanely imbalanced and the only things I heard in chat were people going "this game is terrible". You'd either be matched with a prestige 8 or something and win with no contest having no fun, or be on the opposite team of the prestige 8 and lose with no hope of coming back and having no fun. I'm sure these 150 people who are the dedicated fan base of this game will have fun wiping the floor of the influx of newbies, but this fresh blood will likely have none of it and quit after getting their♥♥♥♥♥handed to them for a few matches.
2) There now exists better casual MOBA titles. This is a pretty cynical thing to say, but honestly it's true. Most of the unique mechanics awesomenauts had in 2012 have now been taken and put into more polished and balanced MOBA games with larger playerbases. For a specific example, Heroes of the Storm by Blizzard Entertainment took the unique powerups, rebalanced them into a talent system, and also took the map system to make it more interesting. And as much as you don't like the game you can't deny that a triple A company with one of the most popular series of games will instantly have a bigger playerbase than a small indie title with playerbase balance issues.
The only thing I'd recommend Awesomenauts for now is couch multiplayer, as the way it's formatted you can easily play with multiple people in the same room without it getting confusing. But unfortunately for some reason they removed local co-op, so I don't even know what to recommend this game for anymore. The music is good along with the graphics? There isn't really another sidescrolling MOBA on the market? All in all I can only recommend this as a curiosity piece at this time since you're not really losing anything due to the fact that it's F2P.

tl;dr: This game is great. Get it.
Endless Legend is a turn based strategy game that takes the best elements of classic series such as Heroes of Might and Magic and Civilization, and combines them to create a product that is greater than the sum of its parts.
The core of the game is to build your empire as one of several extremely unique factions.  There are the Broken Lords, beings that inhabit suits of armor and subsist entirely on Dust, the game's equivalent of gold, bypassing the need for food entirely.  Or there are the Necrophages, a sentient insect race that devour everything in their path, including their own citizens if they desire.  There is a faction that controls the world markets and cannot declare war, and a faction that values diplomacy and can force peace treaties and alliances.  These are just a sample of the factions, and each one brings with it an entirely unique strategy.
Much like the Civilization series, players have an option for how they would like to pursue victory.  In addition to staples like Domination or Scientific victories, there are also more unique victory methods such as the Expansion victory where the goal is to control over 70% of the territories on the map.  There is even a storyline victory,  in which players can race to unlock the secrets of their faction and the world of Auriga as a whole.
Developing territory in this game is incredibly satisfying as well.  Each region in the game can only be occupied by one city, and the owner of that city becomes the owner of that territory, thereby gaining control of any resources that territory may hold.  Developing cities is much more interesting than just building a bunch of buildings as well.  Players can expand the amount of tiles their city exploits by actually building expansion districts that visibly increase the size of their city, in addition to providing increased resource generation.
Combat is a unique affair where both sides battle for six turns.  Units and generals can be outfitted with an assortment of different gear types that affect everything from their damge and defense, to providing unique abilities such as retaliating against everything around the unit.  The battles play out automatically with some strategical assistance from the player.  If the battles aren't decided within the six turns, they are considered a draw.
One the biggest hurdles to overcome when playing Endless Legend is the UI.  While extremely informative and clean, it provides a lot of information that can be daunting to newer players.  My recommendation is to take time to complete the tutorials provided in game, as they cover all of the basics and really help familiarize players with the UI as well.
If you enjoy 4x and turn based strategy games, you owe it to yourself to give this game a shot.  The base game is a great price, and frequently goes on sale, and the expansions only serve to improve the experience.

This game is still one of my favorite games I've ever played. It's Star Wars with a fantastic story, good turn based gameplay and with plenty of hours of content to keep players happy. Set 4,000 years before the events of Episode IV, this game tells the story of the Sith Lords Revan and Malak and their attempt at taking over the galaxy. The Republic is embattled and on the edge of falling to conquest. It is up to you and your rag-tag team of companions to bring an end to the Sith and save the Republic from certain destruction. There are many opportunities for morality choices in this game between the Light and Dark Side to create a varied experience as well as two different endings. This game is a bit simpler than modern Western RPGs in choice and morality scales, but considering its age and how it fits its mechanics in its story, this can be overlooked.
Combat is solid for its intentions. If you are not a player that enjoys turn based and paper RPG-like mechanics like behind the scenes dice rolls for attacks, saves, hits, defenses, stuns etc., then this game is probably going to be on the dry side for you if not completely boring. It's simpler than Dragon Age Origin's combat system and is not an action RPG in the same vein as Mass Effect. (Jade Empire would probably be closer to ME and is sold on GoG with better compatibility for Win 7 and 8 users.) Despite its simplicity, the gameplay is fun and works perfectly in regard to its own rules. You aren't going to find any bugs or glitches in this aspect of the game.
This particular version of the game is superior to its original Xbox counter part in that it has a much easier to use UI and runs faster, smoother and looks better. (Granted the graphics aren't something that have aged as well as other parts of the game regardless of the version played.) However, where the Xbox version completely trumps this one is stability. There are many, many people that have issues getting this game to even run on Windows 7 and 8 machines. The most common issue seems to be with the cutscenes. Turning them off completely will help, though unfortunately you would be missing out on some context in the story if you go this route. If you run Windows 7, I would suggest looking into guides on how to set up compatibility modes for the game. I was able to get the movies to run relatively well on my Win 7 laptop using this video guide:
Unfortunately this doesn't seem to be a universal fix considering some people still report problems running the game after following these instructions.
For Windows 8, I have so far lucked out on my PC. I have recently played about 4 hours or so on a new file and have only experienced one issue of the game minimizing itself during a cutscene. I was able to click back into the game where it started where it left off and showed the complete scene.
I recommend this game because it is still a great RPG and is a wonderful Star Wars experience. Arguably one of the best Star Wars media ever made and is certainly on top of the EU pile. However, I would only look into buying this game during a Steam sale considering its current issues. If you run XP, then you'll likely have very little issue running this game since that is the OS it was released for and the $9.99 price will be a very low risk. Windows 7 and 8 users should be aware that there is a chance that you will never get this game to work properly. For $4.99, as it's often priced during sales, it's not a massive risk and I was personally okay with experimenting on it for the gamble that I could get an excellent game to work on a platform that allows modding as opposed to it's closed system counterpart on the Xbox.

The problem is that with the exception of the early Zelda'esque gameplay Evoland is just not very fun.  There is less than three hours of game and it still feels drawn out.
The puzzle sections see you trudging backwards and forwards along the same path time and time again.  The traps are cheap and the monsters re-spawn which makes reloading and replaying the same stage a chore.
Once the game has evolved to Final Fantasy style random encounters it becomes very annoying as an encounter happens every three to tens seconds on the world map.  There is almost no need for interaction during encounters as the combat is basically: hit with one character heal group with the other.  Walk through some trees.  Repeat with the next encounter.
The Torchlight styled sections could have been fun but the collision detection is so utterly awful that melee hits tend to miss.  Fighting degenerates into mashing the hit button until the area attack is charged.  Again repeat.
Really this game had a lot of potential but there is so little content (repeated ad-nauseam) that I do begrudge the time I spent to complete it.

- The visuals of Anoxemia are immersive and follow a kind of silhouette style. The graphics are dark and gloomy and can be eye-strainingly difficult to see at times, although this adds to the immersion. The colours and light in this game are wonderful, while the jellyfish swimming in the background are magestic. Overall, the graphics quality and visual style of Anoxemia are very decent.
- The audio in this game are muffled and ambient, as you would expect from an underwater game. The sounds are great and reflect that you are underwater. The voice acting is good for the most part, and helps guide you in the game. The music in this game is relaxing and soothing, and it was unexpectedly well made. Overral, the audio of Anoxemia is pretty good.
- In Anoxemia, you go through 38 levels, which each take 2-10 minutes depending on how good you are. I'm around a third of the way throught the levels and I've played just under an hour, so I would say that the length is alright. In each level, you must get to a certain area or collect certain materials. You mostly need to collect some samples of plants which are found along the levels. You do this by navigating the drone while Bailey straggles behind, and he will collect the items/plants. Along the levels you will encounter obstacles which you need to overcome, such as puzzles or enemies. Enemies and mines have to be avoided, and rocks can be pushed or pulled to block or reveal entrances. You need to keep up your energy levels and to keep Bailey oxygenated, and you do this by collecting the energy and oxygen items on the levels. Honestly, I found Bailey to be a liability in this game, while the story does revolve around him, the game is basically just a big escort mission, as you control a drone which does all the work. Bailey just tags along and helps you by dying from asphyxiation. All in all, I found the gameplay of Anoxemia to be refreshing and fun, albeit frustrating at times.
- The story is a major focus for Anoxemia. Personally I found it bland and nothing unique or exciting. The journey of the game was somewhat enthralling but the story behind is was meh. Bailey's narrations in-game are nice, and allow for story development outside of the cutscenes. I won't say much to avoid spoilers, but the story overview can be found in the description on the store page anyway. The story in Anoxemia is sufficient, but fails to captivate.
- This game features a few graphical presets, and very minimal settings for anything else. The controls are kind of confusing to start with, and I had to rebind some controls. The game runs very smoothly even on max settings. There are many small annoyances like getting stuck in rubble which takes too long to diminish, and Bailey gettings stuck on anything due to his lack of AI. On later levels, it becomes almost impossbile to past because whenever I activate a level to open a door, I get sucked into the ground and have to restart the level. Sometimes Bailey clips through the terrain too and gets stuck. It is extremely annoying and I cannot beat the level due to this glitch consistently occuring. The functionality of Anoxemia is too poor for me to continue on with the game.
If you're looking for an underwater adventure such as Song of the Deep, then I suggest you give Anoxemia a try.
I recommend this game due to its cheap price.
I give this game a 4/10, a beautiful underwater adventure game provides substantial entertainment, but is severely broken and frustrating in later stages.
EDIT: I'll have to change my review to negative after playing for a couple more hours. I've started to experience dreadful glitches where I get stuck inside the terrain, so I'm forced to restart levels. I cannot recommend this game anymore unfortunately.
I hope the developer can fix these issue, because otherwise this is a very great game.

Takes the Word Visual Novel literally and includes no interactivity outside of clicking or pressing the spacebar to progress the story.
