Do you like Civ but feel a bit distant to the historical aspects? Give Endless Legend a try. EL is in my opinion the best example of a city/empire building multiplayer game to date. It is clear that it has helped influence titles that came after it.
Quick talking points:
The interface is clean and straightforward.
Resources and tech tree is varried, interesting and complex while not being too daunting.
The races are all interesting and have their own 'quests' which add alot of motivation to build up hero units and explore.
Balance is good in defualt races.
Customization of game type/modes/enviro is good, many options to tailor to your particular play preferences.
Battles are interesting, though autocombat is satisfying and what I prefer to use (it rarely feels unbalanced as in many other games where manual or autobattles can be selected)
The lore actually ties in with the other 'Endless' games, (Dungeon of the Endless, Endless Space) and the art direction is great in personal opinion. The simple designs and colors help keep things disticntive on the worldmap and prevents clutter that many civ games are prone to.
I've put alot more time into the game than listed in offline modes, and lan play is fantastic, rarely does the game drop out of sync and it recovers very well.
The only major gripe is it's inconsistency on MacOS, it appears to have some memory issues as it tends to crash in long sessions, been years since release so its probably not going to get fixed, still the cross platform play works well otherwise and the regular expansions are greatly appreciated and have all added something interesting to the base gameplay.
I have become fan of Amplitude and am eager to see them continue this particular game series as well as the 'Endless' franchise itself in the future.

Avoid this dev at all costs! Look at the forums and Metacritic that point out the abysmal plot, grammar, and story telling. Not only are they unskilled at this, but they are unable to handle criticism. If you sell something to the public, it's got to be good enough to play. This isn't.
The point regarding the wine bottle is that no one who speaks English says that! You say 'I want a bottle of wine', not a 'wine bottle'. Do you get it now? English may not be the dev's first language, but if it's sold in English, tough.
Original review:
Painfully clunky and slow in every aspect. I love RPGs, but the direction and story here are simply terrible.
First, your grandmother asks you to pick up a 'wine bottle' from the pub. 'I'll be happy with my wine bottle' she says when you give it to her. Every piece of dialogue is written like this.
Secondly, you do a quest for an older gent which involves going into the caves beneath his house. All you're told is 'clear it out'. Random attacks happen, and someone throws down a rope. Going back up moves nothing on, because you were supposed to *jump* up onto a cliff face and chase an imp into a smaller cave. You're not told you can jump, or that the quest is up there - but if you don't do this, you'll not advance with the plot.
A witch called Xen storms into town and casually turns your character into a girl. This is the whole plot, from what I can tell. There's no reason for the witch to do this, bar she's taking over villages for no particular reason and boom, gender switch.
I realise this game is cheap, and I wanted to enjoy it. However, the woeful writing and storyline make it agony to play, and I'm sorry I bought this in a bundle. Avoid at all costs. If you want a genuinely enchanting RPG with a positive plot, may I recommend Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale? It's charming and enjoyable, with many hidden plot twists and character stories.

hard to get into, even harder to master, but 100% worth the time and effort. now the game comes only with ARK:SE, its easier to assume new players have access to an environment they can learn at their own pace.
SOTF puts your ability to survive to the real test, forcing players to adapt to random pre-determined events that can make or break your strategy for a game on their own, but subject all players to the same element of risk and reward. there are many ways to win, many more ways to play and have fun, and the games last a pretty standard amount of time, which makes it a more casual-friendly (if very intense) game to play based on time commitment versus the main game (ARK:SE).
there are limited tools to learning how to play out there, but there are plenty of means to do your own research.
is a good resource for learning recipes and requirements to tame certain types of dinosaurs, but SOTF has its own variations on the main game (usually to make it easier to achieve within the smaller timeframe of a SOTF game) that take a bit of learning.
the game is a baptism of fire for the unprepared as it is pure pvp and despite being a stand-alone to the main game, it very much requires some basic knowledge of the main game to get by. being efficient in everything you do is critical and it takes practice to build it up.
would highly recommend that players try the main game first, but hone their PVP skills in SOTF as soon as they are "comfortable" with the PVE elements of the main game. making friends in the regular game is easier as well as there isn't any time pressures on being in the same lobby, and that lobby isnt usually entirely focused on killing everyone else in that lobby!
so tl:dr - playing the main game is almost essential to get started, but isn't required once you start to build up your skill level. if you like a challenge in survival, this game is 100% for you.

A princípio é um jogo que trás uma fórmula simples de jogo. Você, incorporado em Marine Interstellar qualquer, é designado a desativar mecanismos eletrônicos de uma nave já infestadas por alieníginas. O diferencial deste jogo é sua simplicidade. Não há muito o que fazer senão atirar nos inimigos para salvar sua vida. O jogo não conta com um sistema de Check Points muito menos com Health. Totamelmente Perma-Death. Se o alienígina te pegar com um simples hit você morre e é obrigado a começar tudo de novo. O que naturalmente deixa o jogo bem mais interessante devido ao fato que você deve ter um extremo cuidado na hora de enfrentar seus inimigos nos corredores escuros da nave. O clima também não deixa a desejar. Por ser um jogo simples, conta com uma atmosfera bastante cativante. O clima do jogo, com suas músicas de fundo e sua baixa visibilidade, dá um ar de tensão quando os inimigos se aproximam, deixando o jogo bem tenso aos que tentam sobreviver e completar os objetivos. O jogo não dispôe (talvez ainda) de modo MP. Entretanto é um jogo que vale a pena se você busca um pouco de Survive Horror com uma mescla de ação no mais Alien/The thing que possa existir por aí (aos leigos Alien e The thing são clássicos do cinema). Enfim, pelo preço cobrado e a ideia oferecida, vale a pena dar uma chance!

A game that truly feels like Aliens, with all the claustrophobia and hyperlethality of Space Hulk. The way the soundtrack automatically jumps and your FOV tunnelvisions when an alien appears in your field of view might initially seem cheap, but it's actually one of the most immersive ways I've seen a shooter implement a horror mechanic. The music also creeps up should an alien be creeping up on you, which is a godsend when you're too busy blasting away to glance down at your motion tracker and don't realize that a xenomorph's coming from behind. When you're done winding down from the adrenaline pump, having activated a sentry gun in a bottleneck and fled past the waves, there's a neat little snare drum rat-at-tat-tat that lets you know you're off the hook for at least the few seconds. The way your movement rate automatically goes from a sedate jog when all's quiet to a breakneck sprint for survival isn't just for effect or to add spookiness, it actively helps keep you alive when an alien suddenly bursts out from the breach you've got no choice but to brush past. All and all, it creates an extremely atmospheric experience that combines horror and gunplay in way that modern titles can't do with millions of dollars of budget.
There are some wonky things that can ruin seemingly good runs, though. While enemies can only spawn out of extremely obvious and visible breaches, they don't have any kind of animation that leaves them vulnerable. This means that you can be watching your (upgraded) motion tracker, see and hear zero blips anywhere near you, round a corner where there's a breach in the ceiling, and instantly die because an alien spawned right next to you. The solution to that of course is to never take even a fully upgraded motion tracker for granted, but it's still a tad frustrating. The sentry guns are actually relatively intelligent about friendly fire 99% of the time, refusing to shoot through you and instead giving a telltale klaxon to let you know that they have no shot, but since the bullets do have a marginal travel time, it is in fact possible to walk into the flight path of a bullet and (instantly) die. Also, reduced download time meshes poorly with a large battery and unupgraded recharge time, since currently you only recharge when actually downloading. Allowing you to interact with terminals purely to recharge your battery for just a few extra seconds here and there would be a nice touch.
The multiplayer is only splitscreen right now, which is an experience I wouldn't wish on anyone with all the obstrusive graphical elements included. (I'll admit that I have to remove all the graphical elements to have a hope of completing a level as I get used to the system and how dramatically my mouse sensitivity and movement can change on a dime.) Given the snap reflexes needed to Not Die in this game (a "mere" 150ms is the difference between life and instant death), I wonder how they'll handle the netcode for the online multiplayer - it's likely that the only way to reasonably do it without seemingly randomly killing players will be by computing much of the mechanics clientside.
The game itself is a skeleton right now, but it's a skeleton so solid and functional and with so few flaws that I can't wait to see it grow muscles and skin. There's a lot of room for alternate modes: one where upgrades are purchased up front via a pointbuy/cash system at the beginning of the level with no upgrades to be found midlevel, a mode with a hard timer rather than a soft one through ammo count, a mode that would let you tinker with map parameters like doors, average corridor length, and number of objectives and sentry guns... Once networked multiplayer is made, the doors get blown wide open: a mode with aliens under player control, a mode with a human commander browbeating a squad of other humans as stumble through a map with asynchronous intel available to either party... there's nowhere for this game to go but up. I'm not normally an early access guy, but the game as it stands right now is worth $15, and possibly of expansion can only increase your investment.

In space, no one can hear you scream. Or yell in frustration. The good kind of frustration. The kind that makes you keep coming back, then dying. And dying. And dying some more.
Space Beast Terror Fright is an arcade-style shooter / horror game set aboard a randomly generated, pitch-black space installation or ship. From the moment you step on board the foreign spacecraft, hordes of alien beasts not unlike the creatures from the "Alien" series of movies begin breaching the hull of the ship and stalking you. Your objective is to move around the spacecraft, avoiding and killing off aliens in order to find and enable a number of datacores scattered around the ship, then set the ship to self-destruct and finally escape back to the airlock before the entire thing goes boom. Add in a permanent death element and insta-kill enemies and you have one of the most intense, difficult and adrenaline-pumping games in years.
From the getgo, you're launched into an incredibly difficult environment with limited equipment, although for every datacore you find, you recieve upgrades like thermal vision, stronger weapons and faster download times. There are automatic turrets that can be activated all around the ship to defend important chokepoints or protect you from an oncoming assault. The entire game plays out very quickly; sitting around for too long is almost certain doom. Firing your gun illuminates the screen, obscuring your vision behind smoke and muzzle flashes to the point that you can't see even a foot in front of you. Overall, the game feels like a very accurate depiction of the later half of the film "Aliens" - desperate marines rushing through darkness to escape a constantly aggressive and hostile threat.
The grame feels and looks great, from the dark corridors lit up by dim lights that silhouette the shapes of the vicious alien invaders to the beautifully designed helmet-mounted HUD, complete with somewhat dysfunctional motion tracker (which adds to the desperate mood). I've never had a good look at the aliens themselves, so I can't tell you how they look, which is exactly how a horror game villain should be. Sound design is just as fantastic, with gunshots echoing out and overlapping all other noise (potentially masking the sounds of aliens approaching from the rear) as the soundtrack fluctuates to accent the action of the moment. All aspects of the design are extremely well done, immersing you right into the horrific environment of the murky, alien-infested starship.
The controls are incredibly simple, with only three or four buttons aside from the basic movement keys being used altogether. Doors are opened and consoles activated with a single click - the perfect design choice for the panicing space marine. Gameplay, while still relatively simple, can be intense and is always a fresh experience. Sometimes the aliens will breach the ship near a critical data core console, forcing you to stay on your toes as you download the data. The final rush to the airlock is an extremely intense experience, with players sprinting to reach the end amidst the whirring sirens and screaming aliens. The game is very hard alone, though it can be played via classic 4-way splitscreen co-op and will soon have multiplayer added as well. All in all, this game has some of the most intense, terrifying and addicting gameplay I've experienced in a game thus far. Death in a level will not only reset your mission count to zero, but will also remove all the upgrades you've found via datacores amongst other progress, making teamwork and caution paramount. Space Beast Terror Fright - despite its rather long name - is an excellent game, unique in several ways. A proper Aliens game has finally been made and its name is Space Beast Terror Fright. You and your friends are Marines who are given the simple objective of recovering all data cores on a ship and then overload that ships reactors and escaping back to your shuttle before the ship blows. There's just one problem, the ship is completely infested with Aliens.
Ever since I was a kid I have always wanted a game like this. A game where there is no massive story you are just a marine with a job to do on various different locations involving Aliens. This game is essentially Aliens meets Space Hulk vengeance of the blood angels only instead of AI companions it is either just you or 3 of your friends.
You download datacores and all datacores have a chance of giving you an upgrade of which all have their own different levels. For example your basic motion tracker lvl 1 only tells you if something is moving near you. Lvl 2 motion tracker gives you short range blips indicating where enemy positions are and Lvl 3 essentially can detect all motion on the entire ship. You can get infrared vision, better bullets, a map of the ship, more battery life, waypoints pointing to objectives, faster download time of the datacores etc all upgrades have at least 3 more levels to them to improve them such as datacores being downloaded in 7.5 seconds to being download in just 1 second.
To assist you against the aliens the players can activate sentry guns and close off doors to prevent Alien from being able to easily move about the ship. Naturally the Aliens can destroy these doors but the time it takes them can mean the difference between life and death.
Once you have turned off the coolants to the reactor the Marines have 2 minutes to return to the shuttle.
This is a hardcore game you character will die in 1 hit from alien, turret, or fellow marine and once your character is dead so are all his upgrades. If your character gets close to an alien expect him to freak out with adrenaline. He will run quicker but his vision will also be impaired into a sort of tunnel vision. If you manage to complete a mission you carry on the character from the previous mission so you will start a new map with all of your upgrades on that character which will make the mission significantly easier on you and your teammates.
With procedurally generated maps of 3 different level styles, local coop, planned network multiplayer, and hordes of ravenous Aliens how can you go wrong? This is what a proper Aliens game should be and I am very excited to see what the developers will do with this game in the future.
10/10 buy if you are a fan Aliens or Space Hulk. This is what Colonial Marines should have been.

I have decided to write a review that is actually informative and helpful. That being said, this review contains minor spoilers relating to game style and weapon selection.
Do you want to know what you get for $45 with this game? You get several sniper rifles. Half have 5 rounds in the clip, the other half have 7-15. All do more or less the same damage, the ranges are equal, and the scopes vary in the slightest. All of these rifles have indistinguishable feels to them as well regarding how they fire (some have slightly more recoil or a more muffled sound).
You also get secondary weapons, fun right? I guess. There are several smg's that do next to no damage. There is a single smg that easily outpreforms the rest. There is also a shotgun...be ready to use that for the next 6-8 hours of your playtime.
The pistols in your third space are all the same with one exception. The revolver is one shot kill with a chest or headshot. I found myself switching between guns just to feel like I had some choice, but they are nearly identical so it never made a difference.
Now let's talk about how the game works. You are given tasks: get to the safehouse, defend this position, survive this assault, finish off the zombies, find this key. You are always forced to go somewhere, kill everything in order to progress, and then go somewhere else and do the same thing. There is no straying from this formula. Might I mention that the same guns for every mission make these tasks more like chores?
What does the game do well? The question we should really ask is "Who is this game trying to please?" This game is trying to entertain an audience that cares for nothing but aiming and clicking at something and seeing it die. There is no strategy apart from running past as much crap as you can before being forced to clear an area. There is no story aside from "Hitler has a zombie army." There are 3-4 models for the zombies, there are 2 models for the skeleton enemy, and there are a couple other enemies that you will always feel are just an annoyance.
I had fun for about the first 2 hours. Then I realized that the game was not changing. The story does not progress. You spend hours shooting the SAME THINGS with no goal. There is no reward for your efforts aside from seeing a skull explode every time you shoot a zombie from over 50 meters.
How is this different from Call of Duty zombies? It has less selection, less story, less variation between weapons, no increasing difficulty aside from number of zombies that are all equally easy to kill. Is CoD zombies great? It has its flaws, but Zombie Army Trilogy takes a strong backseat with an unoriginal idea and less fleshed out development.
Don't waste your money on all three of this trilogy. If you must, buy the first game and then replay it twice more; this would be no different than playing two and three because they are all the same. Differences between the three? I believe the third has about 4 more enemy types. oh, and the atmosphere changes about two times somewhere in there.
This is a waste. Buy the first or just save your time and money. Stay away from this package. I am sorry that I bought it, hopefully it can be returned.

Fallen Times is an independent first-person-shooter running on the Unity engine and gameplay in a similar fashion to Serious Sam. That means there is plenty of running, pickups, and most importantly, gunning. Oh, and there is a twist. Instead of a muscular action hero blowing apart enemies in a desert with a rocket launcher, you are playing as a kawaii yuri catgirl with an assault rifle (and a variation of other weapons against an even greater variation of enemies).

On a visual spectrum, Fallen Times does have its limitations, especially in the department of animations primarily due to the engine, but for what it manages to pull off, it is very successful. Textures and models are solid and everything looks as it should, whether it be the actual gameplay or the Visual-Novel styled story moments. Environments are semi-open, varied, and beautiful all things considered. I also did not encounter much in the way of slowdown, and load times went very, very quickly.

As for the soundtrack, the game excels. Although I wish the song playing in the trailer made it to the full game, the soundtrack consists of rock music that fits the action-heavy tone of the game, although some more melancholy pieces would have been a nice addition, but no complaints. As for other sounds, except guns that make gun sounds and goat that scream like humans. Yes, you heard that right!

For the controls, the game is great. The menu is very simple to navigate, and it is easy to hop in to each level. Gameplay-wise, it is an old-school FPS that is absolutely old-school in the sense of the word. Freakishly frenetic boss-fights, no regenerating health, a focus on agility/jumping as opposed to stealth, and most importantly, secrets scattered throughout the levels. It may seem basic, but for what the developer has managed, it is quite impressive. The AI is good, noticing when you are close and chasing you down to kill you. The gunplay itself feels good, allowing you to zoom in instead of using iron sights. There is not any gore, but the enemies are still easy to indicate whether you’ve hit them or not thanks to hit-markers. The game is very challenging, but it is by no means impossible, adding further to its old-school influences. Boss fights are hectic and entertaining, and the overall combat feels like a shooter from the mid-late 90s, which is a very good thing!

In regards to replayability, there are many levels and the game is enjoyable enough to warrant multiple playthroughs. The game is never boring, contains a solid story with plenty of heart, and the game is often times hilarious (a gun that shoots chickens for example). On a side note, there are admittedly some typos in the text, which can likely be fixed soon, but they do not detract from the overall experience. In fact, they are quite hilarious. There is no multiplayer, but the single player content alone justifies a purchase. I have spent over twelve hours in my time with this game, but only one hour was registered online, but in that duration, I got a great amount of enjoyment from this game. I did not encounter any glitches in the game during both my plathrouhghs, and likely wont on my third. Fallen Times is a fantastic indie FPS and I am absolutely looking forward to what Dafu Studio will bring us next. It is highly recommended for all fans of classic first-person-shooters or those who like their games simple yet engaging.

I love the concept behind Evoland and I wish I could say the same for the game itself, but I cannot. Clocking in at about 5 hours (optional areas included), Evoland tries to cover a lot of content without delving all that deeply below the surface on any given playstyle.
A very large chunk of the game takes on the form of a 3D turn-based (well, ATB) RPG and this is by far where Evoland suffers the most as random encounters are excruciatingly frequent and rarely do fights consist of more than spamming normal attacks and sometimes tossing out a party heal. Enemies themselves each only have a single attack, missing is surprisingly frequent if you don't grind a bit, and there is no way to use heal items outside of combat.
The other major part of the game, the 2D and 3D top-down Zelda-inspired areas, fairs a bit better, but not by much. You'll fight the same small handful of enemies (skeletons, not-octorocs, not-wizrobes, and a whole lot of bats) from the beginning to the very end in these areas with one or two other enemies appearing here and there. Most of the puzzles in the game are found in these segments, but like most things in Evoland, they rarely provide much of a challenge and often overstay their welcome.
Other aspects of the game simply come off as rushed or otherwise unpolished. There are stars to collect, and some are even well-hidden, but they only give an achievement. There are cards to collect, but there doesn't seem to be any way to view them outside of the card game. The card game itself is somewhat similar to Final Fantasy VIII's Triple Triad, but you are given five cards at random from those you have collected, meaning that it is actually better to actively avoid collecting too many of the weaker cards early on. Some of the writing is clever, but most of it consists of running through RPG cliches and making references for the sake of making references, such as by naming mushroom-shaped enemies 'Zoombas' and having a character named 'Sid'. Of the several optional dungeons in the game, none of them ever pay off with a neat new abilitiy or an optional gameplay evolution or even an optional boss and instead only reward more stars and cards.
Evoland does do a fantastic job of gradually changing up the graphics from start to finish, and both the graphics and the music are impressive at that, but it just doesn't carry this same sense of passion across to the actual gameplay mechanics. Usually, once a new genre or evolution of a genre is introduced the player is handed several new gimmicks to go along with it in rapid-fire succession and then it simply stagnates, as though the jump from 2D to 3D gameplay was the only major innovation to ever happen to RPG's. Players will never get useful things like visible enemies replacing random encounters, interesting things like skill trees, amusingly useless innovations like switching rows in combat, or even many basic functionalities like the ability to block or to use items outside of combat in the RPG sections or the ability to quickswap between items in the Zelda-like sections.
At the end of the day, Evoland has a creative, fun concept which carries it for about half an hour before it falls flat on its face and never really recovers because it simply doesn't run anywhere near far enough with it.

Anoxemia is a great example of a game that wins you over with an elegant design, high quality narration and sound effects, and simple gameplay mechanics that are tough to handle but rewarding. It’s a 2D action game that takes you into the depths of a strange ocean and immerses you into an eerie atmosphere, and guess what? Atmoshpere is  almost everything for me in a game..
One of the main things that attracts attention to Anoxemia, is its apparently simple gameplay. Whereas the controls are intuitive indeed, the actual control of the character is very tricky at times. In the game you actually control an advanced robot drone and the human you follows it around as if he was tied with an invisible rope. Whenever you stop the drone, your character might still move a bit passed it and it could spell disaster when you’re running too close to a mine. This is something that has a lot of potential to become a really fun game. It reminds me of Rainbox Six Vegas 2, one of my all time favourite shooters. I think the major thing the developer needs to focus on is polishing some nice, clean base mechanics and then really pushing for content. The worry with this game could be overdoing it. If executed right, this game could have that simple charm that games like Rainbow Six vegas had. The thing the vegas had and this game didn't is smoothness to the movement. Obviously, this game is very early in its development so I could possibly be too critical in that respect, but it is definitely something that needs to be done right early on.
The planning phase of this game is a really nice feature, but it is hindered a lot (and honestly quite frustrating) by how clunky it is. I think the cameras need a high sensitivity and should controlled with WASD. A and D should look left and right, and W and S should cycle between them. It's nice and quick and can be done without needing to use the mouse for everything. There are like 20 cameras per level and people are going to replay levels a lot so it needs to be fast and convenient in order to avoid it being really frustrating. The last thing you want is a nice quirky feature being ruined by how long it takes to use.
Movement and aiming is something that needs a lot of attention. I feel the base speed should be slightly quicker in general, creeping around everywhere where not much goes on does get a little boring. The aiming is very hard to use due to the glitchyness of it. Couldn't imagine why it is happening but it is very jittery, and I would focus on having cleaner recoil, that was the thing that bugged me about Rainbow six, but you could counter it by going up against the wall. This game (I guess) isn't going in that direction, so clean recoil is a must.
The bots are a little too fast to act. They need to dumbed down a bit by having a delay from when they hear shooting.
Again, It's something I'm sure will be sorted out, but finding out where you are being shot from is a big issue. I can never see the muzzle flare from any guns being fired and there are no damage indicators that I can see.
Story isn't something I expect to get from this game, I really wouldn't care if it is there or not. I think the focus should lie in getting some really good mechanics down and working on fun PvE levels. Because that is where I feel the real value could lie in this game.
Perhaps consider a replay button when you die to go back to the start of the level with your plans already in place with the option to go back and alter the plans instead of wiping them every time.
In short, this could be a game with a lot of playtime value if the Mechanics are cleaned up as soon as possible. It doesn't really need any more features that I can see, just a nice big pollish and then a push for content. I will follow its progress because I really want to see sucess in this title.

Epsilon is not bad for what is being charged at the moment. Epsilon in it's current state (pre-alpha) performs surprisingly well on lower end systems and looks half decent aswell. Epsilon features a few of the game mechanics that made the old Tom Clancy games great such as being able to pre-plan your mission (Rainbow Six 3), the fiber optic camera to scout underneath doors (Splinter Cell and eventually Rainbow Six) and the ability to open doors incrementally to provide much more cover when scouting a room for enemies and making entry kills (Rainbow Six 3). Serellan LLC are known for the subpar game Takedown: Red Sabre but it appears that the devs have taken into consideration what was wrong with the game as a tactical shooter and fixes a few of the problems in Epsilon, however it does carry some of the problems over like the somewhat sluggish movement system and the insanely fast reaction times of the enemy AI at times. Epsilon for what it is worth at the moment is not bad but you may want to hold off buying the game until some of the bugs and gameplay features are ironed out. All in all I like where this game is heading and it is great to see tactical shooters like this and Ground Branch coming back into the gaming world.
Also a message to the devs if they end up reading this:
Don't be afraid to ask the community for suggestions on how to improve the game as we all want to see this become an amazing game and we are happy to help to make this game become better than it already is.

I remember getting this one quickly after playing the first Delta Force game. Man, those were the days!
Not gonna lie: Delta Force 2 is exactly what it is. A sequel at best. There's not much improvement in most departments. This game is basically a big stand-alone expansion of the first DF.
Of course, you could complain that the devs milked the cow a little with this one, but they were answering a legitimate demand from the market. Can't really blame them, right?
Right as you start the game, you will realize that the whole design is pretty similar to Delta Force. The menu is almost the same, but with a different color and different sound effects. On your first mission, you will also acknowledge that the game hasn't changed much visually or gameplay-wise.
But it's still a good FPS. Not great, but good. After all, Delta Force, the first one, was most certainly good. Once again, the campaign missions are diversified and exciting on your first time but they also suffer from the terribly predictable AI which crippled the replay value of the first Delta Force since the characters always do the same things and go to the same locations every single time.
There are some minor additions. A few new items, voice acting during mission briefings and some minor in-game elements/events, but nothing extraordinary.
The main problem is that when Delta Force 2 came out, there were other FPS games on the market which offered more in general, but most especially in the graphics department. The first game of the Unreal franchise quickly comes to mind. Unreal brought unrivaled graphics that came with relatively large areas for the players to explore. DF2 used the Voxel Space Engine which could have been revolutionary if it had been released five years earlier. Unfortunately, when you played Unreal or some other game using a more powerful engine and went back to Delta Force 2, it was a cringy experience even though the available playing area was larger and all that. You enjoyed playing it, but you felt like the Delta Force franchise was definitely at a lower level at that point. When DF2 came out, it didn't feel at all like a AAA title.
Those who are senior gamers in their early 30's will definitely be interested in getting this game. It's cheap nostalgia, even if you never owned it back in the day! Younger players who weren't there back when DF2 came out will most probably be repelled by the aged quality of the game. Can't blame them. If they're looking for low-priced game to play for a few hours, however, they should be satisfied if they aren't too difficult concerning old first person shooters which will inevitably look pretty bad when compared to the monsters they make nowadays.

Space Beast Terror Fright is a game that lets you have an experience very similar to the movie Aliens. The weapon akin to the pulse rifle, the hundreds of xenomorphs, the music, the motion trackers, the sentry guns and their ammo count decreasing too fast, the overall look and feel, and so on. These Aliens elements are integrated to a roguelite skeleton, with a maze of corridors that change each time the player dies and then starts over.
I think that the atmosphere is really nailed perfectly, heavy and atmospheric when the monsters are not here, then intense and a lot more stressful when the xenomorphs are pouring down the corridors with no end in sight. Sentry guns to activate and doors to open/close add a layer of strategy to the shooting. The shooting is very divisive by the way... Invasive Heads Up Display, enormous weapon and its muzzle flash, huge recoil, screen shake... This is where you decide : are you willing to sacrifice slick shooting mechanics for immersion? This time, I say yes. The game is built around that in the first place: the corridors are small and the xenomorphs are huge targets going down in very few bullets. So killing is not difficult at all. However, the feeling of not seeing much and not being in control contributes to make the encounters even more stressful and the monsters more numerous and dangerous than they really are.
Well, except that sometimes there can really be TOO MUCH of them constantly attacking. There are holes in the ceilings that endlessly spawn more and more Aliens as you get closer to them, and some of these nests in the same location can cause some areas to be extremely difficult to get through.
Despite being in early access, Space Beast Terror Fright runs very well on my aging computer. The developers seem to listen to the community (without sacrificing their artistic integrity if possible, since complaints about each element of the immersive interface are bound to keep appearing) and they are set on adding features to the game (such as new monsters or online coop - local coop is already possible), which would be quite welcome. Indeed, the game as it is is an enjoyable and intense experience, but it remains too bare-bones to renew itself on the long term. I am really looking forward see this game grow and get new features, thanks to early access. However I enjoy playing the game as it is, I am satisfied by the experience already, with no unrealistic expectations on how different the game should become!
Edit: online coop was added! However the perfunctory netcode is based on P2P, and the game is only playing smoothly when there is very little lag between the players.

Nearing the end of this game's campaign, I keep getting surprised at how solid it actually is.
I mean, yeah, it was an Xbone launch title and all, so it stands to reason it'd be polished, but it's a great experience nonetheless. The story is good (if a little on the predictable side). The characters are voiced and mo-capped perfectly, lending credibility, emotion, pathos and personality to the game as a whole. I can't stress just how good the mo-cap and VO are. An example: during the (often and brutal) fights, the facial expressions for everyone involved will dynamically change. Severing someone's limb elicits shocked, painful disbelief. Running someone through with your sword elicits grunting agony. Slamming your shield on theirn face makes them go crosseyed and dizzy, trying to keep their composure and consiousness. All of this is clearly discernible during combat.
The combat itself is, like stated above, brutal and fun. It employs a familiar dodge/break defense/attack/parry system with finishers, with two twists. First, there's no EZ mode prompt for parrying, which means you will actually have to pay attention to everyone's movements and patterns to know when they're attacking and when you should hit the parry button. Second, the finishers do what you choose: be that to recharge your health, your special focus meter, extra xp or others. That preference can be switched on the fly. Finishers themselves are two-button prompt events, their complexity varied by type, footing, number of enemies etc
All in all Ryse surprised me. I was expecting a run of the mill action game, what I got was a game that with a little better timing and promotion could have been the launch of a great new franchise borrowing heavily from both Gears of War and God of War. As it stands it's a great one-off.

I'm rather amazed with this game. I actually bought this while it was on sale for like $2 and decided that I couldn't lose trying it out. To name some of the great things about this game:
Music: AWESOME. Totally inspired and changes based on your completion of the game. I don't want to give too many spoilers, so just experience it yourself.
Graphics: Pretty good. It's amazing to see the evolution of how far gaming has come since the old days. This game does a great job of showing how good game development has gotten. All in all. A pretty sound game. I wasn't sure how it was going to play as I was buying it, but like I said before...I'm really glad I did. It's not a difficult game, nor is it a long RPG game, but I would still totally recommend this game for the fun that it brings.

Epsilon is a very early access game.  Having been released in October 2015, Epsilon still shows a lot of promise, though in its current state it still has a long way to go.
This review will be based on what I actually expect from a game which has been released as an early access title.  Scoring represents the current build of the game as of July 27th 2016 and may not apply to future patches.
Epsilon is heavily focused on tactics and planning.  So far, the player has been given the abillity to plot out routes to the objective on the map.  Before the player and the team hops into the the fps action, the area can be surveyed with the security cameras installed around the building.  Sadly this function is completely useless.  For me, tagged enemies did not appear through the walls, and the cameras were too poorly placed for the NPCs to be spotted.  For some reason, the developers felt that it would be more important to place cameras around the empty sparesely-patrolled hallway, instead of ones in the rooms of the building, where the majority of the hostile NPCs are spawned in.  In the game's current state, the map design is sub-par as the game seems to have taken visuals over practical map design, like what EA did with BF4.
Speaking of AI, the AI is primitive.  They fail to properly alert themselves from a nearby gunshot, yet seem to be able to instantly spot the player from a mile away through blurred glass, something that I wish to be improved on, especially since this game is focused on tactics.  In its current state, Epislon's AI is too dumb for its own good but over the course of a year, I can see a lot of improvements which can be done to fix everything and turn this game around.
In its current state, the game has two modes: Elimination and Story.  Strangely enough, neither of these modes have their objectives properly displayed to the player.  I believe story usually consists of the player freeing hostages which the player must scour every room on every floor to find, a very tedious task without the help of proper security camera placement.
Among the many things that fps games must get right, the guns are the most important.  Epsilon approaches this subject with its tiptoes, so to speak.  The player is provided with a variety of weapons, and even more to come, but there is a lack of proper visual feedback when firing shots and I'm sure the community would very much appreciate the application of a better soundscape and visual feedback from shooting and getting shot over new weapons.  Speaking of guns, the pistol is so inaccurate, it's ridiculous.  I emptied a full magazine on someone across the hallway with a pistol and not a single bullet hit.  Why are the pistols more inaccurate than my shotgun?
Personally, I believe the game shows so much potential, but I'm worried that the developers will forget about these major issues with the game.  Here are the following gameplay aspects which should be improved on:
In its current build, Epsilon puts a lot of food on the table.  The command options available for the player to control the team are varied and teases a lot of future features which I hope will be implemented.  Sadly, this content is still unreleased and it'd be unfair for me to review said unreleased content purely based on my predicitions.
A good thing that the game has already done is the self-promotion of its own mechanics.  What I mean by this is that the game silently encourages the player to play this game the way it's meant to be played.  Players who charge into rooms will find themselves easily gunned down.  A tactical approach must be used and it definitely shows that this fps is meant to be played slowly and strategically.  A nice start for a Pre-Alpha Early Access title.
It's in Pre-Alpha, don't expect a fleshed-out story this early.
Epsilon is a breath of fresh air for the indie genre in terms of its visuals.  The game is powered by Unreal Engine 4 (as advertised in the main menu) and at times I found myself wanting to become a staff member of some of the offices thanks to the sleep colour scheme and design of some of the maps.  The game's maps are reminiscent of the Mirror's Edge franchise, which uses white as a base and recurring bright colours as highlights.  Epsilon's maps have a stunning similarity and for the developers to design such a good looking map in such a short time is impressive to say the least, though improvements to gameplay and other more important aspects in the game are due.
The game's current UI is just offensive.  It takes up about a quarter of the entire screen.  This UI doesn't display a minimap or other important information, just teammate health and an endless well of ammunition.  I'd like to see significant improvements to the UI and HUD of the game.
+Immense amounts of potential
+Nice, slow gameplay
+Stunning visuals
+Non-linear gameplay, players can choose their own approach
-Very barebones and primitive
-Counter-intuitive UI
-Dumb AI
-Confusing map design

Reviewing the game in Pre-Alpha, version 1.07. As far as Early Access games go, this one is pretty solid. I also own Takedown: Red Sabre. Epsilon has very well kept some of the best qualities of Takedown and removed the worst qualities.
I like the futuristic setting and design work for Epsilon, it's just a bit futuristic but not to the point that you're using rayguns and fighting martians. It works really well with the new Unreal Engine 4 graphics, which look great, as always.
Epsilon has working squad commands! Your squad feels much more useful in Epsilon than in Takedown because of it. Enemy AI seems to be improved, as I haven't seen the glaring pathing issues that you would sometimes see in Takedown. The sniper and the planning phase mechanics are really fun!
Overall: Good replay value, nice graphics, plenty challenging.
I definitely recommend picking this one up! It's currently got 2 completed maps, no co-op yet, ragdolls, squad commands, It's worth the 8 bucks they're asking for now, and the price will only go up as they keep adding content. But yeah, it's a very fun pre-alpha that on its own, is already better than Takedown minus less maps currently available.

METAL GEAR SOLID V: GROUND ZEROES is the prequel to the highly anticipated fifth installment of the "Metal Gear Solid" series. Tough I would not call it a complete game, it is fun while it lasts.
The content is streched over one entire map, making the scenery somewhat redundant. Fortunatly, there are several different side or special ops next to the "canon" story. I would say the game gets better, the more you play it, since you get more content to play around with. Just like a big sandbox.

Music is typically "Metal Gear"-esque and very fitting, thrilling and emotional.
The controls are a little disorienting at first, but you get used to it very fast. Since I am a mouse & keyboard player, I cannot rate the controls on a controller.
The price is a little too steep for it (considering its just one location). Get this game either as a gift or when on sale. Also, sometimes DOF is not working how its supposed to be, camera angles might be confusing at certain times. An issue which was probably carried over from Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance.
Overall, an awesome game. Reminds me of the good old "Splinter Cell"-Days, but with more possibilities to approach your targets. More please!

GAMEPLAY REVIEW ONLY: The control scheme and player interactivity seems quite reminiscent of the refined version of MGS3 to me (haven't played 4), and i think that's a great thing! I use k+m to play the game and the controls feel very responsive. You have an arsenal of options at your disposal and the game never feels clunky when executing them. When you shoot you have a more significant recoil than in past Metal Gear Solid games and i find that to be a nice addition that adds difficulty and realism to the game; two things which i can imagine being significant in the upcoming "Metal Gear Online."
Two big things that arguably counter this finely tuned control system though are the enemy A.I. system and the new slow motion game mechanic. Even in Hard Mode, i found that the enemy's poor and unrealistic field of view was cotninously taking me out from the immersion. You might be standing in their "realistic" field of vision but they still won't recognize your activity because "you're just a tiny bit too far away", and their patrolling and reconnaissance seems too simple to me personally. The game's iteration of the tranqualizer again (in classic Metal Gear fashion) makes things a bit too easy, and i found myself playing my own version of the game where i would do my best not to come into contact with the enemy whatsoever. If you think about it, the game's enemy A.I. and context is not as difficult and realistic as it could be, it's been like this since the beginning of time and for the most part it's ok....because these games are much bigger than the sum of their parts. The games shouldn't be sadistically hard, but there's undeniable potential for a more cerebral stealth...but that's a discussion for another time...
The slow motion mechanic i previously mentioned seems unneccessary. If you're spotted, the game basically gives you a second chance (a couple seconds as the game world selflessly stops just for you...) in which you can try to take them out before they start the alarm off. You can turn it off though, no harm no foul.
The game world itself is rich and detailed and allows for different strategies and ways to tackle the objectives (as already shown in the official E3 game teasers for TPP. There's a plethora of side missions and fun unlockables that will easily give you plenty of game time with this title.
This is game plays very well, but i personally think it can still reach a higher bar, which im sure it will in one way or the other in TPP.

The first impression of this game by everyone was, "It's not a game it's a tech demo" what this actually is, is what Kojima said it would be, which is a game for the fans to enjoy whilst waiting for the Phantom Pain.
Having played every metal gear game released, I have a background of what to be looking for, in terms of stealth, to be able to choose from a number of options is what this game does really well, you can pick whatever way you wish to go about completing the mission, certain ways got my heart pumping especially on the hard difficulty, I've put 20 hours into this game and I have loved every second, it hasn't gotten boring, it hasn't even felt repetitive, it's just right.
The content of the game is mostly one mission that explains the prologue of Phantom pain, but if you carry on and start the side missions, you are rewarded with some very fun missions to complete, again, whichever way you want to complete them, it's up to you, and the game also includes two "extra ops" missions which are my personal favourites as they offer the player a chance to feel a little bit of nostalgia from MGS1.
Overall this game is pretty decent, and If you pre-order the Phantom Pain you get this included for free, so while you're waiting you can play it, I recommend 30 hours, which is probably what I will get out of this game before The Phantom Pain is released, once again, the emotion that drives Metal Gear Solid has come back even stronger, and as for the Phantom Pain, I can almost be certain that it will be a tear jerker.
A great game, worthy of playing.

Zombie Army Trilogy es una colección de los juegos de la saga Sniper Elite Nazy Zombie Army con ediciones remasterizadas de los primeros dos juegos así como la tercer y ultima parte de la serie. Esta colección marca la primera ocasión en que los juegos están disponibles en consola.
Durante los últimos días de la segunda guerra mundial, Hitler al borde de la derrota recurre a rituales ocultos para crear un ejército de zombies para que combatan a los aliados. Tú formas parte de un grupo de sniper elites que busca detener al ejército de Hitler.
Con un sniper como arma primaria, una pistola y una metralleta o escopeta como arma secundaria, deberás luchar para llegar a puntos específicos de cada mapa. El juego cuenta con una variedad de rifles, cada uno con sus propiedades especificas que van desde rango de la mira, velocidad del disparo, estabilidad y carga de municiones.
Cada misión se estructura de manera que hay zonas seguras a las cuales podrás acceder luego de sobrevivir a una oleada de zombies. Las misiones tienen una duración aproximada de 1 hora cada una.
El juego usa el mismo engine que Sniper Elite, por lo tanto, las físicas de las balas varían en base a ciertas condiciones, como la distancia. Las metralletas y escopetas disponibles en el juego son útiles pero a diferencia de otros juegos, no puedes usarlas como tu arma principal ya que no son tan efectivas y las municiones son limitadas.
Existen varios tipos de enemigos: Zombies con armas, sin armas, zombies snipers, esqueletos, zombies con moto sierras, zombies explosivos, zombies quemados, entre otros. Los jefes de cada zona aparecen junto con una oleada grande y requieren más esfuerzo para eliminarlos.
A pesar de la variedad de enemigos, jugar el juego por tiempos prolongados hace notar que por más enemigos distintitos la estrategia no cambia mucho. Para fines de esta reseña se invirtieron más de 12 horas y cerca del final ya estaba cansado de los mismos tipos de enemigos.
Adicional a esto, el juego está hecho con cooperativo en mente. Si juegas solo encontraras que ciertas partes del juego son difíciles de pasar pero no imposible. Para una experiencia optima les recomiendo jugar con al menos un amigo.
El juego cuenta con un nuevo modo llamado horda en donde tú y hasta 3 amigos deberán luchar por sobrevivir la mayor cantidad de oleadas de zombies posible.
Cabe señalar que el juego solamente cuenta con cooperativo en línea. Durante mi tiempo de juego, jugué en línea por cerca de 3 horas y mi compañero se quejaba de que había un retraso entre sus acciones y lo que reflejaba el juego. Por mi parte yo note momentos en los que su personaje se cambiaba de ubicación sin razón aparente.
Al contar con 3 juegos en un solo paquete, Zombie Army Trilogy ofrece cerca de 15 horas de entretenimiento solamente en la campaña. El nuevo modo horda es una mejora bienvenida aunque es más de lo mismo.
Para aquellos que disfrutan jugar en cooperativo con sus amigos, Zombie Army Trilogy es un juego que no los decepcionara. Desafortunadamente el juego no cuenta con más variedad que extienda su encanto más allá del modo cooperativo.
Lo Bueno:
•	Cerca de 15 horas de campaña
•	Modo Horda
•	Físicas de disparo
Lo Malo:
•	Variedad de enemigos
•	Problemas al jugar en línea
•	Se vuelve aburrido al jugarlo por tiempo prolongado

As others have said, this is an idle game with a D&D theme. That should provide enough interest for many to check the game out.
Beyond those basic elements, what sets Idle Champions apart?
There is a logic puzzle element to play with as you set up the champion formation. Champions interact in different ways depending on their positioning. The artwork is nicely done, especially backgrounds. The devs, artists, and other Codename Entertainment staff all seem very pleasant, and they provide a steady stream of free goodies via their email newsletter and Twitch stream. So far, new content has been added on a regular basis. The stories are sometimes rather funny and tongue-in-cheek.
What might deter people from playing the game, or staying with it?
It's not a role-playing or tabletop gaming experience. It's a themed idle game, so if you don't care for the general pace and style of idlers/clickers this probably isn't for you. It's a bit bug-prone, although the devs have been reasonably active with fixes and the support team has been responsive. And there is an element of pay-to-achieve, so if you take a firm stand against that type of model, you'll want to avoid this game. It's quite possible to progress through most or all achievements without buying any gear or chests, but paying for those can speed the game up considerably.

Reminded me of my childhood. Gameboy > Gameboy Color > Gameboy Advance > NDS.
Very novel game that plays on a player's nostalgia and familiarity. I could say more in that direction, but I'd just be echoing the other existing reviews. Please note,
this game if you are looking for a serious RPG. I'd recommend this game only on discount/bundle and if you have a particular nostalgia for classic RPGs -
Frankly - the game is short and yet still not fool-proof. In all of its gimmicky shine, there are still areas where if the player doesn't match a particular sequence of steps, they could end up getting stuck and need to end the game and restart from last save - particularly in areas where you must travel from 3D-to-2D to complete a puzzle. The player also has freedom to explore and do some main quest steps out of sequence too - for instance I collected the second-half of the Amulet before the first-half - and many of the evolution upgrades during that stage were no where to be seen when going back for the first-half of the Amulet.
To make things worse, there is a lot of backtracking - as if having to do a puzzle all over again wasn't already frustrating enough.
Additionally, there are frustrating challenges here-and-there that just seem unfair. In the Shrine of Babamut, I had to die countless times before I got lucky in the final room where hordes of mobs rushed me from a literal 360 degrees. Or the card mini-game, with its "random" card selection each game - that was also quite unfair. For instance, I had to play Championship mode several times before I even received a stack of cards that didn't resemble the same ones I used in Easy mode with low numbers. Wouldn't be so bad if there was a way to forfeit a card game instead of wasting your time playing dumb cards that make you laugh out loud while the CPU opponent lays down a whole stack of cards that are literally double the strength of your own cards every single time.
All my complaints aside - it is a decent piece of nostalgia for anyone who has enjoyed watching J-RPGs progress into their modern form. Pretty, low-poly graphics and (usually) fun puzzles await you.
I can't recommend it, however, if you are looking for a deep and meaningful RPG with story and character development that immerses and interests you. Such is the reality of a story that can be retold entirely within a minute or less.
I also recommend searching google/youtube for stars/cards chest locations BEFORE you play the game to avoid backtracking as much as possible. I only gave in to referencing the Internet when I was missing only three more cards and stars, and I was severely dissapointed at how they were hidden behind hidden walls and non-existant doors.
- just spoil the whole thing for yourself and get it over with. You will be happier that you didn't waste your time as it becomes severely un-enjoyable to locate chests that offer no challenge aside from dumb-luck.

Pretty much a review encompassing all of the old Delta Force games. This game was the first FPS I ever played. Put simply, there aren't games made today like these anymore. Difficult and brutal these games were, they do not hold your hand like games today. Missions were long, and usually placed you, at the very least, against a whole base of enemies. The worst part being, no saves. You could die at the extraction point of a 30-minute mission and have to re-do the entire mission over. Usually a few shots will kill you, maybe even one if you are unlucky enough. Stealth and movement are important least you find yourself end up getting shot up by 20 hostiles. Getting shot at gave you a terrifying feeling, and fear of have doing everything for naught. Today, games will not give you such a challenge in fear of fustrating the player.
The release of Delta Force marked the beginning of realistic shooters (games like OFP and ARMA) and even today is still an enjoyable game.

There is no Roman experience quite like Ryse: Son of Rome. While games like Total War: Rome only allow you to command troops from above instead of being able to play as the troops themselves, Son of Rome allows you to play as a single soldier. Your character, Marius, will visit Rome, York, and northern England, and although you must always follow a linear path and cannot explore, it is still stunning to gaze at Crytek's beautifully-reproduced environments. In addition, the studio has created impressive cinematic events that make the game truly intense.
The combat system, which is the foundation of the game, has both strengths and weaknesses. While Marius's different attacks, finishers, and bashes are satisfying and awesome, they get repetitive over time, making combat less exciting as you move towards the final stages of the game. What ultimately weakens combat, though, is the lack of different enemies. The game uses the same few skins for the enemies over and over, so you may be fighting three enemies that look absolutely identical, and they will all be doing the same attacks. You can buy new finishers later in the game, though, which keeps you playing. In various parts of the game, you can also create a shield wall, which was one of the best moments of the game; you and your men shield themselves from archers, and flaming arrows hit the shields. It is an amazing experience.
Some of the boss battles are frustrating, and you may even have to look online to see how to complete them. The minotaur chieftian, Chief Glott, is the most frustrating of them all. When he is charging, you must wait until he almost hits you (he will turn yellow) and only then can you successfully counter him. Do not counter prematurely.
The story is the best part of the game. Marius's journey brings him into a vicious feud between Gods, Kings, and Emperors, and Son of Rome even blurs the lines between friend and foe, giving you some doubts about which side you are truly on yourself.
The diverse soundtrack is another highlight of the game. At times it will convey the glory of Rome, the misty forests of northern England, and much more. Once you have completed the campaign, the game allows you to listen to different parts of the soundtrack without having to play the game, which is a nice feature.
There is a multiplayer component, but there are very few people on the servers (if any at all).
To give the game replay value, there are collectibles scattered around the environments; exploring hidden areas gives you access to scrolls, art, and even Son of Rome comics.
The game's campaign took me about six hours to complete, so it is definitely worth it on sale. If you have ever wanted to play as a Roman soldier or gladiator, or if you just want to experience Rome, this game delivers. Recommended.

Attempts to be a return to the classic tactical shooters (Rainbow Six up to 3, SWAT 3 and 4, etc) but fails to remember why those were actually fun. Movement and aiming is incredibly clunky, "story mode" is obnoxious, enemy meshes don't at all fit with the world (generic South American militia in super futuristic cyber land), guns also don't really fit the setting. There are a bunch of parts, but all of them are rough (early access, but read on) and none of them fit well together
Because therein lies the big issue: The devs just don't seem to care. They looked at a checklist of what people have been complaining about since R6 Vegas and they add it:
- Optiwand to mirror under doors? Check, but it moves incredibly slowly and has awkward controls (you move the camera with WASD...). Also, this will switch you back to your primary instantly
- Useful secondary equipment and not just pistols? Sort of. There is a grenade launcher of some form that seems to fire high explosive rounds... that make the terrorists surrender.
- Modern military weapons: Sort of. It looks like they found a generic asset pack of a few FN guns and added that in... which is strange when this is set in a cyber-future land... full of what look like Fidel Castro's dopplegangers
- Squad commands: Surprisingly yes, but it depends on a circular menu (think powers in Mass Effect, but clunkier). And becuase this is an attempt at emulating the games of olde, it involves multiple levels, none of which flows well together.
- Open doors with mousewheel: I have been missing this for years, but it is pointless as two rapid swipes of my wheel opened the door about halfway. So unless I am peaking (which is what the optiwand is for), I don't know why this is here
And that is the thing. Yes, this is early access and most of this can be fixed (better controls and new asset packs). But why is this here in the first place? Why is there a fundamentally flawed command menu? Why would things that worked, and what are clearly inspirations, be changed to not work? There is a fundamental difference between pushing an incomplete game (awkward animations, lack of content, funky AI, all the sound issues I neglected to mention) and pushing one where the mechanics just don't work. Even basic playtesting should have revealed most of those.
A huge step up from this studio's previous (abandoned) game, but still a long way to go.
If you want the gunplay of olde, look into Insurgency. If you want the spirit, consider one of the more recent Rainbow Sixes (Vegas lacks tactics but definitely has the spirit of an R6 game). And if what you miss is the planning, consider Doorkickers or Breach and Clear... or just buy one of the first three Rainbow Sixes.

Epsilon is a team-based tactical shooter currently in the early access stages being developed by Serellan. The game is in a fairly barebones state at present but with a decent foundation already in place; this could potentially grow into a very impressive game down the line. At such a generous pricepoint too; it is most definitely worth a punt even now.
Firstly; the game looks absolutely remarkable, with a unique visual style of colours, outstanding lighting effects and stunning reflections. This aspect alone is very encouraging and makes this one of the most visually impressive early access titles to date. If each environment maintains this standard; Epsilon could stand against many top-end AAA games in graphical terms.
This being in the very early stages though; many aspects are yet to be completed or are even absent at present. The developers have listed a wealth of features and improvements on the horizon which demonstrates they have a clear understanding of their product moving forward. The core of Epsilon is still very playable so far as you get to grips with the concept and mechanics. There are a few bugs and some rough parts but overall; it's a solid platform for the developers to build upon.
The developers Serellan have certainly come under fire previously after the somewhat mediocre Takedown: Red Sabre but this title houses enormous potential and with lessons hopefully learned; I hope they don't make the same mistakes again. With 30% completed and another 12 months projected until the game is ready for a full release; it is certainly one to watch. There is still a considerable amount of work to be done in regards to developing and improving but with such a strong foundation already in place; this could be a very exciting title to follow.

While "Oh...Sir!! The Insult Simulator" is intruiging at first glance, it quickly falls quite short.
(This being my very first review on Steam, expect it to be somewhat unorganized.)
By putting together dialogue fragments, and constructing the most vile and absurd of insults, you progress towards defeating your opponent. You will be using their soft spots against them, hoping for the right words and sentences to show up in your favor. Perhaps they deal with family issues, or perhaps, their Achille's heel is their choice of style. By taking these factors into account, you come up with strategies, forcing you, the player, to think creatively. right?
While I do think the concept in itself is very interesting, the game lacks depth, for multiple reasons.
Firstly, picking up strategies along the way does not turn out to be all that engaging- as the options the player is provided with, are rather limited- both in numbers, but also in terms of function. You quickly figure out, that each sentence/word fits under a certain category. Including that sentence/word in any given sentence, you will earn a bonus, as long as the enemy character, considers that very subject offensive, not considering the context (except for the level of absurdity, which I'll explain futher down). Furthermore, as the number of possible words/sentences is very limited, it gets repetetive, and ultimately rather boring piecing together your insults. This is also creates a sense of inconsistency, as the damage dealt to your opponent's pride meter (?) seems arbitrary. The game does reward you for constructing longer sentences, yet it punishes you, for creating insults that are "too" absurd. While this is great in theory, the criteria for creating an insult the game considers "too absurd", are very vague.
Secondly, the number of playable characters is limited. Attacking those parts of your opponents that are vulnerable, ends up becoming dice roll, rather than analyzing their background story (provided in the selection menu). This breaks their personalities and charms apart, as they end up feeling quite alike. I had hoped, that these characters would have something more to offer, not only in terms of the very few special sentences they each occationally are provided with during "combat", but also a few more alternative character-defining traits, whether it be passives, special abilites or something radically different. I know I'm being very vague, but the purpose of having different characters in the game, is almost entirely pointless.
While the game suffers a bit in terms of the mechanical aspects, I certainly find the aesthetic much fitting. Decent pixel art, as well as some decent voice acting. While the voice acting could have been stepped up by a smidgeon, I wouldn't by any means call it lacking. It is crucial to have solid voice acting for a game about settling arguments through verbal abuse, and I think the game performs as it should in this aspect.
Even though I do have a lot of critizism in relation to the game's contents, I still find it very charming, and there's one particular reason, I'm going to keep myself updated to the game. Considering the price tag, I find it perfectly reasonable, for having spent at the very least 1.5hours of fun. The points I've made on the game, are things, I certainly consider possible to fix.
I think it's perfectly reasonable to criticize me, on behalf of my high hopes. I was perhaps anticipating a more ambitious project when initially booting up the game (Yes I know, it's 2 euros...).
Anyway. Those are just my thoughts.

The aesthetic of this game is amazing. The artstyle, music, and sound all blends amazingly together and that was why I decided to pick the game up. Unfortunately, the game just feels frustatingly impossible.
I understand the game is going for the style of 1920s but the tracks all feel like you're racing on ice. You slide all over the place, slowing you down a lot. Oddly enough, the AI doesn't seem to have the same physics as you do. I've tried drifting through turns and I've tried braking early to accelerate through turns. Neither style seems to work well. You will still often slide uncontrollably, likely causing yourself to stop entirely or slow down dramatically before you can regain control of your car. Sometimes you'll be going straight at a high speed and your car just decides to fishtail with nothing causing it.
Worst of all, the AI cars seem to be a 100x heavier than yours. The AI has no problem shoving you around, a simple tap to the rear end will fishtail you and likely spin you out. If you tap the AI in the rear end, it's like you hit a wall and you just slow down to their pace. Hitting walls will often also make you just stop rather than bounce off them as it should as well.
I was really looking for a fun top down racer but this is not it. The physics are just too bad to find any enjoyment out of this game.

I was looking for some small and short games which I like to play occasionally and stumbled upon to this little gem couple of weeks ago. After my purchase I realized how wrong I was thinking.
Gameplay:
The game looks simple at the beginning. Indeed, there is almost no learning curve, but after your first race it hits you hard that the game is not like your average racing game. It is difficult to win a race and it is also not easy to get used to the viewing angle. Although there are some comments about how bad the viewing angle is, I personally liked it. The cars with different speeds and different handling ratios are well balanced and shows how difficult those cars were handled in 20’s. It is definitely not a simulation, and I don’t think this was the developer’s intention, but they managed to program the physics of the game remarkably good.
Long story short: It takes a while to master but the game is very enjoyable.
Graphics and Sound:
The polygon graphics are funny and gives a great atmosphere to the game. It is a mixture of a comic book and art concept. 
There are some graphical glitches occasionally but nothing which will distract or annoy.
The music is beautiful and doesn’t disturb if you play long. I’m not a fan of this era in terms of music, but when you hear it, you will be in the mood.
I’ve played this game on my 15” Macbook Pro from 2011 on both macOS and Windows 10, and the performance was very good.
Overall surprising great game which I recommend to everyone. A little bit patience for mastering the game is recommended. :)

I love the old school styling and the simple and clear graphics, but the game play is not fun. Basically, it's too difficult and unfortunately not in a fun way. It's made difficult by the poorly utilised perspective that constantly changes and leaves you without sufficient visibility to reliably pick a line or avoid obstacles and other cars.
If your car is heading from the bottom left to the top right, you can see far up the track. However if you are going from the top left to the bottom right you can only see about 10 car lengths ahead. As a single mistake will cost you the race, it becomes a boring chore of repeating the same track until you learn what's coming up in the parts you can't see.  If the camera angles are changed so you can see far enough to drive, I'd try to master this. But at the moment it's simply frustrating and I can't give it my recommendation.

Personally, I find the thought and creativity that is put into developing these games is much more fulfilling than what I have gotten out of the expensive and popular games...this was absolutely dirt cheap and I have to say, objectively worth a lot more than I paid for it. This genre in general is a well kept secret, one that I hope will continue and thrive.

This game... I love this game! The beginning is a bit tough, but the mid-game is really fun!
You start with 4 squad members with average skills. They miss a lot and need to be close to their target in order to hit most of the time. As you complete missions, your squad members gain experience which will gradually increase their performance. Experience is spent on stat points which increase an array of skills which will directly and quickly benefit each squad member. When enough stats are gained, classes become available. Most classes will net your squad member a few benefits, and can be trained up to lvl 3. Each squad member can have 3 classes maxed out at lvl 3.
As missions are completed and time passes, more and more territories are explored and made available to you. Bases need to be connected together using tracks in order to gain resources, and some facilities will boost those resources gained. Missions can be triggered automatically, or you can "ask" for a mission to be plotted in a single region of your choice at a time. Most missions consist of defeating most enemies on a battle map, capturing a marked enemy, rescuing a civilian or escorting several civilians to a specific spot on the battle map. Once the objective is complete, you can complete the mission even if there are still enemies remaining. This game will make a tactician out of you!
There are many strategies in battle and out of combat which will guarantee replayability. What facilities will you build in which city? Will you focus on research early on? Will you manufacture armor and weapons as soon as possible? Which research will you start first?
The game has some bugs which are annoying at times, but still manageable. Sometimes you won't be able to complete a mission because of an enemy outside the map or in a spot you can't reach. The game will sometimes crash when rearranging squad members. Using the unofficial 1.3 patch and widescreen resolution fix, this oldy is a goody.
I give this game a good 9/10. I have completed it once (about 60 hours of gameplay to capture every territory possible) and have started another playthrough. Much fun! I especially love how enemies sometimes fly when you shoot them with shotguns at close range or snipers!

A solid alternative to the XCOM series (both classic and modern ones), the UFO series is a set of real-time squad tactics games that have provided myself with many hours of enjoyment, far more than Steam has logged as I had the original games and likely spent 100s more hours on them in total.
UFO: Aftershock is my favourite from the series, occupying the middle ground in stylistic choices (not as gritty as Aftermath, but not as cartoony as Afterlight) and squad management options, having the most numerous unique factions, and having the most varied selection of weaponry on offer.
However, as the many unjustified reviews will say, there are bugs and glitches in Aftershock that have the potential to ruin games. These bugs can be easily patched however, and a quick Google will take you to the latest, unofficial patch that fixes that vast majority of problems. I managed to complete the game on Steam without a single major bug occuring. They also complain of long campaign times, but in my experience the UFO campaigns take no longer than the XCOM campaigns, averaging 40 hours a run if you aren't trying to speed through it. And some complain of repetitive missions, but again, there is enough variety in enemies and mission types for it to match any other games in the genre I find.
If you like either of the XCOM series, you have every possibility of enjoying this and Aftermath as well. This game stands up so well I even nominated for the Test of Time Steam award, easily worth the £1 it costs on sale.
